en: Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter One:
Now begins the first chapter, titled "The Yoga of Arjuna’s Despondency."
The Commentary composed by the Blessed Śaṅkarācārya: Introduction. Oṃ!
Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; the cosmic egg arises from the unmanifest.
Within this egg, however, are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents.
Having created this world, that Blessed One,
desiring to establish its maintenance, first created Marīci and others, and caused the Prajāpatis to accept the dharma characterized by worldly engagement as declared in the Vedas.
Then, having produced others such as Sanaka, Sanandana, and so forth, He caused them to accept the dharma characterized by renunciation, which is defined by knowledge and dispassion.
For the Dharma taught in the Veda is of two kinds: that characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) and that characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).
It is the cause of the stability of the world;

it is that which is the direct cause of the prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*) for living beings, and which is practiced by those belonging to the castes, such as Brahmins, and by those in the stages of life (*āśramins*), all seeking the highest good.
After a long time, when Dharma was being overwhelmed by Adharma— which arises from the lust of those who perform rituals and is caused by the decline of discriminative knowledge—
and while Adharma was increasing,
that primordial creator known as Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, desiring to fully protect the stability of the world, [appeared] for the sake of guarding the earthly Brahmā and the status of the Brāhmaṇas.
It is said that Kṛṣṇa was born from Vasudeva and Devakī by means of a portion [of Himself].
Indeed, by protecting the status of the brāhmaṇas, Vedic dharma would be protected, for the distinctions of the social orders (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) are dependent upon it.

And that Blessed Lord, eternally endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor, having brought under His control His own Vaiṣṇavī Māyā—the primordial nature consisting of the three modes—[manifested].

Although He is unborn, immutable, the Lord of beings, and by nature eternally pure, enlightened, and free, He appears— through His own *māyā*— as if possessing a body and as if born, bestowing grace upon the worlds.
Even in the absence of any personal motive, out of a desire to favor all beings, He [revealed] the two-fold Vedic dharma to Arjuna, who was submerged in a great ocean of grief and delusion.
He instructed her who was immersed [in grief], thinking that "dharma, when adopted and practiced by those superior in virtue, will attain great expansion.
The omniscient Lord Vedavyāsa committed that dharma, exactly as taught by the Blessed One, to writing in seven hundred verses known as the Gītā.

This very scripture of the Gītā, which constitutes a compendium of the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, has its meaning difficult to comprehend; therefore, for the purpose of revealing that meaning—

Having observed that even though this work has its words, word-meanings, sentences, sentence-meanings, and logic explained by many [commentators], it is nevertheless grasped by worldly people as having many mutually contradictory meanings, I shall provide a concise commentary for the purpose of determining the meaning through discernment.
The brief purpose of this scripture, the *Gītā*, is supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), characterized by the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence along with its causes.
And that [liberation] arises from the dharma consisting of steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self, preceded by the renunciation of all action.

To this very same effect, with reference to the dharma of the meaning of the Gītā, the Blessed One himself has said in the Anugītā: "For that dharma is fully sufficient for the realization of the state of Brahman" (Mbh 14.16.12).
And it is said in that very same place: "Neither a follower of dharma nor a follower of adharma, and indeed neither virtuous nor non-virtuous;
he who is absorbed in the solitary path, silent, not thinking of anything"—and also: "Knowledge has the characteristic of renunciation."
And here too, at the conclusion, it was said to Arjuna: "Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone" (Gītā 18.66).

Furthermore, even that dharma characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), which is prescribed with reference to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*),—though it is a cause for attaining the stations of the gods and so forth—becomes a means for the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) when performed with the intention of offering it to the Lord, being devoid of attachment to results.

Furthermore, for a person of pure being (*śuddha-sattva*), it is established that [action] is a cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by way of attaining fitness for the culmination of knowledge and as a cause for the arising of knowledge.

And with this very meaning in mind, he will say: "Having placed all actions in Brahman" (Gītā 5.10), and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self" (Gītā 5.11).

This scripture, the Gītā, possesses a specific purpose, a connection, and a subject matter, as it specifically manifests this twofold dharma which has the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as its aim: namely, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*) known as Vāsudeva, who is designated as the Supreme Brahman;
for through the knowledge of its meaning, the accomplishment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is attained.
Therefore, I shall make an effort to provide an exposition of that.
In the field of dharma, at Kurukṣetra, my people and the Pāṇḍavas have assembled, desiring to fight; what did they do, Sañjaya? (BhG 1.1)
Saṃjaya said: Then, having seen the Pandava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
Behold, O Teacher, this vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
drawn up in battle array by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple.
In this [army] are heroes, great archers equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great car-warrior.
Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, that bull among men; BhG 1.5.
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas,
as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī— all of them are indeed great chariot-warriors.
But as for those who are distinguished among us, learn of them, O best of the twice-born;
I shall name them to you for the sake of your information, as they are the leaders of my army.

And there are many other heroes who have renounced their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and all are skilled in battle.
That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient;
but this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient.
And in all the divisions, stationed each according to his allotted place,
may you all indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.
Generating joy for him, the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus,
let out a lion’s roar and blew his conch shell loudly.
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded; that sound became tumultuous.
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses,
Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava blew their divine conchs.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta,
and Vṛkodara, the performer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, has the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva have the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
And Kāśya, the supreme archer; Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki.
O lord of the earth, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī,
and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conchs individually.
That tumultuous sound, making both heaven and earth resound, tore apart the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons.
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arrayed for battle, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the emblem of the monkey, raised his bow as the discharge of weapons began.
Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies."
While I am observing these who stand here desiring to fight, with whom among them must I contend in this exertion for battle? (BhG 1.22)
I behold those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they stand ready for battle.
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies, [said: BhG 1.24.
In front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth,
he said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
There, Partha beheld standing his fathers and grandfathers,
as well as teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
Having beheld all those kinsmen standing there— both fathers-in-law and friends in both armies— that son of Kuntī [was overcome].

Overcome by supreme compassion and despondent upon seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle, O Kṛṣṇa, he spoke this: kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdann idam abravīt / dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṃ samupasthitam // BhG 1.28 //
My limbs fail me and my mouth is parched;
a trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end. (BhG 1.29)
The Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand and my skin is burning all over;
I am unable to stand firm, and my mind seems to be reeling.
And I see adverse omens, O Keśava;
nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle.
I desire neither victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
What is the use of kingdom to us, O Govinda, or what use are enjoyments or even life itself?
"For whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
these very people stand here in battle, having abandoned their lives and wealth."
Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers;
maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives.
I do not wish to kill these men, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me,
not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, let alone for the sake of the earth.
O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us even after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
By killing these aggressors, we would only incur sin ourselves.
Therefore, O Mādhava, we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen; for how, having slain our own people, could we be happy?
Even though these people, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil in the destruction of a family nor the sin in betraying friends.
O Janārdana, how is it that we do not know how to turn away from this sin, even while clearly perceiving the evil brought about by the destruction of our own clan?
Upon the destruction of the family, the eternal family traditions perish;
when the dharma is lost, unrighteousness overcomes the entire family.
O Kṛṣṇa, through the overwhelming power of unrighteousness, the women of the family become corrupted;
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, there arises a confusion of castes.
This confusion leads to hell for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself;
indeed, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
By these faults of those who destroy the family and cause the intermixture of castes,
the eternal laws of the birth-groups and the laws of the family are subverted.
O Janārdana, we have heard from tradition that for those men whose family traditions have fallen into ruin, residence in hell is inevitable. BhG 1.44.
Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, were to slay me in battle while I am unarmed and unresisting, that would be better for me.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the floor of his chariot,
casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Commentary on the Gītā composed by Śaṅkarācārya. //1//
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Two. Sañjaya said:
To him, who was thus overwhelmed by compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears, and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words: Bhagavad Gītā 2.1.
Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is unworthy of the noble, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy.
Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (BhG 2.3)
O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are both worthy of worship?
Indeed, it is better to live even on alms in this world than to slay these high-souled gurus;
for by slaying gurus who are motivated by wealth and desire, one suffers right here.
I would enjoy pleasures stained with blood.
And we do not know which is better for us: whether we should conquer them or they should conquer us;
for we have no desire to live after having slain these very men.
Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand arrayed before you.
My nature overwhelmed by the defect of wretchedness, my mind confused about duty, I ask you:
tell me decisively that which would be the highest good.
I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
For I do not perceive that which, even upon attaining prosperous and unrivaled sovereignty on earth, would dispel this grief of mine that withers the senses.
Even sovereignty over the kingdom of the gods.
Saṃjaya said:
Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes,
said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent.
O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies.

And here, the section of the text beginning with "Having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas" and ending with "having said to Govinda, 'I will not fight,' he became silent" should be explained as having the purpose of demonstrating the cause for the arising of defects that constitute the seed of saṃsāra— such as grief and delusion— for living beings.

For instance: by Arjuna, through the causes of delusive cognition such as "I am theirs" and "these are mine" regarding his kingdom, teachers, sons, friends, well-wishers, kinsmen, relatives, and blood-relations, his own grief and delusion— caused by the severance of affection and so forth— were demonstrated.
By the words "How shall I [fight] Bhīṣma in battle," and so forth, [Arjuna],

whose discriminative knowledge was overwhelmed by grief and delusion, although naturally engaged in battle according to his own kṣatriya duty, desisted from that battle and proceeded to perform the duties of another, such as living on alms.

And thus, for all living beings whose minds are possessed by defects such as grief and delusion, there would naturally be both the abandonment of their own duty (*svadharma*) and the practice of what is forbidden.
Even for those engaged in their own duty, the activity of their speech, mind, body, and so forth, occurs only preceded by an intention for results and is accompanied by egoism (*sāhaṃkāra*).

This being the case, because of the accumulation of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—characterized by the attainment of desirable and undesirable births, pleasure, pain, and so forth—continues without ceasing.
Therefore, grief and delusion (*śoka-moha*) constitute the seeds of *saṃsāra*.

Since their cessation occurs through nothing other than self-knowledge (*ātma-jñāna*) preceded by the renunciation of all action (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*), the Blessed One, desiring to teach that for the sake of favoring all the world, spoke [as follows], taking Arjuna as the occasion.
Vāsudeva: "Those who are not to be grieved for," and so forth.
Regarding this, some say: liberation is certainly not attained through mere steadfastness in self-knowledge alone, preceded by the renunciation of all ritual actions (*karma*).
What then? The attainment of liberation results from knowledge conjoined with *śrauta* and *smārta* rites such as the *agnihotra*; this is the definitive meaning established throughout the *Gītā*.
And they cite the scriptural evidence for this point:
"If you will not engage in this righteous battle" (Gītā 2.33), "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47),
"Therefore, perform action itself" (Gītā 4.15), and so forth.

Nor should this doubt be entertained—that Vedic ritual leads to unrighteousness because it involves violence and the like—for how so? Even the duty of a warrior (*kṣatra-dharma*), characterized by battle and involving the killing of teachers, brothers, sons, and others—though exceedingly cruel—is not for the sake of unrighteousness when performed as one's own duty (*svadharma*).
For it is said: "By failing to perform it, you will abandon your duty and reputation and incur sin" (Gītā 2.33).

By saying this, it has been stated with certainty that actions enjoined by Vedic texts such as "as long as one lives," which are characterized by the slaughter of animals and so forth, are not unrighteous (*adharma*) from the very beginning.

That is incorrect; for there is a statement regarding the distinction between the two types of steadfastness—those based on knowledge and those based on action—which rest upon two different forms of intelligence (*buddhi*).

The determination of the reality of the supreme self (paramārthātmatattva) which was made by the Blessed One through the textual passage beginning with "those who are not to be grieved for" and ending with "and having also considered one's own duty"—
that is Sāṃkhya.

The cognition whose object is that [Sāṃkhya], which arises from the determination of the meaning of the context— that the self is a non-agent because of its lack of the six modifications such as birth and so forth— [is the knowledge of Sāṃkhya].
That is the Sāṃkhya understanding;
those wise ones for whom that is appropriate are the Sāṃkhyas.

Prior to the arising of this [final] cognition, there is yoga, characterized by the performance of the means to liberation, which is preceded by the discernment of dharma and adharma and is based on the self’s distinction from the body and so forth, as well as its status as agent and enjoyer.
The cognition whose object is that [yoga] is "yoga-cognition" (yoga-buddhi).
Those practitioners for whom that [discriminative knowledge] is appropriate are the yogins.

Accordingly, the Blessed One distinguished and pointed out two types of intellect (buddhi), saying: "This intellect has been declared to you in the context of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [intellect] regarding Yoga. And he will later describe the distinct culmination of those who follow Sāṃkhya, which rests upon the intellect of Sāṃkhya, as being attained through the yoga of knowledge, stating: "It was proclaimed by me in the past in the form of the Veda."
And likewise, He will declare a distinct culmination through the yoga of action based on the intellect of yoga—saying, "for yogis, by means of the yoga of action.

Thus, relying upon the intellect of Sāṃkhya and the intellect of yoga, the Lord Himself has stated two distinct culminations for knowledge and action, which are based respectively on the intellect of agency and non-agency, and of unity and multiplicity; for He perceives the impossibility of these two being simultaneously present in a single person.

This very statement regarding such a distinction is shown in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: "Desiring this world alone, the Brāhmaṇas who are wanderers go forth into the wandering life" (BAU 4.4.22). Having thus enjoined the renunciation of all ritual action, it continues with the remainder:
"What shall we do with offspring, for us this self is this world? (BAU 4.4.22).
And in that very context, prior to taking a wife, a person is merely an ordinary self; but subsequent to the desire to know Dharma, he [seeks] the means for accomplishing the three worlds:
a son, and two kinds of wealth—human and divine.

In this context, human action—which consists of ritual form—is the means for attaining the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ-loka*), while knowledge (*vidyā*) and divine wealth (*daiva-vitta*) are the means for attaining the world of the gods (*deva-loka*).

By the statement, "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*, BĀU 1.4.17), it is shown that all rituals, such as those prescribed in the Vedas (*śrauta*), belong exclusively to one who possesses ignorance (*avidyā*) and desire (*kāma*).
Having risen above these, [the text continues:]
The statement, "They go forth" (BAU 4.4.22), is prescribed for one who is free from desire and seeks only the Self as the world—that is, for one who has renounced.
This statement of distinction would be untenable if the Blessed One intended the combination of scriptural ritual action and knowledge.
Furthermore, Arjuna’s question, beginning with "If, in Your view, action is inferior to knowledge" (Gītā 3.1), would not be appropriate.

Since the impossibility of intellect and action being performed by a single person was not previously stated by the Blessed One, how could Arjuna— having understood what he had not heard— superimpose upon the Blessed One the false claim that intellect is superior to action, saying, "If you consider intellect to be superior to action"?

Furthermore—if the combination of both wisdom (*buddhi*) and action (*karman*) had been taught for everyone, then it would certainly have been taught for Arjuna as well; in that case, how could there be a question regarding only one of the two when both had been instructed? For instance, when a physician instructs a person seeking to pacify bile (*pitta*) that "both sweet and cold things should be eaten," it is not appropriate for that person to ask, "Tell me which one of these two is the cause for pacifying bile."
It is possible.

Now, even if one were to assume that Arjuna’s question is caused by his failure to discern the meaning of the words spoken by the Blessed One, even so, the Blessed One ought to have given a reply corresponding to that question: "I have taught the combination of knowledge and action; for what reason are you thus deluded?"
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to give an inconsistent reply that is entirely different from what was asked, such as saying, "Two culminations were previously declared by me.

Nor is it logical to claim that all statements regarding the distinction [between the two paths] are justified only when the intention is the conjunction of ritual action (*smārta-karman*) with wisdom (*buddhi*).

Moreover, for a Kṣatriya who knows that fighting is his own duty (*svadharma*) as a ritual act prescribed by tradition (*smārta*), the reproach—"Why do you urge me toward this terrible action?"—is untenable.

Therefore, in the Gītā-śāstra, it is impossible for anyone to demonstrate the combination of self-knowledge with even the slightest degree of ritual action, whether Vedic (śrauta) or Smṛti-based (smārta).

However, for one who—having been engaged in action due to ignorance or defects such as passion—and whose being (sattva) has been purified by sacrifice, charity, or austerity, there arises knowledge concerning the ultimate reality:
"All this is indeed the one Brahman, and it is without an agent."
Even when his [the knower's] action and the purpose of action have ceased, his engagement in activity with effort for the sake of maintaining the world is just as it was before;
however, that which appears as the form of such activity is not "action" (karma) in the sense that it would lead to a combination with knowledge.
Just as the performance of the duties of a kṣatriya by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is not combined with knowledge for the sake of accomplishing the goal of man.
In the same way, because the learned person possesses an equal absence of both the desire for the fruits of action and the ego-sense,
the knower of reality thinks, "I do not act," and does not intend for the fruit thereof.

And just as for one who has consecrated the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and desires heaven and other such rewards, having commenced the performance of rites characterized by *agnihotra* and the like, even if the desire is destroyed midway while he is performing that very *agnihotra* and so forth, that *agnihotra* and the rest do not become "desire-driven" (*kāmya*);
so too does the Blessed Lord demonstrate in various places: "Even while acting, he is not tainted; he does not act, he is not tainted."
As for the statement, "Whatever was done by the ancients in even earlier times—by action alone indeed did Janaka and others attain perfection"—that must be understood after making a distinction.
How so? If, first of all, the ancients such as Janaka and others were knowers of reality (tattvavidaḥ) yet remained engaged in action; [then it refers to their specific case].
Knowing that "these qualities function among the qualities for the sake of gathering the world," they have attained perfection through that very knowledge;
even though the renunciation of action would logically follow, they have attained perfection while remaining engaged in action itself—
the meaning is that they did not perform a formal renunciation of action.
Now, if they are not knowers of reality,
then through action dedicated to the Lord as a means, they attain perfection— either the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) or the perfection characterized by the arising of knowledge.
It should be explained that Janaka and others remained [in this state].

The Blessed One will express this very same meaning for the sake of purifying the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) when He says, "They perform action," and after stating, "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a person attains perfection" (*sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya siddhiṃ vindati mānavaḥ*), He will further describe the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) for one who has attained perfection, saying, "Having attained perfection, as [one realizes] Brahman... (*siddhiṃ prāpto yathā brahma*).
By means of the first [verse], etc.
Therefore, the established conclusion in the Gītā scripture is that liberation is attained through the knowledge of reality alone, and not from its combination with action.
We shall demonstrate how this is so by dividing it according to the relevant sections throughout the work.

Seeing no means of extricating Arjuna— who was there, his mind utterly bewildered regarding dharma, possessed of false knowledge, and submerged in a great ocean of grief— other than through the knowledge of the Self, Lord Vāsudeva, out of compassion, desiring to lift him up, spoke as follows, introducing him to the knowledge of the Self:
The Blessed Lord said:
You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not grieve for the dead or for the living.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others are not to be grieved for;

they are not objects of grief because of their virtuous conduct and because they are eternal by their ultimate nature. You have grieved for those who are not to be grieved for, thinking, "They are dying on my account."
"Separated from them, what shall I do with the pleasures of sovereignty and the like?
You speak words of wisdom—the doctrines and utterances of the wise and intelligent;
thus you display within yourself this contradiction between folly and scholarship, appearing like one who is mad—this is the intended meaning.
For the wise— those who know the Self— do not grieve for those whose life-force has departed, who are dead, nor for those whose life-force has not departed, who are living.

Those whose intellect has the Self as its object are indeed the wise (*paṇḍita*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Having realized wisdom" (BAU 3.5.1). Yet, in the ultimate sense, you grieve for those who are eternal and beyond grief.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "You are deluded.
Why are they not to be mourned?
Because they are eternal. How so?
But indeed, I was never non-existent, nor you, nor these lords of men;
and none of us shall ever cease to be hereafter.

But indeed, never at any time was I not; rather, I certainly was. The intended meaning is that throughout the past births and destructions of bodies, I have always existed eternally, like space within jars and other objects.
Likewise, you were not non-existent.
But they were indeed;
likewise, these lords of men were not merely non-existent, but were indeed;
and likewise, we shall certainly not cease to be.
But we shall indeed exist; all of us, therefore, even after the destruction of this body, in the subsequent time as well.
The meaning is that we are eternal in our essential nature throughout all three periods of time.
The plural number is used because of the persistence of the distinction between bodies, not with the intention of implying a plurality of selves.
Regarding that, he provides an illustration as to how the self is eternal: [BhG 2.13]
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
"One who possesses a body" (*dehī*) is so called because he has a body;
for that embodied self (*dehin*), while this body exists, just as there are various stages— namely, childhood (*kaumāra*), which is the state of being a child or the stage of infancy,
and youth (*yauvana*), which is the state of being young or the middle stage— so too [is there old age].
Old age is the loss of vitality and the state of decrepitude;
these three states are mutually distinct.
There is no destruction of the subsequent states upon the destruction of the first state.
When a second state arises, there is no arising of the Self;
rather, it is observed that the immutable Self itself merely attains the second and third states.
Likewise, in that very same way, a body other than the current one is called "another body" (dehāntara).
The meaning is that its "attainment" is the attainment of another body for the Self, which is indeed changeless.
Being thus wise (dhīra), the intelligent one does not become deluded; he does not fall into confusion.
Even though delusion caused by the destruction of the Self is impossible for one who knows that the Self is eternal, [delusion regarding the body may still arise].

Nevertheless, worldly delusion (*moha*) is observed to arise from the attainment of cold, heat, pleasure, and pain; likewise, delusion arises from separation from pleasure, and grief (*śoka*) arises from union with suffering.
Anticipating this objection from Arjuna, the Blessed One said:
But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
The sense organs, such as the ear and so forth, are called *mātrās* because by means of them objects such as sound are measured (*mīyante*).
The "contacts" (*sparśas*) of the *mātrās* are the conjunctions with sound and the other objects;
these bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain—that is, they provide cold, heat, pleasure, and pain.
Alternatively, "contacts" (sparśa) are the sense objects—sounds and so forth—because they are touched.
Both the "nutriments" (mātrā) and the "contacts" bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain;
for instance, cold is sometimes pleasant and sometimes painful.
Likewise, heat (*uṣṇa*) also has an indeterminate nature.

Pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*duḥkha*), however, have a determinate nature because they do not deviate [from their own essence]. Therefore, cold (*śīta*) and heat (*uṣṇa*) are mentioned separately from those two.
Since those contacts with the senses, such as cold and heat, are subject to coming and going—having the nature of appearing and disappearing—they are impermanent.
Therefore, endure them; that is, bear cold, heat, and so forth with fortitude.
The meaning is: do not give way to joy or dejection on account of them. (BhG 2.14)
Listen to what happens for one who endures cold, heat, and the like:
"O bull among men, that steadfast person whom these do not afflict, who is equal in pleasure and pain—he is fit for immortality. (BhG 2.15)

For those aforementioned opposites, such as cold and heat, do not afflict nor shake that steadfast and wise person who regards pleasure and pain as equal— meaning one for whom pleasure and pain are the same— who remains free from elation and despondency upon encountering happiness or sorrow, because he perceives the eternal Self.

Established in the vision of the nature of the eternal Self, and enduring the pairs of opposites, he becomes fit—that is, capable—for immortality, meaning for the state of being immortal, which is liberation.

// BhG 2.15 // Furthermore, for this reason as well, it is proper to endure cold, heat, and so forth without succumbing to grief and delusion, because: "The unreal has no being; the real never ceases to be."
The end of both of these has been perceived by those who see reality.
For that which is non-existent and unreal—such as cold, heat, and so forth, along with their causes—there is no existence, no becoming, and no being.
For cold, heat, and so forth, along with their causes, do not exist as real entities when examined by means of valid cognition;
for they are transformations,
and transformations are inconstant.
Just as the configuration of a jar or similar object, when examined by the eye, is non-existent because it is not perceived apart from the clay,
so too every modification is non-existent because it is not perceived apart from its cause;
for it is not perceived prior to its birth or after its destruction.
The non-existence of the effect, such as a jar, and its cause, such as clay, follows from their non-perception apart from that [ultimate] cause.

If it is argued that "if that [non-existence] were non-existent, it would follow that everything is non-existent," we say no; for in every case two cognitions are perceived: the cognition of existence and the cognition of non-existence.
That object regarding which cognition does not err is real;
that object regarding which cognition errs is unreal.
Thus, the distinction between the real and the unreal is established as being dependent upon cognition.
In all cases, two cognitions are apprehended by everyone as being in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa), unlike [the case of] "blue lotus"; for example:
"the pot exists" (san ghaṭaḥ), "the cloth exists" (san paṭaḥ), and "the elephant exists" (san hastī).
Thus it is in all cases.
Of those two cognitions, the cognition of a jar and so forth is subject to deviation;
and this has already been demonstrated.
But the cognition of existence [itself] does not [arise].
Therefore, the object of the cognition of a jar and so forth is non-existent,
because of its variability.
But it is not the object of the cognition of existence,
because that cognition is non-erroneous.
If it is argued that when the jar is destroyed and the cognition of the jar deviates, the cognition of "existence" (*sat*) also deviates, we say no;
for the cognition of "existence" is observed even in the case of a cloth.
That cognition of "existence" has only the qualifier as its object.
If it is argued that the cognition of a jar is also seen following another jar, just like the cognition of a real entity, we say no;
because it is not observed in the case of cloth and other such things.
If it is argued that even the cognition of existence (*sad-buddhi*) is not perceived when the jar has perished, we say no;
this is because of the absence of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
Being a cognition whose object is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), in the absence of the substantive, the qualifier cannot logically occur—what, then, would be its object?
But it is not so, because for a correct cognition there is no absence of an object.

If it is argued that co-referentiality (ekādhikaraṇatva) is not tenable when the qualificand, such as a jar, is absent, we say no; for co-referentiality is observed even when one of the two is absent, as in the case of a mirage where one thinks, "This is water."
Therefore, since the body and so forth, along with their causes— the dualities— are non-existent, their coming into being does not exist;
likewise, for the existent Self, its non-existence or unavailability does not exist,
because, as we have stated, it is never absent from anything.

Thus, the end—the determination—of both the self and the non-self, of both the existent and the non-existent, has been seen and apprehended by the seers of reality as follows: "The existent is indeed existent; the non-existent is indeed non-existent," regarding these two as previously described.
The word "that" (tad) is a pronoun, and Brahman is everything;
its name is "that," and its state of being so is "reality" (tattva).
The true nature of Brahman;
those whose character is to perceive that are the "seers of reality" (tattva-darśinaḥ), by those seers of reality.

The intended meaning is this: you too, relying on the vision of those who perceive reality, should abandon grief and delusion; and having resolved in your mind that these dualities—such as cold and heat, which are both fixed and unfixed in nature—are merely transformations that are non-existent and appear falsely like water in a mirage, you must endure them.
What, then, is that which exists as the Real and exists at all times? It is said:
"But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this imperishable. (BhG 2.17)
"Indestructible" means that whose nature is not subject to destruction.
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from what is non-existent. "Know that" means understand it.
What? That by which this entire world is pervaded—that is, encompassed—by the Brahman known as "Being," just as jars and other objects are encompassed by space;
[and] destruction, meaning non-perception or non-existence.
"Of the imperishable" (*avyayasya*) means that which does not perish; it does not undergo increase or decrease, hence it is "imperishable.
This Brahman, designated as "Being," does not perish—that is, it does not deviate—from its own nature, because it is partless, unlike the body and so forth.
Nor does it pass away by means of what belongs to the self,
because of the non-existence of anything belonging to the self;
just as Devadatta passes away due to the loss of wealth.
But Brahman does not pass away in this manner.
Therefore, no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable Brahman;
no one, not even the Lord, is capable of destroying the Self.
For the Self is indeed Brahman, because action is contradictory within one's own self. What, then, is that which is non-existent, which deviates from its own existence? It is said:
These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
Those things which possess internal destruction are "finite" (*antavat*).

For example, just as the persistent cognition of existence regarding a mirage and the like is severed at the conclusion of an investigation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that [severance] is its "end."

Likewise, these bodies—like dream-bodies, illusory bodies, and so forth—are finite; they are said by the discerning to be finite for the eternal, embodied, indestructible, and immeasurable Self. Thus, the terms "eternal" and "indestructible" are not redundant, because there are two kinds of eternity and two kinds of destruction recognized in the world.

Just as a body that has been reduced to ashes and has passed beyond sight is said to be "destroyed," and just as even while existing, one who has undergone a transformation into another state— becoming afflicted by disease and so forth— is said to be "destroyed";
in this context, the meaning of the words "eternal" and "indestructible" is that he is unrelated to both these kinds of destruction.
Otherwise, the self might be eternal like the earth and other elements;
so that this [eternity] should not [be attributed to the self in an inappropriate sense], he says "of the eternal, the indestructible.
This means "of the immeasurable," i.e., of that which is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), being undeterminable by means of valid cognitions such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Is it not the case that the self is determined by scripture and previously by perception and other means? No;
because the self is established by itself.
For the search for means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs within oneself, the cognizer who desires to know;
indeed, one does not first proceed to determine an object of knowledge (*prameya*) without having previously cognized the self as "I am thus.
For there is no one for whom that which is called the "self" is unknown.

The scripture, however, is the final means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it attains the status of a means of valid knowledge for the Self by merely removing the superimposition of attributes that do not belong to it, and not by making known an object previously unknown. Thus says the Śruti: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).
Since the Self is thus eternal and immutable, therefore fight;
the meaning is that you should not desist from battle.
For here, the necessity of performing battle is not being enjoined.
For he, though indeed engaged in battle, remains silent because he is obstructed by grief and delusion;
therefore, the Blessed One merely removes that obstruction for him. Thus, "fight" is a mere restatement (anuvāda), not an injunction (vidhi). // BhG 2.18 //

The Blessed One has cited two Vedic verses as witnesses for this point: that the scripture of the Gītā is intended for the cessation of the causes of saṃsāra, such as grief and delusion, and is not an incitement to action.
As for what you think—that Bhīṣma and the others are being slain by me in battle, and that I alone am their slayer—this is not so.
This understanding of yours is indeed false. How so?
"He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks of it as slain—both these do not understand; this neither slays nor is slain. (BhG 2.19)

He who perceives— that is, understands— this embodied being under discussion as the slayer, the agent of the act of killing, and he who thinks of him as another as slain, [thinking] "I am slain" by the destruction of the body, as the object of the act of killing—
both of these do not understand, that is, they have failed to know, the Self due to a lack of discrimination.

The meaning is that those two who perceive the Self—the object of the notion of "I"—as "I am the slayer" and "I am slain" through the destruction of the body, are ignorant of the true nature of the Self.
This is because this Self does not slay; that is, it does not become the agent of the act of killing, nor is it slain; that is, it does not become the object of that action.
Because of its changelessness.
(BhG 2.19) The second verse—explaining how the Self is changeless—is as follows:
"It is never born, nor does it ever die."
Having come into being, this [Self] shall not cease to be hereafter;
it is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient.
It is not slain when the body is slain. (BhG 2.20)
It is not born, it does not arise; the meaning is that no modification of a real entity characterized by birth exists for the Self. Likewise, it does not die.
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "ca" (and);
thus, by saying "it does not die," the final modification characterized by destruction is negated.
Alternatively, the word "kadācit" (at any time) is connected with all the negations of modifications: "it is never born," and so forth.
It never dies; that is to say,
because this self, having come into being and experienced the act of becoming, will not thereafter cease to be— that is, it will not go to non-existence again— therefore it does not die.
For that which, having existed, will no longer exist, is called "dies" by the world.
From the word "or" (vā) and from the word "not" (na), this Self either did not exist and will come to be like the body, or it will not exist again;
therefore, it is not born.
For that which, having not existed, comes into being, is said to be "born";
the self is not like this;
therefore, it is not born.
Since it is so, it is unborn;
since it does not die, it is eternal.
Although by the negation of the two modifications at the beginning and the end, all modifications are effectively negated, [the text specifies these two].

Nevertheless, the negation of the modifications occurring in the middle state must be performed by their own specific terms, so that there may be a negation of all unmentioned modifications as well, such as those of youth and so forth.
Thus he says, beginning with "eternal" (*śāśvata*):
by the term "eternal," the modification characterized by decay is negated.
Eternal existence is "śāśvata";
it does not diminish in its own nature because it is partless.
Nor is there decay through the loss of qualities,
because it is devoid of qualities. Furthermore, a modification characterized by growth, which is the opposite of decay, is also denied— by the term "ancient" (purāṇa).
For that which is accumulated through the addition of parts increases and is called "new";
however, since this Self is partless, it was already new even in the past, and thus it is "ancient" (purāṇa) in the sense that it does not increase.
Likewise, it is not slain.
In this context, the root *han* should be understood in the sense of "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) in order to avoid redundancy;
the meaning is "it is not transformed. Thus, even while being struck—that is, while being transformed—the bodies [remain].
In this mantra, the six modifications of being—the transformations of worldly objects—are denied in the Self.
The meaning of the sentence is that the Self is devoid of every kind of modification.
Since this is so, its connection with the preceding mantra is: "Therefore, both of them do not know. (BhG 2.20)
Having established by means of the mantra "He who knows him as the slayer" that he is neither the agent nor the object of the act of killing,
and having stated the reason for this— his changelessness— in the verse "He is not born," he concludes the matter asserted:
"He who knows him as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable..."
How, O Pārtha, does that person cause anyone to be killed, or whom does he kill?
The connection is as follows: "he who knows" refers to one who knows that which is indestructible—devoid of the final modification of existence, eternal, and free from transformation.

How, in what manner, does that learned person, who is thus qualified, kill—that is, perform the act of killing—or how does he cause to be killed, that is, instigate a killer? [He kills or causes to be killed] this Being, whose characteristics were stated in the preceding mantra, who is unborn (devoid of birth) and immutable (devoid of decay).
How could such a person kill or cause to be killed?
"He does not kill anyone in any way, nor does he cause anyone to be killed in any way"— in both cases, the meaning is indeed a negation (*ākṣepa*), since the sense of a question is impossible;

and because the state of being unchanging, which is the meaning of the reason, is the same [for all], the Blessed One intended the prohibition of all action for the wise person to be the subject matter of this section.
The objection raised by the word "hanta" is stated for the sake of providing an illustration.
Seeing what specific reason for the impossibility of action does the Blessed One perceive in a wise man that he rejects all actions with the words "How can that person [act]?"?
[Objection: But has it not already been stated that the immutability of the Self is the specific cause for the impossibility of all actions?
It has been stated that this is true;
however, it is not a specific cause [for the wise man's lack of grief],
because the wise man is distinct from the immutable Self.
If it is argued that for one who has realized the immovable post, action is no longer possible, we say no;
because the state of being a knower belongs to the Self (ātman),
not to the aggregate of the body and so forth.

Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the Self is uncomposite, the Knower, and immutable; thus, since action is impossible for that Knower, the objection—“How can he be a person?”—is appropriate.

Just as the Self, though remaining immutable, is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) as being perceived by the non-discriminative cognition of the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti-aviveka-vijñāna*) regarding objects such as sound brought forward by the intellect, even so, through the cognition of the discrimination between Self and non-Self (*ātmānātma-viveka-jñāna*), the Knower is called the Self which is in reality immutable, even though it is by means of a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) whose nature is unreal (*asatya-rūpā*).

From the statement regarding the impossibility of action for the wise, it is understood that the Blessed One’s settled conclusion is that those actions which are enjoined by the scripture are prescribed for the ignorant.

If it is argued: "But surely knowledge (*vidyā*) is also prescribed only for one who is ignorant, since prescribing knowledge for one who has already realized it would be as useless as grinding what is already ground;
in that case, the distinction that 'rites are prescribed for the ignorant, not for the knower' is untenable"—we say: no.
This is because a distinction between the existence and non-existence of what is to be performed is logically established.

After gaining knowledge of the meaning of injunctions such as the *agnihotra*, for the ignorant person who possesses the cognition "I am the agent" and "this is my duty," and who performs the *agnihotra* and other rites preceded by the gathering of various means, there exists that which is to be performed.
But it is not the case that, as in the injunction regarding the nature of the Self such as "one is not born," there is anything to be performed subsequent to the knowledge of that meaning;

rather, this distinction is logically established because nothing other than the knowledge of the oneness and non-agency of the Self— such as "I am not the agent" and "I am not the enjoyer"— arises [from it].
Furthermore, for one who perceives the self as "I am the doer," the cognition that "this must be done by me" necessarily arises;
with respect to that [cognition], such a person is qualified for action.
Thus, actions are possible for him [the unenlightened];

and because of the statement, "He is ignorant, for both of them do not know," and because there is a statement regarding the specific enlightened one that implies the non-performance of action, how could that person [be subject to karma]?
Therefore, only the specific enlightened seeker of liberation—who perceives the changeless Self—has the qualification for the renunciation of all actions.

For this very reason, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having distinguished between the learned followers of Sāṃkhya—whether they be ignorant or wise—and the performers of ritual action, causes them to grasp two distinct disciplines: "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, and by the yoga of action for the Yogins.
Likewise, the Blessed Vyāsa said to his son: "Now, there are these two paths," and so forth.
And thus: "The path of action first, and renunciation afterwards.

The Blessed One will demonstrate this very division again and again: "One who does not know reality, whose self is deluded by egoism, thinks 'I am the doer'; but one who knows reality," [thinks otherwise].
"I do not act";
likewise, "having mentally renounced all actions, he remains," and so forth.

In this regard, some who consider themselves wise say: "The knowledge that 'I am the one Self, changeless and a non-agent, devoid of the six modifications of existence beginning with birth' does not arise in anyone; yet it is only when such knowledge exists that the renunciation of all action is taught.
That is not so.
This is because it would follow that the instruction of the scripture, beginning with "it is not born," etc., would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, they must be asked: "If, by the power of the scriptural instruction, there arises the knowledge of the existence of dharma and adharma as well as the knowledge of the agent's connection to another body, why then does the knowledge of that very Self's immutability, non-agency, unity, and so forth, not likewise arise from the scripture?"
If it is argued that this is because [the Self] is not within the scope of the instruments of action (*karaṇa*), we say no;
for there is the scriptural testimony: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).
The mind, refined by the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher, as well as by tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and other virtues, is the instrument for the vision of the Self.
And thus, since there exist inference and scripture for the sake of attaining that [knowledge], to claim that knowledge does not arise is mere audacity.
Furthermore, it must be admitted that when knowledge arises, it necessarily sublates the ignorance that is its opposite;
and that ignorance has been shown as: "I am the slayer," and so forth.
"I am killed"—thus neither of those two realizes [the truth].
Here, it is shown that the self's agency (*kartṛtva*), its objecthood (*karmatva*), and its causative agency (*hetu-kartṛtva*) regarding the act of being killed are produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
And this is the same for all actions; agency and so forth are produced by nescience (*avidyā*) because the self is changeless (*avikriyatva*).

For an agent who possesses modification impels another, who has become the object of his action, saying, "Do this. Thus, Lord Vāsudeva, by the words beginning with "How that person," prohibits both the agency and the causative agency of the wise man in all actions without distinction, for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of the wise man's qualification for ritual action.
But where, then, is the qualification for the wise? This has already been stated previously: "for the Sāṅkhyas, by means of the yoga of knowledge.
And likewise, he will speak of the renunciation of all actions with the words, "all actions by means of the mind," and so forth.
If it is argued that because of the expression "with the mind" (manasā), there is no renunciation of vocal and bodily actions, we say no;
for [the text] specifies "all actions" (sarva-karmāṇi). If it is argued that this refers only to all mental actions, we say no.
Since verbal and physical activities are preceded by mental activity, they cannot occur in the absence of such mental activity.
If it is argued that one should renounce all actions with the mind—excluding those mental actions which are the causes of scriptural verbal and physical acts—the answer is no;
for there is the specific qualification: "neither acting nor causing others to act."
If it is argued that this renunciation of all actions (sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa) was spoken by the Blessed One for one who is dying and not for one who is living, we say no;
for the qualification "the embodied one dwells in the city of nine gates" would be untenable.
Indeed, it is not possible for one who is dead to dwell in that body through the renunciation of all actions.
If it is argued that the connection "having renounced in the body" applies to one who neither acts nor causes others to act, but not to one who "dwells in the body," we say no;
for it is established everywhere that the Self is changeless,
and because the action of sitting requires a locus.
Moreover, because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is independent of that [action],
the word *nyāsa* preceded by the prefix *sam-* here has the sense of "abandonment" (*tyāga*), not the sense of "depositing" (*nikṣepa*).

Therefore, we shall demonstrate in various subsequent passages within the section on the knowledge of the Self that, according to the Gītā scripture, only one who possesses knowledge of the Self has the qualification for renunciation, and not for action. (BhG 2.21)
Now we shall speak of the subject at hand.
Therein, the indestructibility of the self has been asserted.
To the question "In what way is that so?", it is said:
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new,
so too does the soul, casting off worn-out bodies.
The embodied soul enters into other new bodies.

Just as in the world a person, having cast off worn-out garments that have reached a state of decay, takes up others that are new, even so the embodied Self, having cast off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones; the meaning is that the Self is indeed changeless, just like the person.
Why is it changeless? He says:
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it.
Weapons do not cut this embodied being under discussion; because it is partless, they do not effect a division of its parts.
"Weapons" refers to swords and the like.
Likewise, fire does not burn it;
even the fire does not reduce it to ashes.
Likewise, the waters do not moisten it.
For water has the capacity to bring about the disjunction of parts by causing the moistening of a composite substance;
that [capacity] is not possible in the case of the partless self (*ātman*).
Likewise, wind destroys a viscous substance by drying up its moisture.
Yet even the wind does not wither this self.
Since it is so, therefore:
This is indestructible, this is unburnable, this is undissoluble, and indeed, it is unwitherable.
This is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
Since swords and other such weapons, being the mutual causes of destruction for one another, are unable to destroy this self, it is therefore eternal.
Because it is eternal, it is omnipresent;
because it is omnipresent, it is like a pillar.
"Steadfast" means this Self is immovable because of its steadfastness;
therefore, it is eternal and ancient.
It is not produced from any cause whatsoever;
the meaning is that it is ever-new.
One should not raise the objection that there is tautology in these worlds.
For, by this very verse alone— beginning with "It is neither born nor does it die"— the eternity and changelessness of the Self have been stated.
Whatever is said there regarding the subject of the Self does not exceed the meaning of this verse.
Some [repetitions] are by way of the word, while others are by way of the meaning;
because the reality of the self is difficult to understand, [the Buddha] brings it up again and again, employing different words to express that very same reality.

The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva explains how the unmanifest reality (avyakta-tattva), having come within the range of the intellect of transmigrating beings as that which is not subject to transmigration, may lead to the cessation of saṃsāra.
Furthermore—
This Self is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable;
therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
This Self is unmanifest because it is not an object for any of the instruments of perception; thus, it is "unmanifest" (avyakta).
For this very reason, it is inconceivable (acintya).
For whatever falls within the range of the senses becomes an object of thought.
But this self, because it is not within the range of the sense faculties, is inconceivable;
for that very reason, it is unchangeable, unlike milk, which is subject to transformation by the addition of a ferment such as curd.
And because it is partless, it is changeless;
for nothing that is partless is ever observed to be subject to modification.
Because it is changeless, this Self is said to be unchangeable.
Therefore, having understood this Self in the manner thus described, you ought not to grieve, thinking, "I am the slayer of these," or "these are being slain by me.
[Now] this is said while accepting the impermanence of the self:
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, even if you consider this [self] to be constantly born or constantly dying, even then you ought not to grieve in this manner.
Moreover, the word "iti" has the sense of acceptance.
You consider this very self under discussion to be "constantly born"— meaning you think it is born again and again with the birth of various bodies according to worldly convention—
and likewise, you consider it to be "constantly dying" with each respective destruction, thinking "it is dead, it is dead."
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, even though the self is thus, you ought not to grieve in this way;
for the destruction of that which is born and the birth of that which is subject to destruction are both inevitable. (BhG 2.26)
And this being so:
"For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore, you ought not to grieve over that which is inevitable. (BhG 2.27)

For one who has been born—that is, for one who has attained birth—death is certain and inevitable; and for one who has died, birth is likewise certain. Therefore, this matter characterized by birth and death is unavoidable.
Since this matter is unavoidable, you ought not to grieve over it.
Furthermore, it is not proper to grieve even for those beings whose nature consists of the aggregate of body and organs, because:
"Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their dissolution; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (BhG 2.28)

"Unmanifest in origin": those beings whose beginning is unmanifest—meaning invisible, imperceptible—are the elements consisting of the aggregates of effects such as sons, friends, and the like. These beings are "unmanifest in origin" prior to their birth;
having been born, they are "manifest in the middle" until death;
and they are indeed "unmanifest in dissolution," for those whose end, or death, is again the unmanifest—invisibility.
The meaning is that even after death, they attain only a state of non-manifestation (*avyaktatā*).
And so it has been said:
"Having emerged from the unseen, he has once again gone to the unseen."
"He is not yours, nor are you his; why this vain lamentation? (Mahābhārata, Strīparvan 2.13).
In this context, "why this lamentation" means: what is the point of this wailing or delirious speech regarding beings who are like illusions—beings that were unseen, seen, and then vanished?
Furthermore, the subject under discussion, the Self (*ātman*), is difficult to discern.
But why do you reproach me alone when the cause of delusion is common to all?
How is this Self so difficult to understand? To this he says:
"Someone beholds it as a wonder."
One speaks of this as a marvel,
and another likewise hears of it as a marvel;
yet even after hearing it, no one at all truly knows it.
Like a marvel—meaning like a wonder never seen before, extraordinary, and appearing suddenly—one person perceives this Self as a marvel;
another speaks of it likewise as a marvel;
and yet another hears of it as a marvel.
Having heard, seen, or even spoken of it, no one at all knows this self;
or rather, he who perceives this self is like a marvel,
and he who speaks of it or hears of it is indeed someone among many thousands.
Therefore, the intention is that the Self is difficult to understand.
Now, concluding the subject matter of this section, he says:
"O Bhārata, this embodied one is eternally indestructible within the body of everyone."
Therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings.
The embodied self (*dehin*), being eternal and always present in all states, is indestructible because it is partless and eternal.

In this regard, it is "indestructible in the body" (*avadhyaḥ śarīre*); since it is omnipresent, even while residing in stationary objects and the like, this embodied self is not destroyed when the body of any living being is slain.
Therefore, with respect to all beings such as Bhīṣma and others, you ought not to grieve.
It has been stated here that, with respect to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*), neither sorrow nor delusion is possible.
This is not only the case with respect to the ultimate reality, but furthermore:
"Having also considered your own duty (*svadharma*), you ought not to waver."
For indeed, there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war.

"Even your own duty"—your own duty is battle for a Kṣatriya; having regard even for that, you ought not to waver or deviate. The intention is that [you must not depart] from the natural duty of a Kṣatriya, which arises from one's own innate nature (*ātma-svābhāvya*). Furthermore, that battle—by way of conquering the earth—is for the sake of dharma and for the sake of protecting the subjects; thus, being not devoid of dharma, it is supremely righteous (*dharmyam*).
Therefore, for a Kṣatriya, no other duty exists that is more conducive to his welfare than this righteous war; for this is so.
And why must that war be undertaken? It is said:
"By chance has come to you this open door to heaven."
O Pārtha, happy are the Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this.
And for those Kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a battle— arrived by chance and unasked for, like the gateway to heaven opened and flung wide—
are they not happy?
[And] even though this [battle] has presented itself as a duty—
But if you will not engage in this righteous battle,
then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you will incur sin.

But if you do not engage in this lawful battle, ordained as consistent with dharma, then by its non-performance, having abandoned your own duty and the fame resulting from encounters with the great gods and others, you will incur only sin.
Not only is there the abandonment of one's own duty and fame—
And people will speak of your undying infamy;
for one who has been highly esteemed, ill repute is worse than death.
Moreover, after the battle, people will speak of your undying and long-lasting infamy.
For one who has been honored for qualities such as being righteous and brave, infamy is worse than death; the meaning is that for one so highly esteemed, death is better than infamy. (BhG 2.34)
Moreover:
"The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will now incur contempt. (BhG 2.35)
Out of fear of Karṇa and others, the great car-warriors—Duryodhana and his followers—will think and consider that you have desisted and withdrawn from the battle, and not out of compassion.
And having been highly esteemed by them, Duryodhana and the rest, as one endowed with many virtues, you will again fall into insignificance and lightness of status.
Moreover:
"And your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, censuring your prowess; what indeed could be more painful than that? (BhG 2.36)

Your enemies, your adversaries, will speak many various kinds of unspeakable and unutterable words, censuring and reviling your prowess that was manifested in battles such as those against the Nivātakavacas. What indeed could be more painful than that suffering arising from such censure?
The meaning is that there is no suffering more grievous than that.
Furthermore, when [the battle] is being waged by Karṇa and the others, [Arjuna said]:
"Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore, arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle. (BhG 2.37)
Either slain you shall attain heaven— being killed, you will reach the celestial realm—
or having conquered heroes such as Karṇa and others, you shall enjoy the earth.
The intention is that, in either case, there is gain for you alone.
Since this is so, therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, for battle; the meaning is: having made the resolve, "I shall conquer my enemies, or I shall die. (BhG 2.37)
In that regard, listen to this instruction for one who fights with the understanding that battle is his own duty:
"Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, then engage in battle; thus you shall not incur sin. (BhG 2.38)
Having made pleasure and pain equal and the same, and having likewise not made attachment and aversion [so],
and similarly having made gain and loss, victory and defeat equal— then engage in battle; strive.
"By fighting in this manner, you shall not incur sin"—
this is the incidental instruction.
The worldly principle for the removal of grief and delusion has been stated in such verses as "Having also considered your own duty," and so forth.
But it is not with that as its primary purport;
for here the vision of ultimate reality is the subject under discussion.
And that which was stated is now being concluded—"this has been declared to you"—in order to demonstrate the distinction between the subjects of the scriptures.

For, since this division of the subject matter of the scripture has been demonstrated here, the scripture—which concerns the two-fold steadfastness (niṣṭhā) of the Sāṃkhyas through the yoga of knowledge and of the Yogins through the yoga of action—will be easily heard by the listeners, and they will grasp it with ease according to the division of its subject matter; therefore, He says:
"This wisdom has been declared to you in respect of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] in respect of Yoga."
Endowed with that intellect by which, O Pārtha, you shall cast off the bondage of action.

This wisdom—knowledge concerning the discrimination of the ultimate reality in the context of Sāṃkhya—has been declared and explained to you; it is the direct cause for the cessation of the defects that are the root of saṃsāra, such as grief and delusion.

Now, however, hear this wisdom which will be spoken of immediately hereafter regarding Yoga—the means for attaining that [Sāṃkhya]—consisting of the performance of action in the form of Karma-yoga for the sake of propitiating the Lord through detachment and the prior abandonment of the pairs of opposites, as well as Samādhi-yoga.

And he praises that intellect for the sake of creating interest: "Endowed with that intellect which has Yoga as its object, O Pārtha, you shall cast off the bondage of action"—the meaning is that this is because you will attain knowledge caused by the grace of the Lord. Furthermore:
In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.

In this path to liberation, namely Karma-yoga, there is no destruction of the "abhikrama"—"abhikrama" meaning "abhikramaṇa," which is the commencement; its destruction does not exist as it does, for example, in the case of agriculture and the like.
The meaning is that in the sphere of Yoga, the commencement does not have an uncertain result.
Furthermore, unlike medical treatment, there is no "pratyavāya" (adverse effect or obstacle) that occurs.

However, even a very small amount of this dharma—the practice of the yoga-dharma—when performed, protects and saves one from great fear, namely the fear of saṃsāra characterized by birth, death, and so forth. (BhG 2.40)
That very intellect which has been described in Sāṃkhya and in Yoga, and whose characteristics will be explained hereafter—
O joy of the Kurus, that intellect is of the nature of resolute determination; it is single in this world.
For the intellects of those lacking resolve are indeed many-branched and infinite.

The intellect characterized by resolve— that is, having the nature of certainty— is indeed one, subverting the various branches of other contrary forms of cognition because it is produced by valid means of knowledge on this path to the highest good.
O descendant of Kuru,
as for those others who possess contrary understandings,
their [teachings] are endless, shoreless, and unceasing due to the proliferation of various sectarian branches.

Samsara becomes eternally extended and vast; and when the cognitions of infinite distinctions cease due to the power of the discerning intellect produced by right knowledge, samsara also comes to an end. Those cognitions have many branches—that is, they possess numerous branches—and thus they are "many-branched."
"Many divisions"—this refers to the fact that, according to the different branches [of the Vedas], cognitions are indeed infinite.
Of whom? Of those who lack resolve; the meaning is: of those who are devoid of the discriminative cognition produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (BhG 2.41)

Those whose intellect is not characterized by resolve— those unwise ones who utter this flowery speech, O Pārtha, being devoted to the ritualistic declarations of the Vedas and asserting that "there is nothing else"— [are deluded]. (BhG 2.42)

O Pārtha, those who are devoid of wisdom—meaning those who lack intelligence and discernment—speak these words which are about to be described: words that are "flowering," like a tree in bloom, appearing beautiful and pleasant to hear when being recited; words characterized as mere verbal rhetoric.

They are "delighting in the talk of the Vedas," meaning they take pleasure in Vedic statements that illuminate numerous types of explanatory discourses (*arthavāda*), results, and means to those ends.
Those who are habitually inclined to speak thus: "There is nothing other than ritual actions that accomplish results such as the attainment of heaven"—
they are those whose very selves are desire, who look toward heaven, and [who follow the path] that yields birth as the fruit of action.
It abounds in various ritual actions directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power.
"Those whose nature is desire" means those whose essence is desire;
"those intent on desire" is the meaning.
"Those for whom heaven is the highest goal" means those for whom heaven is the supreme human aim (*puruṣārtha*); they are those who prioritize heaven.

"Bestowing birth as the fruit of action"—the fruit of action is *karma-phala*; birth itself is the fruit of action, hence "birth-as-the-fruit-of-action. That which bestows this is "bestowing birth-as-the-fruit-of-action," referring to that speech. The word "they proclaim" (*pravadanti*) is to be supplied from the context.

"Abounding in specific rituals": specific rituals are *kriyā-viśeṣāḥ*; that speech in which these are numerous is "abounding in specific rituals"—that speech by which objects such as heaven, cattle, and sons are predominantly proclaimed. Regarding "the attainment of enjoyment and power": enjoyment (*bhoga*) and power (*aiśvarya*) are "enjoyment-and-power" (*bhogaiśvarye*);
their attainment or reaching is "the attainment of enjoyment and power" (*bhogaiśvarya-gatiḥ*).
The intention is that those fools who speak words abounding in those specific ritual acts which serve as the means for attaining that [heaven] continue to revolve in saṃsāra.
And of them—
those who are attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [speech].
A resolute intellect is not established in meditative concentration.
For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power— those for whom enjoyment and power are the sole objects of affection, who have identified themselves with them,
and whose minds are carried away by that speech abounding in various ritual actions, thereby obscuring their discriminative wisdom—
the resolute intellect pertaining to Sāṃkhya or Yoga is not fixed upon samādhi. Samādhi is so called because everything is concentrated therein for the experience of the Puruṣa.

The internal organ is the intellect (*buddhi*); in that state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is "not enjoined," meaning it does not exist. // BhG 2.44 // He now states the result for those whose minds are devoid of such discriminative intellect and whose nature is driven by desire:

"The Vedas concern themselves with the three qualities; be free from these three qualities, O Arjuna. Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, beyond the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self."

"Having the three qualities as their subject matter": *traiguṇya* (the three qualities) is *saṃsāra* (transmigration), which is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) that must be illuminated by them; thus, those Vedas are "having the three qualities as their subject matter.
But you, O Arjuna, become free from the three qualities; the meaning is: become desireless.
Free from the pairs of opposites: the terms *dvandva* (pairs) refer to the two categories that are the causes of pleasure and pain and which stand in mutual opposition;
therefore, become one who has emerged from these, a *nirdvandva*.
Constantly established in goodness: always take refuge in the quality of *sattva*.

Likewise, you should be free from the pursuit of acquisition and security; for "acquisition" (yoga) is the taking up of what has not yet been acquired, and "security" (kṣema) is the protection of what has already been acquired.
Since it is difficult for one whose primary concern is acquisition and security to engage in what is truly beneficial, you should therefore be free from the pursuit of acquisition and security.
Be self-possessed and vigilant;
this is the instruction for you as you perform your own duty.
(BhG 2.45) If one does not look toward those infinite fruits which are declared for all the rites prescribed in the Vedas, [then...]

For what purpose are those [Vedic rites] performed for the sake of the Lord? Listen: "Whatever purpose there is in a small reservoir when there is water overflowing everywhere, such is the purpose of all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses true knowledge. (BhG 2.46)

Just as in the world, whatever purpose, result, or utility— such as bathing or drinking— exists in various limited water sources like wells or ponds, all that same purpose is accomplished in its entirety even by water that has overflowed everywhere.
The meaning is that it is included therein. Thus, whatever purpose there is in all the Vedas and in the rituals prescribed in the Vedas— namely,
the fruit of those rituals— that very same purpose is attained by a Brahmin who has renounced the world and understands the reality of the supreme truth.

The meaning is this: whatever fruit of knowledge exists anywhere—comparable to a place flooded with water—all that becomes as large as that [knowledge] and is included within it. Just as when the primary die has been won, all the lower stakes are gathered together, even so everything that people do well, and whatever they know, all that converges upon him who knows what he [the Self] knows (ChāU 4.1.2).
Thus says the Śruti;
and He will also say, "all action in its entirety.
Therefore, prior to attaining the qualification for steadfastness in knowledge, one who is qualified for action [should perform it].
Action that serves as the means for constructing wells, tanks, and other such works must also be performed.
And for you:
"Your entitlement is to action alone; never to its fruits."
Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction for you.
Your authority lies only in action, not in steadfastness in knowledge.
And while performing that action, let there be no authority over the fruits; the meaning is that at no time, in any state whatsoever, should there be thirst for the fruit of action.
