When you have craving for the fruit of action, then you would become the cause for the attainment of that fruit of action;
thus, do not become a cause for the fruit of action.
For when one engages in action impelled by craving for the fruit of action, then one becomes the cause for the very birth that is the fruit of action.
If the fruit of action is not desired, what is the use of action which is of the nature of suffering?
Thus, let there be no attachment for you toward inaction; let there be no pleasure in non-performance. (BhG 2.47)
If action is not to be performed by one who is motivated by the fruits of action, then how should it be performed? It is said:
"Established in yoga, O Dhananjaya, perform actions, having abandoned attachment."
Having become the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga.
Established in yoga, perform actions solely for the sake of the Lord;

even in that regard, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment with the thought, "May the Lord be pleased with me," when action is performed free from thirst for results, there arises perfection characterized by the attainment of knowledge born from the purification of the mind.
The non-establishment [of the Self] arises from the opposite of that; being equal—that is, identical—with respect to both their establishment and non-establishment, perform your actions.
What is this yoga, established in which you are told to "perform"?
This indeed is that: equanimity toward success and failure is called Yoga.
Furthermore, regarding the action performed for the sake of worshipping the Lord while endowed with the intellect of equanimity—it is from this action [that one attains the goal].
For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in wisdom. Miserable are those whose motive is the fruit of action.

By far— that is, by a great distance and indeed to an extreme degree— is inferior, base, and lowly the action performed by one seeking fruits, compared to the action characterized by the yoga of wisdom (buddhi-yoga), which is endowed with the intellect of equanimity;
for [the former] is the cause of birth, death, and so forth, O Dhanañjaya.

Since this is so, therefore seek—pray for—the refuge, the support, and the cause for attaining fearlessness in the intellect whose object is Yoga, or in the Sāṃkhya intellect born from its maturation;
the meaning is: "Become one who has taken refuge in the knowledge of the supreme reality.
For those wretched and miserable ones who perform inferior action are motivated by desire for results, being driven by thirst for the fruits of their deeds.
For the Śruti declares: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable" (BAU 3.8.10).
Now, hear what fruit one attains by performing one's own duty while endowed with the intellect of equanimity:
"One whose intellect is disciplined abandons here both good and evil deeds. (BhG 2.50)
Therefore, strive for yoga; yoga is skill in actions.

One who is "endowed with intelligence" (*buddhi-yuktaḥ*)—that is, one endowed with an intelligence whose object is equanimity toward action (*karma-samatva-viṣayayā buddhyā*)—abandons and relinquishes both good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛte*), meaning merit and sin, in this very world, by means of the attainment of knowledge through the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*). Therefore, apply yourself—that is, strive—for the yoga of the intelligence of equanimity. For yoga is skillfulness (*kauśalam*) in actions; it is that state of skillfulness (*kuśala-bhāvaḥ*) consisting of the intelligence of equanimity toward success and failure while engaged in one's own duty (*sva-dharma*), characterized by a mind surrendered to the Lord (*īśvarārpita-cetastayā*).
For that indeed is skillfulness by which even those actions whose very nature is bondage turn away from their inherent nature through the realization of equality.
Therefore, become one who is endowed with the realization of equality.
For the wise, endowed with discernment, abandon the fruit born of action;
liberated from the bond of birth, they go to the state that is free from all suffering.
The phrase "having abandoned the fruit born of action" is connected with the distant word [in the verse].

The attainment of desirable and undesirable bodies is the fruit born of action—that is, produced from actions. Because those who are "endowed with wisdom"—meaning those endowed with the wisdom of equanimity—having abandoned and relinquished that fruit, become "sages," that is, possessors of knowledge; for this reason...

"Completely liberated from the bondage of birth"—birth itself is the bondage; thus, "liberated from the bondage of birth. Being liberated from the bondage of birth even while still living, they go to the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which is called liberation (*mokṣa*), meaning free from all affliction (*anāmaya*).

Alternatively, beginning with the words "O Dhanañjaya, through the yoga of the intellect," the intellect characterized by the vision of the ultimate reality—which is like water overflowing everywhere—is produced by the purification of the *sattva* resulting from the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).
Because it is heard that [this state] is the direct cause for the abandonment of good and evil deeds and so forth.
(BhG 2.51) It is now stated when the intellect (*buddhi*), purified by the practice of yoga, will be attained:
"When your intellect shall cross beyond the thicket of delusion..."
Then you will attain detachment from what is yet to be heard and from what has already been heard.

When— at which time— your intellect (buddhi), having transcended— that is, having passed beyond— that turbidity consisting of delusion (moha-kalila), which is of the nature of delusion and takes the form of non-discrimination, by which [turbidity] the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is defiled with respect to the object [of knowledge], thereby clouding the awakening that discriminates between the Self and the not-Self; the meaning is that it will attain a state of extreme purity.
At that time, you will attain *nirveda*—dispassion toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard;
the meaning is that at that point, both the hearing and what was heard will appear fruitless to you.

If you ask, "When, through the transcendence of the turbidity of delusion, shall I obtain the wisdom born of self-discrimination and thus reach the fruit of Karma-yoga, which is the Yoga of the Supreme Reality? listen to this:
When your intellect, which has been perplexed by the Vedas, stands firm and unwavering in meditative concentration, then you shall attain Yoga.

When your intellect— having become conflicted, variously opposed, and distracted by the various scriptural hearings (*śruti*) that proclaim the manifold relationships between means and ends, and which are characterized by engagement and withdrawal— shall stand firm, having become steady, motionless, and free from the agitation of distraction in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Samādhi" is the self (ātman) because the mind is concentrated (*samādhīyate*) upon it; "in that self" means in that [self].
"Immovable even there" means free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The intellect (*buddhi*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
At that time, you will attain yoga; you will obtain discriminative wisdom (*viveka-prajñā*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Having obtained the seed for a question, Arjuna spoke, desiring to know the characteristics of one who has attained the wisdom of meditative absorption:
Arjuna said:
O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi?
What would one of steady wisdom speak? How would he sit? How would he move?

He whose wisdom is established in the realization, "I am the Supreme Brahman," is one of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*). What is the description of that person of steady wisdom? What is his speech—how is he described by others—when he is established in *samādhi*, O Keśava?

What would one whose intellect is steady—that is, one whose wisdom is established—himself speak? What would he sit, or how would he walk? What is his posture, or what is his manner of walking? This is the meaning:
by this verse, the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established are being questioned.

For, regarding both the one who from the very beginning renounces actions and proceeds to steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, and the one who [proceeds] by means of the yoga of action— from the verse beginning with "He abandons" up to the end of the chapter— the characteristics of the man of steady wisdom and his means of attainment are taught.
For throughout the entire inner science (adhyātma-śāstra), those very characteristics of one who has accomplished the goal are taught as the means (sādhana),
because they are to be achieved through effort.
Regarding those which are both means to be accomplished by effort and characteristics, the Blessed Lord said:
When one abandons all desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha, and is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be established in wisdom. (BhG 2.55)

When— at which time— one completely abandons, thoroughly relinquishes, and casts off all desires— that is, every variety of longing— O Pārtha, those that have entered the mind, having entered the heart; for when all desires are abandoned, since there is no cause for satisfaction and only the remnants necessary for maintaining the body remain, one might fall into activity like a madman or a person intoxicated.

Therefore, it is said: when one is satisfied in the Self alone—that is, in the very nature of the inner self—by means of the Self itself, being independent of external gains; and having attained the nectar-like essence of the vision of the supreme truth, one possesses the conviction that "enough" of anything else; such a person is called a man of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*), a wise one in whom wisdom born from the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self is established and firmly rooted.

Having renounced the desires for son, wealth, and worlds, the renunciant (saṃnyāsī) who delights in the Self and finds sport in the Self is one whose wisdom is established; this is the meaning. Furthermore:
"One whose mind is unperturbed in sorrows and who is free from longing in pleasures..."
Free from passion, fear, and anger, one whose intellect is steady is called a sage.
One whose mind is not agitated or disturbed when internal and other such sufferings have arisen is "one whose mind is undisturbed" (*anudvigna-manāḥ*).

Likewise, one from whom longing or thirst has departed when pleasures are obtained— meaning one who does not increase further in pleasure like a fire fed with fuel— is "one whose longing has departed" (*vigata-spṛhaḥ*).
One from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed—that is, one in whom passion, fear, and anger have been removed—is "one whose passion, fear, and anger have departed.
He is called a sage of steady intellect, a man of steady wisdom, and a renunciant at that time.
Furthermore—
He who is entirely free from attachment, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious— his wisdom is firmly established.

That sage who is everywhere without attachment—even toward body, life, and so forth—and is free from all clinging; who, having encountered various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious, and having obtained each such thing, neither rejoices nor feels aversion; who, upon obtaining what is auspicious, is neither satisfied nor elated.
And the meaning is that he does not feel aversion even upon encountering the unpleasant.
For him who is thus free from both elation and despondency, wisdom born of discernment becomes firmly established.
(BhG 2.57) Furthermore—
And when he completely withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses, as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established. (BhG 2.58)

When this ascetic, engaged in the culmination of knowledge, properly withdraws and fully draws back [the senses]—just as a tortoise, out of fear, withdraws its own limbs from all sides—so too does one established in knowledge withdraw the senses from the objects of the senses, that is, from all sense-objects.
For such a person, "wisdom is firmly established"—this statement has already been explained. (BhG 2.58)

In that regard, although the senses of even a sick man who does not partake of sense objects are withdrawn like the limbs of a tortoise, the passion for those objects is not withdrawn. How is that passion withdrawn? It is said: "The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food;
but the taste [for them] remains. Even that taste turns away from him upon seeing the Supreme. (BhG 2.59)

Although the objects of the senses— and by extension, the senses themselves which are indicated by the term "objects"— cease for even a fool who is abstinent, who does not take in sense-objects, and who stands in difficult austerity, they do so with the exception of *rasa*; that is, excluding *rasa*, which is attachment (*rāga*) toward sense-objects.

The word *rasa* is well-known in the sense of "passion" (*rāga*), as seen in such expressions as "one who acts by his own *sva-rasa*," "one who possesses taste" (*rasika*), and "one who knows taste" (*rasajña*).

That taste, which consists of attachment, also ceases for this ascetic who, having seen and realized the supreme reality of the ultimate truth—Brahman—abides in the thought, "I am indeed That. The meaning is that his cognition of objects becomes seedless.
There is no severance of this taste as long as right vision (*samyag-darśana*) is absent.

For even of a wise man who strives, O son of Kuntī,
the turbulent senses violently carry away the mind.

O Kaunteya, because the senses of even a wise and intelligent man—who is striving, that is, making an effort—are turbulent by nature and prone to agitation, they indeed throw the person off balance and distract him toward sense objects;
and having distracted him, they forcibly and openly carry away the mind of one who possesses discriminative knowledge, even while he is looking on. (BhG 2.60)
Therefore, having restrained all those [senses], one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. (BhG 2.61)

Restraining all those [senses]—having performed their restraint, that is, their subjugation—one should sit disciplined and composed, being intent on Me; "intent on Me" means one for whom I, Vāsudeva, the inner Self of all, am the supreme goal, thinking, "I am none other than He. For the yogi who sits in this manner, whose senses remain under control through the power of practice, his wisdom is firmly established.
Now, that which is the root of all calamities for one who is about to be defeated is stated here:
"When a person dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment, desire is born; and from desire, anger is produced. (BhG 2.62)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the destruction of discernment; and from the destruction of discernment, one perishes.

In a person who meditates—that is, who reflects upon and perceives specific objects such as sound and the rest—attachment, which is clinging or affection, arises toward those objects. From that attachment, which is affection, desire or thirst (tṛṣṇā) is born. From desire, when it is obstructed by something, anger is produced.
From anger arises delusion (*saṃmoha*), which is a lack of discrimination regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
For one who is angry, being thus deluded, even reviles his teacher.

From delusion comes the confusion of memory (*smṛti-vibhrama*); that is, there is a confusion or failure of the memory produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) instilled by the teachings of the scriptures and teachers—namely, the non-arising of memory when the conditions for its production are present.
Then, from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The destruction of the intellect is said to be the inner organ’s (*antaḥkaraṇa*) incapacity for discerning between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
From the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
For a person exists only so long as his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is capable of discriminating between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done regarding its objects.
When it is incapable of that, the person is indeed destroyed.
Therefore, the meaning is that through the destruction of that internal organ—the intellect—he perishes; that is, he becomes unfit for the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha).
The longing for sense objects has been declared to be the root of all misfortune;
now, therefore, this cause of liberation is stated:
"But moving among sense objects with the senses free from attachment and aversion..."
With his senses under his own control, the self-governed man attains serenity.
"Free from attachment and aversion": attachment and aversion are "rāga-dveṣau";
for the activity of the senses is naturally preceded by these two.
In that regard, he who is a seeker of liberation [should engage] with unavoidable objects through the senses, such as the ears and so forth, which are free from those two.

While practicing, one who perceives [the truth]—having brought the senses under his own control and having them become submissive through those senses that are self-governed—he, being one whose inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is subject to his will, attains serenity. Serenity is clarity, a state of well-being. (BhG 2.64)
It is said: what happens when there is serenity?
"When there is serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him;
for the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes established. (BhG 2.65)
In serenity, the abandonment—that is, the destruction—of all sufferings, both internal and otherwise, arises for this ascetic.

Furthermore, because the intellect of one whose mind is serene, whose internal organ is composed, quickly—that is, swiftly—becomes fully established; it becomes established all around like the sky, meaning it becomes motionless in its very nature as the Self.

Thus, for one whose mind is serene and whose intellect is established because his duty has been accomplished, the meaning of the statement is that he should act with senses free from attachment and aversion toward unavoidable objects that are not contrary to the scriptures. This very serenity is now being praised: The meaning of the statement is that he should act with senses free from attachment and aversion toward unavoidable objects that are not contrary to the scriptures.
This very serenity is now being praised:
For one who is not disciplined, there is no discernment; for one who is not disciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness? (BhG 2.66)

The meaning is that it does not exist, is not found, and does not come into being; for one who is unyoked— that is, whose internal organ is not composed— there is no cognition regarding the true nature of the Self,
nor is there any meditative cultivation consisting of an intense application toward the knowledge of the Self for such an unyoked person.
Likewise—there is no peace, that is, no tranquility, for one who does not negate and who does not cultivate attachment to the knowledge of the Self.
For one who is not tranquil, whence can there be happiness? Indeed, that which is happiness is the cessation of the thirst for indulgence in the objects of the senses.
Craving for sense objects is not [true] craving;
indeed, it is suffering itself.
The meaning is that as long as craving exists, not even a mere scent of happiness can arise. (BhGS 2.66)
Why is it said that the intellect of one who is undisciplined does not exist?
"For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away his wisdom, just as the wind carries away a ship upon the waters. (BhG 2.67)

For when the mind follows— that is, conforms to— the senses as they move, proceeding toward their respective objects, that mind, having engaged through the conceptualization of sense-objects, "carries away" the wisdom of this seeker; it destroys the discernment born from the discrimination between the Self and the not-Self.

How so? Just as the wind, having diverted a boat from its course upon the water—that is, in the midst of the ocean—carries it toward a wrong path, even so, having snatched away wisdom directed toward the Self, the mind causes it to become directed toward sense objects.
Having stated the various arguments for the point introduced by the words "for one who strives" (*yatataḥ*), and having established that point, he concludes:
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.

Since the defect in the functioning of the senses has been demonstrated, therefore, O mighty-armed one, the wisdom of that ascetic whose senses have been restrained in every way—in all their various forms such as the mental and so forth—from the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, is firmly established. This worldly and Vedic activity ceases for one who has attained discriminative knowledge and whose wisdom is steady, because it is an effect of ignorance; thus, upon the cessation of ignorance, it ceases.
And because ignorance ceases due to its opposition to knowledge,
he says the following to clarify this point:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake."
That in which all beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
That which is night for all beings— that night which, by its nature of darkness, causes the non-discrimination of all objects—
what is that ultimate reality which is the object of the one whose wisdom is established?
Just as it is indeed day for those who roam by night, yet it is night for others.

In the same way, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*) is like night to all beings whose ignorance stands in the place of nocturnal wanderers; for it is not within the range of those who lack the corresponding cognition. In that state characterized by the sleep of ignorance, the self-controlled one (*saṃyamī*), possessing restraint, remains awake and alert.
The meaning is "the yogi who has conquered the senses.
In that night of ignorance, characterized by the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, beings are said to be awake even while they are actually asleep;
in that night, those who perceive dreams are as if asleep.
That night, because it is of the nature of ignorance, belongs to the Sage who perceives the ultimate reality;
therefore, actions are enjoined only during the state of ignorance,
not during the state of knowledge.
For when knowledge exists, ignorance perishes like the darkness of night at the rising of the sun.

Prior to the arising of knowledge, ignorance—being grasped by the cognition of its validity—takes the form of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit, and thus becomes the cause of all ritual activity.
It is not possible for that which is grasped by the cognition of its invalidity to serve as a cause for ritual action.
For one who possesses the knowledge that "the action enjoined by the Veda, which has become the means of valid cognition, is my duty," the agent engages in action;
however, for that knower of the Self who understands that "all this variety of difference is merely ignorance," there is eligibility only for the renunciation of all actions, not for engagement.
And so the Lord will demonstrate his eligibility for the steadfastness in knowledge alone through such passages as "those whose intellect is fixed on That, whose self is That," and so forth.
If it is argued that even in that case, activity would be impossible due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that prompts it, we say no;
for the cognition of the self has the self as its own object.
Indeed, the self does not depend upon a prompting means of valid cognition with respect to itself.
Precisely because it is the self,
and because the validity of all means of knowledge culminates in that [self];
for once the nature of the self has been realized, the conventional operation of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge is no longer possible.
For the final means of knowledge negates the subjecthood of the self; and in the very act of negating it, it itself becomes non-authoritative,
just as the means of knowledge operative during a dream does upon waking.
Furthermore, in the world, it is observed that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serves as the cause for engaging in activity toward the apprehension of an object.
Therefore, it is established that one who knows the Self has no qualification for ritual action.
(BhG 2.69) Only for the knower who has renounced all desires, the ascetic whose wisdom is firmly established, is there the attainment of liberation.
But [this is not so] for one who has not renounced, who is driven by desires; wishing to establish this point by means of an illustration, He says:
"Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness."
In the same way, he into whom all desires enter attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.

Just as the waters flowing from all directions enter the ocean— which, though being filled with water, remains established immovably, its stability consisting in its lack of motion— and which, while remaining itself unchanged and abiding in its own nature,

is not affected; even so, all desires— specific longings arising from the proximity of sense-objects— enter that person who, like the ocean, remains unmodified, and they all dissolve away within his very self.
They do not bring themselves under their own control;
he attains peace and liberation, and not the other who desires sensual pleasures.
"Desires" (kāmāḥ) are those objects which are desired; one whose nature it is to desire them is a "desirer of desires" (kāma-kāmī).
The meaning is that such a person does not attain [the goal] at all.
Since this is so, therefore—
The man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing,
without the sense of "mine," and without egoism— he attains peace.

Having abandoned—that is, having completely renounced—all desires without exception, that person who is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) "moves about," meaning he wanders with only the activities necessary for mere subsistence remaining;

being "free from longing" (*niḥspṛhaḥ*), meaning one from whom longing has departed even regarding the mere maintenance of the body and life; and being "without the sense of 'mine'" (*nirmamaḥ*), meaning one who is devoid of the obsession "this is mine" even toward possessions necessitated by the mere maintenance of the body and life.
"Free from egoism" (nirahaṃkāraḥ) means being devoid of self-conceit based on such grounds as possessing learning and so forth.

One who is thus constituted is a man of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña), a knower of Brahman; he attains—that is, reaches—peace, characterized by the cessation of all the miseries of saṃsāra and known as Nirvāṇa; the meaning is that he becomes one with Brahman. // BhG 2.71 //
This very steadfastness in knowledge is praised: "This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Even at the time of death, by remaining established in this, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman. (BhG 2.72)
This aforementioned state is "Brahmic" (*brāhmī*), meaning it pertains to Brahman; it is the abiding in the very form of Brahman after having renounced all action.
O Pārtha, having attained and reached this state, one does not become deluded—that is, one does not fall into confusion.

Abiding in this aforementioned Brahmic state, even at the end of life, in the final stage of existence, one reaches—meaning one attains—the extinction in Brahman (*brahma-nirvāṇa*), which is the bliss of Brahman, liberation.

What need is there to say more? He who, having renounced even while still a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*), remains established in Brahman alone for as long as he lives, attains the extinction in Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇa*).

Thus ends the second chapter in the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-Pūjya-pāda, the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
BhG 3, Third Chapter: Śaṅkara’s Commentary.
Two types of intellect, pertaining to the subjects of engagement and withdrawal, have been pointed out by the Blessed One in the scripture.
Regarding the two types of wisdom mentioned as "wisdom in Sāṅkhya" and "wisdom in Yoga":

from the verse beginning with "When he completely renounces desires" up to the end of the chapter, having taught that those who rely on the wisdom of Sāṅkhya must practice renunciation, it is stated that their fulfillment of purpose is achieved through steadfastness in that very [renunciation], concluding with the words, "This is the state of Brahman."
And to Arjuna, having recourse to the intellect of Yoga, He said, "Your right is to action alone; let there be no attachment to inaction," thereby declaring that action itself must be performed,
but not that the attainment of the highest good results from that alone.

Observing this, Arjuna, his mind becoming deeply perplexed, said: "How is it that, having taught me—who am a devotee seeking my own welfare—the very means for attaining the highest good, namely steadfastness in the wisdom of Sāṅkhya, you now enjoin me to action, which is fraught with many visible evils and whose fruit is the attainment of a welfare that is at best only indirect and uncertain? Thus, Arjuna’s state of confusion was entirely justified."
The corresponding question begins with "If [the teacher] is superior" (jyāyasī cet) and so forth;

How then could the Blessed One speak such a contradictory matter to Arjuna?

In this regard, it might be argued that liberation through knowledge alone—by abandoning the Vedic rites—is prohibited only for householders, but not for those in other stages of life (*āśrama*).

How so? Therefore, the intended meaning is as follows: the Lord, having first established the synthesis of knowledge and action for all stages of life as the settled doctrine of the Gītā, subsequently—in order to encourage those who are incapable of such synthesis due to their lack of dispassion and so forth—declared that liberation is attained through knowledge alone, without action, for those in other stages of life. This is because he will later say, "For one whose mind is unsteady, yoga is difficult to attain" (Gītā 6.36). In that regard, [the opponent claims] that even though the Smārta rites exist for householders, they are disregarded as if they did not exist, and it is stated that liberation comes from knowledge alone.
This too is contradictory.

How so? For how can discerning people determine that liberation through knowledge conjoined with Smārta rites is denied specifically for the householder, but not for those in other stages of life (āśramas)?

Furthermore, if Smārta rituals are combined with the knowledge of those who have renounced worldly life (*ūrdhva-retas*) as a means to liberation, then let it be accepted that for the householder (*gṛhastha*) as well, there is a combination only with Smārta rituals and not with Śrauta ones. Or,

if it is argued that for the householder alone there is a combination of both Śrauta and Smārta rituals for the sake of liberation, whereas for those who have renounced worldly life, liberation comes from knowledge combined solely with Smārta rituals—
this being the case, the householder would be burdened with a great deal of exertion, having placed upon his head the many forms of suffering consisting of both Śrauta and Smārta rituals.

Now, if it is argued that liberation belongs only to the householder because of the great amount of exertion involved, and not to the other stages of life (*āśrama*) because they are devoid of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta-nitya-karma*), that too is incorrect.

For in all the Upaniṣads, in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and in the Yoga-śāstra, the renunciation of all actions is ordained for one desiring liberation as a limb of knowledge; furthermore, both Śruti and Smṛti ordain both the option and the combination of the stages of life.
Is it then established that there is a combination of knowledge and action for those in all stages of life?
No, because for one desiring liberation, the renunciation of all actions is prescribed:
"Having withdrawn from worldly life, they then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).

Therefore, they say that among these ascetic practices, renunciation is superior: "Renunciation alone surpasses them" (NāU 2.78), and "They declare renunciation to be superior to these austerities" (NāU 2.79).
And also: "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality" (NāU 2.12).
"From the very practice of celibacy one should go forth," and so on, are the scriptural texts (*śruti*).
"Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon."
Having seen that cyclic existence itself is devoid of essence, and desiring to see what is essential,
they renounce the world without having married, relying upon supreme dispassion.
Thus Bṛhaspati also spoke to Kaca:
"A living being is bound by action and is liberated by knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who perceive the further shore do not perform ritual action."
Thus ends the instruction of Śuka.
Here too, [it is said]: "Having renounced all actions with the mind," and so forth.
Furthermore, since liberation is not something to be produced by action, for one who desires liberation, action is purposeless.
If it is argued that the obligatory rites (*nitya*) must be performed for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), we say no;
for the incurrence of transgression applies only to those who have not renounced.

Indeed, it is impossible to conceive of a transgression for a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) arising from the non-performance of the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*) and other such duties, in the same way as it is conceived for householders (*karmiṇaḥ*) who have not renounced, such as students (*brahmacārin*).

It cannot be maintained that the production of a positive entity in the form of sin (*pratyavāya*) occurs simply from the non-existence of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), because of the scriptural teaching that the arising of an existent from a non-existent is impossible: "How can the existent be born from the non-existent? (ChāU 6.2.2). If the Veda were to assert that sin arises—even though it is impossible—from the non-performance of what is enjoined, then it would follow that the Veda, being a cause of harm, is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Because performing or not performing what is enjoined results only in suffering,
it would follow that the scripture is a producer (*kāraka*) and not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), which would render its meaning untenable;
and this is not accepted.

Therefore, actions do not belong to renunciants; hence, the combination of knowledge and action is untenable. Furthermore, Arjuna’s question—“If you consider wisdom to be superior to action”—would otherwise be inconsistent.

For if the Blessed One had stated in the second chapter that knowledge and action must be practiced by you in combination, then Arjuna’s question—"O Janārdana, if you consider wisdom to be superior to action"—would be inappropriate. If it had been told to Arjuna that both wisdom and action were to be practiced by him, then that wisdom which is superior to action would have already been declared; so why then do you urge me toward this terrible action, O Keśava?
Thus, this question is not justifiable in any way.

Nor is it reasonable to assume that the Blessed One had previously stated to Arjuna that his own higher wisdom was not to be practiced, such that the question "If [your] wisdom is higher... would have been appropriate.

If, however, the Blessed One had previously stated that because knowledge and action are contradictory for a single person, their simultaneous performance is impossible and thus they must be performed by different persons, then this question beginning with "If the renunciation of works were superior" would be appropriate.

Even if one were to assume that the question arises from a lack of discrimination, the Lord’s reply would still not be appropriate, as it pertains to duties to be performed by different types of persons.
Nor can the Lord’s reply be imagined to be based on ignorance;
for from this very fact—that the Lord’s reply is seen to concern the distinct bases of knowledge and action to be practiced by different persons—it follows [that he is omniscient].
The combination of knowledge and action is untenable.
Therefore, the conclusion established in the Gītā and all the Upaniṣads is that liberation results from knowledge alone.
Furthermore, the request, "Tell me with certainty which one of the two—knowledge or action—is superior," would be inconsistent if both were possible to be combined as a single path.
And by means of the restrictive emphasis [on "only"], He will show Arjuna that the possibility of steadfastness in knowledge arises from the injunction, "Therefore, you must perform action alone.
Arjuna said:
"O Janārdana, if You consider wisdom to be superior to action..."
Why then, O Keśava, do you urge me toward this terrible deed?

If, O Janārdana, you consider that knowledge— understood as wisdom— is superior and more excellent than action, then if both wisdom and action are intended to be combined, it would follow that one is the means to the highest good; thus, Arjuna’s statement that "wisdom is superior to action" would be inconsistent, as it implies that wisdom is an instrument distinct from and additional to action.
It would have been accomplished;
for that very thing could not, in terms of its result, be distinct from that [action].
And thus, the Blessed One has declared that the intellect which brings about the highest good is superior to action.

He seems to reproach the Blessed One as it were, asking, "Why do you instruct me to perform an action that brings about what is not beneficial? And when he says, "O Keśava, why do you enjoin me to this terrible, cruel deed characterized by violence?",
that too is not tenable.
Now, if it were the case that the Blessed One had taught a combination of all [actions] with Smārta ritual action alone, and Arjuna had understood it thus,
then how could such a statement as "Why do You urge me toward this terrible action" (BhG 3.1) be appropriate?
Furthermore—
With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, bewildering my intellect.
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one path by which I may attain the highest good.
As if it were mixed,
even though the Blessed One speaks with distinct clarity;
nevertheless, to me of dull intellect, the Blessed One’s speech appears as if it were mixed.
Therefore, you seem to confuse my intellect;
for while you have set out to remove the confusion of my intellect, how is it that you instead cause further delusion?
Thus I say:
"You seem to confuse my intellect.

But if you think that it is impossible for a single person to perform both knowledge and action—which have different agents—then, this being the case, having determined which of these two, either knowledge or action, is appropriate for Arjuna according to his state of intellectual capacity and disposition, speak; tell me.
"By which knowledge or by which action— by either one of these— I might attain, or reach, the highest good.
For if knowledge had been spoken of by the Blessed One as being merely subordinate to the path of action (karma-niṣṭhā),
then how could Arjuna’s desire to hear be directed toward a single subject, such that he asks, "Tell me one of these two"?

For it was not previously stated by the Blessed One that He would speak of only one of the two— either knowledge or action— and not both, such that [Arjuna], considering the impossibility of attaining both for himself, might have sought after only one. (BhG 3.2)
The answer was indeed in accordance with the question;
the Blessed Lord said:
"O sinless one, in this world, a twofold steadfastness was declared by me of old."
For the followers of Sāṃkhya, by means of the yoga of knowledge; for the yogis, by means of the yoga of action.

O sinless one, in this world, for the members of the three twice-born classes who are entitled to the performance of the meaning of the scriptures, there are two kinds of *niṣṭhā*— that is, two types of steadfastness regarding what is to be practiced. This was declared by me, the omniscient Lord, in the past at the beginning of creation, after creating living beings and revealing the traditional transmission of the Vedic meaning as the means for their attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good.

Regarding that, as to what those two kinds of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) are, he says: therein, by means of the yoga of knowledge—knowledge itself being the yoga—the steadfastness of the Sāṃkhyas is declared; these are those who possess the discriminative discernment regarding the self and the non-self, who have practiced renunciation from the very stage of the student life (*brahmacarya*), whose purpose is well-ascertained through the higher knowledge of the Vedānta, who are wandering mendicants of the supreme order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*), and who abide in Brahman alone.
The meaning is that "the steadfastness of the yogins who are performers of action has been declared by means of karma-yoga"— that is, karma itself is the yoga, and thus it is karma-yoga.

If the Blessed One intended, desired, had stated, or would state in the Gītā or in the Vedas that knowledge and action should be practiced in combination by a single person for the sake of a single human goal, then why would he here, to Arjuna who has approached him as a dear disciple, speak of two distinct steadfastnesses in knowledge and action performed by different persons?

If, however, it were imagined that the Blessed One’s intention was: "Once Arjuna has heard both knowledge and action, he will practice them himself, while for others I shall declare that they are to be practiced by different persons," then the Blessed One would be imagined as being possessed of attachment and aversion, and thus not an authoritative source;
and that is improper.
Therefore, by no reasoning whatsoever can there be a combination of knowledge and action.
That which was stated by Arjuna regarding the superiority of wisdom over action remains established because it has not been refuted; furthermore,
that steadfastness in knowledge is to be practiced only by renunciants, as it is taught that they and [those devoted to action] are to be practiced by different persons.
It is understood that the Blessed One has indeed approved this very point.

Not independently;

Just as one sees one's own self within oneself, as if in the surface of a mirror.
This is because of such traditional teachings as these.

The meaning is that the person does not reach or obtain this.

For what reason, then, does one not attain freedom from action through the non-commencement of actions?
It is said: because the very commencement of action is the means to freedom from action.
For there is no attainment of the goal without a means;

Therefore, he says: "Nor indeed by renunciation alone.

Nor does one attain—meaning reach—the perfection characterized by freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*), which is steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, merely through renunciation alone, that is, through the simple abandonment of action devoid of knowledge.

For what reason, then, does a person not attain the perfection characterized by freedom from action through mere renunciation of action alone, being devoid of knowledge? In response to this expectation for a reason, he says:
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature.
For indeed, no one ever at any time, even for a moment, remains without performing action.

Why? Because every living being is driven—that is, set in motion—helplessly and without independence by the qualities (guṇas) born of nature, namely sattva, rajas, and tamas, which arise from nature; "the ignorant one," is the completion of the sentence.
For it will be said later, "he who is not shaken by the gunas";

As for the objection that action is impossible for the wise because they are free from the influence of the qualities, that is answered by the fact that even the wise, while remaining established in their own nature, may engage in action for the sake of the world's welfare. This is also supported by the statement: "For the maintenance of the world, even the man of knowledge must perform action" (Gītā 3.25). Therefore, there is no contradiction. ||| He who, being unattached, performs actions merely for the purification of his own self, having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, attains the supreme peace. By performing actions without attachment, he purifies himself through the fire of knowledge and reaches the highest goal. This is also supported by the statement: "For the maintenance of the world, even the man of knowledge must perform action" (Gītā 3.25). Therefore, there
He who sits restraining his organs of action while dwelling on the objects of the senses with his mind is a deluded soul; he is said to be a hypocrite.

He who sits remaining with his organs of action, such as the hands and so forth, restrained—that is, withdrawn—yet remembers and contemplates the objects of the senses, the sense-objects, with his mind, he is called one of deluded soul; that is, one whose inner self is deluded, a hypocrite, a pretender, or one of sinful conduct. (BhG 3.6)
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent.

But he who, on the other hand, being ignorant yet qualified for action, O Arjuna, restrains the organs of perception with the mind and undertakes action through the organs of action—speech, hands, and so forth—what does he undertake? It is said: being unattached, free from desire for fruits, he performs the yoga of action; he is superior to the other, who follows a false course of conduct. (BhG 3.7) Since this is so, therefore:
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the mere maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction.
That which is prescribed by the scriptures as constant and obligatory is "niyata" (fixed) action;
whatever action one is authorized to perform for the sake of its fruit, even if its result is not explicitly mentioned in the texts, that is niyata karma—
perform that, O Arjuna.

For action is superior— that is, more excellent— in terms of its fruit; for indeed, from *akarma* (non-action), that is, from non-performance or non-undertaking, even the maintenance of the body— the sustenance of the physical frame— would not be accomplished for you, nor would it reach fulfillment, due to such non-action.

Therefore, the distinction between action and inaction is seen in the world. Furthermore, that which you think—that action should not be performed because it leads to bondage—is also incorrect. How so?
"Except for action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action."
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
Since the Śruti states, "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice" (TaittS 1.7.4), the Lord is sacrifice.
That which is performed for His sake is action for the sake of sacrifice.
Apart from that action, this world is occupied by other action; he who performs action is "one bound by action" (TaittBhā 3.1.6)—he whose bondage is action is this one "bound by action."
But not for the sake of sacrifice.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, for that purpose—for the sake of sacrifice—perform your action, being free from attachment, that is, devoid of attachment to the fruits of action. 3.9.
For this reason as well, the duty must be performed by the one who is authorized:
"Having created all beings together with sacrifice, Prajāpati said of old: 'By this shall you propagate; let this be the milch-cow that grants your desired objects. (BhG 3.10)
Having created in the past—at the beginning of creation—the three social orders (varṇas) together with sacrifice, Prajāpati, the creator of beings, spoke thus:
"By means of this sacrifice, you shall multiply; that is, perform increase, which is growth or procreation.
Let this sacrifice be for you the milch-cow that grants all desired objects."
It is called the "milk-cow of desired objects" because it milks forth—that is, yields—the desired and cherished fruits of specific results.
How so?
By nourishing the gods with this [sacrifice], may those gods nourish you in return.
Cultivating one another, you shall attain the highest good.
Nourish and strengthen the gods, Indra and the others, by means of this sacrifice;
may those gods nourish and satisfy you with rain and other blessings.
Thus, nourishing one another in this way, you shall attain the supreme good characterized by liberation through the gradual acquisition of higher knowledge.
Or you shall attain heaven or the highest good.
Furthermore:
"For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire."
He who enjoys what has been given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief.

For the gods, being nourished by sacrifices— that is, strengthened and gratified by sacrifices— will indeed give and bestow upon you the desired and cherished enjoyments, such as women, cattle, sons, and so forth.
Without giving back those enjoyments bestowed by those gods, [one does not attain the goal].
The meaning is "without having discharged the debt.
To these gods;
he who eats merely gratifies his own body and senses—he is indeed a thief, a robber, a stealer of the property of the gods and others. (BhG 3.12)
But those who eat the remnants of the sacrifice, being virtuous, are liberated from all sins;
however, those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin.
Those whose habit it is to eat the remnants of food—called *amṛta* (nectar)—after having performed sacrifices to the gods and other rites, are "eaters of sacrificial remnants";

such saintly persons are liberated from all sins, that is, from all evils produced by the five slaughter-houses beginning with the hearth, as well as from others generated by violence committed through negligence. But those who eat for the sake of self-maintenance alone—they are themselves sinful and consume sin; they cook and prepare food solely for their own sake and for their own benefit. (BhG 3.13)
Furthermore, the prescribed action must be performed by the one who is authorized;
for action is indeed the cause for the continued functioning of the wheel of the world.
How so? It is said:
From food beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice rain arises; and sacrifice originates from action.
From food that has been eaten and transformed into blood and semen, living beings are visibly produced and born.
From rain—that is, from *parjanya*—comes the production of food, the "origination of food.
From sacrifice comes *parjanya*.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
According to the traditional law (smṛti), "Sacrifice is the unseen potency (apūrva);
and that sacrifice originates from action."
The activity of the officiating priests and the sacrificer is "action" (*karma*);
that sacrifice, which is the *apūrva* (unseen potency) arising from that [activity], is "born of action" (*karma-samudbhava*).
Regarding where such action as this originated, he says:
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable.
Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice.
Action has its origin in Brahman;
"Brahman" here means the Veda. Know—that is, understand—that action has that [Veda] as its origin, its cause, and its illuminator.

Furthermore, "Brahman" refers to that which is called the Veda, originating from the Imperishable (*akṣara-samudbhava*). That which has the Imperishable—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—as its source is "originating from the Imperishable.
The meaning is that Brahman is the Veda.

Since this Brahman originated directly from the Imperishable known as the Supreme Self, like the breath of a person, it is "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*) because it illuminates all objects of knowledge.

Although it is all-pervading, it is eternally established in sacrifice because the performance of sacrifice is its primary purpose. O Pārtha, he who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion lives in vain— evil-minded, delighting only in the senses.

Thus, he who is qualified for action in this world but does not follow the wheel of the universe set in motion by the Lord in this manner— preceded by the Vedas and sacrifices— is an *aghāyuḥ*; that is to say, one whose life (*āyuḥ*) is evil (*agham*), meaning one whose livelihood is sinful.

"One who delights in the senses" (*indriyārāmaḥ*) means one whose pleasure, enjoyment, or play (*āramaṇam*) with sense-objects is by means of the senses; such a person, O Pārtha, lives in vain—that is, fruitlessly.
Therefore, the meaning of this section is that action must indeed be performed by the ignorant person who is so qualified.
Prior to attaining the fitness for steadfastness in self-knowledge, the performance of *karma-yoga* for that purpose is required by the unenlightened person who is thus qualified.

Having established that "it must certainly be performed" starting from the verse, "Not by abstaining from actions" (Gītā 3.4), up to the end of the passage, "Even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for you through inaction" (Gītā 3.8),

and having further established— incidentally— for the qualified person who does not know the Self— that the performance of action is necessary through the section beginning with, "Action other than that for the sake of sacrifice" (Gītā 3.9), up to the end of the passage, "He lives in vain, O Pārtha" (Gītā 3.16).
Many reasons have been stated,
and the faults incurred by not performing that [action] have also been proclaimed.
(BhG 3.16) Since this is the case, must everyone follow the wheel thus set in motion?

Or rather, [is it] that state which is not yet attained by those who do not know the Self, even while they are engaged in the yoga of knowledge—the very state that is to be reached through the practice of the previously mentioned karma-yoga as a means, and which is to be practiced by the Sāṃkhyas who know the Self?
Anticipating such a question from Arjuna, or else, for the sake of establishing a clear understanding of the meaning of the scripture, [the Lord says]:
"Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas, being freed from false knowledge, [distinguish themselves] from those possessed of false knowledge..."
"Having renounced the necessary pursuits such as the desire for sons and so forth, they then practice the life of a mendicant, motivated solely by the maintenance of the body.

For them, there is no other duty apart from steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self" (BAU 3.5.1). Revealing this intended meaning of the Śruti as that which is to be established here in the Gītā-śāstra, the Blessed Lord says:
But for that person who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed. (BhG 3.17)

But that Sāṃkhya who is established in the knowledge of the Self, who finds delight in the Self— meaning his delight is in the Self alone and not in sense objects— and who is thus "delighting in the Self" (ātma-rati), as well as being "satisfied by the Self" (ātma-tṛpta), meaning satisfied by the Self alone and not by food, flavors, and so forth; that man, that human being, that renunciant (saṃnyāsī), is also "contented in the Self alone" (ātmany eva ca santuṣṭaḥ).

For contentment indeed arises in everyone upon the acquisition of external objects; disregarding that, he who is satisfied in the Self alone and is free from thirst for everything—of such a knower of the Self, there exists no duty to be performed, meaning none remains to be done. (BhG 3.17)
Moreover:
"He has no purpose whatsoever in this world through action, nor any through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object. (BhG 3.18)

For one who delights in the Supreme Self, there is no purpose or need for action performed; nor, then, can there be any harm known as transgression resulting from non-performance. Indeed, in this world, there is not the slightest harm—whether consisting in the incurrence of sin or characterized by self-destruction—that arises from non-action.

And for him, there is no dependence upon any purpose among all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects; that is, there is no dependence consisting of an action to be accomplished for the sake of some motive or purpose.
There is no goal to be achieved by depending on any particular being as a support, such that an action for its sake would have to be performed.
But you do not abide in this right vision, which is like a place flooded with water on all sides. (BhG 3.18) Since it is so—
therefore, perform constantly the action that ought to be done, remaining unattached.
For by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.

Therefore, unattached—free from clinging—always and at all times, perform and carry out the duty that must be done, the obligatory ritual action. For by performing it unattached—that is, by doing work for the sake of the Lord—a person attains the supreme liberation through the purification of the mind; this is the meaning.
And because: [3.20]
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
therefore, you should also act, having regard for the maintenance of the world.
For it is by action alone that the wise Kṣatriyas of old set out—that is, they were engaged in—attaining perfection, which is liberation.
Who were they? Janaka and others, such as Janaka, Aupatiprabhṛti, and so forth. If they had already attained right vision, [how could this be?]

Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the world (lokasaṃgraha), because they were under the influence of *prārabdha-karma*, they attained perfection (*saṃsiddhi*) while not renouncing action—that is, together with action itself; this is the meaning. Alternatively, if Janaka and others had not yet attained right vision (*samyagdarśana*), then the verse should be explained as follows: "They attained perfection gradually by means of action that served as a means for the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*). This is the intended sense.
Now, if you think that Janaka and others in the past performed their duties even while remaining ignorant,

and therefore it is not necessarily required that another who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśana*) perform action for the sake of having accomplished his purpose— even so, you are dependent on the karma already set in motion. "Gathering the world" (*lokasaṃgraha*) means precisely the prevention of the world from proceeding along wrong paths.
Seeing that very purpose, you ought to act accordingly.
To explain for what reason the maintenance of the world (*loka-saṃgraha*) must be performed, it is said:
"Whatever a superior person does, that very thing other people do."
Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
Whatever action the best or foremost person performs, that very same action the other, inferior person performs, following after him.
Furthermore, whatever standard—whether worldly or Vedic—the best person establishes, the world follows that; the meaning is that the world accepts that very thing as its authority.
If you have a doubt here regarding the duty of maintaining the world, then why do you not look at me?
For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever that must be done in the three worlds;
there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.

For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever—nothing at all—that remains to be done in the three worlds. Why? Because there is nothing unattained, not yet reached, that remains to be attained or reached.
Nevertheless, I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage unweariedly in action at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
For if, moreover, I were not to engage at any time whatsoever in action, being untiring and diligent, then men would follow my path— that of one who is preeminent—
in every way, O Pārtha. (3.23)
These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action;
I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings.
All these worlds would perish and be destroyed due to the absence of the karma that is the cause for the maintenance of the world, were I not to perform action;
furthermore, I would be the author of confusion (saṃkara),
and by that reason, I would ruin these creatures.

The meaning is: "If I, who have set out for the sake of favoring all beings, were to cause injury—that is, inflict harm—it would be unbecoming of me, the Lord. (BhG 3.24) Furthermore, if you, like me, possessed the realization that your purpose has been accomplished...
Whether one is a knower of the Self or another, even though for that Self there is nothing further to be accomplished, the welfare of others alone remains to be done; thus he says:
"O Bhārata, as those who are unlearned act, being attached to action," [so should you act].
Thus, a wise man, though unattached, should act with the desire to bring about the welfare of the world.

Just as some ignorant people act, O Bhārata, being attached to action with the thought, "The fruit of this action shall be mine," so should the wise man who knows the Self act, remaining unattached. For what purpose does he act in that manner?
Listen to that: "desiring to effect," meaning wishing to bring about, "the welfare of the world" (loka-saṃgraha).
Thus, for one who desires to effect the welfare of the world—whether it be Me, the knower of the Self, or anyone else—there is no other duty to be performed except for the welfare of the world.
Therefore, this is taught to that knower of the Self:

The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not cause a disturbance of intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all works by performing them himself.

"Buddhi-bheda" means the breaking or unsettling of the intellect— that is, the intellect in the form of a determination such as "this must be done by me" or "the fruit of this action must be enjoyed. He should not produce or generate that in the ignorant, the undiscriminating, those who are attached to action, and those possessed of attachment toward action.
What indeed should he do?
The wise man should encourage and cause all actions to be performed by others, while himself, being disciplined and diligent, performs only those actions appropriate for the ignorant.
He asks: how does the ignorant, the one lacking knowledge, become attached to actions? To this, he says:
All actions performed in every way by the qualities of nature, one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. (BhG 3.27)

Nature (prakṛti) is the primordial source (pradhāna), the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas. One whose self is deluded by egoism (ahaṅkāra)— possessing the misconception that the aggregate of the body and the senses is the self— performs all actions, both worldly and scriptural, in every way, through the modifications of the qualities of that nature which take the form of the body and the senses.
"By that [egoism], the fool—whose internal organ (the self) is characterized by various and manifold forms—is one whose nature consists of the body and the instruments of action;
being possessed of the conceit of being the body and the instruments, he, through ignorance, imagining actions to belong to himself, thinks, "I am the doer of this or that action. (BhG 3.27)

But the wise man who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one— knowing the distinction between the qualities and their functions, and realizing that "it is the qualities acting upon the qualities"— is not attached.
But the knower of reality, O mighty-armed one—of what is he the knower of reality?
The meaning is: he is the knower of reality regarding both the division of the qualities (guṇas) and the division of actions (karma).

The qualities (guṇas), which are of the nature of instruments, abide within the objects that consist of the qualities; realizing that "the Self does not [abide there]," one does not become attached—that is, one does not form an attachment.
But those who are utterly deluded by the qualities of material nature (prakṛti) become attached to the actions of the qualities.
One who knows the whole should not disturb those dull-witted ones who do not know the whole.

Being thoroughly deluded and bewildered by the qualities of *prakṛti*, they become attached to the actions of the qualities—that is, to the "qualities-and-actions"—thinking, "We perform action for the sake of its fruit. One who knows the Whole (*kṛtsnavit*), being a knower of the Self, should not himself cause those people—who are attached to action, who lack complete knowledge, who see only the fruits of action, and who are dull-witted—to waver; for the meaning is that he should not cause such a division in their understanding, which would constitute causing them to waver. (BhG 3.29)
Furthermore, how should an ignorant person who is entitled to action and seeks liberation perform that action? It is said:
"Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self (adhyātma), being free from desire and free from the sense of 'mine-ness,' fight, freed from feverish anxiety. (BhG 3.30)

Renouncing all actions by casting them into me, Vāsudeva—the Supreme Lord, the Omniscient, and the Self of all—with a mind directed toward the inner self through the intellect of discernment, with the realization: "I am the agent; I act for the sake of the Lord like a servant";

furthermore, being free from desire (*nirāśī*), having abandoned hope, and being free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*)—you who have cast off the notion of "mineness"—fight, free from fever, free from distress, and free from grief.
The meaning is "being present.
Regarding that which has been stated with its authoritative basis—that action must be performed according to my view: "Those men who constantly practice this teaching of mine..."
Those who possess faith and are free from malice are also liberated from their actions.
Those men who always follow and conform to this, my teaching— being full of faith, believing, and free from envy toward me, Vāsudeva, the supreme teacher—
they too, being such as these, are liberated from the bonds of action known as dharma and adharma.
But those who, being envious, do not follow this teaching of mine...
Know them to be utterly deluded regarding all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of discernment.
But those who, being opposed to this, find fault with my teaching and revile it, do not practice it and do not follow my thought;
know them, understand them, to be deluded in all knowledge—deluded in every branch of learning—and ruined, having gone to destruction, being devoid of discernment. (BhG 3.32)
But for what reason do they not follow your teaching, yet instead practice the dharma of others?
Why do they not conform to their own dharma?
Being opposed to you, how is it that they do not fear the fault of transgressing your command? To this, he says:
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature;
all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish?

One acts—that is, performs an action—in a manner that is similar and corresponding to one's own nature (*prakṛti*). What is this "nature"? It refers to the predispositions (*saṃskāra*) such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) performed in previous lives, which become manifest at the beginning of the present birth.
That is one's nature;
every living being, even one possessed of knowledge, acts in accordance with that very nature— how much more so, then, a fool?
Therefore, living beings—meaning sentient creatures—follow their own nature;
what can restraint, which takes the form of prohibition, do to me or to anyone else?
The completion of the sentence is: "Nature is difficult to restrain. (BhG 3.33)
If every living being acts solely in accordance with its own nature, and there is no one whatsoever devoid of such nature, then,
since the scope for human effort would be untenable and the scriptures would consequently be rendered useless, this is said:
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of each sense-organ;
one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries. (BhG 3.34)
Regarding each sense-organ and its object—that is, toward the objects of all the senses such as sound and so forth—attachment arises toward what is desired and aversion toward what is undesired;
thus, attachment and aversion necessarily occur with respect to every sense-object. In this regard, the scope of human effort and the purpose of the scripture is stated:
one who has engaged in the practice of the scriptural teaching should, from the very outset, not fall under the sway of attachment and aversion.
For that nature which belongs to a person impels him toward his own activity only when preceded by passion and aversion;
at that time, there occurs the abandonment of one's own duty and the performance of the duty of another.
But when one restrains passion and aversion through their antidotes, then the person comes to possess the vision of the scriptures alone.
One is not under the sway of nature;
therefore, one should not come under the control of those two, passion and hatred.
For they are the adversaries of this person, creating obstacles on the path to the highest good like two robbers on a road—this is the meaning. (BhG 3.34)

In that regard, one impelled by passion and hatred may even misunderstand the meaning of the scriptures, thinking, "The duty of another must certainly be performed because it is a duty. That is incorrect:
"Better is one's own duty, though deficient in quality, than the duty of another well-performed. Death in one's own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear. (BhG 3.35)
One's own duty (svadharma), though deficient in qualities (viguṇa)—that is, even if lacking excellence—is better than the duty of another, even if that other duty is performed with perfection.
Death while established in one's own duty is better than life while established in the duty of another.
Why? Because the duty of another brings fear; for it brings forth fear characterized by hell and other such states. (BhG 3.35)

Although it has been stated that "for a person who meditates on sense objects, desire and aversion arise, which are the roots of ruin" (Gītā 2.62) and "desire and aversion are indeed his adversaries" (Gītā 3.34), those statements were made regarding a state that is distracted and undetermined.
Desiring to know this very point in a concise and certain manner—thinking, "Once that is known, I shall exert effort to eradicate it"—Arjuna said: [Arjuna said:]...
Now, by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?
Now, by what cause impelled does this person perform and practice evil deeds, even against his own will, like a servant driven by a king? O Vārṣṇeya, you are born of the Vṛṣṇi clan;
the phrase "as if constrained by force" is used as an illustration, referring to being commanded like a servant by a king.
The Blessed One said: "Listen, I shall tell you of that enemy who causes all misfortune, about whom you ask. BhG 3.36.
This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of passion (rajas);
all-devouring and most sinful—know this to be the enemy here in this world.
"Lordship (bhaga) is the designation for the sixfold aggregate consisting of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, splendor, dispassion, and liberation. Thus,
that Vāsudeva in whom this hexad of sovereignty and the rest exists eternally and in its entirety, without any obstruction— [he is called Bhagavān].
"He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings,
and who knows both knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called 'Bhagavān'.
Thus, Vāsudeva is to be called Bhagavān because he possesses the discerning knowledge (vijñāna) whose objects are origin and the other states.
Regarding "desire" (*kāma*): this desire is the enemy of all the worlds, for it is the cause by which all misfortunes are encountered by living beings.
When that very desire is thwarted by someone, it transforms into anger (*krodha*).

Therefore, anger too is this same [desire]; it arises from the quality of *rajas*. "The quality of *rajas*" (*rajo-guṇa*) means *rajas* and its quality; that from which it originates is "arising from the quality of *rajas*" (*rajo-guṇa-samudbhava*), which refers to desire.
Or rather, it is the emergence of the quality of *rajas*.
For desire, once arisen, sets *rajas* in motion and thereby impels the person.
Indeed, the lamentation of those suffering—who are driven by egoism through craving and engaged in the activities of *rajas* such as service—is heard.
"Mahāśana" means one whose eating is great;
for this very reason, he is "mahā-pāpmā" (of great sin).
For, impelled by desire, a living being commits evil.
Therefore, know this desire here in this cycle of existence to be the enemy.
How is it an enemy? He makes this clear through illustrations:
As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust,
and as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this [Self] covered by that.
Fire, which is luminous by nature, is covered by its own smoke, which is non-luminous;
or as a mirror is covered by dust;
and just as the embryo is covered and concealed by the *ulba* (inner membrane) and the *jarāyu* (outer membrane) that envelop it, so too is this [Self] covered by that [intellect]. (BhG 3.38)
What, then, is this that is denoted by the word "this" (idam), which is said to be covered by desire?—
"Knowledge is veiled by this, O son of Kuntī, by the eternal enemy in the form of desire, which is as difficult to satisfy as fire. (BhG 3.39)
Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the man of knowledge;
for the man of knowledge knows, "By this [ignorance] I have previously been led into misfortune," and thus he remains in a state of constant suffering.
Therefore, this [desire] is the eternal enemy of the wise man, but not of the fool.
For the latter, perceiving desire as a friend at the time of craving, realizes only when the resulting suffering has arrived: "I have been brought to a state of misery by craving."
Not only previously;
therefore, he is the eternal enemy of the wise man alone.

In what form? In the form of desire (*kāmarūpeṇa*). Desire is his very form, thus he is "desire-formed" (*kāmarūpa*); by him who is difficult to fill—difficult to fill because his filling occurs with suffering—and by that fire, there is no end or sufficiency for him.
"And by that [desire], fire exists.
In response to the inquiry— "Upon what basis does desire, acting as an obstacle to knowledge, become the enemy of the entire world?"— the Lord says:
For when the enemy's stronghold is known, its destruction can be easily accomplished;
thus it is said: "The senses, the mind, and the intellect are called his strongholds;
through these he deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge. (BhG 3.40)
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be the seat and support of this desire.
By means of these supports—the senses and so forth—this desire deludes, that is, it causes manifold confusion, veiling and obscuring the knowledge of the embodied soul.
Since this is so:
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses and utterly abandon this evil which destroys knowledge and realization.

Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first of all— having restrained and brought under control the senses— abandon, cast off, this evil-doing sin, namely desire, which is the enemy under discussion and the destroyer of knowledge and realization; "knowledge" (jñāna) here refers to the understanding of the Self and other principles derived from scripture and the teacher.

"Discrimination" (*vijñāna*) refers specifically to the experience of that [object]. Abandon—meaning renounce from yourself—that which destroys, i.e., causes the destruction of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and discrimination (*vijñāna*), which are the causes for attaining the highest good. (BhG 3.41)

It has been said: "First, having restrained the senses, slay desire, the enemy. In that regard, it is now stated what the basis for slaying desire is: "They say the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses."
But the intellect is superior to the mind; and he who is beyond the intellect is superior even to that.

The wise say that the five senses, beginning with hearing, are superior (*parāṇi*)— meaning more excellent— relative to the gross, external, and limited body, on account of their subtlety, internality, pervasiveness, and so forth. Likewise, the mind, whose nature consists of volition and conceptualization, is superior to the senses.

Likewise, the intellect (*buddhi*) is superior to the mind, being of the nature of ascertainment. Furthermore, he who is internal to all objects of perception ending with the intellect—him, the embodied one, desire, joined with its supports such as the senses, deludes by way of obscuring knowledge; this has been stated. But he is beyond the intellect.
He is the seer of the intellect; He is the Supreme Self. What follows from this?
Having thus known that which is beyond the intellect, and having steadied the self by means of the self—
By which you may slay the enemy, O mighty-armed one, who takes the form of desire and is difficult to overcome.

Thus, having realized— that is, having known— the Self which is beyond the intellect, and having steadied it— meaning having performed a perfect stabilization by properly concentrating the self through the mind itself which has been refined—
he should abandon this enemy, O mighty-armed one; that is,

he should abandon this one whose form is desire, who is difficult to approach (durāsada), meaning whose attainment (āsādana) is reached with great difficulty, and who possesses many insuperable particularities.

Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjya-pāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya). //3//
Bhagavad Gītā 4:
