Now begins the Fourth Chapter (Śaṅkara’s Commentary).
This yoga, characterized by steadfastness in knowledge, which has been described in these two chapters, is renunciation (sannyāsa) having the means of karma-yoga;

it is that in which the entire meaning of the Vedas—both that characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and that characterized by withdrawal (nivṛtti)—is fully contained. And in all the Gītās, this very yoga is intended by the Blessed Lord.
Therefore, considering the meaning of the Vedas regarding worldly engagement to be complete, the Blessed Lord praises it by recounting the lineage.
The Blessed Lord said: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat declared it to Manu; and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
At the beginning of creation, I taught this Yoga, which has been described in these two chapters, to Vivasvat, the son of Aditi,
for the purpose of bestowing strength upon the Kṣatriyas who protect the world;
endowed with that power of Yoga, they become capable of preserving the Veda.
When the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are protected, they are capable of protecting the world;
it is imperishable because its fruit is imperishable,
for the fruit called liberation belonging to this state characterized by steadfastness in right vision never perishes.
And that Vivasvat told it to Manu;
Manu spoke it to his son Ikṣvāku, the first king.
Thus, the royal seers have known this which was received through tradition.
O scorcher of foes, after a long time, that yoga was lost here on earth.

Thus, this Yoga—which had been handed down through the lineage of the Kṣatriyas—was known by the royal sages (*rājarṣis*), who are both kings and sages. That Yoga, O scorcher of foes (*parantapa*), was lost over a long period of time here on earth, its traditional transmission having been broken.

The term *para* refers to those who have become adversaries to oneself; one who "scorches" (*tāpayati*) them with the rays of his valor and splendor, like the sun, is a *parantapa*, meaning a scorcher of enemies. *Bhagavad Gītā 4.2*

Having encountered people who have lost control over their senses and having observed that this world has fallen away from the goal of human endeavor, I have declared to you today this very same ancient Yoga, for you are My devotee and My friend; indeed, this is the most supreme secret. (BhG 4.3)
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today;
for you are My devotee and My friend.
Indeed, this is a secret, because this yoga is the supreme knowledge—this is the meaning. (BhG 4.3)
Lest anyone should think that what was spoken by the Blessed One was contradictory, Arjuna spoke as if raising an objection for the sake of clarification:
"Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier;
how then am I to understand this—that You taught [this] in the beginning? (BhG 4.4).

"Another [birth] was yours more recently in the house of Vasudeva, while the supreme [birth] was your first birth, your manifestation at the beginning of creation, that of Vivasvat, the Sun. How may I understand this so that its meaning is not contradictory—that you, who yourself first taught this yoga, are the very same one who has now taught it to me? (BhG 4.4)
Dispelling the doubt of the foolish who suspect that Vāsudeva is neither the Lord nor omniscient, the Blessed Lord spoke as follows; for Arjuna’s question was indeed based on this point:
"Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna.
I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe" (BhG 4.5).

"Many births of mine have passed away and gone by, O Arjuna, as well as yours; I know them all, but you do not know them, because your power of knowledge is obstructed by dharma, adharma, and so forth. I, however, because my nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, possess unobstructed power of knowledge; thus, I know them."
O scorcher of foes! (BhG 4.5) How then is there birth for you, who are the eternal Lord, even in the absence of merit and demerit? To this it is said:
"Though being unborn and of imperishable nature, and though being the Lord of all beings..."
Presiding over my own nature, I manifest through my own power of illusion (māyā).
Although he is unborn, being devoid of birth; and although he is of an imperishable nature, his essence being characterized by undiminished power of knowledge;
and although he is the Lord of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, possessing the quality of sovereignty.
My own *prakṛti* is indeed my Vaiṣṇava *māyā*, consisting of the three *guṇas*, under whose control this entire world exists;
by which the world, being deluded, does not know its own true Self, Vāsudeva.
Having presided over—that is, having brought under control—that *prakṛti* of mine, I manifest, appearing as if possessing a body, as if born, through my own *māyā*, the *māyā* of the Self.
Not from the perspective of ultimate reality, but as in the world.
And when, and for what purpose, does that birth occur? It is said:
"Whenever, O Bhārata, there is a decline of Dharma..."
When there is an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.

Whenever there is a decline, a decay, of Dharma— characterized by the system of social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) and serving as the means for the worldly prosperity and ultimate liberation of living beings, O Bhārata— and whenever there is the uprising,
the emergence, of Adharma, then I manifest Myself through My creative power (māyā).
For what purpose?
"For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evildoers, and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age. (BhG 4.8)
For the protection and preservation of the virtuous who abide on the true path,
for the destruction of evildoers who commit sinful acts,
and furthermore, for the purpose of establishing righteousness— the perfect establishment of dharma— it is for that sake that I come into being.
In age after age—that is, in every successive age. O Arjuna, he who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, upon leaving the body, does not come to rebirth; he comes to Me.

He who knows in truth— that is, according to reality and as it has been described— this birth of Mine to be of the nature of *māyā*, and My work to be the protection of the virtuous and so forth, as My divine (*divya*), non-material (*aprākṛta*), and sovereign (*aiśvara*) power; having abandoned this body, he does not come again to birth, that is, to rebirth.
"He who comes to me thus, O Arjuna, is liberated.
This path to liberation has not been set forth now for the first time.

What then? Even in the past—those who were free from passion, fear, and anger, who were absorbed in Me and took refuge in Me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state. (BhG 4.10)
"Free from passion, fear, and anger"—passion (*rāga*), fear (*bhaya*), and anger (*krodha*) are collectively "passion-fear-anger";
those from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed (*vīta*) or vanished are "free from passion, fear, and anger.
"Consisting of Me" (*manmaya*) refers to the knowers of Brahman who perceive non-difference from the Lord.
"Having taken refuge in Me alone, the Supreme Lord"—

the meaning is that they are established in exclusive knowledge. "Many," meaning numerous, [attain perfection] through "knowledge-austerity," where knowledge itself regarding the Supreme Self is the austerity.
By that knowledge and austerity, being purified and having attained supreme purity,
they have come to— meaning fully reached— my state, which is the state of the Lord, liberation.
The qualification "by the austerity of knowledge" (jñāna-tapasā) is the indicative mark that steadfastness in knowledge is independent of other forms of austerity. [Objection:
In that case, you must possess attachment and aversion, since you bestow the nature of the Self upon some and not upon others.
It is not from all [that I receive gifts]. Thus it is said:
"In whatever way people surrender unto me, even so do I reward them;
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect. (BhG 4.11)

In whatever way, by whatever means, for whatever purpose, and with a desire for whatever fruit people approach Me, I honor them—that is, I favor them—by granting that very fruit; this is because they have no desire for liberation.
For it is not possible for a single person to simultaneously possess both the desire for liberation and the desire for [worldly] fruits.
Therefore, he satisfies those who seek specific fruits by granting those fruits; those who act as prescribed but do not seek fruits and are seekers of liberation (mumukṣu) by granting knowledge;
and those who are already wise, renunciants, and seekers of liberation by granting liberation.
"Likewise, by removing the suffering of those who are afflicted"—the meaning is that I favor those who approach Me in whatever manner they do so;
however, I do not favor anyone on account of passion, hatred, or delusion.
In every way, human beings follow the path and course of conduct of Me, the Lord, in all My states.

Those who, being entitled to a particular action because they desire its fruit, exert themselves in that action— those humans are referred to here as "all," O Pārtha, in every way and by all means. If you, the Lord, being free from defects such as passion and the like, possess an equal desire to favor all living beings and are capable of bestowing all fruits, then why is it that those seeking liberation, through the knowledge that "Vāsudeva is everything" (Gītā 7.19), [do not attain their goal]?
"Why do they all not resort to you alone?
Listen to the reason for this:
Desiring success through their actions, people here worship the deities."
For success born of action is quickly attained in the world of men.
Desiring, longing for, and praying for the success of their actions—the accomplishment of results—they worship the deities such as Indra, Agni, and others here in this world.
Now, he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know;
he is like an animal.
Thus, according to the Vedic scripture, "He [attains] the worlds of the gods" (BAU 1.4.10).
For those who sacrifice to separate deities and desire fruits, it is because they quickly—that is, swiftly—return to the world of men;
for it is in the world of men that there is authority over the scriptures.
Because of the qualification "quickly indeed in the world of humans," the Blessed One shows that the attainment of the fruits of action occurs in other [realms] as well;
however, the distinction is that in the world of humans there is the eligibility for actions such as those pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*).
And for those performers of action who belong to the various castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), the accomplishment of the fruit born of action—arising from action—comes quickly.

[Question: Why is there this restriction that the entitlement to perform actions such as those pertaining to caste and stage of life exists only in the human world and not in other worlds? What is the cause of this?

Alternatively, it was stated [in Gītā 4.11]: "Human beings, endowed with the distinctions of caste, stage of life, and so forth, follow my path in every way. For what reason, then, do they follow your path specifically and by rule, and not that of another? It is said in reply:
"The fourfold social order was created by me according to the divisions of qualities and actions."
Know Me also as the author of that [action], yet the non-agent and immutable.

The fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) consists of exactly four castes; this was created and produced by me, the Lord, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with, "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth" (Ṛgveda 10.90.12; Yajurveda 31.11).
This was done according to the division of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), that is, by the division of qualities and by the division of actions.
The qualities (guṇas) are sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Among these, the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, who is characterized by sattva—that is, for whom sattva is predominant—are tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, and so forth (Gītā 18.42). The duties of a Kṣatriya, for whom rajas is predominant with sattva as a subordinate factor, are heroism, splendor, and the like.

The duties of the Vaiśya consist of agriculture and so forth, characterized by Rajas as the subordinate quality and Tamas as the predominant one; the duty of the Śūdra is service alone, characterized by Tamas as the subordinate quality and Rajas as the predominant one. Thus, the meaning is that the fourfold order has been created by Me according to the division of qualities and duties.
And this fourfold caste system does not exist in other worlds;
therefore, the qualification "in the human world" is specified.
Well then, since [the Creator] is the agent of the action consisting of the creation of the fourfold caste system and so forth—
"Therefore, you are joined with the fruit of that [action]; thus, you are neither eternally liberated nor the eternal Lord.
It is said in reply: "Even though, by means of the conventional usage of *māyā*, I am the agent of that action, know me in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) to be a non-agent;
for this very reason, know me to be immutable and not subject to transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*). (BhG 4.13)
But as for those actions of which you consider me to be the agent from the perspective of ultimate reality, I am in fact not their agent. For this reason:
"Actions do not taint me, nor do I have any desire for the fruits of action.
He who understands me thus is not bound by actions. (BhG 4.14)
Those actions do not smear me, because there is an absence of egoism regarding their being the initiators of the body and so forth;
nor is there any longing or thirst for the fruits of those actions on my part.
However, it is logical that those actions smear those transmigrating beings who possess the conceit "I am the doer" and have a longing for actions and their fruits.
"Because of the absence of that [egoism], actions do not smear me.
In this way, whoever else also recognizes Me as the Self—realizing "I am not the agent, nor is there any desire for the fruit of my action"—is not bound by actions.
The meaning is that even for such a person, actions that initiate a body and so forth do not come to pass. (BhG 4.14)
"I am not the doer,
nor do I have any longing for the fruits of my actions"— having realized this, even the seekers of liberation of old performed their duties.
Therefore, perform action alone, as it was performed by those of old even before them.
Knowing this, perform action just as it was performed by those seekers of liberation who have passed away in the past;
therefore, you must indeed act,
neither remaining silent nor undertaking renunciation.

Therefore, since it was also practiced by those who preceded you— if you are ignorant of the Self, then for the sake of purifying the Self; if you are a knower of reality, then for the sake of sustaining the world—
the ancestors, such as Janaka and others, performed it even earlier than before.
It is not something performed or ceased by me at this present moment. (BhG 4.15) In that case, if action must be performed, I shall do it simply because of your word;
what is the use of this qualification?

Regarding the statement, "What was done by the ancients was done even more so by those before them" (Gītā 4.15), it is said in reply: because there is indeed a great disparity regarding action. How so?
Even the wise are deluded in this matter as to what is action and what is inaction.
I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil.
"What is action? And what is inaction?"—even the wise and intelligent are deluded, having fallen into confusion regarding this matter of action and so forth.
Therefore, I shall declare to you both action and inaction, by knowing which—that is, by understanding which—you will be liberated from the evil of transmigratory existence.
And you should not think thus: [that this is too difficult for you].
What is called "action" (karman) is the movement of the body and so forth, as is well known in the world;
"inaction" (akarman), on the other hand, is the absence of such activity, namely, remaining silent.
What is there to be understood in this regard? Thus [is the question].
Why? It is said:

"For that which is to be understood regarding action, and that which is to be understood regarding improper action (vikarman), and that which is to be understood regarding inaction (akarman)—the course of action is profound. (BhG 4.17)
For since there is indeed something to be understood even regarding action prescribed by the scriptures,
and there is certainly something to be understood regarding "vikarman" (forbidden action),
so too there is something to be understood regarding "akarman" (inaction) or silence; thus, the word "to be understood" must be supplied in all three cases.
Because the course—the true nature or reality—of action (and by implication, of inaction and mis-action) is profound, difficult, and hard to understand; this is the meaning of the verse. (BhG 4.17)
But what is that reality regarding action and so forth which was promised to be explained as that which must be understood? It is said:
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. (BhG 4.18)
Regarding action (*karman*): action is that which is performed; it is mere activity (*vyāpāra-mātra*).

One who should perceive "non-action" (*akarma*)—the absence of action—in that action; and likewise, one who perceives "action"—the presence of activity—in non-action, [which is merely] the absence of action because both engagement and withdrawal depend upon an agent: for indeed, the entire conventional usage of action, factors of action (*kāraka*), and so forth, without having reached any real entity, exists only on the plane of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*). As for action...

He who sees [action in inaction] and sees [inaction in action] is wise among men; he is a disciplined yogi and a performer of all actions— he is praised as one who perceives the mutual nature of action and inaction.
Now, is this not a contradiction that is being stated— that one should see inaction in action,
and action in inaction? For indeed,
action cannot be inaction, nor can inaction be action.

In that regard, how could the seer perceive what is contradictory? He does not. From the perspective of the deluded world, that which is in fact non-action appears as action, and likewise, action itself appears as non-action.
In that regard, for the purpose of seeing things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-darśana*), the Blessed One said: "He who sees non-action in action," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no contradiction, because [the attributes] such as intelligence (*buddhimattva*) are logically established;
furthermore, by the term "that which is to be understood" (*boddhavya*), seeing things as they truly are is expressed.
Furthermore, liberation from the inauspicious could not occur through erroneous knowledge; for it has been said: "Knowing which, you shall be liberated from the inauspicious" (Gītā 4.16).
Therefore, since actions and inaction are grasped erroneously by living beings, the Lord’s statement beginning with "He who sees inaction in action" is intended to remove that erroneous apprehension.
Moreover, there is no action here that exists as the locus of action.
Like jujube fruits in a bowl,
there is no action that is not the locus of action, because non-action is simply the absence of action.
Therefore, action and non-action are perceived in a contrary manner by worldly people.
Just as there is water in a mirage, or silver in mother-of-pearl;
surely, for everyone, action is indeed action and never deviates from its nature.

That is not so, because when one is on a boat that is moving, mountains standing on the bank—which are themselves motionless—are perceived as having a movement contrary [to the direction of the boat].
Because one perceives the absence of motion in objects that are nearby even as they move, and because one perceives motion in objects that are distant even while they remain still;
so too here, the perception of action in what is non-action—thinking "I am acting"—and the perception of non-action in action are instances of erroneous perception.
To refute this, it is said: "He who sees non-action in action," and so forth.

Thus, because the world is repeatedly deluded by the persistence of utterly perverted views, it forgets again and again—even though it has heard the truth repeatedly—the reality that has been explained; and by repeatedly introducing spurious arguments, it raises objections.
Therefore, the Blessed One provides the answer over and over again.
And having observed that the true nature of reality is difficult to discern,

the absence of action (karmābhāva) in the self— established by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning— is stated in such passages as "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable" (Gītā 2.25) and "It is neither born nor does it die" (Gītā 2.27), and will be further explained hereafter.

In that Self, where there is an absence of action—that is, inaction—there is an extremely deep-seated perception of action contrary to reality; for even the wise are deluded in this regard, as it is said: "Even the seers are confused as to what is action and what is inaction" (Gītā 4.16). Having superimposed action, which has the body and so forth as its locus, upon the Self, they think:
"I am the agent; this is my action."
And [the thought], "I must experience the fruit of this action. Likewise, [the thought], "I shall remain silent,
so that I may be effortless, free from action, and happy"— this is the cessation of the activity based on the body and the instruments [of action] caused by that [desire].
Having superimposed happiness upon itself, the world imagines, "I do nothing; I sit silently in comfort.
In this regard, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "He who sees inaction in action" in order to remove this perverted vision of the world.
And here, action—which is indeed action—residing in the body and its instruments, is superimposed by everyone upon the Self, which is devoid of action and changeless.

Since even a wise man thinks, "I am doing," and because action— which is well-known to all the world as inherent in the self— is like the movement of trees standing on a riverbank [appearing to move in the opposite direction], he who sees "non-action"— the absence of action— as it truly is, like the absence of motion in trees; [that person sees.]

And when there is inaction— that is, when the activities of the body and the organs have ceased— because one superimposes action upon the Self, thinking "I sit happily, silent and doing nothing," due to the underlying motive of egoism,
he who perceives action even in that inaction,
and who thus knows the distinction between action and inaction, is wise and learned among men.
He is the disciplined yogi who performs all actions;
the meaning is that he is liberated from inauspiciousness and has accomplished what was to be done.
This verse has been explained differently by some.
How so? It is said that obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), when performed for the sake of the Lord, are called "non-action" (*akarma*) by way of figurative usage because they lack [worldly] fruit.
And their non-performance is "action" (*karman*);
and that, because it results in demerit (*pratyavāya*), is called "action" by way of figurative usage alone.
In that regard, regarding obligatory action (*nitya-karman*), he who perceives it as "non-action" (*akarma*) does so because of the absence of [desirable] fruit;

just as even a cow that is a milch-cow is called a "non-cow" (*agauḥ*) when she does not yield the fruit known as milk, so it is here. Likewise, regarding non-performance—that is, non-action—of the obligatory rite, one should perceive it as "action," for it yields the fruit of demerit (*pratyavāya*) such as rebirth in hell.

This explanation is not tenable, because liberation from the impure would be impossible through such knowledge. It would contradict the statement spoken by the Blessed One: "Having known which, you shall be liberated from the impure" (Gītā 4.16).
How so? Liberation from evil might indeed result from the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), but not from the knowledge that they lack a fruit.
For the knowledge that obligatory rites have no fruit does not have liberation from evil as its result.
The knowledge of obligatory action (*nitya-karma*) has been enjoined,
but it was not spoken by the Blessed One in this context;
by this, the view that there is action in what is non-action is refuted.
For it is not the view that "non-action is action" which is enjoined here as something to be performed; rather, there is merely the necessity of performing what is obligatory (nitya).
Nor would any result accrue from the knowledge that "no transgression occurs through the non-performance of what is obligatory."
Nor is non-performance [of prescribed acts] enjoined as an object of knowledge;
nor is liberation from evil through the false view that "this is action" or "this is inaction," which constitutes wisdom.
Logical consistency,
the performance of all actions, and so forth, as well as the fruit [of liberation], are established either as praise or as a logical consequence;
for false knowledge alone is directly of an unwholesome nature— how could liberation from unwholesomeness come from anything else?
For darkness does not become the remover of darkness. But is it not the case that the perception of inaction in action, or the perception of action in inaction, is not false knowledge?
What then is the secondary cause for the existence or non-existence of the fruit?
No, because even from the secondary knowledge of action as inaction, no fruit is heard of [in scripture].
Nor is any distinction gained by abandoning what is heard and imagining what is not heard.
It is possible to state by one's own words that there is no fruit for obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), and that from their non-performance there would be a fall into hell;
what, then, is the purpose of saying "he who sees inaction in action" and so forth through such a pretext, which consists in deluding others?
By explaining it in that very way, the Lord’s spoken word would clearly be imagined as being intended for the delusion of the world.
Nor is it proper to say that this matter should be protected by means of deceptive speech, nor that it would become easily understood if it were stated again and again using different words;
for the meaning already stated very clearly in the verse, "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47), need not be stated again.
In all cases, that which is praiseworthy must be understood and indeed performed;
it is not said that one should understand something that serves no purpose.
Furthermore, false cognition does not become an object to be known, nor does the appearance of an object presented by such cognition;

nor does the production of a non-existent result arise from the non-performance of eternal duties due to their non-existence, because of the scriptural statement: "Of the non-existent, there is no being" (Gītā 2.16).
Furthermore, it has been shown [in ChāU 6.2.2]: "How could being be born from non-being?
Since the birth of being from non-being is thus prohibited, one who asserts that being arises from non-being would effectively be saying that non-being becomes being, and being becomes non-being.
And that is illogical,
because it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
nor would a treatise (*śāstra*) enjoin fruitless action, since [action] is of the nature of suffering.
Furthermore, since suffering cannot logically be an effect produced intentionally,

if one were to accept that falling into hell results from not performing [the prescribed acts], it would lead only to misfortune. In either case— whether by performing or not performing— the scripture would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with one's own accepted position for one who, having accepted that action is eternally fruitless, then says it is "for the sake of the fruit of liberation.
Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "action in which there is inaction" is exactly as it was heard;
and thus it has been explained.
Thus we have this verse (BhG 4.18):
This very vision of action as inaction and so forth is being praised: "He whose undertakings are all devoid of desire and purposeful resolve..."
The wise call him a sage whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
For one who perceives as described, all undertakings—whatever actions are commenced—are "undertakings" (samārambhāḥ) that are free from desire and intention;
they are devoid of desires and the intentions that cause them, being performed merely as purposeless activity. If he acts out of engagement, it is for the sake of maintaining the world.

If he has desisted from action merely for the sake of subsistence—him whose actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge; "knowledge" here refers to the vision of action as non-action and so forth regarding action and the like;
that itself is the fire, and he is one whose actions characterized as auspicious and inauspicious have been burnt by that fire of knowledge.
The wise who know Brahman call him a sage from the perspective of the ultimate truth.

(BhG 4.19) But he who perceives "inaction" and so forth in action and the like, by virtue of that very perception of inaction and so forth, becomes free from action— a renunciant whose movements are for the sake of mere subsistence— and does not engage in action,
even though he previously engaged in it due to a lack of discrimination.
But he who, having commenced action, should later attain the correct vision of the Self, seeing no purpose in any action, surely renounces action along with its means; yet,
if for some reason the renunciation of action is impossible, he remains free from attachment to both action and its fruit.

Since he has no personal motive, even though he engages in action for the sake of maintaining the world as before, he does not do anything at all because his actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge; thus, his action becomes non-action. Demonstrating this point, He says:
"Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented, and independent."
Even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.

Having abandoned self-conceit regarding actions as well as attachment to their fruits— meaning one who is eternally content and free from longing for sense objects through the aforementioned knowledge—
one is "without support" (nirāśraya), which means devoid of a support.
A "support" (āśraya) is that which one relies upon in order to desire to accomplish the goals of human life.
The meaning is that it is devoid of any basis for accomplishing results, whether seen or unseen.
Action performed by the wise person is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, truly non-action,
because he is perfected in the vision of the self as being devoid of activity.
Since for one who has become thus there is an absence of any personal motive, it follows that action along with its means must indeed be abandoned.

However, because it is impossible to emerge from that [state of action], even though he engages in action as before— either out of a desire to maintain the world order (*loka-saṅgraha*) or out of a wish to avoid the reproach of the learned— he does nothing at all, because he is perfected in the realization of the Self as being beyond action (*niṣkriya*).
On the other hand, he who is the opposite of those previously mentioned— having already realized the Self within the Brahman, the innermost of all, which is actionless even before the ocean of karma—

being devoid of desire for seen or unseen objects of enjoyment, perceives no purpose whatsoever in actions aimed at seen or unseen ends; thus, having renounced all action along with its means, the ascetic, whose activity is limited to the mere maintenance of the body and who is established in knowledge, is liberated.
To demonstrate this point, he says:
"Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action solely for the sake of the body, one incurs no sin. (BhG 4.21)
"Nirāśīḥ" means one from whom desires have departed; he is "nirāśīḥ. "Yata-cittātmā": "citta" is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
"ātmā" is the external aggregate of the body and the senses.

He whose mind and self are both restrained and controlled is one whose mind and self are restrained (*yata-cittātman*). He who has abandoned all possessions is one by whom every possession has been relinquished (*tyakta-sarva-parigraha*).
Performing action that is merely for the purpose of maintaining the body—and even there, devoid of egoism—he acts.
He incurs neither *kilbiṣa*— that is, undesirable evil— nor *dharma*.
For even *dharma* is indeed undesirable *kilbiṣa* for one seeking liberation,
because it brings about bondage.
Therefore, he is liberated from those two;
the meaning is that he is liberated from saṃsāra.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "bodily action alone" (śārīraṃ karma kevalam), what is intended by "bodily action" (śārīraṃ karma)? Is it action performed by means of the body?
Or rather, is "bodily action" that which has as its sole purpose the maintenance of the body?
What follows from this: is bodily action that which is accomplished by the body, or is the body that which has as its sole purpose the maintenance of the body?
It is said: if bodily action were intended to mean action accomplished by the body, then it would include actions with both seen and unseen purposes.
For one who says, "Even while performing with the body an action that is prohibited, one incurs no sin," a contradictory statement would result.

Furthermore, for one who says, "While performing with the body an action prescribed by scripture, whether for a visible or invisible purpose, one incurs no sin," there would be the consequence of prohibiting what has not been established as forbidden.

Because of the qualification "performing bodily action" and the use of the word "kevala" (exclusive/alone), it follows that action accomplished by speech and mind—being the subject of injunctions and prohibitions and denoted by the terms *dharma* and *adharma*—is [excluded].
It would be stated that "one incurs sin while performing [it]";
in that case as well, if one follows the position that [the act] is enjoined by speech and mind, the statement regarding the incurrence of sin would result in a contradiction;
and even if one follows the position that it is something prohibited, it would be a mere restatement of an existing fact and thus useless.

But when bodily action is intended as having the sole purpose of maintaining the body's existence, then, while not performing any other action— whether seen or unseen, whether understood through injunctions or prohibitions, and whether accomplished by body, speech, or mind— one uses those very same instruments (body, etc. solely for the purpose of maintaining the body, as indicated by the use of the word "kevala" (solely).
Free from the conceit "I am the doer," one who performs what is merely the movement of the body and so forth according to worldly perception incurs no sin.
Since for such a person the acquisition of "sin"—which is denoted by the word *kilbiṣa*—is impossible, he does not incur the "sin" that is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Because all actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge, he is liberated without obstruction; thus, this is merely a restatement of the result of the right vision previously described.
Thus, by accepting the meaning that the body is merely action (karma),
it becomes faultless.

For an ascetic who has renounced all possessions, since there is no possession of food and so forth for the sake of maintaining the body, [the body's sustenance must come] through begging and the like.

When the necessity of maintaining the body has arisen, the text—beginning with the words, "unasked for, unprepared, obtained by chance" (Mbh 14.46.19; Baudhāyana-dharma-sūtra 21.8.12)—reveals the means by which an ascetic obtains food and other necessities for the sake of bodily sustenance, as permitted by such scriptural injunctions; thus he says:
"Content with what is obtained by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy..."
Being the same in success and failure, even after acting, he is not bound.

Content with what is obtained by chance (*yadṛcchā-lābha-santuṣṭaḥ*): "obtained by chance" refers to gain that comes unbidden; "content with that" means having developed the sense of sufficiency (*alaṃ-pratyaya*). "Transcending the pairs" (*dvandvātīta*): even when struck by pairs such as cold and heat, one whose mind does not become dejected is said to have transcended the pairs.
Free from envy, devoid of malice, and with a mind free from enmity;

equanimous and equal toward gain or loss occurring by chance, whether in success or failure— such a yogi is the same in the acquisition or non-acquisition of food and other means for the maintenance of the body, remaining free from both joy and dejection.
Seeing no action in what is action and so forth,

being established in the vision of the Self as it truly is, one performs actions such as wandering for alms— actions carried out by the body and other instruments merely for the purpose of maintaining the body— while thinking, "I do nothing at all" (Gītā 5.8), because "the qualities act upon the qualities" (Gītā 3.28).
Thus, always reflecting in this way and seeing the absence of agency in himself, he performs some action such as wandering for alms;
yet, because he conforms to worldly convention, he becomes an agent in actions like begging for alms, even though agency has been superimposed upon him by worldly people.
But by his own experience, born from the authority of the scriptures and so forth, he remains indeed a non-doer.
Thus, even after performing actions such as wandering for alms—which serve the sole purpose of maintaining the body and whose agency has been superimposed upon him by others—he is not bound;
for action, along with its cause, which is the cause of bondage, has been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. This is merely a restatement of what was previously said. (BhG 4.22)

By the verse beginning with "Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action" (Gītā 4.20), it is shown that when one who has commenced action becomes endowed with the realization of the Self as the inactive Brahman, then— although the abandonment of action follows for him who perceives the absence of agent, action, and purpose— if for some reason that abandonment is impossible, he should remain in that same action as before.
"Even for one who has engaged in action, he does nothing at all" (Gītā 4.20)—thus the absence of action has been demonstrated.
For him in whom this absence of action has been shown, it is said: "For one whose attachment has passed away, who is liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge..."
For one who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, all karma is entirely dissolved.

For one who is free from attachment, whose interest has ceased in every respect, who is liberated, and whose bonds such as merit and demerit have been removed; for one whose mind is established in knowledge— that is, one whose consciousness is fixed upon knowledge itself— for him,

as he performs or carries out action for the sake of sacrifice, for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice, his entire action— meaning that action which exists together with its future fruit— is completely dissolved.
The meaning is that it perishes. But for what reason does an action being performed dissolve entirely without initiating its own effect? It is said:
because—The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman.
Through that concentration on the work of Brahman, one must go to Brahman alone.
The instrument by which the knower of Brahman offers the oblation into the fire is itself Brahman;

he perceives it as such, seeing that it has no existence apart from the Self, just as one perceives the absence of silver in mother-of-pearl. This is what is meant by the statement: "Brahman alone is the offering."
Just as that which is silver is actually mother-of-pearl;

so too, when the words "brahma arpaṇam" are not taken as a compound, the meaning is that whatever is perceived in the world with the notion of an offering (arpaṇa) is, for this knower of Brahman, Brahman alone. Likewise, the oblation (havis) is Brahman; that which is grasped with the notion of an oblation is, for him, Brahman alone.
Likewise, "in the fire that is Brahman" (*brahmāgnau*) is a compound word;
the fire, too, is indeed Brahman.
The meaning is that where it is offered by Brahman as the agent, Brahman alone is the agent.
Whatever oblation was offered by him, that sacrificial act is Brahman alone;
whatever fruit was to be attained by him, that too is Brahman alone.

Through the concentration on the action of Brahman—wherein the action is Brahman and the concentration is upon it—one who possesses that concentration on the action of Brahman reaches Brahman alone as the goal.
Thus, even an action performed by one desiring to gather the world is,

from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthatas*), non-action (*akarma*), because it is sublated by the realization of Brahman (*brahma-buddhi*). This being so, it is all the more appropriate to establish the nature of sacrifice (*yajñatva*) for knowledge— even for one who has withdrawn from action and renounced all works— in order to praise right vision (*samyag-darśana*).

That which is well-known as the sacrificial implements such as the ladle (*arpaṇa*) and so forth in the context of sacrifice is, for one who perceives the ultimate reality, Brahman itself from the perspective of the inner self (*adhyātma*).
Otherwise, if everything were Brahman, the specific designation of the ladle and other implements alone as being Brahman would be purposeless.
Therefore, for the wise person who realizes that "all this is indeed Brahman," there is an absence of all ritual action.
And because of the absence of the notion of agency:
for no action known as sacrifice is ever observed to be devoid of the notion of agency;

every action, such as the Agnihotra and others, is observed to possess the notion of agency regarding the specific recipient deity presented by the words [of the mantra], as well as the conceit of being an agent and the expectation of a fruit.
It is not that which possesses an intellect that perceives distinctions between the agent, the instrument, and the fruit, nor is it devoid of the conceit of agency and the desire for results.

This action, however, is one in which the intellect has destroyed the perception of distinctions between the agent, the instrument—beginning with the offering—and the fruit through the realization of Brahman; therefore, that is indeed non-action (akarma).
And so it has been shown: "He who sees non-action in action" (Gītā 4.18).

This is shown by such passages as: "Even though engaged in action, he does nothing at all" (Gītā 4.20), "The qualities act among the qualities" (Gītā 3.28), and "The disciplined knower of reality should think, 'I do nothing at all'" (Gītā 5.8).
And demonstrating this in various instances, [the scripture] effects the sublation of the notion of distinctions between action, its factors, and its results.
For it is observed that in the case of the optional *agnihotra* and other such rites, there is an abandonment of the optional *agnihotra* etc. through the sublation of desire (*kāma*).
Likewise, it is observed that actions performed intentionally, unintentionally, and so forth, initiate specific types of effects.

Similarly here as well, for the wise person whose cognition of distinctions among the factors of action—the agent, the instrument, the action, and the fruit—is sublated by the cognition of Brahman, even ritual action becomes non-action through mere external movement.
Therefore it is said: "everything is dissolved" (Gītā 4.23).
Regarding this, some say: "That which is Brahman, that is the ladle and so forth."
Indeed, Brahman itself, existing as the fivefold set of causal factors such as the sacrificial ladle and so forth, performs that very action.
In this regard, the cognition of the ladle and other implements is not to be negated;
rather, the cognition of Brahman is to be superimposed upon the ladle and the rest.
Just as there is the notion of Viṣṇu and others in an image, or the notion of Brahman in a name and so forth;
this might indeed be the case if this section were not intended for the purpose of praising the sacrifice of knowledge.

In this context, however, having introduced right vision—which is designated as the "sacrifice of knowledge"—alongside many specific actions designated as "sacrifices," the Lord praises knowledge, saying: "The sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects, O scorcher of foes" (Gītā 4.33).
And in this regard, the statement beginning with "the offering to Brahman" is fully capable of establishing the nature of knowledge as a sacrifice.

Otherwise, if everything were Brahman, the specific designation of Brahman-hood for the offering and so forth would be purposeless. As for those who say that the vision of Brahman is superimposed upon the offering and so forth—just as the vision of Viṣṇu is superimposed upon an image—or as [the vision of the Supreme Self is superimposed] upon names and so forth; [this is not the case].
In this context, the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) would not be intended for them,
because such knowledge has as its object the act of offering and so forth;
nor is the fruit of liberation attained through the knowledge that consists in the mental visualization [of the sacrifice].
And it is said that "by that [knowledge], Brahman alone is to be attained";
furthermore, it is contradictory [to claim] that liberation as a fruit is obtained without right vision (*samyag-darśana*),
and there is also a contradiction with the nature of things (*prakṛti-virodha*).
Furthermore, right vision (*samyag-darśana*) was introduced in the verse, "He who sees inaction in action" (Gītā 4.18), and at the end as well, right vision is concluded with that very same theme.

The chapter concludes by praising right vision alone through such statements as, "The sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice of material objects, O scorcher of foes" (Gītā 4.33) and "Having attained knowledge, one attains supreme peace" (Gītā 4.39).
Thus, the chapter is exhausted.

In this regard, it is untenable to claim that the vision of Brahman is enjoined upon the sacrificial implements and so forth without context—just as the vision of Viṣṇu is enjoined upon an image—because [the text] speaks of "offering" (*arpaṇa*) and the like.
Therefore, this verse has the meaning exactly as it has been explained.
Now, having established that right vision (*samyag-darśana*) is a sacrifice, other sacrifices are introduced for the purpose of praising it:
Some yogis offer sacrifice to the divine alone;
others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.
That sacrifice by which the gods themselves are worshipped is the divine sacrifice; other yogis, who are performers of action, attend to that very sacrifice—they perform it, is the meaning.
[They offer it] into the fire of Brahman, [which is] "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (TaittU 2.1) and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss" (BAU 3.9.28).

That which is Brahman—direct and immediate, the Self that is within all—as stated in such passages as [BAU 3.4.1], and which is devoid of all attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and thirst, and from which every distinction has been negated by the words "not this, not this" [BAU 4.4.22], is denoted by the term *brahman*.
That which is both *brahman* and *agni* (fire)—intended here in the sense of being the locus of the oblation—is the *brahmāgni*; in that *brahmāgni*...

Others, who are knowers of Brahman, offer as an oblation— by means of the Self alone— that very Self which is designated by the word "sacrifice" (since the word *yajña* is listed among the names of the Self in the *Nirukta* 14.11), which is in reality the Supreme Brahman itself, yet is joined with limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and possesses all the attributes superimposed upon those adjuncts; they cast it, in the form of an oblation, into that same Self characterized as described above.
The vision of the conditioned self as being nothing other than the nature of the unconditioned Supreme Brahman—
that is the oblation they offer into that fire;
the meaning is that the renunciants are those who are established in the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.

This very sacrifice characterized by right vision (samyag-darśana), which was introduced in the verses beginning with "The offering to Brahman" (brahmārpaṇam) among the sacrifices such as the sacrifice to the gods (daiva-yajña),
is praised for the sake of glorification in the passage beginning with "Knowledge-sacrifice is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects, O scorcher of foes" (Gītā 4.33).
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
Others, the yogins, offer the sense organs, such as the ears and so forth, into the fires of *saṃyama*. The plural number is used because *saṃyama* differs for each individual sense organ.
They offer them into those very fires of *saṃyama*;
the meaning is that they practice the restraint of the senses.
Others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses;
that is, they consider the perception of non-prohibited objects by means of the ears and other senses to be an oblation into those fires of the senses.
Furthermore—
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.

"All functions of the senses" (*indriya-karmāṇi*) means the actions of the senses. Likewise, "functions of the vital breath" (*prāṇa-karmāṇi*): *prāṇa* is the internal air; its functions are contraction, expansion, and so forth. And these [functions], others say, [are offered] into the fire of self-restraint yoga (*ātma-saṃyama-yogāgni*).
Self-restraint in the self is *ātma-saṃyama*.
That very fire of yoga—in that fire of the yoga of self-restraint—they offer as an oblation; they cast it in.
The meaning is that they cause it to dissolve, having made it blaze with the discernment of wisdom (viveka-vijñāna), just as [a fire] is kindled by oil when lit by knowledge.
Others likewise perform sacrifices of material objects, sacrifices of austerity, and sacrifices of yoga.
And there are ascetics of firm vows who perform the sacrifice of knowledge through the study of the scriptures.

Those who perform the expenditure of wealth at sacred fords with the intention that it is a sacrifice are performers of the sacrifice of wealth (*dravya-yajña*). Those ascetics for whom austerity is the sacrifice are performers of the sacrifice of austerity (*tapo-yajña*).
Those for whom yoga—characterized by breath control, withdrawal of the senses, and so forth—is the sacrifice are performers of the sacrifice of yoga (*yoga-yajña*).

Likewise, others are those for whom the sacrifice is study and knowledge (*svādhyāya-jñāna-yajña*). "Sacrifice of study" refers to those for whom the sacrifice is the recitation of the *Ṛg* Veda and other scriptures according to rule; "sacrifice of knowledge" refers to those for whom the sacrifice is knowledge, that is, the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures. These are the ascetics (*yatayaḥ*), whose nature is constant effort (*yatana-śīlāḥ*).
Those whose vows are firmly resolved are called *saṃśita-vrata*; they are those whose vows have been properly sharpened, refined, and made keen.
Furthermore:
others offer the out-breath (*apāna*) into the in-breath (*prāṇa*), and likewise the in-breath into the out-breath.
Having restrained the movements of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they are devoted to the practice of prāṇāyāma.
In the apāna—that is, in the function of the apāna—they offer, they cast, the prāṇa, that is, the function of the prāṇa;
the meaning is that they perform the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) known as pūraka.
Others likewise offer the apāna into the prāṇa.
And they perform the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) called recaka;

this refers to the movements of prāṇa and apāna: the movement of prāṇa is the exit of air through the two primary nostrils, while the movement of apāna is the downward flow by way of the opposite process.
These are the movements of prāṇa and apāna.
Having restrained and suppressed these [senses], those devoted to *prāṇāyāma*—meaning those intent on *prāṇāyāma*—perform the *prāṇāyāma* known as *kumbhaka*.
Furthermore:
others, with regulated food intake, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths.
All these, too, are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice.

Others, being those whose food is restricted— meaning those for whom food is restricted and measured— offer the vital breaths, which are specific types of air, into the vital breaths themselves; that is,
whichever particular wind is being mastered, they offer the other varieties of wind into that very one.
They become as if they have entered therein.

All these are knowers of sacrifice—those whose impurities have been worn away by sacrifices; that is, those whose impurities have been destroyed and eliminated by the sacrifices performed according to the prescribed injunctions.
Having thus completed the sacrifices as described—
Those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman;
for one who does not sacrifice, even this world does not exist—how much less another, O best of the Kurus? (BhG 4.31)

"Eaters of the nectar of sacrificial remnants" (*yajña-śiṣṭāmṛta-bhujaḥ*): that which remains from sacrifices is "sacrificial remnant" (*yajña-śiṣṭa*); that sacrificial remnant is also nectar, hence "nectar of sacrificial remnants. Those who eat that are "eaters of the nectar of sacrificial remnants.

Having performed the aforementioned sacrifices, they eat at the time remaining after them food called "nectar," as enjoined by the rules; thus they are "eaters of the nectar of sacrificial remnants. They go—that is, they proceed—to the eternal Brahman, the ancient one, if they are seekers of liberation.
This is understood by implication as referring to the lapse of time.

O best of the Kurus, this world—which is common to all living beings—is not for him who lacks even one of the aforementioned sacrifices; he is a non-sacrificer (*ayajña*). How much less, then, could there be anything else accomplished by superior means?
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action, and by knowing this, you shall be liberated.

Thus, these various and manifold sacrifices described above are spread out and extended at the mouth—the gateway—of the Veda; they are said to be spread at the mouth of Brahman because they are understood through the gateway of the Veda, such as, for example, "We offer the vital breath into speech," and so forth.
Know all those sacrifices born of action to have arisen from bodily, vocal, and mental acts, and not from the Self.
For the self is indeed devoid of activity;
knowing this, you will be liberated from the impure.
These [actions] do not originate from my activity.
"Knowing thus, 'I am inactive and indifferent,' you shall be liberated from the bondage of transmigratory existence through this right vision; this is the meaning.
(BhG 4.32) By the verse beginning with "The offering is Brahman" (4.24), the nature of right vision as a sacrifice has been established.
Furthermore, many kinds of sacrifices have been taught.

By those who have achieved the purpose and goal of human endeavor, knowledge is praised. How so?— "O scorcher of the foe, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
for all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge. (BhG 4.33)
O scorcher of the foe, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects— that which is accomplished by means of material substances—
for the sacrifice consisting of material objects initiates a result,
whereas the sacrifice of knowledge does not initiate a result.
Therefore, it is superior—that is, more praiseworthy.

How so? Because all action—entirely and without exception, O Pārtha—is completed and subsumed within knowledge, which is the means to liberation and which is like water flooding everywhere. This is the meaning.

"Just as when one has won at dice, the lower stakes are gathered together, even so all that good which creatures do comes together unto him who knows what he knows"—so says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.4).
Now, by what means is this distinguished knowledge attained? It is said:
Know that through prostration, through inquiry, and through service;
the wise who have seen the truth will instruct you in that knowledge. (BhG 4.34)
Know—that is, understand—by what method that [knowledge] is attained:
by approaching the teachers through prostration; "prostration" (praṇipāta) means falling down very low, that is, a long-lasting salutation.
What is bondage? What is liberation?
What is knowledge?
And what is ignorance?
By means of such inquiries,
by service, by attendance upon the guru, and so forth.
The teachers, won over by your humility, will instruct and explain to you that knowledge characterized as previously described—those who possess knowledge.
For even among those who possess knowledge, some have the habit of perceiving reality as it truly is, while others do not;
therefore, he specifies "the perceivers of reality."
The knowledge taught by those who possess right vision becomes capable of accomplishing its purpose;
it is not so with others—this is the Lord’s opinion.
And this being the case, the following statement is also valid:
Knowing this, O Pāṇḍava, you will not again fall into such delusion;
by means of it, you shall see all beings without exception within yourself, and then within me.

Having known that knowledge which has been taught by them, and having attained it, you shall not again fall into such delusion as you have now fallen into, O Pāṇḍava. Furthermore, by means of that knowledge, you will see all beings without exception— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— directly within yourself, the inner self, as "these beings abide in Me," and likewise in Me, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, as "these [beings are] in Me."
The meaning is that you shall behold the oneness of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara), which is well-established in all the Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, what is the majesty of this knowledge?—
even if you are the most sinful among all sinners...
By the boat of knowledge alone, you shall cross over all evil.

Moreover, even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, a greater sinner than all those who commit evil, you shall cross over all evil— the ocean of sin— by means of the raft of knowledge alone, having made knowledge itself your boat. For in this context, even dharma is called "evil" for one who seeks liberation.
How does knowledge destroy evil?
This is explained with an illustration:
"Just as a blazing fire, O Arjuna, reduces fuel to ashes,"
In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

Just as a well-kindled, thoroughly ignited fire reduces pieces of wood to ashes, O Arjuna, so too the fire of knowledge—the fire that is knowledge itself—reduces all actions to ashes; the meaning is that it renders them seedless.
For the fire of knowledge cannot directly reduce actions to ashes in the same manner as it reduces fuel.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that right vision (*samyag-darśana*) is the cause for rendering all karma seedless.
By implication, that karma by which a body has already been commenced perishes only through experience, because its fruit has already begun to manifest; as it is said:
"For him, there is only a delay as long as he is not released from this body; then he shall be united. Consequently, those [karmas] whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest...
It reduces to ashes all those very actions performed prior to the arising of knowledge, as well as those performed simultaneously with knowledge, and even those performed over many past lives.
Since this is so, therefore—
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
Indeed, there exists nothing here equal to knowledge—nothing so purifying, sanctifying, or effecting purity.

That knowledge, one who is perfected through yoga—that is, refined and rendered fit by means of both the yoga of action (karma-yoga) and the yoga of meditative concentration (samādhi-yoga)—being a seeker of liberation, finds and attains within himself after a long time; such is the meaning.
The means by which the attainment of knowledge occurs with certainty is taught:
"The one possessed of faith, who is devoted to it and has his senses restrained, obtains knowledge;
having obtained knowledge, he attains supreme peace before long. (BhG 4.39)
One who possesses faith and is faithful attains knowledge.
Even among those who possess faith, some may be slow in their progress; therefore, he says: "devoted to that."
One may be devoted to attending upon the guru and so forth, and possess faith in the means for attaining knowledge;
yet, even if intent upon that, one might still have uncontrolled senses. Therefore, he says: "one whose senses are restrained" (*saṃyatendriya*).
He is one whose senses (*indriyāṇi*) are restrained (*saṃyatāni*), meaning turned away from sense-objects (*viṣayebhyaḥ*).
One who is thus endowed with faith, devoted to that [knowledge], and has his senses restrained, necessarily attains knowledge;
whereas external acts such as prostration are not invariably effective,
since they may arise from deceit and the like.
But that [attainment] does not follow from mere possession of faith and so forth; therefore, knowledge is the exclusive means for attaining [the goal].
What, then, would result from the attainment of knowledge? It is said: having attained knowledge, one reaches the supreme peace called liberation—cessation—in no long time, that is, very quickly.
That liberation occurs very quickly through right vision is a well-ascertained truth established by the logic of all the scriptures. (BhG 4.39)
In this matter, no doubt should be entertained, for doubt is indeed most evil. Why is this so? It is said:
The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (BhG 4.40)

The ignorant one, the one who does not know the Self, the one lacking faith, the one who lacks conviction in the words of the Guru and the scriptures, and the one of a doubting nature— one whose mind is full of doubt— perishes.
Although both the ignorant and the faithless perish, they do not perish in the same way as the one of a doubting nature.
But the one of a doubting mind is the most wicked of all.
Why? Because for him there is not even this common world;
likewise, there is no world beyond.
It is not happiness, because even therein doubt arises for one whose nature is doubt, whose mind is characterized by doubt.
Therefore, doubt must not be entertained.
Why?
O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been severed by knowledge, and who possesses self-mastery.

"By one who has renounced actions through yoga"—that is, by that seer of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) by whom actions known as merit and demerit have been renounced through yoga characterized by the vision of the ultimate truth—how is he "one who has renounced actions through yoga"?

To this he says: "by one whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge"—that is, one by whom doubt has been rent asunder by knowledge characterized by the vision of the identity of the Self and the Lord; such a person is "one whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge."

For one who has thus renounced action through yoga, those actions—which are seen as the movements of the *guṇas*—do not bind that self-possessed and vigilant person; they do not produce results such as undesirable states, O Dhanañjaya. (BhG 4.41) Because, through the practice of karma-yoga, one whose doubts have been severed by knowledge—which arises from the destruction of impurity—is not bound by actions, precisely because his actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge.
And because one who possesses doubt regarding the practice of knowledge and action perishes—
therefore, having severed with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart which has arisen from ignorance, take refuge in yoga and arise, O Bhārata! (BhG 4.42)

Therefore, with the sword of knowledge— knowledge being right vision (*samyag-darśana*) which removes defects such as grief and delusion, and that very [vision] being the sword or scimitar— one should cut away this most evil [ignorance], born of ignorance— that is, produced from non-discrimination— which resides in the heart, meaning it is situated in the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is "of oneself" because doubt has the self as its object.
For another person's doubt does not require being severed by that other person such that it would need to be qualified as "one's own"; therefore,
even a doubt concerning oneself belongs to oneself alone.
Having cut asunder this doubt, which has become the cause of your own destruction, practice yoga—the performance of action that is the means to right vision; this is the meaning.
"Arise now for battle, O Bhārata! (BhG 4.42).

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher of the Paramahaṃsa order. //4//
Bhagavad Gītā 5:
Now begins the fifth chapter (Śaṅkara-bhāṣya).
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions and again you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better. BhG 5.1.

"You praise—commend and speak in favor of—renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which is the abandonment of ritual actions, specifically those special duties enjoined by the scriptures; yet you also praise yoga, which is the necessary performance of those very same actions. Therefore, I have a doubt as to which is better for me: is the performance of action superior?"
Or rather, what is that abandonment?
It is that which should be practiced as more praiseworthy.

And therefore, regarding these two—renunciation of action and the yoga of action—you think: "That which is better, more praiseworthy, between these two, by the practice of which I might attain the highest good."
Since it is impossible for both of these to be practiced by a single person simultaneously, tell me with certainty which one among them is your preferred choice.
— o)O(o—
Declaring His own intention for the sake of a definitive conclusion, the Blessed Lord said:
"Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good."
But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.

Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the abandonment of actions, and Karma-yoga is their performance; both of these bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), that is, they effect liberation by being causes for the arising of knowledge.
Although both are causes of the supreme good, nevertheless, between those two causes of the supreme good, Karma-yoga is superior to mere renunciation of action; thus [the Lord] praises Karma-yoga.
To the question "Why?", he says:
He who neither hates nor desires should be known as a perpetual renunciant.
For one who is free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is easily liberated from bondage.
He should be known as a karma-yogin and a perpetual renunciant— he who hates nothing and desires neither pain nor pleasure, nor the means to achieve them.
The meaning is that such a person, even while engaged in action, is to be understood as a perpetual renunciant.
For one who is free from the pairs of opposites and devoid of dualities, O mighty-armed one, is easily released from bondage without effort.

—o)O(o— Since renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and karma-yoga are to be practiced by different persons and are mutually contradictory, it would logically follow that there must also be a contradiction regarding their results; however, it might be argued that both lead only to the highest good (niḥśreyasa). To this, the following is said:
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
even by being established in one correctly, one obtains the fruit of both.
The ignorant, not the wise, declare Sāṃkhya and Yoga to be separate and having contradictory, distinct results;

however, the wise, who possess knowledge, maintain that their result is one and non-contradictory. How so? Because even though there is only one [result], one who is "well-established" in both Sāṃkhya and Yoga—that is, one who has practiced them correctly—[attains it].
Both obtain the fruit; for that very same fruit of the supreme good belongs to both. Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the fruit.

[Objection: But having introduced the topic with the terms "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) and "karma-yoga," why does he here state the identity of the fruits of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which was not the subject under discussion?

[Response: This is not a fault; for although Arjuna posed his question referring solely to renunciation and karma-yoga, the Blessed Lord, without abandoning those very topics, gave his reply by employing different terminology—namely "Sāṃkhya" and "Yoga"—while incorporating the specific distinction intended by Himself.

It is the Blessed One’s view that those very two—renunciation and the yoga of action—when conjoined with knowledge, its means, equanimity of intellect, and so forth, are denoted by the terms "Sāṃkhya" and "Yoga.
Therefore, there is no introduction of an irrelevant subject.
—o)O(o— How does one obtain the fruit of both by the correct practice of even one? It is said:
"The state which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas is also reached by the Yogins."
He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one—he truly sees.

That state known as liberation which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas— those renunciants established in knowledge— is also attained by the Yogas; those who, having offered their actions to the Lord as a means for attaining knowledge and without desiring the fruits for themselves, perform [their duties], are the Yogas, the practitioners of yoga.
The intention is that even by them [the followers of Yoga], one goes [to the goal] by means of attaining the renunciation of action through the knowledge of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-jñāna).
Therefore, he who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one because their fruits are identical—he sees correctly; this is the meaning. // BhG 5.5 //
—o)O(o—If that is so, then renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) alone is superior because of its connection with yoga.
How then is this stated: "But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action" (Gītā 5.2)?

Listen to the reason for this: you asked which of the two—renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) or the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*)—is superior, referring only to those two as they are commonly understood. In response to that, I stated that "the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action" without regard to knowledge.
However, when dependent upon knowledge, renunciation is what I intended by the term *sāṃkhya*.
And that alone is the yoga of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-yoga).
As for the Vedic yoga of action (karma-yoga), because it has that [ultimate truth] as its purpose, it is figuratively designated as "yoga" and "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa).
How is it that it has that as its purpose? It is said:
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman before long.
But absolute renunciation is difficult to attain—that is, to reach—without yoga, meaning without the practice of yoga.
A sage (*muni*) is one who is joined with yoga; that is, joined with Vedic *karma-yoga* in the form of action dedicated to the Lord, performed without regard for results.
He is called a sage because he contemplates (*manana*) the true nature of the Lord.

Because it is characterized by steadfastness in the knowledge of Brahman as the Supreme Self, the renunciation under discussion is called "Brahman. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Renunciation is Brahman; for Brahman is the Supreme. He attains—that is, reaches—Brahman, which is the ultimate renunciation characterized by steadfastness in the knowledge of the supreme reality, before long, that is, very quickly.
Therefore, I have said that the yoga of action is superior. (BhG 5.6)
Furthermore, when one is thus disciplined in yoga as the means for attaining right vision— purified in self, having conquered the self, and mastered the senses—
Having become the self of all beings, even while acting, he is not tainted.

One who is joined with yoga— meaning one disciplined in yoga— is a pure self, one whose being is purified, one who has conquered the self, one who has mastered the body, and one who has subdued the senses; and he whose self has become the self of all beings— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— is "one whose self has become the self of all beings," which means he is a seer of reality (samyag-darśin).
Acting in this manner, even while performing action for the sake of gathering people to himself, he is not tainted; the meaning is that he is not bound by actions. (BhG 5.7)
— o)O(o —
And since he does not act from the perspective of ultimate reality, therefore the knower of truth should rightly think: "I do nothing at all."
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing;
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, and even closing them—
he should maintain the conviction that it is the senses alone that operate among the objects of the senses.
Being disciplined and concentrated, he should reflect—that is, he should contemplate.
A "knower of reality" (*tattva-vid*) is one who knows the reality (*tattva*) of the self's true nature; the meaning is that he is a seer of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
When or how does he, ascertaining reality, reflect? To this it is said:
The word "should think" (manyeta) is to be connected with what precedes.

For that knower of reality who thus perceives only inaction even in actions— the activities of all the organs of action— being one of right vision, his qualification is solely for the renunciation of all works, because he perceives the non-existence of action.

For one who has set out to drink water from a mirage with the cognition that it is water does not, even upon knowing the absence of water there, continue to act for the purpose of drinking in that very place.
But he who, on the other hand, does not know the Truth yet is engaged in the yoga of action— he who performs actions by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment— [is superior].
He is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

Having placed [the mind] in Brahman and having surrendered it to the Lord, thinking "I perform action for His sake," he who performs all actions like a servant for the sake of his master—having abandoned attachment even to the fruit of liberation—is not smeared by sin; he is not bound, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (BhG 5.10)
—o)O(o—The fruit of that action would be merely the purification of the *sattva* alone; for it is said:
"By means of the body, the mind, the intellect, and even by the senses alone..."
Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

With the body, the physical frame, the mind, and the intellect—each being purely devoid of the sense of "mine"—one performs action for the Lord alone, thinking, "Not for my own fruit"; thus, even with the senses, one acts while empty of the notion of "mine. The word "purely" (*kevala*) is connected individually with each term, beginning with the body, in order to exclude the sense of ownership in all activities.
Yogis who are performers of action perform their work, having abandoned attachment to its fruits, for the sake of self-purification—that is, for the purification of the mind (sattva).
Therefore, since your qualification lies in that very sphere, perform action alone. (BhG 5.11)
And because:
"The disciplined one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains the peace that is final."
One who acts impelled by desire, being attached to the fruit, becomes bound.

Being thus composed, thinking "I perform action for the sake of the Lord, not for the sake of my own fruit," and having abandoned— that is, relinquished— the fruit of action, he attains peace known as liberation; that is, he attains the final state (*naiṣṭhikīṃ*) which exists in the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhāyāṃ bhavāṃ*), according to the sequence of purification of being, attainment of knowledge, renunciation of all actions, and steadfastness in knowledge— this is the remainder of the sentence.
Furthermore, one who is undisciplined and unconcentrated acts according to his own desire.
"Kāra" means acting; "kāma-kāra" means acting according to desire.
By that "kāma-kāra"—the meaning is: by being impelled by desire.
Thinking, "I perform this action for the sake of my own fruit," one who is thus attached to the fruit becomes bound;
therefore, the meaning is that you should be disciplined (yukta). (BhG 5.12)
But he who perceives the ultimate reality—
he, having renounced all actions with his mind, remains happily as a master of himself.
The embodied self in this city of nine gates neither acts nor causes action to be done.

"Having renounced all actions"— that is, having completely abandoned all actions, whether they be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), or prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*). The meaning is that one abandons all those actions with the mind through the intellect of discernment, by perceiving the absence of action within action and so forth.
He sits, he remains in happiness.

Having abandoned the activities of speech, mind, and body, free from exertion, with a serene mind, and having turned away from all external purposes other than the Self—he is said to "sit in happiness.
"The master" means one who has conquered the senses.
Where and how does he dwell? To this he says: "In the city with nine gates. There are seven openings on the head which are the gateways for the self's perception.
Two openings below are for the discharge of urine and feces;
