with these doors, the city called the body is said to have nine gates, being like a city with a single sovereign, the Self.
And that city is presided over, as it were, by citizens—namely, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, along with their objects and purposes—which produce cognitions of manifold fruits.
In that city of nine gates, the embodied self remains, having renounced all action.
Why specify this further?
"For every embodied being—whether a renunciant or a non-renunciant—dwells in the body alone;
therefore, the qualification [of 'renunciant'] is useless.

To this it is replied: "But that ignorant embodied being who perceives the self as consisting merely of the aggregate of the body and the senses, thinks 'I am sitting' whether in a house, on the ground, or on a seat."
For one who perceives the self as consisting of the body alone, the notion "I sit" with respect to the body is not possible, just as it would not be in the case of a house.
However, for one who perceives the self as distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, the notion "I sit" in the body is indeed appropriate.

Furthermore, the mental renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the actions of others—which have been superimposed upon the supreme Self through ignorance—is possible by means of knowledge, that is, through discriminative wisdom.

For one who has attained the knowledge of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*) and has renounced all ritual actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsī*), even though he is like a householder, his seat is indeed in the city of the body with its nine gates;
for as long as the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of karma whose fruits have already begun (*prārabdha-phala*) persist, specific cognition (*viśeṣa-vijñāna*) arises only within the body.
Thus, the qualification "dwells in the body" does indeed serve a purpose, since it depends on the distinction between the perceptions of the knower and the ignorant.

Although it has been stated that one remains having renounced the body, the organs, and actions—which have been superimposed upon the Self through ignorance—nevertheless, one might suspect that agency and causality could still be inherent in the Self; anticipating this, he says: "Neither acting himself, nor causing the body and organs to act—that is, not setting them in motion toward activities.
Why? Because that agency and causality which belongs to the embodied being, if it were inherent in its own nature, would not be possible through renunciation.
Is it as with a moving object, where motion would not exist upon the cessation of the activity of going? Or is it that agency does not belong to the self by its own nature?
To this it is replied: the self possesses neither agency nor causality by its own nature.
For it has been said: "This is declared to be unchangeable" (Gītā 2.25), and "Though situated in the body, O son of Kuntī, it neither acts nor is tainted" (Gītā 3.26);
and also from the Śruti: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7). // BhG 5.13 //
Moreover:
"The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world."
But it is nature that proceeds toward the connection with the fruits of action.
The Lord, the Self, does not by itself act, saying "do," nor does it create or produce for the world the most desired objects of action such as chariots, jars, or palaces;
nor does it bring about the connection with the fruit of the action for one who has made a chariot or the like—that is, the connection with the result of action.
If the embodied soul does not do anything at all by itself, nor cause anything to be done, [how can there be agency?]
What then is it that, acting and causing others to act, brings about this activity?

It is said: "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) means one's own being; it is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) characterized by ignorance, which is *māyā*. This will be explained in the passage beginning with, "For it is divine" (*Gītā* 7.14).
— o)O(o—
But from the perspective of ultimate truth,
the All-pervading Lord does not take on the sin or even the merit of anyone.
Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.

The All-pervading Lord neither takes nor accepts the sin of anyone, even of His devotee; nor does He accept the merit performed by His devotees. If so, for what purpose is merit—consisting of worship, sacrifice, charity, fire-offerings, and so forth—performed by devotees? To this He says: "Knowledge"—that is, discriminative wisdom—is covered by ignorance.
Because of that, undiscriminating transmigrating beings fall into delusion, thinking, "I do," "I cause to be done," "I shall eat," and "I cause to be eaten. Thus they go to delusion. (BhG 5.15)
But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge, like the sun, reveals that which is beyond. (BhG 5.16)

But by that knowledge with which [ignorance] has been destroyed by the discriminative knowledge concerning the Self, those living beings who were deluded because they were shrouded by ignorance—for those beings, that knowledge, like the sun, illuminates all objects of knowledge; that is the supreme reality, the ultimate truth. —o)O(o—
Those whose intellects are absorbed in that supreme knowledge which has been revealed, whose very selves are that, who are established in that, and who have that as their ultimate goal—
having shaken off all impurities by means of knowledge— they go to the state from which there is no return.
Those whose intellect has gone into that Brahman are "tad-buddhayaḥ";
those for whom that very Supreme Brahman is the Self are "tad-ātmānaḥ";
and those whose steadfastness—meaning firm adherence and intentness—is upon that [Brahman] after having renounced all actions, remaining established in that very Brahman, are "tan-niṣṭhāḥ."

And those for whom that alone is the supreme resort—that is, the highest goal and ultimate destination—are "those whose resort is that" (*tat-parāyaṇāḥ*); the meaning is that they find delight solely in the Self.
Those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge—such persons of true wisdom go to non-return, which is the absence of further connection with a body;
for their taint has been shaken off by knowledge, meaning the defect that causes saṃsāra, such as sin and so forth, has been shaken off or destroyed by the aforementioned knowledge.
The meaning is: those ascetics whose impurities have been shaken off by that knowledge.
— o)O(o—
Regarding those whose ignorance of the Self has been destroyed by knowledge, it is said how those wise ones perceive reality:
"In a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant..."
The wise perceive with an equal vision toward both a dog and an outcaste.

In one endowed with knowledge and discipline— where "knowledge and discipline" (*vidyā-vinaya*) means both knowledge and discipline, and discipline (*vinaya*) is restraint— one who is thus endowed with those two, being both learned and disciplined, whether it be a Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, or even an outcaste (*śvapāka*).
The wise perceive with equanimity:
toward a sattvic brahmin who is endowed with learning and discipline and possessed of the highest refinement,
and toward a rājasic cow of middling quality.

Those whose nature it is to perceive that Brahman— which is utterly untouched by the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, as well as by the impressions (*saṃskāras*) born of them, and likewise by *rājasa* and *tāmasa* impressions— in its absolute state of pure isolation within that which is devoid of impressions, such as elephants and the like, being equal, one, and changeless; they are the wise.
Those who perceive with equanimity.

— o)O(o)— But surely they are unworthy of whose food one may not eat, for they are possessed of faults, according to the traditional law (smṛti): "From the equal and the unequal, the unequal and the equal [are distinguished] by virtue of their reception of honor" (Gautama-dharma-sūtra 2.8.20).
They are not possessed of faults. How so?—“For those whose minds are established in equanimity have already conquered rebirth even here.
For Brahman is indeed faultless and equal; therefore, they are established in Brahman. (BhG 5.19)
Even while still living in this very world, those wise ones who possess equal vision have conquered— that is, brought to an end— the cycle of birth (sarga),

they whose minds (the internal organ) are established in equanimity toward all beings, remaining motionless within Brahman; for although it is faultless, their mind is perceived by the deluded as if it were possessed of faults when directed toward those who are faulty, such as the wicked and the like.
Nevertheless, it is "untouched by those defects," meaning it is faultless and devoid of defects;
for consciousness is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and is therefore not divided by differences among its own qualities.
And the Blessed One will state that desire and the other [afflictions] are properties of the field (*kṣetra*), because they are beginningless and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Nor do the ultimate particularities (*viśeṣa*) exist as differentiators of the self (*ātman*).
Since no valid means of knowledge can establish their existence as distinct from each body,
Brahman is therefore uniform and one;
thus, they are established in Brahman alone.
Therefore, not even a trace of fault touches them, because they lack the conceit of viewing the aggregate of the body and so forth as the self;
for [the notion of "I"] has as its object the conceit of viewing the aggregate of the body and so forth as the self.
But that sūtra— “The unequal and the equal [are distinguished] by means of the unequal and the equal, on account of worship”— is due to the qualification [of the recipient] as an object of worship;

for it is observed that in the case of giving gifts and performing worship, the connection with specific qualities, such as "one who knows the Veda," "one who knows the six auxiliary limbs," or "one who knows the four Vedas," is the cause [of distinction].
But since Brahman is free from connection with all qualities and defects, it is logical that "they are established in Brahman.
Furthermore, while [the rule] beginning with "by the equal and the unequal" refers to the sphere of ritual action (*karma*),
this present context concerns the renunciation of all actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*).
"Having begun with 'all actions by means of the mind,' [this continues] until the end of the chapter. (BhG 5.19)
— o)O(o— Since Brahman, the Self, is faultless and equanimous, therefore:
one should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor should one be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant.
Steady in intellect, undeluded, the knower of Brahman abides in Brahman.
One should not rejoice—that is, one should not feel elation—upon obtaining or attaining something pleasant and desired;
nor should one be agitated upon obtaining or encountering something unpleasant and undesired.
For it is only those who perceive the self as consisting merely of the body that experience joy and dejection upon the acquisition of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
This is not only because for one who perceives the Self,
the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant is impossible;
furthermore, it is for one whose intellect is firm and free from doubt, [realizing] that the one Self is the same and faultless in all beings.

He would be steady-minded, undeluded, and free from delusion; he is a knower of Brahman as described, established in Brahman, and a non-performer of action—meaning one who has renounced all actions. (BhG 5.20)
Furthermore: Established in Brahman,
with his self unattached to external contacts, he finds that happiness which is in the Self.
With his self united through yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.

Regarding "external contacts" (*bāhya-sparśeṣu*): they are external and they are contacts, hence "external contacts. They are called "contacts" (*sparśāḥ*) because they are touched; these are the objects such as sound and the rest. In those external contacts, he whose self—that is, his internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*)—is unattached is "one whose self is unattached" (*asaktātmā*). Being devoid of delight in sense-objects, he finds or attains [peace].

"He finds that happiness which is in the Self"—this is what is meant. "With his self united through yoga with Brahman": yoga with Brahman is *samādhi*; one whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the self—is joined, concentrated, and occupied with that yoga of Brahman is "one whose self is united through yoga with Brahman."
One enjoys—that is, pervades—imperishable happiness.
Therefore, one who desires imperishable happiness within the self should withdraw the senses from the fleeting pleasure of external objects; this is the meaning. (BhG 5.21)
— o)O(o—
And for this reason, one should turn away from them: "For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the very source of suffering."
O son of Kuntī, they have a beginning and an end; the wise man does not delight in them.

For since those enjoyments— that is, experiences— born of contact arise from the contact between the sense organs and their objects, they are indeed sources of suffering, because they are produced by ignorance;
for internal and other forms of suffering are seen to have precisely those [enjoyments] as their cause.
From the word "eva" (only/just), it is understood that as it is in this world, so it is in the next world as well.
Having realized that not even a mere scent of happiness exists in saṃsāra, one should withdraw the senses from the mirage of sensory objects;
for they are not merely sources of suffering.
And they have a beginning and an end;
for the beginning of enjoyments is the contact between the sense organs and their objects, and the end is precisely the separation from them.
Therefore, having a beginning and an end, they are impermanent.
The meaning is: because they exist only for a middle moment.
O Kaunteya, the wise person—the discerning one who has realized the reality of the supreme truth—does not delight in those enjoyments;
for delight in sense objects is seen only among the utterly deluded.
Just as in the case of cattle and other such beings. (BhGS 5.22)

—o)O(o— This fault, which is the adversary of the path to the highest good, is the most grievous, the cause for the attainment of all misfortune, and difficult to ward off; therefore, one must exert great effort toward its avoidance. Thus the Blessed One said:
"He who is able to endure [the body] even here, prior to liberation from the body..."
He who restrains the impulse arising from desire and anger is a disciplined man; he is happy.
He who is able—that is, capable—of enduring and withstanding [the impulse] even while living here, prior to the release of the body, meaning until death;

the setting of death as the limit is because the surge arising from desire and anger is inevitable for one who lives, for it has infinite causes; the meaning is that as long as there is death, one must not feel secure.

Desire (*kāma*) is that thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) which arises toward a pleasant object—whether it be currently perceived through the senses, heard, remembered, or previously experienced—that is a cause of happiness.
Anger (*krodha*) is that aversion (*dveṣa*) toward things that are disagreeable to oneself—causes of suffering—which are being seen, heard, or remembered.
The impulse (*vega*) from which those two, desire and anger, arise is called the "impulse born of desire and anger" (*kāma-krodhodbhavo vegaḥ*).
The impulse arising from desire is characterized by signs such as horripilation and eyes and face beaming with joy, and consists of an agitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The impulse arising from anger is characterized by signs such as trembling of the limbs, perspiration, biting the lips, and bloodshot eyes. He who is able—that is, capable—to endure, to withstand, that impulse born of desire and anger; [he is a sage].
Thus disciplined, that man is a yogi and is happy in this world.
"And in what state, established in Brahman, does one attain Brahman? To this, the Blessed One said:
He who finds happiness within, whose recreation is within, and likewise whose light is solely within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction that is Brahman.

He who has happiness within is "one whose happiness is internal" (*antaḥsukha*); likewise, he whose delight, pleasure, or play is only within the self is "one whose delight is internal" (*antarārāma*).
Similarly, he whose light or illumination is only within the self is "one whose light is internal" (*antarjyotis*).
Such a yogi, having become Brahman while still living here, attains—that is, reaches—the extinction in Brahman, the bliss in Brahman, which is liberation. //BhGS_5.24//
Furthermore: The seers whose taints are exhausted attain the Brahman-nirvana.
With their doubts severed, self-restrained, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

The sages who possess right vision, who have renounced the world, whose impurities are exhausted, whose sins are destroyed, who are faultless, whose doubts are severed, whose perplexity is gone, who are self-controlled, whose senses are restrained, and who delight in the welfare of all beings— meaning they are devoted to the well-being and favor of all creatures and are non-violent— attain the liberation of Brahman-Nirvāṇa. (BhG 5.25)
Furthermore: For ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained—
For those who have realized the Self, the state of Brahman and Nirvana exists on all sides.

For those ascetics and renunciants who are free from desire and anger—desire and anger being "kāma-krodhau," and they are free from these two—who have restrained their minds, that is, whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are controlled; for such persons who have known the Self—that is, those by whom the Self has been realized—they possess the extinction into Brahman, which is liberation, both while living and after death. "Those who have known the Self" means those by whom the Self has been understood and realized.
The meaning is: of those who have realized the Self, that is, those who possess right vision. (BhG 5.26)

-o)O(o- It has been stated that for renunciants established in right vision (*samyag-darśana*), there is immediate liberation. Furthermore, Karma-yoga— performed by dedicating all states of being to the Lord, Brahman, with the thought "I act for the sake of the Lord"— leads to liberation through the sequence of purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), attainment of knowledge (*jñāna-prāpti*), and renunciation of all actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*).
The Blessed One has spoken [on this] at every step and will speak [further];

now, intending to explain in detail the yoga of meditation (dhyāna-yoga), which is the internal means for right vision (samyag-darśana), he taught these verses that serve as the aphorisms (sūtra) for it:
Having cast external objects outside and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils; BhG 5.27.
The sage whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, who is intent on liberation, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is indeed always liberated. (BhG 5.28)

Having made external contacts—namely, sounds and the rest—which are objects such as sound that have entered into the internal intellect through the doors of the ears and so forth, one does not think about them; thus, those external sounds and the rest are truly kept outside.
Having thus placed them outside, the phrase "and having placed the eyes between the eyebrows" is to be supplied [from the preceding verse].
Likewise, having made equal the prāṇa and apāna breaths moving within the nostrils;
"one whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained" (yatendriya-manobuddhiḥ) means one by whom the senses, the mind, and the intellect are restrained (yatāni = saṃyatāni);
he is a sage (muniḥ) because of his contemplation (mananāt), that is, a renunciant (saṃnyāsī).

Thus, one who is solely intent on liberation—meaning a sage for whom liberation alone is the supreme goal (*ayana*) and the ultimate resort (*parā gati*)—should become one whose desire, fear, and anger have vanished;
that is, one from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed.
Such a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) is one who always conducts himself in this manner.
He is already liberated;
for him, no further liberation needs to be accomplished.
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. (BhG 5.29)
It is now stated what is to be known by one whose mind is thus concentrated:
the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity—in the form of the agent of sacrifices and the form of the deity;
the great Lord of all worlds, the supreme ruler of all worlds; and the friend of all beings, of all living creatures.

Knowing Me as Nārāyaṇa— the benefactor who is indifferent to any return favor, who dwells in the hearts of all beings, who is the presiding authority over the fruits of all actions, and the witness of all conditions— one attains peace, which is the cessation of the entire cycle of worldly existence.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant and teacher of the supreme state of liberation. //5//
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Six (The Commentary of Śaṅkarācārya)

At the end of the immediately preceding chapter, the verses beginning with "Having cast out contacts externally" (Gītā 5.27) were taught as aphorisms for the yoga of meditation (*dhyāna-yoga*), which is an internal means toward right vision (*samyag-darśana*). This sixth chapter is now commenced as a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon those aphorisms.

In this regard, since action is an external limb of the yoga of meditation, and since action must be performed by the qualified householder until he becomes capable of ascending to the yoga of meditation, the Lord praises that action here.

Now, for what purpose is this establishment of a limit for ascending to the yoga of meditation? For is it not the case that prescribed action must simply be performed as long as one lives? No; because of the specific qualification: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means" (Gītā 3.3).
Furthermore, because the connection is made only with tranquility (*śama*) for one who has already ascended,

if both tranquility and action were intended as duties for both the seeker of ascent and the one who has ascended, then the qualification by way of the distinction between the objects of tranquility and action— namely, "for the seeker of ascent" and "for the one who has ascended"—
as well as the making of this division, would be purposeless.
Among those belonging to the stages of life (āśramin), some are desirous of ascending to yoga,
some have already ascended, and others are not desirous of ascending.

If it is argued that those who have not yet climbed are excluded, and that— relative to them— the distinction and the assignment of the qualifiers "one who wishes to climb" and "one who has climbed" are indeed appropriate, we say no;
for this is because of the statement "of that very [person]."
Furthermore, because of the mention of "yoga" [in the previous verse], it is said that for one who has already ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*)—
that is, for the very same person who previously desired to ascend to yoga— tranquility (*śama*) alone is to be practiced;
this is stated as the reason for the fruit of yoga.
Therefore, there is no obligation for anyone to perform any action throughout their entire life;
this is also because of the statement regarding one who has fallen away from yoga.
Furthermore, if yoga were prescribed for a householder who is a performer of ritual actions in the sixth chapter, [it would contradict the present teaching].
Even for one who has fallen away from yoga, since he attains the course of action and the fruit of action, the apprehension of his destruction would be untenable.

For an action that has been performed—whether optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*)—necessarily initiates its own fruit, since liberation is eternal and thus not something to be newly produced. Furthermore, we have already stated that because an obligatory action is known through the authority of the Veda, it must necessarily have a fruit.
Otherwise, it would follow that the Veda has no purposeful meaning.
Furthermore, the statement regarding "falling away from both" would not be meaningful if ritual action existed,
because there would be no possible cause for such a falling away from action.
If it is argued that because one has surrendered the performed action to the Lord, the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent, we say no;
for it is logical that surrendering [the action] to the Lord is a cause for even greater fruit.
If it is argued that this is solely for the sake of liberation, [we reply: no.
If it is argued that the dedication of one's performed actions to the Lord, when accompanied by yoga, leads only to liberation and not to any other fruit—
and therefore, since he has fallen away from yoga, the apprehension of his destruction is indeed appropriate— [the answer is] no.

This is because of the injunction for the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) in such passages as "solitary, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and possessions" (Gītā 6.10) and "established in the vow of celibacy" (Gītā 6.14). Furthermore, statements such as "free from desire and possessions" would not be appropriate for a householder;
moreover, the question regarding one who has fallen away from both [paths] would otherwise be logically untenable.

If it be argued that by the word "unsupported" (anāśrita), the status of being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) and a yogi is stated for the ritualist alone, and that the status of being a renunciant and a yogi is thereby prohibited for one who maintains no sacred fires and performs no action, we say: no;
because the intent is to praise the renunciation of the desire for fruits of action, which is an external limb (bahiraṅga) with respect to the yoga of meditation.
A renunciant and a yogi are not merely one who is without fire and without action; rather, even one who performs action is so,
provided he has renounced attachment to the fruits of action and practices the yoga of action for the sake of purifying his being.
He is praised as being both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi.

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single sentence to simultaneously offer praise for the renunciation of attachment to the fruits of action and the prohibition of the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*).

Nor does it deny the well-known status of renunciation and yoga—which is prescribed for the ultimate renunciant who is without fire and without ritual action—in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Yoga-śāstras.

The Blessed One [has spoken thus], and because of the contradiction with his own words: "Having renounced all actions with the mind... he remains neither acting nor causing to act" (Gītā 5.13); "silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady-minded" (Gītā 12.19).

The Blessed One has shown his own words in various places, such as: "The man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing" (Gītā 2.71) and "one who renounces all undertakings" (Gītā 12.16).
A prohibition against the fourth stage of life would contradict these.

Therefore, for the sage who desires to ascend to yoga and has entered the state of a householder, the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*, when carried out without regard for their fruits, serves as a means for ascending to the yoga of meditation by way of purifying the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*).
Thus, he is praised as both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi.

He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not one who merely maintains no sacred fires, nor one who merely abstains from action.

"Unattached" (*anāśrita*) means not attached (*na āśritaḥ*). To what? To the fruit of action (*karma-phalam*), that is, the result of actions; he is unattached to that. The meaning is that he is free from craving for the fruits of action.
For whoever possesses craving for the fruit of action becomes dependent upon that fruit of action;
this one, however, is the opposite of that,
and is therefore not dependent upon the fruit of action.
Being thus constituted, he performs—that is, carries out—the obligatory duty that must be done, which is the opposite of optional rites such as the Agnihotra and the like.
Any such practitioner of action (karmī) is distinguished from other practitioners of action;
for this reason, it is said: "He is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi."
Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) means abandonment; he who possesses that is both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi.
Yoga is the concentration of the mind; he who possesses that is a yogi. One endowed with such qualities is to be considered [a true renunciant and yogi].
It should not be thought that only one who has abandoned the sacred fires and is inactive is a renunciant and a yogi.
One from whom the fires that constitute the limbs of ritual action have departed is "niragni" (without fire).
And one for whom actions—specifically those rites such as austerity and charity that do not depend on the sacrificial fire—are no longer present, is "akriya" (without action). BhG 6.1.
But surely, it is well known in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Yoga-śāstras that the state of being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) and a yogi belongs only to one who is without fire and without ritual action;
how then can it be said here that the state of being a renunciant and a yogi is [also] established for one who possesses fire and performs ritual action?
This is not a fault.
Because both [states] are intended to be accomplished through a certain figurative application of the term.

How so? He is a *saṃnyāsin* because of his renunciation of the intention for the fruits of action, and he is a *yogin* because of his performance of action as an auxiliary to yoga and because of his abandonment of the intention for the fruits of action, which is a cause of mental distraction; thus, both titles are used in a secondary sense.
However, to show that the primary sense of renunciation and yoga is not intended here, he says:
"Know that which they call renunciation to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogin without having renounced his purposeful intentions. (BhG 6.2)

That which is characterized by the renunciation of all actions and their fruits—the ultimate renunciation (*paramārtha-saṃnyāsa*)—is what those who know the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* call "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*).
Know, O Pāṇḍava, that Yoga, which is characterized by the performance of action, is that very same ultimate renunciation;
for Karma-yoga, which is characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*), is [identical] with that ultimate renunciation characterized by withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).

In response to the inquiry, "Having accepted what kind of similarity is that state [of similarity] being asserted? this is said: Indeed, there is a similarity between Karma-yoga and ultimate renunciation (*paramārtha-saṃnyāsa*) by way of their agent.

For he who is an ultimate renunciant, by virtue of having abandoned all means of action, renounces the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) directed toward all actions and their fruits—the cause of desire which is the motive for worldly engagement.

This practitioner of action (karma-yogin), while indeed performing action, renounces the mental resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding its fruit. Intending to demonstrate this point, He says: "For" (hi)—because no one whatsoever who has not renounced their resolve—that is, whose resolve or intention (abhisandhi) has not been renounced or abandoned—can become a yogin, that is, one possessed of meditative composure (samādhāna). No such practitioner of action can be established in yoga if his purpose remains unrenounced.
The meaning is that it is not possible [to achieve this otherwise],
because the mental resolve for the fruit is a cause of distraction of the mind.
Therefore, any practitioner whatsoever who has renounced the mental resolve for the fruit would be a yogi, possessed of concentration and having an undistracted mind.
The intention is that [he is called a *saṃnyāsī*] because he has renounced the mental resolve for the fruits [of action], which is the cause of distraction of the mind.

Furthermore, because he performs actions as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), or because he has abandoned the mental resolve for the fruits of action—which is the cause of distraction of the mind—he possesses both the state of a yogi and the state of a *saṃnyāsī*. This is what is intended by the term.

Thus, with reference to the commonality of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) based on the agent in both ultimate renunciation and the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*), it was stated for the purpose of praising karma-yoga that "know that which they call renunciation to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava" (Gītā 6.2).

Having praised Karma-yoga as being equivalent to renunciation (saṃnyāsa) on the grounds that it is an external means for the Yoga of Meditation (dhyāna-yoga), which is independent of its fruits, [the Lord] now demonstrates that Karma-yoga is the means for attaining Dhyāna-yoga: "For the sage who desires to ascend to Yoga, action is said to be the cause;
for that same person once ascended to Yoga, tranquility is said to be the cause. (BhG 6.3)
The meaning is: for one who desires to ascend— that is, one who wishes to climb but has not yet climbed, being unable to remain established in the yoga of meditation.
Of whom is he who desires to ascend?
Of the sage (muni), meaning one who has renounced the fruits of action. What does he desire to ascend to? Yoga.
Action is said to be the cause, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

However, for one who has ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*), tranquility—that is, peace (*upaśama*) consisting in withdrawal from all actions—is said to be the cause, the means of accomplishment for that very person who has ascended to yoga; this is the meaning.
To the extent that one desists from actions, [to that same extent...]
To that same extent, the mind of one who is free from exertion and has conquered the senses becomes concentrated;
being so, he quickly becomes established in yoga.
And thus it was said by Vyāsa:
There is no wealth for a brahmin such as this: namely, singleness, equanimity, truthfulness, virtue, steadfastness, the laying aside of the rod, and uprightness.
"And then there is cessation from activities.
(Mbh 12.175.37) Now, it is said when one becomes established in yoga:
"When indeed one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions..."
When one has renounced all volitional constructions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.

When the yogi, with his mind being concentrated, does not become attached— meaning he does not form the notion that such attachment is a duty— to the objects of the senses (the sense-objects being sound and so forth) nor to actions, whether they be obligatory, occasional, optional, or prohibited, because he perceives them as being devoid of purpose;

"One who has renounced all mental constructs" (*sarva-saṃkalpa-saṃnyāsī*) means one whose nature is to renounce all mental constructs—the causes of desire for objects pertaining to this world and the next.
"One who has ascended to yoga" (*yogārūḍhaḥ*) means one who has attained yoga; that is what is said at that time.

From the statement "one who has renounced all volitions" (sarva-saṃkalpa-saṃnyāsī), the meaning is that one should renounce all desires and all actions; for all desires have their root in volition—indeed, "desires have volition as their root, sacrifices arise from volition" (Manu 2.3), and "O Desire, I know your root; you are born indeed from volition."
I shall not form a conceptualization of you; therefore, you shall not exist for me.
This is because of such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as [Mahābhārata 12.177.25].

Furthermore, when all desires are abandoned, the renunciation of all actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*) is established, according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as: "As is one's desire, so is one's resolve; as is one's resolve, so is the action one performs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).

This is also evident from such Smṛti texts as, "Whatever a living being does, all that is the movement of desire" (Manu 2.4), and by logical reasoning as well—for indeed, if one were to renounce all volitions, one would not even be capable of moving a limb.
Therefore, by the statement "one who has renounced all volitions," the Blessed One causes one to abandon all desires and all actions. (BhG 6.4)
When one has thus ascended to yoga, then by that means the self is uplifted from the cycle of existence, which is a mass of misfortunes. Therefore:
"One should uplift the self by means of the self; one should not let the self sink."
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

He should lift up his own self, which is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; "from there" means he should raise it upward, bring it to the state of being established in yoga—this is the meaning. He should not cause himself to sink, nor lead himself downward.
One should not cause oneself to go downward;
for the self alone is the friend of the self,
since there is no other friend whatsoever.
Even a kinsman, though he may exist for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, is actually adverse to liberation,
because he is a locus for the bonds of affection and the like.
Therefore, the restriction is appropriate: "The self alone is indeed the friend of the self.
The self alone is the enemy;
even that external enemy who causes harm is one instigated by the self itself. Thus, the restriction that "the self alone is the enemy of the self" is indeed logical.
It has been said: "The self alone is the friend, the self alone is the enemy of the self.
In this regard, it is now explained: what are the characteristics of the self that is the friend of the self, and what are the characteristics of the self that is the enemy of the self?
The self is the friend of that self by whom the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would act as an enemy, like an enemy.
The self is the friend of that self;
that self is the friend of the self by whom the very self has been conquered—
that aggregate of causes and effects (the body) has been brought under control by him.

The meaning is "one who has conquered the senses. However, for one who lacks self-control—that is, for one whose self is unconquered—the self itself would exist in the state of an enemy, in the condition of being an adversary;
just as an external enemy is harmful to oneself, so too would the self act as an enemy.
The meaning is that the self would thus act to its own detriment.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is fully concentrated within, amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor. (BhG 6.7)

For one who has conquered the self—that is, for that renunciant whose self (the aggregate of the body and senses) has been conquered and who is tranquil, meaning whose internal organ is serene—the Supreme Self remains concentrated, existing in the state of being his very own Self; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he should remain the same amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as in honor and dishonor—that is, in respect and humiliation.
One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is steadfast and has conquered the senses,
for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same— he is called a yogi who is disciplined.

One whose self (the internal organ) is satisfied by knowledge and realization: "knowledge" (jñāna) is the thorough understanding of the categories of things as taught in the scriptures, while "realization" (vijñāna) is the personal experiential verification of those very things known through the scriptures; he whose self (antaḥkaraṇa) has become satisfied—having attained the sense of "enough"—by means of both that knowledge and realization is one whose self is satisfied by knowledge and realization.
The meaning is that he becomes immovable like a peak,
and one who has conquered the senses.
One who is such as this is said, or described, as "yukta," meaning "concentrated.
That yogi is one for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal; he is one to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same—such is the "sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcana.
Furthermore—
One who possesses an equal mind toward friends, allies, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen— and even toward the virtuous and the wicked— is preeminent.
The half-verse beginning with "suhṛd" constitutes a single compound word.
"Suhṛd" refers to one who benefits others without expecting a return; "mitra" refers to one who possesses affection.
An *ari* is an enemy;
one who is indifferent (*udāsīna*) does not take the side of anyone;
and one who is neutral (*madhyastha*) is a well-wisher of both opposing parties.
"An enemy" is one who is unpleasant to oneself;
"a kinsman" is a relative. Toward all these—whether they be virtuous followers of the scriptures, or even the wicked who perform prohibited acts—one should have an equal mind.
The meaning is that one's mind should not be preoccupied with such thoughts as "Who is this? or "What is his action?"
"Is distinguished," or "is liberated"—these are alternative readings.
The meaning is that he is the best among all those who have ascended to yoga.
Precisely for this reason, in order to attain such a supreme fruit—
The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline himself. (BhG 6.10)

The yogi, a meditator, should constantly and at all times yoke—that is, concentrate—his self, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while staying alone and without companion in a secluded place such as a mountain cave;
by the qualifying terms "staying in seclusion" and "alone," the meaning is that he should do so after having renounced worldly life.
One whose mind and body are restrained is called *yata-cittātmā*; here, "mind" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and "self" refers to the physical body.
"Free from desire" means one whose thirst has departed; "without possessions" means being devoid of all things held as one's own.
Even while being a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), the meaning is that one should practice yoga having abandoned all possessions.
Now, for one who is practicing yoga, the rules regarding posture, diet, conduct, and so forth must be stated as the means for achieving yoga.
The characteristics of one who has attained yoga, as well as its fruits and so forth, are now commenced;
therein, the posture (āsana) itself is first described:
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other— BhG 6.11.
Having established for oneself a firm and motionless seat in a place that is clean, pure, and secluded by nature or through refinement— a seat that is neither too high nor too low,
and which has cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass as its upper layers— that is, a seat upon which cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass are placed one above the other.
In this case, the sequence of the cloth and the other items is the reverse of the order in which they are mentioned.
Having established [the image], what then? Having made the mind one-pointed therein, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained.
Sitting on his seat, he should practice yoga for the purification of the self.
Having sat down there on that seat, one should practice yoga.

How? Having withdrawn [the mind] from all objects and having made the mind one-pointed, one whose activities of the mind and senses are restrained—meaning, he for whom the activities (*kriyā*) of the mind and the senses (*cittendriya*) are controlled—is "one whose activities of the mind and senses are restrained."
For what purpose should he practice yoga? To this he says: "for the purification of the self," that is, for the sake of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The external seat has been described;
now it is stated how the body is to be supported:
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady,
gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction— BhG 6.13.
"Body, head, and neck" refers to the body, the head, and the neck; holding these straight and motionless—
since movement can occur even for one who holds them straight— the text specifies "motionless" (*acalam*) to exclude that possibility.
"Steadfast" means having become steady.
"Having gazed at the tip of his own nose" means having performed a thorough looking or seeing;
the word "iva" (as if) should be understood as elided.

For it is not the gazing at the tip of one's own nose that is intended here; what then? It is the convergence of the vision of the eyes, and that is intended as being dependent upon the concentration of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
If the intention were merely to look at the tip of one's own nose, the mind should be concentrated on that alone, not on the Self.
For the author will later state that the mind is to be concentrated on the Self, saying, "having made the mind established in the Self."

Therefore, by the elision of the word "iva" (as if), the very meeting of the gaze of the eyes is called "looking intently. This means not looking at the quarters, that is, maintaining one's gaze between the directions.
Furthermore—
With a tranquil self, free from fear, and established in the vow of celibate studentship,
one should sit disciplined, with the mind restrained, the heart fixed on Me, and intent upon Me as the supreme goal.
One whose inner organ (ātman) is profoundly tranquil is "praśāntātmā";
one who is free from fear is "vigatabhīḥ";
and one who stands firm in the vow of celibacy is "brahmacārivratasthaḥ."

"Brahmacarya" is the vow of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), consisting of service to the teacher, eating alms-food, and so forth; "established in that" means he should be a performer of those practices. Furthermore, "having restrained the mind" means having withdrawn the fluctuations of the mind.
"With mind on Me" means one whose mind is fixed on Me, the Supreme Lord; being thus "yoked," that is, composed in meditation, he should sit—that is, remain seated.
"Having Me as the supreme goal" means he for whom I am the highest aim.
A certain person, being lustful and possessing a mind fixed on women,
does not perceive the woman alone as the supreme object;
rather, he perceives the king or a great deity as such.
But this one has his mind fixed on Me and regards Me as the supreme goal.
(BhG 6.14) Now, the fruit of yoga is being described:
Thus constantly engaging the self in yoga, the yogi of restrained mind...
He attains peace, which culminates in Nirvana and is centered in Me.

Practicing yoga and performing concentration in this manner according to the prescribed method, the yogi—whose mind (*mānasa*) is restrained and controlled (*niyata*), meaning his mental faculty is disciplined—attains peace (*śānti*), which culminates in liberation (*nirvāṇa-paramā*); that peace for which liberation is the ultimate goal, which is established in Me (*mat-saṃsthāṃ*), meaning dependent upon Me.
He reaches it; he attains it. (BhG 6.15)

Now, the regulation of food and other matters for the yogin is stated: "But yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all; nor for him who is habituated to excessive sleep, nor for him who is ever awake, O Arjuna. (BhG 6.16)
For one who eats too much—that is, one who eats beyond the measure of food appropriate for oneself—there is no yoga;
nor is there yoga for one who does not eat at all.

As the Śruti declares: "That food which is measured to the self protects it and does not harm it; that which is more than this harms it, and that which is less than this does not protect it. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 9.2.1.2)
Therefore, a yogi should not eat more or less than food measured by his own capacity.

Alternatively, for one who eats in excess of the quantity of food prescribed in the Yoga Śāstra for a yogi, there is no yoga. For it has been said: "One half [of the stomach] should be for food with its condiments, and the third for water."
One should leave the fourth [space] remaining for the purpose of the movement of the wind.
Such is the measure [of time], and so forth.
Likewise: "O Arjuna, yoga does not belong to one who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, nor indeed to one who is excessively awake.
How, then, does yoga come to be? It is said:
For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in performing actions,
and moderate in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
For one whose food and movement are disciplined: "food" (āhāra) is that which is taken in, namely nourishment;
"movement" (vihāra) is the act of moving, namely the stepping of the feet;
he for whom these two are disciplined—that is, regulated in their measure—is "one whose food and movement are disciplined. For such a person...
For one whose activity is thus disciplined— that is, for one whose activities in their duties are constant—
and for one whose sleep and wakefulness are thus disciplined— that is, for one whose sleep and wakefulness are regulated by fixed times—

for such a yogi who is disciplined in food and recreation, disciplined in activity, and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering; it is called the "destroyer of suffering" because it destroys all sufferings.
The meaning is that yoga becomes the destroyer of all the suffering of saṃsāra.
Now, it is said when one becomes united [in yoga]:
"When the well-restrained mind abides in the Self alone..."
When one is free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be disciplined. (BhG 6.18)

When the mind—thoroughly restrained, specifically controlled, disciplined, and having attained one-pointedness—abandons the thought of external objects and abides in the Self alone, meaning it attains stability within its own nature;

and when the yogi is free from longing, such that all desire or thirst for seen and unseen sense-objects has departed from him, then at that time he is said to be "yoked," that is, concentrated. (BhG 6.18)
An analogy is given for that concentrated mind of the yogi:
"As a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker—this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices yoga of the self. (BhG 6.19)

Just as a lamp, well-lit and placed in a windless spot—that is, situated in a place free from wind—does not flicker or move; this is the simile used by those who know yoga and perceive the movements of the mind. It is remembered and contemplated for the yogi whose mind is restrained, whose internal organ is controlled, who is practicing yoga, and who is performing the concentration of the Self.
This is the meaning.

BhG 6.19: When the mind, having become one-pointed through the power of the practice of yoga and resembling a lamp in a windless place, comes to rest—restrained by the cultivation of yoga—wherein the mind comes to rest, restrained by the service of yoga; [that state is called yoga].
And where, seeing the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the self.
At whatever time the mind ceases— that is, it reaches a state of stillness, being restrained from all sides and suppressed through the practice of yoga,

the performance of yoga— at that very time, perceiving and apprehending the Self, which is the Supreme Consciousness whose nature is light, by means of the self, i.e., the internal organ purified by concentration, one finds satisfaction, one experiences contentment, within one's own Self.
Moreover:
"That absolute bliss which is beyond the senses and perceivable by the intellect—he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality. (BhG 6.21)
The word *ātyantikam* means that the happiness becomes absolutely final; its meaning is "infinite.

That which is "grasped by the intellect" (*buddhi-grāhyam*) means it is grasped by the intellect alone, independent of the senses; thus, it is "beyond the senses" (*atīndriyam*), meaning it transcends the range of the senses and is not produced by sense-objects.
He knows—that is, he experiences—such happiness at that time (*yatra*) when [the state arises].
Moreover, this wise man, established in the true nature of the Self, does not waver from it; in reality, he does not fall away from the essential nature of Truth—this is the meaning.
(BhG 6.21) And furthermore: Having attained which, he considers no other gain to be superior to that.
Established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.
Having attained which—having obtained which self-attainment—one does not consider or think that there is any other attainment, any further gain, superior to it.
Moreover, established in that reality of the Self, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering characterized by the falling of weapons and the like.
Beginning with the verse "Wherein the mind comes to rest" and so forth, Yoga has been described as a particular state of the Self distinguished by various attributes.
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as Yoga;
that Yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency. (BhG 6.23)

One should know—that is, one should understand—that "the disjunction from the conjunction with suffering" (duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga) means: conjunction with sufferings is "conjunction with suffering" (duḥkha-saṃyoga);
disjunction from that is "disjunction from the conjunction with suffering.
One should know—that is, one should understand—that this very disjunction from the conjunction with suffering is designated as "Yoga" by virtue of its contrary characteristic. This is the meaning.

Having summarized the fruit of yoga, the necessity of practicing yoga again by means of renewed effort is now stated for the purpose of prescribing determination (*niścaya*) and freedom from despondency (*anirveda*) as the means of achieving yoga.
That yoga, which possesses the aforementioned fruit, must be practiced with determination—that is, with firm resolve—and with a mind free from despondency; "not despondent" means *anirviṇṇa*.
What is that? It is the mind (*cetas*); the meaning is: by that mind which is devoid of despondency. (BhG 6.23)
Furthermore:
Having abandoned all desires born of volition without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses from every side by the mind alone— BhG 6.24.
Having abandoned all desires— which are born of volition, meaning those desires for which volition is the source— completely and without remainder; furthermore,
having restrained the entire collection of the senses from every side by means of the mind itself endowed with discrimination,
one should gradually attain tranquility through the intellect held with fortitude.
Having made the mind abide within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
One should gradually, and not suddenly, cease—that is, one should bring about cessation—by means of what? By means of the intellect;
of what kind? [The following:]
"With steadfastness held"—that is, with steadfastness (dhṛti) held, meaning endowed with fortitude.

Having made the mind "established in the Self" (ātma-saṃstham)—meaning established in the Self, such that the Self alone is everything and there is nothing else apart from It—one should not think of anything at all.
This is the supreme rule for yoga. (BhG 6.25)
In this regard, the yogi who has set out to establish the mind thus within the Self [should act as follows]:
"From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause he should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. (BhG 6.26)
From whatever cause— be it sound or any other— from whichever object the mind, which is by its very nature defective, wanders excessively, being fickle and therefore unstable,
from each and every such cause such as sound, one should restrain it by investigating the true nature of that respective cause.

Having restrained the mind from its objects such as sound, and having rendered those respective objects mere appearances by determining their true nature through the cultivation of detachment, one should bring this mind under control within the Self alone—that is, one should bring it to a state of subjection to the Self.
Thus, by the power of the practice of yoga, the mind of the yogi becomes tranquil within the Self alone. (BhG 6.26)
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is tranquil,
whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint.

He whose mind is perfectly tranquil—that is, one whose mind is exceedingly calm—is a person of tranquil mind; indeed, supreme happiness, which is unsurpassed, comes to and approaches such a yogi. "With passion stilled" means that the passion (*rajas*) of afflictions such as delusion (*moha*) has been destroyed. "Become Brahman" refers to one who is liberated while living, possessing the firm conviction that "all is Brahman. "Brahman-become" means stainless, being free from merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and other such taints. (BhG 6.27)
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taints,
easily attains the infinite bliss of contact with Brahman.

Thus practicing yoga according to the sequence described, the yogi—free from obstacles to yoga, always and at all times free from stain (vigata-kalmaṣa), that is, free from sin—attains with ease, without effort, that bliss which is "touching Brahman," meaning that bliss whose contact is with the Supreme Brahman; he enjoys, that is, pervades, that which is absolute, existing beyond all limits, most excellent, and unsurpassed. // BhG 6.28 //

Now, the fruit of yoga—which is the vision of the oneness of Brahman and the cause of the cessation of all saṃsāra—is demonstrated: One whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere. (BhG 6.29)

One whose self is disciplined by yoga, whose internal organ is concentrated, and who possesses equal vision everywhere— seeing his own Self abiding in all beings, and seeing all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as having attained oneness within the Self— beholds them thus in all things, despite their apparent inequality from Brahmā down to the stationary world.
He whose vision— knowledge— is equal toward all beings, without distinction, having as its object the oneness of Brahman and the Self, is one who sees with equality everywhere.
(BhG 6.29) The fruit of this vision of the oneness of the Self is now stated:
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me.

He who sees Me as Vāsudeva, the Self of all, everywhere in all beings, and sees the entire multitude of beings beginning with Brahmā within Me, the Self of all—for him who thus perceives the oneness of the Self, I, the Lord, do not pass away; I shall not become invisible to him.
And he does not pass away from Me; that wise man does not pass away from Me, Vāsudeva, nor does he become invisible to Me.
Because he and I are of one essence;
for one's own self is indeed dear to oneself, and since I am the very one who perceives the unity of the Self in all. (BhG 6.30)
Having thus restated the right vision whose meaning was explained in the preceding verses, its fruit—liberation—is now declared:
"The yogin who, established in unity, worships Me as dwelling in all beings, he dwells in Me, regardless of how he conducts himself. (BhG 6.31)
In every way and by all means, even while engaged in worldly activity, the yogin who possesses right vision abides in Me, the supreme state of Viṣṇu;
he is eternally liberated,
meaning he is not obstructed by anything on the path toward liberation.
Furthermore:
"Moreover, O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere—whether it be pleasure or pain—that yogi is considered supreme. (BhG 6.32)
"By way of self-likeness" (*ātmaupamyena*): that by which the self (*ātman*) is itself compared is a "comparison" (*upamā*);
the state of that comparison is "likeness" (*aupamya*). By that likeness of self, O Arjuna, he who sees all things equally—that is, as identical—in all beings.
And how does he see with equanimity? It is said: just as happiness is desired by me, so too is happiness agreeable to all living beings.
The word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and. Or else, just as suffering is disagreeable and undesired by me, so too is suffering [undesired] by all living beings.
Thinking, "It is undesirable and disagreeable," he views pleasure and pain as agreeable and disagreeable with equanimity toward all beings by means of the analogy of himself;
he does not act in a way that is disagreeable to anyone.
The meaning is "non-violent.
He who is thus non-violent and established in right vision is considered—that is, intended—the supreme, most excellent yogi among all yogis. (BhG 6.32)
Observing that this yoga, characterized by right vision as previously described, is difficult to accomplish, Arjuna, desiring to hear the certain means for its attainment, said:
"O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by You, I do not see how it can have a steady endurance because of the mind's restlessness. (BhG 6.33)

O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga which has been described by You as equilibrium and equanimity, I do not perceive—that is, I do not attain—a firm and unshakable stability in it, because of the restlessness of the mind.
What [do I not perceive]? A steady and immovable state.
That is not established—for the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (BhG 6.34)
For the mind is indeed restless.
"Kṛṣṇa" is a form derived from the root *kṛṣ*, meaning "to draw.
He is called Kṛṣṇa because he draws away (attracts) the faults of his devotees, such as their sins and so forth.
The vocative form of that [word] is "he kṛṣṇa.
For indeed, the mind is restless— not only exceedingly restless, but also "pramāthi," meaning it has the nature of agitating.
It crushes the body and, by distracting the senses, brings them under the control of another. Furthermore, it is powerful and exceedingly strong, such that it cannot be restrained by anyone.
Because it is difficult to restrain.
Furthermore: "Firm like a serpent made of fiber, it is uncuttable.

I consider the restraint—that is, the suppression—of such a mind to be as difficult as that of the wind; the intention is that I consider it even more difficult than the restraint of the wind. (BhG 6.34)
The Blessed Lord said: It is exactly as you say—
without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain.
But by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is mastered.

Without doubt, there is no uncertainty regarding this: "The mind is restless and difficult to restrain," O mighty-armed one! However, [it is controlled] by practice—practice being the repeated occurrence of a similar mental state upon some level of the mind—and by dispassion—dispassion being the absence of craving resulting from the cultivation of seeing the defects in the enjoyment of seen and unseen objects.
And by that dispassion, the movement of the mind in the form of distraction is seized;
thus, that mind is seized, restrained, and suppressed—this is the meaning. (BhG 6.35) Furthermore, for one whose self is not yet disciplined, by that—
"Yoga is difficult to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my conviction.
But it can be attained by one who has mastered the self through effort and by means of the proper method."

"For one whose self is uncontrolled"— that is, one whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇam*) is not restrained by practice and dispassion— it is my conviction that yoga is difficult to attain for such an uncontrolled person, being reached only with great hardship. On the other hand, however, he whose self— that is, the mind— is brought under control through practice and dispassion, [for him it is easily attained]."
With a self brought under control, by that very self which is controlled and striving— making further effort— it is possible to attain Yoga through the means previously described.
In that state, by undertaking the practice of Yoga, those actions which are the causes for attaining this world and the next are renounced.

Thinking, "I have not attained right vision, which is the fruit of the perfection of yoga and the means to liberation," and fearing the ruin of one whose mind wavers from the path of yoga at the time of death, Arjuna said:
"One who is lacking in self-restraint, yet endowed with faith, whose mind has strayed from yoga..."
O Kṛṣṇa, failing to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does he reach?

One who is lacking perseverance, though endowed with faith and a sense of conviction regarding the path of yoga, and whose mind wavers at the time of death due to yoga— such a person of lost memory, having failed to attain the perfection of yoga, that is,
the fruit of yoga which is right vision (samyag-darśana), what goal does he go to, O Kṛṣṇa? (BhG 6.37)
O mighty-armed one, I hope that he who has fallen away from both, being bewildered on the path of Brahman and without support, does not perish like a scattered cloud.
Does someone who has fallen away from both— the path of action and the path of yoga— not perish like a scattered cloud,

being without support and without refuge, O mighty-armed one, having become utterly deluded on the path of Brahman, the way to the attainment of Brahman? You, Kṛṣṇa, ought to sever this doubt of mine completely.
For indeed, no one other than you is found to be capable of cutting through this doubt.

O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever and remove this doubt of mine entirely. For there is no other seer or god besides you who could be the one to sever—that is, to destroy—this doubt; since such a person is not found and cannot exist, the meaning is that you alone are capable of severing it. (BhG 6.39)
The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him;
for no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever comes to a miserable state.
O Pārtha, for him there is no destruction whatsoever, neither in this world nor in the other world beyond.
"Destruction" means the attainment of a birth inferior to one's former state; that does not exist for one who has fallen from yoga.
For, my dear, no doer of good, no performer of auspicious deeds, ever goes to an evil or miserable state.
Because he extends himself (*ātman*) in the form of a son, the father is called *tāta*;
likewise, because the son is indeed the father, the son is also called *tāta*.
Furthermore, the disciple is also called "son."
Because he does not go [to hell]. But what happens to him?—
Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds, and having dwelt there for eternal years, [he returns].
One who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous.

The renunciant who has set out on the path of Yoga, by his own capacity, having reached and traversed the worlds of the merit-performers— those who have sacrificed with the Aśvamedha and other rites— and having dwelt there for eternal, perpetual years, when that enjoyment is exhausted, he is born again in the house of the pure, the prosperous, and the illustrious who act according to the injunctions; thus is one fallen from Yoga reborn.
Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in this world.
Or else, he is born— not from a family of the prosperous— but in the family of poor yogis who are wise and intelligent;
for this indeed is true birth,
which occurs in the family of poor yogis.
Compared to what has preceded it, such a birth in this world as in a family with the aforementioned qualities is more difficult to obtain and more difficult to attain through suffering.
For this reason:
there he regains that same connection with wisdom belonging to his previous body.
And from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even further for perfection.
In that family of yogis, he regains that same connection with wisdom—the connection with wisdom belonging to his previous body—from his former existence;
and from that prior impression (*saṃskāra*), O descendant of Kuru, he strives—that is, he exerts effort—further and more intensely for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
How is it that there is a conjunction with the intellect and the impressions of a previous body? To this it is said:
"By that very same former practice, he is indeed carried away even against his will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound. (BhG 6.44)
That practice which was performed in a previous birth is "prior practice";
by that very [practice], being powerful, he is carried toward perfection, because even though he has fallen from yoga, he is not [entirely] helpless.

This is so provided that no action characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the like—which is stronger than the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from the practice of yoga—has been performed.
Then one is carried away by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the practice of yoga;
however, if unrighteousness (*adharma*) has been made more powerful, it indeed overcomes even that latent impression born of yoga.
But upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue], the impression born of yoga (yogaja-saṃskāra) itself initiates its own effect;
the meaning is that there is no destruction of it even after it has endured for a long time.
Therefore, even a renunciant who has fallen from yoga—one who, though desiring to know the nature of yoga and wishing to practice the path of yoga, has failed—is [nevertheless saved].
By implication, even that person transcends—that is, surpasses and casts off—the fruit of performing the rituals prescribed in the Vedas, which is the Word-Brahman (śabda-brahman).
How much more so for one who, having understood Yoga, remains steadfast in it and practices it?
And for what further reason is the state of a yogi superior? — [as follows:]
But the yogi who strives with diligence, having his impurities completely cleansed and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal.

"Striving with effort" means striving intensely. In that state, the wise yogi, having his impurities completely cleansed— meaning his sins are purified— and having attained perfection through many births, [reaches the goal].
Having accumulated a certain measure of the collection of impressions (*saṃskāra*) over many births,
and having become perfected through that accumulation performed over many births— one who has attained right vision (*samyag-darśana*) thus goes to the supreme, most excellent goal.
Since this is so, therefore:
The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge;
and the yogi is superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. (BhG 6.46)
The yogi is superior to the ascetics;
even among those possessed of knowledge— where "knowledge" here refers to proficiency in the meaning of the scriptures—
the yogi is considered, known, to be superior and more excellent than even them.
The yogi is superior to the performers of ritual acts such as the Agnihotra; since he is more distinguished than those who possess such rites, therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.
Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me,
full of faith— he is considered by Me to be the most disciplined.

Among all yogis— even those devoted to the meditation on Rudra, the Ādityas, and others— he who, with his inner self— that is, his internal organ— fixed on Me, Vāsudeva, and being full of faith, worships and serves Me,
he is considered by Me to be the most disciplined (yuktatama), meaning he is preeminently endowed with yoga; this is My intention.

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya). //6//
Bhagavad Gītā 7:
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge and Realization" (Śaṅkara’s Commentary).

Having introduced the seed of the question with the words: "Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith— he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined" (Gītā 6.47), [the Lord proceeds].
Desiring himself to express that "my true nature is such as this" and that "one should thus have one's inner self absorbed in me," the Blessed Lord said:
"O Pārtha, with the mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me..."
Listen to that by which you shall know me fully and without doubt. (BhG 7.1)

O Pārtha, he whose mind is attached to Me— the Supreme Lord endowed with the attributes about to be described— is "one whose mind is attached to Me" (mayyāsaktamanāḥ). Practicing yoga, that is, effecting the concentration of the mind, he is "one who has Me as his refuge" (madāśrayaḥ), meaning one for whom I alone, the Supreme Lord, am the refuge.
For whoever desires some human goal resorts to a certain means for its accomplishment— be it a ritual such as the Agnihotra, austerity, or charity—
but this yogi resorts to Me alone as his support; having abandoned all other means, he becomes one whose mind is attached to Me alone.

Since you, being such as you are, will know me— without doubt, in their entirety, and in all my perfections such as majesty, power, strength, sovereignty, and other qualities— exactly as I am, namely,
"the Blessed Lord is indeed thus," listen to that which is being told by me.
And that knowledge concerning Me— this wisdom along with its full realization— I shall declare to you in its entirety,
by knowing which nothing further remains here to be known. (BhG 7.2)
I shall declare to you this knowledge, together with realization—that is, accompanied by direct experience—in its entirety and without remainder.

He praises that intended knowledge in order to attract the listener: "Having known that knowledge, there remains nothing else here further to be known as a means for achieving the goals of human life;
nothing whatsoever is left over."
The meaning is that he who thus knows the reality of the Self becomes omniscient;
therefore, because it yields such a distinguished fruit, this knowledge is difficult to attain. (BhG 7.2)
How so? It is said:
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection;
and even among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (BhG 7.3)
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives— that is, exerts effort— for perfection, for the sake of attainment. And even among those who have attained perfection,
it is only those who strive for liberation who are truly perfected.
"Indeed, among them, only someone knows Me as I truly am.
[Having thus drawn the listener's attention by creating interest, He says:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect," BhG 7.3.
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.
The "earth" (bhūmi) is said to be the subtle element of earth (pṛthivī-tanmātra), not the gross [element], because of the statement: "Prakṛti is divided eightfold.
Likewise, water and the others are also called subtle elements alone—water, fire, air, and space.
By "mind" (manas), the ego (ahaṃkāra) is understood as the cause of the mind;
by "intellect" (buddhi), the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva) is understood as the cause of the ego;
and by "ego," the unmanifest (avyakta) conjoined with ignorance (avidyā) is meant.

Just as food mixed with poison is called "poison," so too the unmanifest primal cause (avyakta-mūlakāraṇa), when possessed by the latent impression of egoism (ahaṃkāra-vāsanā), is called "egoism" (ahaṃkāra),
because egoism is the impelling factor.
For in the world, egoism alone is seen to be the seed of all activity.

Thus, this aforementioned nature of mine, my sovereign power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), is divided eightfold; it has come to possess these distinctions. But know that there is another, higher nature of mine, different from this one.
O mighty-armed one, that which has become the individual soul (jīva), by which this world is sustained.

This other [nature] is not the supreme; it is inferior, impure, productive of evil, and characterized by the bondage of saṃsāra. But know that My other nature, distinct from this aforementioned one, is the supreme—purified, My very self, consisting of the individual soul (jīva), characterized as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and serving as the cause for the maintenance of life, O mighty-armed one.
By which [nature], having entered within, this world is sustained;
understand that all beings have this as their source. I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

Understand—that is, know—this: all beings have these two, characterized as the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), as their source (*yoni*). These two, the higher and the lower *prakṛtis*, are the source of all beings;
for my *prakṛti* is the source and the cause of all beings.
Therefore, I am the origin—the birth—and likewise the dissolution—the destruction—of the entire, complete world.
The meaning is that, by means of the two natures (*prakṛti*), I, the omniscient Lord, am the cause of the world.
Since that is so:
There is nothing whatsoever else higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread.
Other than Me, the Supreme Lord, there is no other cause whatsoever;
that is to say, I alone am the cause of the universe,
O Dhanañjaya.

Since this is so, therefore all beings, this entire world, are woven upon me, the Supreme Lord; that is to say, they are strung together, interwoven, pervaded, and threaded through me—just as a cloth is on long threads, or as clusters of jewels are on a string. (BhG 7.7)
By which specific qualities are you distinguished such that all this is woven upon you? It is said: "O son of Kuntī, I am the taste in the waters; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun;
I am the sacred syllable *praṇava* in all the Vedas; I am the sound in the ether; and I am the manly vigor in men. (BhG 7.8)
"I am the taste": that which is the essence of water is taste; the meaning is that within me, who have become that taste, the waters are woven.
This applies everywhere in the same way.
Just as I am the taste in water, so am I the radiance in the moon and the sun;
I am the syllable Om, the Praṇava, in all the Vedas.
In Me, who have become the Praṇava, all the Vedas are woven together;
