likewise, as sound is the essence within space (ākāśa),
space is woven in Me.
Likewise, I am the *pauruṣam*—the essential nature of the Puruṣa—from which the perception of "man" arises among men; in Me, that Puruṣa, all men are woven together.
I am the fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in the fire.
I am the life-force in all beings, and I am the austerity among ascetics.
"I am the pure, fragrant scent in the earth.
In me, who have become that scent, the earth is woven.
The purity of the scent is shown in the context of the earth by its very nature, for the purpose of indicating the purity of taste and other qualities in water and the rest.

However, the lack of merit in odors and so forth belongs to transmigrating beings due to their association with particular elements, depending on factors such as ignorance and demerit. Furthermore, I am the heat and the light in the fire; likewise, I am the life-force in all beings.
That by which all beings live is Life;
and among those who practice austerity, I am austerity;
in that austerity, within Me, the ascetics are woven. (BhG 7.9)
Know Me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.

Know Me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal and ancient seed that causes the sprouting of all beings. Furthermore, I am the discerning power of the intellect belonging to the wise who possess that power of discrimination;
and I am the brilliance, the courage, of those who possess that brilliance.
And I am the strength of the strong, devoid of lust and passion;
I am the desire that is not contrary to dharma among living beings, O bull of the Bharatas.
I am strength, capability, and the vigor of the powerful; and that strength is free from desire and passion. Desire and passion constitute "kāma-rāgau."
*Kāma* is desire for objects that are near at hand due to craving;

*rāga* is passion or attachment toward objects already attained. Free from both these *kāma* and *rāga*, I am the strength and the essence (*sattva*) intended merely for the maintenance of the body and so forth, and not that which is the cause of craving and passion for those in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsārin*).
Furthermore: "Not contrary to dharma.

That desire toward living beings which is not contrary to dharma—that is, not contrary to the meaning of the scriptures—such as the desire for food, drink, and so forth, for the sole purpose of maintaining the body, that desire I am.
Thus, O bull of the Bharatas.
Furthermore:
"And whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)..."
Know that they arise from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.

And whatever states or entities there are that are characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*) and produced from *sattva*, those characterized by passion (*rājasa*) and produced from *rajas*, and those characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*) and produced from *tamas*—
whatever states arise for living beings through the power of their own karma;
Know that all these beings without exception are born from Me alone;
even though they are thus born from Me, nevertheless I am not dependent on them nor subject to their control.
Just like those who wander in saṃsāra;
moreover, they are under my control and dependent upon me.
Even though the Supreme Lord is of such a nature—eternally pure, enlightened, and free by nature, and the Self of all beings— [He is perceived otherwise by the ignorant.]

The Blessed One demonstrates His compassion by thinking, "The world does not recognize Me, who am devoid of qualities and the cause of the burning away of the seeds of the defects of worldly existence.
And for what reason is this ignorance of the world? It is said:
"By these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world..."
Deluded, it does not recognize Me, who am beyond these and immutable.

By these three states consisting of the qualities (guṇas)—the transformations of the qualities appearing in the forms of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth—this entire world of living beings has been deluded; having been brought to a state of non-discrimination, they do not recognize Me. [I am] beyond these aforementioned qualities, distinct from them, and immutable, meaning free from decay and devoid of all modifications of being such as birth and the like. (BhG 7.13)
How, then, does one transcend this divine illusion (māyā) of Viṣṇu, which consists of the three qualities? It is said:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, composed of the qualities, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (BhG 7.14).

This divine Māyā of mine—the Lord Viṣṇu—is indeed my very nature; for this aforementioned Māyā of Mine, consisting of the Guṇas, is difficult to overcome (duratyayā), meaning that its transcendence or crossing over is achieved with great difficulty. This being so, those who, having renounced all duties, take refuge in Me alone—the wielder of Māyā, who am their own Self—with their whole being, they cross over and transcend this Māyā which deludes all beings.
The meaning is that they are liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
But if those who have taken refuge in you cross over this illusion, why do not all take refuge in you? To this it is said:
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me;
their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have taken recourse to a demonic nature.

The foolish evildoers—those who perform sinful deeds, the lowest among men, the most base—do not take refuge in me, the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. Their wisdom has been carried away by my *māyā*, their intellects are utterly deluded, and they have resorted to a demonic nature characterized by violence, falsehood, and the like.
On the other hand, those who are the best among men, performers of meritorious deeds—
O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom.
O Arjuna, four kinds of virtuous people—those who have performed meritorious deeds—resort to and serve Me:
the distressed (ārta), who is seized by affliction and overwhelmed by thieves, tigers, disease, and so forth;
and the seeker of knowledge (jijñāsu), who desires to know the true nature of the Blessed Lord.
One who seeks wealth desires riches;
one who possesses knowledge is a knower of the reality of Viṣṇu, O bull among the Bharatas. Among these, the man of knowledge, who is ever-steadfast and devoted to the One alone, is preeminent.
For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me.
Among those four, the man of knowledge (jñānī), who knows reality, becomes eternally disciplined because of his knowledge of reality;
he is singularly devoted,
for he perceives no other object of worship.
Therefore, that single-minded devotee is distinguished—he attains excellence or superiority; the meaning is that he excels others.
For because I am the Self, I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge.
For it is well known in the world that the self is dear;
therefore, because the Knower is the very Self, Vāsudeva is dear to him—this is the meaning.
And since that Knower is indeed my own Self, he is exceedingly dear to me, Vāsudeva.
Are the three beginning with the distressed (ārta) then not dear to Vāsudeva? No. What then?—All these are indeed noble; however, the man of knowledge (jñānin), in my view, is My very Self.
For he, with a disciplined mind, is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
All these three are indeed noble and excellent; the meaning is that they are all dear to me.
For no one who is devoted to Me can be unloved by Vāsudeva.
The distinction is that the man of knowledge (jñānī) is exceedingly dear.
Why is that? To this He says: "But the man of knowledge is My very Self; he is none other than Me—this is My conviction, My settled opinion."

The meaning is this: that man of knowledge, being one whose self is disciplined and whose mind is concentrated, thinking "I am indeed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva and none other," has set out to ascend— that is, he has begun to go toward Me alone, the Supreme Brahman, the unsurpassed goal to be reached.
The man of knowledge is praised once more:
"At the end of many births, the possessor of knowledge attains Me, realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great-souled one is very rare. (BhG 7.19)

At the end—that is, upon the completion—of many births characterized by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of seeking knowledge, one who possesses knowledge, whose wisdom has reached full maturity, attains Me, Vāsudeva, the inner Self, through direct perception.
How? By realizing: "Vāsudeva is everything.
He who thus realizes Me, Nārāyaṇa, as the Self of all, is a Great Soul (*mahātman*).
There is no other equal to him, nor any superior;
therefore, it is said that he is very difficult to find among thousands of men. (BhG 7.19)
The cause for the failure to realize that "the Self alone is everything, [namely] Vāsudeva," is stated as follows:
"Deprived of knowledge by various desires, they resort to other deities, adhering to their respective rules of conduct, constrained by their own natures. (BhG 7.20)

Those whose knowledge—meaning their discriminative wisdom—is carried away by various desires for objects such as sons, cattle, heaven, and so forth, resort to other deities; that is, they attain deities other than Vāsudeva, who is the Self. Adhering to—that is, relying upon—this or that specific rule well-known for the propitiation of a deity, they are constrained by their nature, meaning by their own inherent disposition arising from the particular impressions acquired in previous births.
Restrained by their own selves;
and of those seekers of desire—
whichever form of deity any devotee desires to worship with faith, [I make that faith of his steady].
Whatever firm faith each person has, that very faith I make for them.
Whichever seeker of desire, being endowed with faith and being a devotee, wishes to worship— that is, to honor— a particular form of a deity,
for that very seeker of desire I ordain and stabilize that same unwavering, firm faith.
By whatever [faith] one was previously engaged according to one's own nature, such that one wishes to worship a particular form of a deity with faith—
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that deity;
and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone.
Endowed with that faith ordained by Me, he strives—that is, exerts himself—for the propitiation, the worship, of that deity’s form.

And from that deity’s form, once it has been propitiated, he obtains his desired objects; for they have been ordained and fashioned by Me alone, the Supreme Lord, who is omniscient and knows the distribution of the fruits of actions.
Since those desired objects were ordained by the Blessed One, the meaning is that he necessarily obtains them.
In the word-splitting *hitān*, the quality of being beneficial (*hitatvam*) must be understood as applied figuratively to desires;
for desires are not beneficial to anyone.
Because they are finite, involve the exertion of means, and belong to those who lack discrimination and are full of desire—for these reasons—[they are not beneficial].
But for those of small intelligence, their fruit is finite;
the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, while My devotees come to Me as well.
But the fruit for those of small intelligence, those of little wisdom, is perishable and comes to an end.
"Sacrificers to the gods" (*devayājaḥ*) refers to those who sacrifice to the gods;
they go to the gods.
"My devotees come even unto Me.
Thus, although the effort is equal, they do not take refuge in Me alone for the sake of infinite fruit;
"Alas! How painful this is!"—in this way the Blessed Lord manifests His compassion. (BhG 7.23)
For what reason do they not take refuge in me alone? It is said:
"The unintelligent, not knowing my supreme nature—which is imperishable and unsurpassed—regard me, who am unmanifest, as having come into manifestation" (BhG 7.24).

The unintelligent— those lacking discrimination— who do not know my supreme state, which is the nature of the Supreme Self, think of me, though I am the eternally established Lord, as having now attained manifestation and clarity after being previously unmanifest and without light; they do not know my imperishable, unsurpassed, and absolute state, which is free from decay.
The meaning is that they think thus.
To explain what the cause of that ignorance is, it is said:
"I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā."
Deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and immutable.
The intended meaning is: "I am not manifest to the whole world; I am manifest only to certain of My devotees.
Enveloped by *yoga-māyā*: *yoga* is the conjunction or arrangement of the *guṇas*; that itself is *māyā*, hence *yoga-māyā*.
He is covered by that *yogamāyā*; the meaning is that he is concealed.
For this very reason, this deluded world does not recognize Me, the unborn and imperishable.
I know all beings that have passed away, those that are present, O Arjuna, and those yet to come; but no one knows Me.
That yogic power (yogamāyā) by which the world does not recognize me, being enveloped by it—
that very same yogic power of mine, though it is my own, does not obstruct the knowledge of me, the Lord who am the wielder of illusion;
just as the illusion of another magician likewise does not obstruct his own knowledge.

Since this is so, therefore: "But I know—I am aware of—the beings that have passed away, those that have transcended; and of the present beings, O Arjuna, and the beings yet to come, I know them all."
But no one knows me, except for my devotee who has me as his sole refuge;
it is precisely because of the absence of knowledge regarding my true nature that he does not worship me.
(BhG 7.26) By what obstacle to the knowledge of my true nature, however, are all beings born obstructed such that they do not know me?
In response to this inquiry, he said:
"O Bhārata, O scorcher of foes, at the time of creation, all beings fall into delusion through the confusion of dualities arising from desire and hatred. (BhG 7.27)

"Arising from desire and aversion": desire and aversion are "desire-and-aversion"; that which arises from those two is "arising from desire-and-aversion," and by that [it is meant]. When there is an expectation for a specific [agent], he says this: "by delusion regarding the pairs. Delusion caused by the pairs is "delusion regarding the pairs," and by that.

Those very same desire and aversion, mutually opposed like cold and heat, having as their objects pleasure, pain, and the causes thereof, and being joined with all beings at the appropriate time, are designated by the term "dualities" (*dvandva*). When desire and aversion, having attained their own nature through the acquisition of pleasure,

pain, and their causes, then produce delusion (*moha*)— which, by bringing wisdom under its own control, is the cause of the obstruction to the arising of knowledge regarding the reality of the supreme Self— for all beings.
For knowledge regarding objects as they truly are does not arise even for one whose mind is under the sway of the defects of desire and aversion, even with respect to external things;
what need is there to mention that knowledge would not arise for one whose intellect is possessed by those two, who is utterly deluded, and for whom there are many obstacles within the inner self?

Therefore, O Bhārata, descendant of the Bharata lineage, all beings are deluded by this dualistic delusion arising from desire and hatred; they are deluded— that is, rendered utterly confused— at the time of creation, which is birth.
"At the time of birth"— this means, O scorcher of foes, all beings as they are being born go, that is, proceed, under the very influence of delusion; such is the intended meaning.
Since this is so, therefore all beings, their wisdom obstructed by that delusion of the pairs of opposites, are utterly bewildered and do not know Me, who am their very self.
For this very reason, they do not worship Me as their own self.

Now, to show the intended meaning—namely, who are those liberated from this delusion of the pairs of opposites who, having known You according to the scriptures, worship You as their own self—it is said:
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end—they, freed from the delusion of dualities and firm in their vows, worship Me. (BhG 7.28)

But for those people whose evil has reached its end, who have almost completed it, and who are exhausted of it— those of meritorious deeds in whom there exists merit that is the cause of the purification of beings—
those of meritorious deeds, being freed from the delusion of dualities, freed from the aforementioned delusion of dualities, they worship Me, the Supreme Self, with firm vows.
In this very way, those whose knowledge is certain through the vow of renouncing everything that "the ultimate reality is not otherwise" are called those of firm resolve.
For what purpose do they devote themselves? It is said:
"Those who, having taken refuge in Me, strive for liberation from old age and death..."
They know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self, and all of action in its entirety.

Those who, having taken refuge in Me, the Supreme Lord, strive with their minds concentrated on Me for the sake of liberation from old age and death—that is, for the purpose of being released from old age and death—they know that which is the supreme Brahman; they know the entire Adhyātma, the reality concerning the inner self in its totality;
and they know all Karma in its entirety. (BhG 7.29)
Those who know Me as the presiding deity of the elements, the presiding deity of the divine, and the presiding deity of sacrifice—
they, with disciplined minds, know Me even at the time of death.
Those who know Me as "sādhibhūtādhidaiva"— that is, together with the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva;
and those who know Me as "sādhiyajña," together with the adhiyajña.
And at the time of departure, even at the time of death, those whose minds are disciplined and whose hearts are composed know Me. (BhG 7.30)

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 8:
Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Imperishable Brahman."
(The commentary composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkarācārya-Bhagavatpāda.
By means of the passage beginning with "They know that Brahman in its entirety," the Blessed One has taught the seeds of Arjuna’s questions.
Therefore, for the purpose of those questions, Arjuna said:

What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma), O Supreme Person? And what is declared to be the objective world (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine realm (adhidaiva)?
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice (adhiyajña) here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?
To resolve these questions in their proper order, the Blessed Lord said:
The supreme, imperishable Brahman is called the Self by nature;
the emission that brings about the origin of the existence of beings is designated as action.

The Imperishable (akṣara) is that which does not perish; it is the Supreme Self, according to the Vedic revelation: "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9).
Furthermore, the syllable *oṃ* is not to be understood here, because it is distinguished by the subsequent qualification: "The single-syllabled Brahman is *oṃ*" (Gītā 8.13).
Furthermore, the qualification "supreme" (paramam) is most appropriately applied to the unsurpassed, imperishable Brahman;
for that very Supreme Brahman has as its own nature (svabhāva) the state of being the inner self (pratyag-ātma-bhāva) in every body.
One's own state is one's own nature, which is called the inner self (adhyātma).

That reality which, with reference to the self (ātman) and the body, proceeds as the inner self (pratyag-ātman) and culminates in the supreme Brahman, is called "the internal" (adhyātma); it is denoted by the term *adhyātma*.
"The producer of the manifestation of the states of beings" (*bhūta-bhāvodbhava-kara*) means that which brings about the arising (*udbhava*) of the state (*bhāva*) of beings (*bhūta*);
the sense is that it is the cause of the production of the actual entities of beings.
*Visarga* means relinquishment; it is the renunciation of substances such as *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings intended for a deity.
This very sacrifice, characterized by such relinquishment, is designated as "action" (*karma*), meaning it is denoted by the word "action."
For from this which has become the seed, through the sequence of rain, food, and so forth, all beings—both stationary and moving—arise.
(BhG 8.3) The perishable state is the *adhibhūta* (the field of material elements), and the *puruṣa* (the individual soul) is the *adhidaivata* (the field of the divine).
And I alone am the *adhiyajña* (the presiding deity of sacrifice) here in this body, O best of embodied beings. (BhG 8.4)
It is called *adhibhūta* because it exists with reference to the multitude of living beings (*prāṇijāta*).
What is this? It is the *kṣara*, that which perishes; "perishable" (*kṣara*) means subject to destruction, namely any entity whatsoever that possesses birth—this is the meaning.
He is called *puruṣa* because "all this is filled by him," or because he "dwells in the city" (*puri-śayana*);
he is the *Hiraṇyagarbha* situated within the sun.
He who favors the instruments of all living beings is the presiding deity (adhidaivata).
The presiding sacrifice (adhiyajña) is the deity named Viṣṇu, who presides over all sacrifices.
For according to the Vedic revelation, "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice" (TaittS 1.7.4).
That Viṣṇu is indeed myself. In this context, within this body, I am the presiding deity of that which is sacrifice; thus, I am the *adhiyajña*.

For sacrifice, O best of embodied beings, is inherent in the body because it is accomplished by means of the body; thus, it has the body as its locus. And at the time of death, remembering Me alone, one leaves the body behind.
Whoever departs [at that time] attains My state; there is no doubt about this.
At the time of the end, at the time of death, he who departs— leaving behind and casting off the body (kalevara)— while remembering Me alone, the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu,
he attains My own state, the Vaiṣṇava reality.
There is no doubt whatsoever in this matter— that he either does or does not attain it.
This rule is not restricted to my domain alone. What then?
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state. (BhG 8.6)

Whatever state of being—whatever specific deity—one remembers and contemplates while abandoning and relinquishing the body at the end, at the time of death when the vital breaths depart, to that very state remembered one goes, and to no other, O son of Kuntī; for one who is "constantly permeated by that state"—that state being the constant mental preoccupation which has been cultivated through repeated recollection—is thus "permeated by that state. (BhG 8.6)
Since the final meditation is thus the cause for attaining another body, therefore, at all times remember Me and fight;
with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. (BhG 8.7)

Therefore, at all times, remember me according to the scriptures; and while fighting, perform your duty as a warrior. You, whose mind and intellect are offered unto Me, Vāsudeva—you, being one whose mind and intellect are thus offered unto Me, shall come to Me alone, just as you have remembered Me.
There is no doubt; no uncertainty exists in this matter. Furthermore:
with a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not wandering toward anything else...
Contemplating the supreme divine Person, O Pārtha, he goes to Him.

By means of that [mind] of the yogi which is joined with the yoga of practice— that is, the mind which has Me as its object of dedication, characterized by the recurrence of uniform cognitions uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, and which is thus joined with that yoga, being occupied solely therein.

With a mind that does not go elsewhere—that is, with a mind whose nature is not to wander to any other object—he goes to, or reaches, the supreme, unsurpassed, divine Person who exists in the solar orb, O Pārtha, while constantly reflecting upon Him, that is, while meditating on the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher. (BhG 8.8)
And what kind of Person does he go to? It is said:
"He who should meditate upon the Seer, the Ancient, the Instructor, subtler than the subtlest."
The sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable,
who has the splendor of the sun and stands beyond darkness.

Whoever should meditate upon— that is, reflect upon— the Seer, the one of transcendent vision, the omniscient, the Ancient, the Primeval, the Instructor, the Ruler of the entire world, subtler even than the subtle,
the Sustainer and Ordainer of all that arises from the fruits of action, who distributes it in manifold ways to living beings; [he shall attain the Supreme Goal].
"Of inconceivable form" means that although his form exists, it is not fixed and cannot be conceived by anyone; thus he is "of inconceivable form.
"Sun-colored" means that his color is like that of the sun, possessing the light of eternal consciousness; thus he is "sun-colored.
"Beyond darkness."
The connection with the preceding verse is that he goes while contemplating that Supreme beyond the darkness of delusion characterized by ignorance.
Furthermore:
"At the time of departure, with an unshaken mind..."
Endowed with devotion and by the power of yoga,
having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows,
he attains that supreme, divine Person. (BhG 8.10)

At the time of departure— that is, at the time of death— one who is endowed with devotion (*bhakti*), which means joined with worship, and also endowed with the power of yoga (*yoga-bala*)— the meaning being that one is joined with the power of yoga characterized by the stability of the mind produced by the accumulation of impressions born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— with a steady mind, free from wavering, [attains the Supreme].

Having first brought the mind under control within the heart-lotus, and then, by means of the upward-moving channel (*nāḍī*), having caused the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter and remain between the eyebrows through the sequence of conquering the stages (*bhūmi-jaya*), that wise yogi—being thus perfectly vigilant—approaches and attains that Supreme Person, higher than the highest, characterized as "the Seer, the Ancient," and so forth; He is divine, consisting of light.
[It might follow from this that Brahman is attained merely by following the path of yoga, even without the knowledge of Brahman.]

This is called [the introduction]. Furthermore, by means of the method about to be described, the Blessed One provides a designation for Brahman—which is sought to be understood—as characterized by the qualifiers "known through the Vedas" and "beginningless," and as the qualified object itself:
"That Imperishable which those who know the Vedas declare, and into which the self-controlled ascetics, free from passion, enter."
I shall declare to you in brief that goal, desiring which they lead the life of celibacy (brahmacarya).
That which does not perish is the imperishable (*akṣara*), the indestructible; so say those who know the Vedas, those who understand the meaning of the Vedas.
For there is a scriptural passage: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas speak of this very imperishable as 'not coarse,' 'not subtle,' and so forth," thus describing it by way of negating all specific attributes.

Furthermore—into that which [the ascetics] enter, that is, they enter when perfect vision (samyag-darśana) has been attained; those "ascetics" (yatayaḥ) are those whose nature is striving; "those free from passion" (vīta-rāgāḥ) are those from whom passion (rāga) has departed or vanished; and desiring to know that Imperishable (akṣara)—this being the completion of the sentence—they practice celibacy (brahmacarya) under a teacher; that state (pada), known as the Imperishable, that state to be reached, I shall declare to you in brief.
"Saṃgraha" means a compendium; by that, I shall speak—that is, I shall declare—in brief.
"O Blessed One, he who among men meditates upon the syllable Om until the end of his life..."
"Which world indeed does he conquer by means of that?
To him he said: "O Satyakāma, this syllable *oṃ* is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman," beginning thus, and continuing with the statement:
"But he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), he is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāman chants," and so forth.
And having begun with "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (KaṭhU 1.2.14), [it continues]:
"That goal which all the Vedas proclaim,
and which all austerities declare;"

And by such statements as, "I shall tell you that goal in brief, desiring which they practice the life of celibacy— namely, 'Om'" (KaṭhU 1.2.15), the Supreme Brahman is presented in the form of its designator.
Whether as a mere image or as a symbolic representation,
the meditation on the syllable *oṃ*— intended for those of dull or middling intellect as a means to realize the Supreme Brahman, which was said to yield the fruit of liberation after some time—
that very same thing is intended here as well in the passage beginning with "the ancient poet, the ruler" (Gītā 8.9) and "that imperishable which the knowers of the Vedas speak of" (Gītā 8.11).

Thus, the meditation upon the syllable *oṃ*— which serves as the means for realizing the Supreme Brahman introduced [in the previous verse] in the form previously described, and which has liberation at a later time as its fruit— must be explained along with the practice of *yoga-dhāraṇā*.
For this purpose, the subsequent portion of the text is commenced, including whatever else may arise incidentally (*prasaktānuprasakta*).
Restraining all the gates of the body, confining the mind within the heart,
and fixing one's vital breath (prāṇa) in the head, he remains established in the practice of yogic concentration.

Having restrained all the doors— that is, having controlled all those gates of perception— and having fixed the mind within the heart, that is, having brought it to rest and rendered it motionless within the lotus of the heart;

then, with the mind thus mastered, having ascended upward through the channel that goes upwards from the heart and having placed the vital breath (prāṇa) in the head, he stands intent upon maintaining the concentration of yoga.
And focusing on that very same [thought]— uttering the single-syllabled Brahman "Om" and remembering Me—
whoever departs, casting off the body, he attains the supreme goal. (BhG 8.13)

Uttering— that is, pronouncing— the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," which is the designation of Brahman; and while recollecting— that is, contemplating— Me, the Lord, who am the referent of that syllable, he who departs— that is, dies— he, abandoning— that is, relinquishing— the body, the physical frame (the phrase "abandoning the body" serves to qualify the act of departing, meaning the soul's departure occurs through the relinquishment of the body).
The meaning is not by the destruction of one's own nature; he thus goes, that is, proceeds, to the supreme, most excellent goal.
Furthermore: He who, with a mind focused on no other, remembers Me constantly and perpetually—
I am easily attainable, O Pārtha, by that yogi who is constantly disciplined.
"One whose mind is not directed elsewhere" means one whose consciousness does not dwell on any other object; such a person is "one whose mind is not directed elsewhere.
The yogi who constantly—that is, at all times—remembers Me, the Supreme Lord:
by the words "constantly" and "always," uninterruptedness is expressed.
The word "constantly" (nityaśaḥ) expresses a long duration of time;
it does not mean six months or a year.
What then? The meaning is: he who remembers Me continuously for as long as life lasts.
I am easily attained with ease by that yogi, O Pārtha, who is ever-disciplined—that is, whose mind is always concentrated.
Since this is so, therefore, being single-minded, one should remain ever-concentrated on Me. (BhG 8.14)

"What would come of your accessibility? To this it is said: "Listen to what happens through my accessibility: having attained Me, there is no rebirth in that which is transient and an abode of suffering."
The high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not return.
Having come unto me—that is, having come unto me, the Lord—and attaining my own nature, they do not obtain, they do not undergo, rebirth, which is re-origination.
What kind of rebirth do they not obtain?
To answer this, he states its qualification: "the abode of suffering," meaning the locus or support of sufferings such as those that are internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth.
Birth is called the "abode of suffering" because sufferings adhere to it;
moreover, it is not merely an abode of suffering,
but is also impermanent and unstable in its very nature.
Great-souled ascetics who have attained the supreme and most excellent perfection known as liberation do not undergo such rebirth again;
however, those who do not attain Me return once more. (BhG 8.15) But what else is there that, having been attained, leads to a return? This is explained:
O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return;
but for one who has attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
"Bhuvana" means that in which beings exist;
"brahma-bhuvana" is the world of Brahmā,
meaning the realm of Brahmā (brahma-loka).
All worlds, including the world of Brahmā, are subject to return; they possess the inherent nature of recurring.
But, O Arjuna, son of Kuntī, having attained Me alone, there is no further birth, no further rebirth.
Why, then, are the worlds, including the world of Brahmā, subject to return?
Because they are limited by time. How so?—Those who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas...
Those people who know day and night understand that the night ends after a thousand yugas, and so does the day.
They know that day of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, the Virāj, to extend for a thousand yugas— that is, a day whose limit or conclusion consists of thousands of yugas.
They likewise know his night to end after a thousand yugas, being equal in measure to the day.
Who are they? He says: "They are the knowers of day and night," meaning those people who know the calculation of time.
Since they are thus limited by time, they are worlds that return again. (BhG 8.17)
That which occurs on the day of Prajāpati and during the night is now described: "At the arrival of the day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of the night, they dissolve back into that very thing called the unmanifest. (BhG 8.18)
From the unmanifest [comes] the unmanifest, which is the state of sleep of Prajāpati.
From that unmanifest, the manifest entities—meaning all creatures characterized as stationary and moving—are produced; that is, they become manifest.
At the arrival of the day (*ahar-āgama*), at that time which is the arrival of the day, during the period of Brahmā’s awakening.
Likewise, at the arrival of night, at the time of Brahmā’s sleep, all manifested beings dissolve right there into that which was previously called the unmanifest.

[This is stated] for the purpose of avoiding the faults of the "arrival of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the "destruction of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*), and to demonstrate the fruitfulness of the engagement with the scriptures on bondage and liberation;
for the multitude of living beings, having come into existence again and again under the power of the latent impressions of karma rooted in afflictions such as ignorance, dissolves involuntarily.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate detachment from saṃsāra, he said this: "This very same collection of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha; it comes forth at the arrival of day. (BhG 8.19)
The multitude of beings— the aggregate of beings characterized as both stationary and moving— which existed in the previous kalpa, is this very same one and not another.
Having come into being again and again at the arrival of day,
it dissolves again and again at the arrival of night, at the end of the day, being helpless and lacking independence.
O Pārtha,
at the arrival of day, it comes forth and is born again, indeed helplessly.
(BhG 8.19) Regarding that Imperishable which was introduced:
The means for attaining that has been indicated by such passages as, "Om, the single-syllabled Brahman" (Gītā 8.13).
Now, with the desire to indicate the very nature of that Imperishable, this is said:
"By this path of Yoga, this is to be reached."
But beyond that unmanifested state, there is another eternal unmanifested being which does not perish even when all beings perish.
"Other" means distinct and different.
From what? From that which was previously mentioned.
The word "tu" (but/however) is intended to specify the distinction of the intended imperishable from the unmanifest.
The existent is the supreme Brahman called the Imperishable.
Since there is the possibility of it being suspected to possess the same characteristics even while being distinct [from the individual soul], he says "other" (*anya*) in order to exclude that;
"other" means having different characteristics.
And that [Self] is unmanifest and beyond the range of the senses;
it has been stated that it is "higher than that.
But why is it higher?
The intention is that there is another, distinct state of being from the aforementioned unmanifest (avyakta), which is characterized by ignorance and serves as the seed for the multitude of beings.
That eternal, ancient state does not perish even when all beings, beginning with Brahmā, perish. (BhG 8.20)
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they say He is the supreme goal, that abode of Mine reaching which they do not return.
That which is called the unmanifest and the imperishable— them they call the unmanifest state, the supreme goal.
Having reached that supreme state, from which they do not return to worldly existence, that is my supreme abode.
This means "the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. The means for attaining that is now stated:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone."
In whom all beings abide, and by whom all this is pervaded.
The Puruṣa is so called because he dwells in the city (puri) or because of his fullness (pūrṇatva).
He is the Supreme (para), O Pārtha; "supreme" means beyond all comparison (niratiśaya).
Since there is nothing superior to the Puruṣa,
he is attainable through devotion that is characterized by knowledge, non-dual, and directed toward the Self—
that Puruṣa within whom all beings abide as their internal, intermediate, and effectual states.
For the effect indeed exists within its cause,
by which Person this entire world is pervaded and encompassed, just as jars and other objects are by space.

Since the path to the realization of Brahman must be explained for those yogis under discussion— who have fixed their intellects on Brahman through the syllable *praṇava* and who attain liberation after some time— the verse beginning with "In what time" (*yatra kāle*) is intended to present that specific meaning.
The presentation of the path of non-return is stated for the purpose of praising the other path:
"I shall declare that time at which yogis, having departed, go either to non-return or to return, O bull of the Bharatas" (BhG 8.23).
The phrase "at which time they depart" is to be connected with the distant [verb].

"At which time" means at that particular time; "non-return," meaning no further rebirth, and "return," which is the opposite of that—these refer to both yogins and those who perform ritual actions (karmis).
But as for the performers of action, they are "yogins" by virtue of their qualities, due to the qualification "of yogins through the yoga of action.
At what time departing [from the body] dead do yogins go to non-return,
and at what time departing do they go to return?
I shall describe that time, O bull among the Bharatas.
He speaks of that time as follows:
"Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice."
Departing from there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Agni is the deity presiding over time;
likewise, Jyotis is also a deity presiding over time.
Alternatively, Agni and Jyotis are deities exactly as they are heard in the sacred texts.

However, the primary designation is according to the time, as in the expression "at that time," like a grove of mango trees (*āmra-vana*). Likewise, *ahar* refers to the deity presiding over the day; *śuklaḥ* refers to the deity of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*).
The six months of the northern course of the sun constitute the path;
in this regard also, it is established elsewhere that "the deity itself is the path" (BAU 4.3.4). This principle applies here as well.
Those who have set out upon that path—having died—go to Brahman: namely, those who know Brahman, those who meditate upon Brahman, and people who are devoted to the meditation on Brahman.
The phrase "in succession" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For those who possess immediate liberation and are established in right vision, there is no going or coming anywhere;
as the Śruti states: "His vital breaths do not depart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).

Your vital breaths are indeed absorbed in Brahman; you are composed of Brahman and have become one with Brahman. Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight and the six months of the sun’s southern course—attaining the lunar light during that time, the yogi returns.
Smoke is night, as well as the deities presiding over smoke and the night; likewise, "black" refers to the deity of the dark fortnight;
and "six months of the southern course" refers, as before, to the deity itself.

There, having reached the lunar light—which exists in the moon—the yogi who performs ritual action attains and enjoys the fruit of his sacrifices and other works; upon the exhaustion of that merit, he returns again to this world.
These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be the eternal courses of the world.
By the one, a person goes to non-return; by the other, he returns again.
The white and the black; "white" refers to that which is bright, and "black" refers to that which is dark, because [the former] illuminates through knowledge, while [the latter] lacks that.

These two paths, the white and the black, belong indeed to the world of those who are qualified for knowledge and action; these two paths are not possible for the entire world [of beings]. They are eternal and constant.
Because of the eternity of saṃsāra, according to the intended doctrine;
therein, by means of one [path], the white, one goes to non-returning.
By the other [path], one returns once again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.
O Pārtha, knowing these two paths— the one leading to saṃsāra and the other to liberation— as they have been described,
no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, O Arjuna, at all times remain disciplined in yoga and composed in mind.
Listen now to the majesty of that yoga:
[it excels] in the Vedas, in sacrifices, and in austerities.
Having understood all this, the yogi transcends whatever fruit of merit is prescribed for acts of giving and attains the supreme, primordial state.

When the Vedas have been properly studied, when sacrifices have been performed with excellence, when austerities have been well-practiced, and when gifts have been rightly bestowed— whatever fruit of merit (puṇya-phalam), that is, the fruit of merit,
is ordained by the scripture for these acts, he transcends, passing beyond, all such categories of fruit.

Having understood this and having correctly grasped the meaning stated by way of the resolution of the seven questions, and having practiced it, the yogi attains and reaches the supreme, most excellent, divine station—the "first," meaning that which exists at the beginning, the causal Brahman. (BhG 8.28)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Imperishable Brahman," in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya). //8//
Bhagavad Gītā 9:
Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Sovereign Knowledge and the Sovereign Secret."
(Śaṅkara’s Commentary:
In the eighth [chapter], the yoga of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) with attributes was taught by means of the channels (*nāḍī*) and other [gateways].
And its fruit was specified as the attainment of Brahman at another time through the sequence beginning with the radiance of fire (*agny-arcis*), characterized by non-return (*anāvṛtti*).
In this regard, since the fruit of attaining liberation is realized through this very method and not otherwise, the Blessed Lord spoke as follows, wishing to dispel that doubt:
"But this most secret [knowledge] I shall declare to you, who are free from carping."
This knowledge, together with realized wisdom—by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil.
This knowledge of Brahman, which is about to be declared and has been stated in the preceding chapters, is referred to as "this" by bringing it to mind;
the word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of specifying a distinction.

This alone is the right knowledge that is the direct means for attaining liberation, according to such scriptural and traditional texts as "Vāsudeva is all" (Gītā 7.12), "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2), and "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Nothing else is so, according to scriptural texts such as, "Now, those who know otherwise than this, having other rulers, belong to worlds that are perishable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2).
I shall declare—that is, I shall speak—to you, who are free from envy, that which is most secret, that which is most to be guarded.
What is it? Knowledge. Of what kind is it?
That which is accompanied by consciousness and joined with experience—
having known and attained that, you shall be liberated from the impurity of the bondage of saṃsāra.
And that is—
This is the royal science, the royal secret, this supreme purifier;
it is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable.
It is the royal science among sciences, because it possesses an excellence of brilliance;
for this knowledge of Brahman shines forth with preeminence above all other sciences.
Likewise, it is the secret of secrets, the king of secrets;
it is the purifier, the sanctifier, this supreme among all purifiers, the cause of purity, the most excellent knowledge of Brahman.

Since it reduces to ashes in a mere moment even the karma accumulated over many thousands of births—including both merit and demerit along with its very roots—what more need be said of its purifying power?
Furthermore: "pratyakṣāvagamam" means that which has an understanding through direct perception, like the understanding of pleasure and so forth.
Although something may possess many qualities, it is observed to be contrary to dharma;
however, the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna) is not contrary to dharma in that way.
However, it is righteous (*dharmya*), meaning not departing from the Dharma.
Even so, one might think it is difficult to accomplish; therefore, he says: "It is very easy to perform, like the discerning knowledge of jewels."
In this regard, it is observed that other actions which require little effort and are easily accomplished yield small results, whereas those that are difficult to perform yield great results;
thus, one might conclude that this [practice], because it is easily accomplished, would result in the exhaustion of its fruit.
He said: "It is imperishable.
It is called imperishable because, unlike action, it has no exhaustion in terms of its fruit.
Therefore, the knowledge of the Self is to be trusted. (BhG 9.2)
But those persons who lack faith in this dharma, O scorcher of foes,
fail to reach me and return to the path of the mortal cycle of rebirth.

Lacking faith, devoid of conviction, they are atheists regarding the true nature and the fruit of this dharma which is self-knowledge; being doers of evil, they have adopted the secret doctrine of the Asuras, which is the view that the self is merely the body.
These sinful men, thirsting for life, are faithless.
"O scorcher of foes!

'Without attaining Me, the Supreme Lord'—the meaning is: without even attaining mere devotion, which is a specific path toward My attainment and for which one should have no doubt regarding the attainment of Me."
They turn back; they proceed with certainty.
Where? On the path of death-and-transmigration (*mṛtyu-saṃsāra-vartman*). Transmigration joined with death is "death-and-transmigration" (*mṛtyu-saṃsāra*);
its path is the way leading to the attainment of hell, the animal realm, and so forth.
The meaning is that they abide in that very [Self].
Having turned Arjuna’s attention toward Himself by means of praise, He says:
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded."
All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them.
By me—by that which is my supreme state, by me whose form is unmanifest (*avyakta-mūrti*)—this entire world is pervaded and filled.
"Unmanifest form" means that my own nature (*svarūpa*) is not manifest; thus, it is by me who am of unmanifest form, meaning by one whose essential nature is beyond the range of the senses.
In Me, whose form is unmanifest, all beings— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— abide as resting in Me;
for no being whatsoever can be fit for worldly transaction if it is devoid of a self.
Therefore, they abide in Me, existing through My very self by virtue of possessing a Self;
for this reason, it is said that "they abide in Me.
Because I alone am the Self of those beings, it appears to those of deluded intellect that I abide in them.

Therefore I say: I do not abide within those elements, because I lack any physical contact with them; indeed, I am subtler than even space. For an entity that is non-conjunct cannot exist anywhere in the state of being contained. (BhG 9.4)
Therefore, because of this very state of non-attachment, it is said of Me:
"Behold My divine yoga: the beings do not dwell in Me;
yet My Self, the sustainer of beings and the source of all beings, does not dwell in the beings. (BhG 9.5)
Nor do the beings beginning with Brahmā abide in Me;
behold My yoga—My skillful means, My divine sovereignty, the sovereign power belonging to Me as the Lord.
The meaning is: behold My yoga, which is the true nature of My self.
And thus scripture shows its state of non-attachment due to its lack of association: "Unattached, for it does not cling" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
Behold this other wonder: though it is unattached, it sustains all beings, yet it does not abide in beings.
Because it has been demonstrated by the aforementioned reasoning that its existence as a real entity is untenable,
how then can it be said, "This is my self"?

Having distinguished [the self] from the aggregate of the body and so forth, and having superimposed the sense of "I" upon that [aggregate], one designates it as "my self" in accordance with worldly convention.
Furthermore, unlike worldly people who do not know that the Self is distinct from the self,
he is a "bhūta-bhāvana," meaning one who brings beings into existence, generates them, or causes them to grow.
Establishing the meaning expressed by the two preceding verses through an illustration, he says:
Just as the great wind, moving everywhere, is eternally situated in space, even so, understand that all beings abide in Me. (BhG 9.6)

Just as in the world the wind, which is situated in space and rests eternally and always in space, goes everywhere—thus it is "all-pervading" (sarvatraga) by virtue of its great magnitude—so too, understand and know that all beings remain within Me, who am all-pervading like space, yet without any attachment.
Thus, at the time of their existence, all beings abide in Me just as the wind abides in space. These—
All beings, O son of Kuntī, go to my own nature at the end of a kalpa;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth.
O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa, at the time of dissolution, all beings go to my lower, inferior nature which consists of the three guṇas;
then, again at the time of creation, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send forth—that is, I produce—those same beings as before.
Thus, [I create] that which is characterized by ignorance—
Taking hold of My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature.

Having taken hold of— having brought under my control— my own nature, I project again and again this entire present multitude of beings, born from nature, which is powerless and rendered subject to others by defects such as ignorance,
through the power of nature— that is, through the power of its own inherent nature.

In that case, one might argue that for that Supreme Lord who ordains this diverse multitude of beings, there would be a connection with merit and demerit caused by those [actions]. To this, the Blessed One says:
"And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya."
He sits as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
And those actions that cause the unequal creation of the multitude of beings do not bind me, the Lord, O Dhanañjaya.

He states the reason for the non-connection with those actions: "seated like one who is indifferent," meaning seated like some indifferent person who is an onlooker, because of the self's changelessness;
"unattached," meaning free from attachment to the fruits [of action].
Free from conceit— that is, devoid of the thought "I am doing" regarding those actions—
therefore, for others as well, the absence of the conceit of agency and the absence of attachment to the fruit are the causes of non-connection [with karma].
Otherwise, the fool is bound by his actions like a silkworm; this is the intended meaning.
[Objection: In that regard, it is stated in a contradictory manner: "I project forth this multitude of beings" and "I remain as if indifferent.
To resolve this, He says:
Under my supervision, nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves.

By Me, acting as the supervisor— whose nature is pure consciousness alone and who is changeless as the witness— my Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas and is characterized as ignorance (avidyā), the primordial nature (prakṛti), brings forth and produces the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
And thus says the Vedic mantra:
The one God, hidden in all beings,
all-pervading, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of actions, and the dwelling place of all beings.
"The witness, the perceiver, alone and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).

By this cause, by this motive—namely, His presiding over it—the world, O son of Kuntī, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, including all that is moving and unmoving, revolves through all its states.
For every activity of the world has as its motive the attainment of being an object for the Seer: "I shall enjoy this," [and so forth].
I see this, I hear this, I experience pleasure.
"I experience suffering;
for that purpose, I shall do this,
and I shall know this."
Thus, [this knowledge] culminates in the realization that begins with "I am He" and ends in the realization of the ultimate;
and such mantras as "He who is its overseer in the highest heaven" (Ṛgveda 8.7.17.7, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.9) demonstrate this very meaning.

Furthermore, since there is no other conscious entity apart from the one God—who is pure consciousness acting as the presiding overseer of all and who, in the ultimate sense, has no connection with any enjoyment—there being no other enjoyer, the question "for what purpose is this creation? and its answer are both untenable; for [the Vedas ask]:
"Who indeed knows? Who here has declared it?"
From such Vedic mantra passages as, "Whence was this born? Whence is this emanation? (Ṛgveda 8.7.17.8), and so forth;
and it has been shown by the Blessed One: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.15).

Thus, though I am eternal, pure, enlightened by nature, omniscient, and the very Self of all living beings, the deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human form; they do not recognize my supreme state as the Great Lord of all beings. (BhG 9.11)
The deluded, lacking discrimination, despise me— that is, they treat me with contempt and show me disrespect—
because I have resorted to a human body, a form connected to humanity,
meaning that I am acting through a human body.

Not knowing My supreme state—the supreme reality of the Self, which is like space and even more internal than space—those wretched ones strike Me, their own self, who am the Great Lord of all beings, the supreme ruler of all creatures. And thus, by that cultivation of contempt for Me, they are struck down. (BhG 9.11)
How so?— "Those whose hopes are vain, whose actions are vain, whose knowledge is vain, and who are bereft of discernment,
have resorted to a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric. (BhG 9.12)
Those whose hopes, expectations, and blessings are in vain are "moghāśāḥ.
Likewise, their ritual acts— such as the *agnihotra* and other rites performed by them— are also in vain (*mogha-karmāṇaḥ*), because of their contempt for the Blessed One.
Because they disregard that which has become their very self, their actions become merely vain—that is, fruitless—and thus they are "those of vain action" (mogha-karmāṇaḥ).
Likewise, they are "those of vain knowledge" (mogha-jñānāḥ), meaning those whose knowledge is vain or fruitless;
for them, even knowledge would be entirely without result.
The intention is that they become devoid of discernment and lacking in discrimination.

Furthermore, they have resorted to—that is, taken refuge in—a Rākṣasī nature, which is the innate disposition of Rākṣasas; and an Āsurī nature, which is the innate disposition of Asuras, which is deluding, which causes delusion, and which asserts that the body is the self. [They say:
"Cut! Break!"
Drink, eat,
seize the property of others!
The meaning is that those whose habitual disposition is to speak in such a manner become performers of cruel deeds; for the Śruti declares: "Those worlds are called non-celestial" (Īśa Upaniṣad 3).
On the other hand, those who are full of faith and have set out upon the path to liberation characterized by devotion to the Blessed Lord—
But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, taking refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings.

But those of great resolve, O Pārtha, whose minds are not mean, having known Me— the Lord, the source of all beings, the imperishable cause of the elements such as ether and of all living creatures— worship and serve Me with single-minded devotion, having taken refuge in My divine nature, which is characterized by tranquility, self-control, compassion, faith, and other such qualities. (BhG 9.13)
How so?— constantly glorifying me, striving with firm vows, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (BhG 9.14)

Constantly and at all times glorifying Me, the Blessed One whose nature is Brahman, and striving— exerting themselves through virtues characterized by the withdrawal of the senses, tranquility, self-control, compassion, non-violence, and so forth— and being firm in their vows (those whose vow is firm, stable, and unshakable), and bowing down to Me, the Self dwelling in the heart, they worship and serve Me with devotion, remaining ever-disciplined.
In what various ways do they worship? It is said:
"Others also, sacrificing by means of the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as one, as distinct, and in many ways as the one whose face is everywhere. (BhG 9.15)
By the sacrifice of knowledge— that is, by the sacrifice which is knowledge itself concerning the Blessed Lord—
others, abandoning other forms of worship, worship Me, the Lord;
and they worship that knowledge through the vision of ultimate reality, worshipping by means of oneness, seeing that the Supreme Brahman is indeed one.
And some worship that very Lord Viṣṇu as abiding in distinct forms through the differentiation of the sun, moon, and so forth;
others worship that same Lord, who exists in many ways as the all-facing Universal Form (viśvarūpa), as that universal form which faces all directions and exists in many modes and various manners.
If they worship in many ways, how is it that they worship You alone? To this he says:
"I am the sacrifice (kratu), I am the oblation (yajña), I am the ancestral offering (svadhā), and I am the medicinal herb (auṣadha)."
I am the mantra; I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.
I am the *kratu*, the various types of Vedic ritual; I alone am the *yajña*, the Smṛti-based sacrifice. Furthermore, I am the *svadhā*, the ancestral food offering.
That which is given to the ancestors;

I am the "medicine" (auṣadha), that which is eaten by all living beings, designated by the word "medicine," common to rice, barley, and so forth. Or else, I am the "svadhā," the food common to all living beings.
"Medicine" refers to a remedy for the purpose of alleviating disease.
"Mantra" is I, by which the oblation is offered to the ancestors and the deities.
I alone am the clarified butter and the oblation.
I am Agni; that fire into which the oblation is offered is I myself. I am both the oblation and the act of offering.
Furthermore—
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather;
I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and likewise the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas.
I am the father, the progenitor of this world; I am the mother, the nurturer;
I am the ordainer, the dispenser of the fruits of actions to living beings.
The Grandfather is the father of the father;
the Knowable is that which is to be known;
the Purifier is the sanctifying syllable Om.
And also as the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus [Vedas].
Furthermore:
He is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend.
I am the source, the dissolution, the support, the treasure-house, and the imperishable seed.
Destiny is the fruit of karma;
the sustainer is the nourisher; the lord is the master.
He is the witness of the deeds and omissions of living beings;
He is the dwelling in which living beings reside;
and He is the refuge for the afflicted.
He is the remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge;
He is a friend who benefits others without expectation of anything in return; and He is the source and origin of the universe.
"Dissolution" (pralaya) is so called because in it all things dissolve; likewise, "abode" (sthāna) is that in which they abide;
and "repository" (nidhāna) is a storehouse for living beings to enjoy at a later time.
The seed is the cause of sprouting for those things characterized by sprouting;
it is imperishable because it persists as long as saṃsāra endures,
and indeed, nothing ever sprouts without a seed.
And because sprouting is observed constantly, it is understood that the continuum of the seed does not perish.
Furthermore:
I heat [the world], I withhold the rain, and I release it.
I am indeed both immortality and death, O Arjuna; I am both the existent and the non-existent.
Becoming the sun, I heat [the world] with certain fierce rays; with certain rays I release the rain;
having released it, I withdraw it again with certain rays for eight months, and then I release it once more during the rainy season.
The nectar of the gods and the death of mortals;
that which exists as belonging to something is "sat" (the existent).
And that which is the opposite of this, O Arjuna, is indeed non-existent;
yet the Blessed Lord is not absolutely non-existent, nor are existence and non-existence themselves the cause and effect.

Those knowers of knowledge who worship and meditate upon me with the aforementioned modes of withdrawal— through sacrifices consisting of the cognitions of oneness, difference, and so forth— they attain me alone, each according to their respective cognition. But those who are ignorant and desirous of objects of desire—

Those learned in the three Vedas, the drinkers of soma who have purified their sins by performing sacrifices, pray for the path to heaven; having reached the holy world of the lord of the gods, they [return].
In heaven, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures.

The knowers of the three Vedas— those who know the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*— who drink the Soma, meaning those who consume the Soma juice; thus purified of sin and cleansed of impurity by that very drinking of Soma, they worship Me in the form of the Vasu and other deities through sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*, and thereby attain the heavenly state— the going to heaven, where heaven itself is the goal.
They pray;

and having attained and reached merit and the fruit of merit, they enjoy and partake of divine, celestial, and extraordinary divine enjoyments— the pleasures of the gods— in the world of the Lord of Gods, the abode of Śatakratu.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted;
thus do those who have followed the dharma of the three Vedas.
Those who desire objects of desire obtain only what has been experienced before and what is already gone.

Having enjoyed that vast and extensive heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter— that is, they descend back to— the world of mortals. Thus, in the manner described, those who have resorted solely to the dharma of the three Vedas— namely, Vedic ritual action— and who desire objects of desire, undergo the process of going and coming, that is, the cycle of departure and return.
They obtain only the state of going and returning;
the meaning is that they do not obtain independence anywhere.
// BhG 9.21 // Furthermore, those who are free from desire and possess right vision—
For those people who worship Me, thinking of no other,
and who are constantly devoted to Me— I carry their acquisition and preservation.
Those people who, being renunciants, worship Me by meditating upon Me as their very Self— having realized that the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is non-different from them and not separate—

I carry out both the *yoga* and the *kṣema* for those perceivers of the ultimate truth who are eternally devoted and constantly engaged in practice; *yoga* is the attainment of what has not been attained, and *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been attained— I bring about both of these.

"But the man of knowledge, I consider to be My very Self" (Gītā 7.18), and "he is dear to Me" (Gītā 7.17). Since this is so, they have become My very Self and are dear to Me. Now, one might object: does the Blessed Lord not indeed carry the burden of the yoga and kṣema (acquisition and preservation) of other devotees as well?
True, He certainly carries it.
However, this is the distinction: other devotees, for their own sake, themselves seek security and acquisition (yoga-kṣema);
but those who perceive nothing else do not seek security and acquisition for their own sake.
Indeed, they harbor no craving for their own life or death.
They have the Blessed One alone as their refuge;
therefore, the Blessed One himself provides for their acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema).
[Objection: But surely there are other deities besides you, and those devoted to them worship those very deities. How is it that they worship you alone?
This is indeed so:
"Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule. (BhG 9.23)

"Even those who are devotees of other deities—being devoted to other deities, they sacrifice and worship with faith, endowed and followed by a sense of conviction—they too, O son of Kuntī, sacrifice to me alone, though in a manner not according to the prescribed rule; the meaning is that they sacrifice preceded by non-rule, which is ignorance. "Why do they sacrifice in a manner not according to the prescribed rule? It is said: because—"
For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall.

For I am indeed the deity and the enjoyer, as well as the Lord, of all sacrifices—both those prescribed by the Śruti and those prescribed by the Smṛti. Indeed, it has been said: "The sacrifice has Me as its master;
I alone am the Adhiyajña here" (Gītā 8.4). Thus, the sacrifice belongs to Me.
Thus, they do not recognize Me in truth as I am;
and therefore, having sacrificed according to improper rites, they fall away—they deviate from the fruit of their sacrifice.
(BhG 9.24) Even those who, being possessed of devotion to other deities, sacrifice according to improper rites, [fall away].

For them also, the fruit of sacrifice is inevitable. How so?—“Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me. (BhG 9.25)

Those whose vow, discipline, and devotion are directed toward the gods go to the gods; those whose vow is directed toward the ancestors—meaning those devoted to the ancestors who are intent on rites such as the *śrāddha*—go to the ancestors, such as the Agniṣvāttas and others; and those who worship spirits—meaning the worshippers of spirits such as Vināyaka, the hosts of Mothers, the Four Sisters, and so forth—go to the spirits.
Those who sacrifice to me, the Vaiṣṇavas whose nature is to worship me, go to me alone.
The meaning is that even though the effort is equal, those who do not resort to me alone out of ignorance become partakers of meager fruits.
Not only does My devotee obtain the infinite fruit characterized by non-return, but I am also easy to worship. How so?—
“Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water...”
Therefore, I eat what is offered with devotion by one whose self is disciplined.
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—
that offering of a leaf and so forth, presented with devotion and brought forward with a pure heart, I accept and partake of from that person of purified mind.
Since this is so, therefore—
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me.
Whatever you do as spontaneously obtained, whatever you eat,
and whatever you offer in sacrifice— whether performing a Vedic (śrauta) or traditional (smārta) oblation— [all that is done for Me].
Whatever you give— gold, food, clarified butter, and so forth— to the Brahmins and others,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī,
perform that as an offering unto Me, a dedication to Me.
Listen to what happens for you who act in this way:
"In this manner, you shall be released from the bonds of action through the very fruits of good and evil;
with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you shall come unto Me. (BhG 9.28)

By means of actions that have good and evil fruits— those actions whose fruits are good and evil, desirable and undesirable— by those very bonds of action, which are indeed the fetters of action, you shall be liberated by performing such dedication unto Me.
This is what is called the yoga of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yoga*): it is renunciation because [action] is performed through self-surrender to Me, and it is yoga because it is action;
thus, you are one whose inner organ (*ātman*)—that is, your mind—is joined with that yoga of renunciation, being "one whose self is joined with the yoga of renunciation."
Being truly liberated from the bonds of karma even while living, you shall come to me—that is, you will reach me—once this body has fallen.
[Objection: In that case, the Blessed One must possess attachment and aversion, since he favors his devotees.
That others [do not] is not so;
for: "I am equal toward all beings; there is none hateful to Me and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I also am in them. (BhG 9.29)
I am equal toward all beings;
none is hateful to me, nor is any dear.
I am like fire: just as fire does not remove the cold for those standing at a distance, [so too do I not bestow grace upon those who are far from me].
He removes [the darkness] from those who draw near;
likewise, I favor my devotees and not others.
But those who worship me, the Lord, with devotion—they are in me by their very nature.
The signs of passion do not exist for me toward them;
and I abide toward them by my very nature alone, not toward others. It is not on this account that I have hatred toward them. (BhG 9.29)
Listen to the majesty of devotion to Me:
"Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved. (BhG 9.30)
Moreover, even if one is of very bad conduct— meaning one whose behavior is extremely wicked and utterly contemptible— if he worships Me with undivided devotion, being devoted to no other,
he is to be regarded as indeed virtuous and of right conduct;
for he has rightly resolved as it truly is.
Because that is a virtuous certainty. Having cast off external wickedness through the power of right internal resolve,
he quickly becomes righteous in nature and attains eternal peace.
O son of Kuntī, declare with confidence: "My devotee perishes not."
He quickly and swiftly becomes one whose nature is Dharma, having a mind fixed on Dharma alone;
constantly and eternally, he enters and attains peace and tranquility.
Listen to the ultimate truth:
O Kaunteya, make a firm resolve; declare this certain vow:
"My devotee—who has surrendered his inner self to Me—does not perish.
(BhG 9.31) Furthermore:
For even those who may be of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they, O Pārtha, attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in me. (BhG 9.32)

For, O Pārtha, by taking refuge in me—that is, by accepting me as their support—even those who may be of sinful birth—those whose origin is sinful, meaning those of sinful birth or lowly descent—even they go to the supreme goal. Who are they? He says: women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras; even they attain the highest state.
How much more so, then, O Brahmins, meritorious ones, and royal sages—
having reached this transient and unhappy world, worship Me!
How much more so, then, those meritorious Brahmins born of merit, as well as the devoted royal sages (*rājarṣis*)—those who are both kings and sages.

Since this is so, having reached this world—the human realm—which is impermanent, momentary, fragile, and devoid of happiness, and having obtained the state of humanity which is difficult to find and is the means for accomplishing the goals of man, worship and serve Me. (BhG 9.33)
How so?—Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me. Thus, with your self disciplined and having Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. (BhG 9.34)
You, whose mind is fixed on me, Vāsudeva—become one whose mind is absorbed in me;
likewise, become my devotee;
become a sacrificer to me, habitually performing worship unto me.
And bow down to Me alone;
having disciplined and concentrated your mind, you shall come to Me alone as the Lord.
Thus, regarding Me as the Self—since I am indeed the Self of all beings and the supreme goal, the highest refuge—you shall go to Me who am such; this is the connection with the preceding word.
The meaning is: being one who has me as the supreme goal.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Royal Science and the Royal Secret," in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjya-pāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Ten: The Yoga of Manifestations (with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya)
In the seventh chapter, the true nature (*tattva*) and the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed One were revealed, as they were in the ninth.
Now, those various entities (*bhāva*) in which the Blessed One is to be meditated upon must be stated;
furthermore, the true nature of the Blessed One must be stated, even though it has already been mentioned.
Because it is difficult to understand, for this reason the Blessed Lord said:
"O mighty-armed one, listen once more to My supreme word."
That which I, desiring your welfare, shall speak to you who are well-disposed toward me.

Furthermore, O mighty-armed one, listen again and again to my supreme word, which reveals the unsurpassed reality— this most excellent speech for you who are so delighted, for you take great pleasure in my words as if drinking nectar.
Then—out of a desire for their welfare and a wish for their benefit—I shall speak. [BhG 10.1] To the question "For what purpose should I speak?", He says:
"Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know My origin."
For I am indeed the source of the gods and of the great seers in every respect.
The hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know me; they do not understand.
What is it that they do not know? My origin, my power, and the excellence of my sovereign might.
Or rather, "origin" means arising or birth;
even the great sages such as Bhṛgu and others do not know [Me].
Why do they not know? It is said: because I am the cause, the beginning, of the gods and the great sages in every way, that is, in all respects.
Moreover:
"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins. (BhG 10.3)
He who knows me as unborn and beginningless—
since I am the source of the gods and the great seers,
and no other origin for me exists.
Therefore, I am unborn and without beginning;
being without beginning is the reason for being unborn.

He who knows—that is, understands—Me as the unborn and without beginning, the Great Lord of the worlds (lokamaheśvara), the great Lord of all worlds, the Fourth (turīya) who is devoid of ignorance and its effects, he is undeluded, being free from delusion.
