Among mortal men, he is liberated— will be liberated— from all sins, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally. (BhG 10.3) Furthermore, for this reason also, I am the Great Lord of the worlds:
Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, calmness, pleasure, pain, birth, non-existence, fear, and even fearlessness; BhG 10.4.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the capacity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) to comprehend subtle objects and so forth; for they say that one who possesses this is "intelligent" (*buddhimān*).
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the comprehension of categories such as the self (*ātman*) and other principles.
Non-delusion is activity preceded by discernment regarding present objects to be understood. Forbearance is the state of an unaltered mind when reviled or struck.
Truth is speech uttered exactly as it was seen, heard, or personally experienced, for the purpose of transferring that understanding to another; such is called truth.
Dama is the calming of the external senses; śama is the calming of the internal organ;
sukha is delight.
Suffering is torment;
existence is arising;
non-existence is the opposite of that.
Fear is terror,
and fearlessness is its opposite.
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy— [these are the eightfold qualities].
The various states of beings arise from Me alone.
Non-violence is the non-affliction of living beings; equanimity is even-mindedness;
contentment is satisfaction and the sense of sufficiency regarding acquisitions.
Austerity is the infliction of bodily pain preceded by the restraint of the senses;
charity is the distribution [of goods] according to one's capacity;
fame is renown caused by righteousness.
Disrepute, however, is infamy caused by unrighteousness.

These aforementioned states—intellect and the rest—arise for living beings, that is, for sentient creatures, from Me alone, the Lord, as various and manifold kinds, according to their own respective actions.
Furthermore—
The seven great sages of old and likewise the four Manus,
whose offspring are these creatures in this world, were born of my mind and possess my own nature.
The seven great sages, Bhṛgu and the others, who belong to the past,
as well as the four Manus known as the Sāvarṇas—
they all possess my nature, their realization is directed toward me, and they are endowed with Vaiṣṇava power.
Those Manus and great seers were produced by me from my mind alone; they are born, that is, they have arisen.
From the creation of these Manus and great seers come these creatures in this world, characterized as both stationary and moving.
He who knows in truth this manifestation and this yoga of mine—
He applies himself to yoga with unwavering discipline; of this there is no doubt.

This aforementioned manifestation (*vibhūti*), expansion (*vistāra*), and yoga— meaning either the application (*yukti*) of one's own nature or the power of yogic sovereignty (*yoga-aiśvarya-sāmarthya*) consisting of omniscience born of yoga, which is called "yoga"—
he who knows this yoga of Mine in truth (*tattvataḥ*), that is, according to reality (*yathāvat*).
He is joined with, that is, connected to, yoga characterized by stability in right vision, which is unshakable and immovable.
There is no doubt here; there is no doubt regarding this matter.
(BhG 10.7) By what kind of unshakable yoga is he joined? It is said:
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with such realization, worship me.
I am the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the source and origin of the entire world;
from Me alone proceeds the entire world in its modified form, characterized by the functions of maintenance and destruction, and the experience of the fruits of action.
Thinking thus, the wise—those who have realized the truth of the ultimate reality—worship and serve Me.

Endowed with devotion means being possessed of *bhāva*; *bhāva* is the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of an intense attachment to the reality of the ultimate truth; the meaning is that they are joined or united with that.
Furthermore—having their minds fixed on Me, their life-breaths dedicated to Me, they enlighten one another.
And constantly speaking of me, they find contentment and delight.
"Mac-cittāḥ" means those whose minds are fixed on me;
"mad-gata-prāṇāḥ" means those whose vital functions—such as sight and so forth—have gone to and reached me; the meaning is that their senses have been withdrawn into me.
Or rather, "having their life-breaths gone into Me" means having their very existence centered on Me; thus,
making each other understand and realize this, and speaking to one another about Me as distinguished by qualities such as knowledge, power, and valor.
They are satisfied, they attain complete contentment, they rejoice, and they obtain delight, as if through union with a beloved.
For those devotees who, being steadfast, worship Me in the ways described above— those who worship Me constantly, with discipline, and with love— BhG 10.9.
I bestow upon them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me.

For those who are constantly disciplined, eternally devoted, whose external longings have all ceased, and who worship Me—by what motive, such as self-interest? No; He says: "with love as the primary motive. Love means affection; the meaning is: for those who worship Me preceded by such love.

I give, I bestow, *buddhi-yoga*: *buddhi* is right vision (*samyag-darśana*) concerning my true nature; the union with that is *buddhi-yoga*. By which *buddhi-yoga*, characterized by right vision, they approach—that is, attain—Me, the Supreme Lord, as their very self, as the Self itself? Who are they? Those who worship Me through the modes such as being "intent on Me" (*mac-citta*). (BhG 10.10)
In response to the inquiry— "For what purpose, or for whom, do you grant those devotees of yours the yoga of wisdom that destroys the cause obstructing their attainment of You?"— He says:
"Out of compassion for them alone, I [dispel] the darkness born of ignorance."
Abiding within their very self, I destroy [this ignorance] with the shining lamp of knowledge.

Out of compassion—that is, for the sake of their welfare—thinking, "How indeed might it be well for them?", I, remaining within my own being (*ātma-bhāva*), which is the internal disposition (*antaḥ-karaṇāśaya*) of the Self, dispel with the lamp of knowledge the darkness of delusion (*moha-andhakāra*). This darkness is born of ignorance through lack of discrimination, characterized by false notions. That lamp of knowledge takes the form of discriminative cognition; it is anointed with the oil of devotion and grace, and is fanned by the wind of resolute application to the contemplation of Me.

The meaning is: by means of the lamp of knowledge—which functions through wisdom refined by the purificatory disciplines such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which rests upon an internal organ characterized by dispassion, which stands in a windless chamber with the mind’s attachment and aversion toward sense objects turned away from them, and which is radiant with right vision born of meditation in constant one-pointedness.
Having heard of the Lord’s manifestations and yoga as described, Arjuna said:
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, the Ultimate Purifier; You are the eternal, divine Person, the Primal God, the unborn, and the all-pervading Lord.
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the supreme abode, the supreme splendor, the pure, the sanctifying, the most excellent and preeminent.
You are the eternal, perpetual, divine Person, the primordial God who exists at the beginning of all gods, the unborn, the all-pervading Lord whose nature is to pervade all.
Such as this—
"All the seers, as well as the celestial seer Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have declared this of you; and you yourself tell it to me. (BhG 10.13)
The sages Vasiṣṭha and all the others say this of you; likewise the celestial sage Nārada,
and Asita Devala says exactly the same, as does Vyāsa.
And you yourself tell me this very thing. (10.13) I consider all this that you tell me, O Keśava, to be the truth; for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know Your manifestation. (10.14)
I consider all this that has been spoken by the seers and by you to be truly and indeed real,
O Keśava, as you speak and declare it to me.
For neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know Your manifestation or Your origin.
Since you are the origin of the gods and all others, therefore— O Supreme Person, O Creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the universe— you alone know Yourself by Yourself.

You alone, by yourself, know and understand Yourself—the Lord who possesses unsurpassed power of knowledge, sovereignty, strength, and other faculties; O Supreme Person! You are the "Nourisher of Beings" (bhūta-bhāvana) because You cause all beings to come into existence.
O creator of beings,
O lord of beings,
O ruler of all creatures!
O God of gods, O Lord of the world!
You ought to speak without omission of Your divine self-manifestations.
By those manifestations through which you abide pervading these worlds.
"You ought to speak, you ought to tell [them] in their entirety;
for divine are your self-manifestations.
Those which are your own manifestations, those you ought to speak.
By which manifestations and expansions of Your own majesty You remain pervading these worlds.
// BhG 10.16 // O Yogin, how may I know You by constantly meditating upon You?
In what various forms, O Blessed One, are You to be contemplated by me? // BhG 10.17 //
How may I know You, O Yogin, as I constantly contemplate You?
In what various states and things, O Blessed One, are You to be thought of and meditated upon by me?
[BhG 10.17] O Janārdana, [tell me] in detail Your yoga and Your manifestations.
Speak further, for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar.

O Janārdana— [the term] *janārdana* being a form derived from the root *ard*, meaning "to go," [and so called] because you cause the destruction of *asuras* (those beings who are the adversaries of the gods), sending them to hell and other such realms— you have described in detail your own yoga, the specific power of your mastery over yoga (*yogaiśvarya-śakti-viśeṣa*), and the extent of your manifestations (*vibhūti*). Furthermore, O Janārdana, you are prayed to by all people for the purpose of the human goals of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Or rather:
speak again, even though it has been said before, for there is no satiety—no complete satisfaction—for me as I listen to the nectar of words issuing from your mouth. (BhG 10.18)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Behold, O best of the Kurus, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations according to their preeminence; there is no end to my expansion."

"Come now, O best of the Kurus, I shall describe to you those divine manifestations of Myself—which exist in heaven—that are My own sovereign powers. I shall describe each of those principal manifestations according to their importance;
however, it is not possible to describe them in their entirety even in a hundred years."
The meaning is that there is no end to the extent of my manifestations (*vibhūti*). First of all, listen to this:
"O Guḍākeśa, I am the Self (*ātman*) abiding in the heart (*āśaya*) of all beings."
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
"I am the Self, the innermost Self, O Guḍākeśa;
'Guḍākā' means sleep, and its 'īśa' (lord) is Guḍākeśa,
meaning one who has conquered sleep."
Or, as "He of Thick Hair":
I, the Self, the innermost Self (pratyag-ātman), who dwells within the heart—the abode—of all beings, am to be meditated upon constantly.
And by one unable to do that, I am to be contemplated in the subsequent states.
Since I alone am the beginning, the cause, as well as the middle—the duration—and the end—the dissolution—of all beings;
and thus I am to be meditated upon: among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu, and among luminaries I am the radiant Sun.
Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.
Among the twelve Ādityas, I am the Āditya named Viṣṇu;
among luminaries, I am the radiant Sun;
and among the Maruts—the various classes of Marut deities—I am he named Marīci.
Among the stars, I am the moon, Śaśin.
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāma Veda; among the gods, I am Vāsava;
among the senses, I am the mind; and among beings, I am consciousness.
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāma Veda;
among the gods, such as the Rudras and Ādityas, I am Vāsava, Indra;
and among the eleven senses, beginning with the eye, I am the mind—that mind which consists of volition and conceptualization.
Of beings, I am consciousness—the mental function of the intellect that is eternally manifest within the aggregate of the body and its organs.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth;
among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
Among the eleven Rudras, I am Śaṅkara;
among the Yakṣas and Rakṣasas, I am Kuvera the lord of wealth;
and among the eight Vasus, I am Pāvaka the fire.
Among peaked mountains, I am Meru.
O Pārtha, know me to be Bṛhaspati, the foremost among priests;
among army commanders, I am Skanda; and among bodies of water, I am the ocean.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be the chief and foremost among the domestic priests and royal chaplains—namely Bṛhaspati;
for he is the principal domestic priest of Indra.
Among the leaders of armies, I am Skanda, the commander of the divine host.
Of the lakes and those bodies of water dug by the gods, among all such waters, I am the ocean.
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; of words, I am the single syllable Om;
of sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña); and of immovable things, I am the Himalaya.
Among the great seers (maharṣis), I am Bhṛgu;
among words and speech characterized by syllables, I am the single syllable, the syllable Om;
among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña).
Among the immovable things that possess stability, I am the Himalaya;
among all trees, I am the Ashvattha; and among the divine seers, I am Narada.
Among the Gandharvas, I am Citraratha; and among the perfected ones (siddhas), I am the sage Kapila.
Among all trees I am the aśvattha;
and among the divine seers (devarṣis) I am Nārada. Those who, being gods, have attained the state of seers due to their vision of the mantras are the divine seers (devarṣis); among them, I am Nārada.
Among the Gandharvas, I am the one named Citraratha;
among the Siddhas—those who by birth alone have attained excellence in righteousness, knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty—I am the sage Kapila.
Know me, O best of the Kurus, as Uccaiḥśravas, the horse born of the nectar of immortality, among horses.
Among lordly elephants, I am Airāvata; and among men, I am the sovereign of men.

Among horses, know me to be Uccaiḥśravas by name, the king of horses; know me to have arisen from the nectar—that is, to have been produced during the churning for the sake of the nectar. Among the lordly elephants, the masters of beasts, know me to be Airāvata, the offspring of Irāvatī.
The phrase "know me" (tam mām viddhi) carries over [from the previous sentence].
And among men—that is, among human beings—know me to be the lord of men, the king.
Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt; among cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow;
and I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and among serpents, I am Vāsuki.
Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt born from the bone of Dadhīci;
among milch-cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhuk) belonging to Vasiṣṭha, which yields all desires, or rather, I am the universal wish-fulfilling cow.
Among progenitors, I am Kandarpa, the god of love;
among serpents—that is, among the various species of snakes—I am Vāsuki, the king of snakes.
And among the Nāgas, I am Ananta; and among the aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa.
Among the ancestors I am Aryaman, and among those who restrain, I am Yama.
Among the Nāgas, I am Ananta; among the distinguished Nāgas, I am the Nāga King. Among the aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa; I am the king of the water-deities.
Among the ancestors, I am he named Aryaman; I am the king of the Pitṛs.
Among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama;
among the Daityas, I am Prahlāda; I am Time among those who calculate;
and among beasts, I am the king of beasts, while among birds, I am Vainateya.
Among the Daityas of Diti’s lineage, I am known by the name Prahlāda;
among those who calculate, I am Time (Kāla), the reckoning of those who perform calculation;
and among wild beasts, I am the king of beasts—the lion or the tiger.
And I am Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, Vainateya, among the winged birds. I am Pavana among the purifiers; I am Rāma among those who bear weapons;
I am the Makara among fish, and I am the Jāhnavī among rivers.
Among those that purify, I am Pavana, the wind;
among wielders of weapons, I am Rāma—the son of Daśaratha, Rāma;
and among aquatic creatures such as fish, I am the species known as the Makara.
Among flowing streams, I am the Jāhnavī, the Gaṅgā.
O Arjuna, I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations;
among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātma-vidyā); and among those who debate, I am the dialectic.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations— of all emanations— I am their origin, their sustenance, and their dissolution, O Arjuna.

Although it was stated at the outset that I am the beginning and the end of "beings" (bhūtānām) specifically as those presided over by individual souls (jīva), the distinction here is that I am the beginning, middle, and end of the entire process of creation without such qualification.

Among the sciences, I am the science of the inner self (*adhyātma-vidyā*), because it has liberation as its purpose; among those who debate, I am the formal debate (*vāda*), because it is the means for determining the truth—
therefore, I am that.
By way of the speakers, it is the varieties of speech—namely *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*—that are understood here as "of those who debate" (*pravadatām*).
Among letters I am the letter *a*; and among compounds, I am the copulative compound (*dvandva*).
I alone am inexhaustible Time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.
Among letters—that is, among phonemes—I am the letter *a*;

among compounds, I am the *dvandva* compound; and among all collections of compounds, I am likewise. Furthermore, I alone am the imperishable time (kāla), well known by such names as the moment (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Or rather, I am the Supreme Lord, the Time even of time;
I am the Ordainer who dispenses the fruits of action, facing all directions for the entire world.
I am death that carries away all, and I am the source of those things yet to be.
Among women, I am fame, fortune, eloquence, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forbearance.
Death is of two kinds: that which takes away wealth and so forth, and that which takes away life. Of these, that which takes away life is said to take everything away.
The meaning is "I am He.
Alternatively, the Supreme Lord is the "All-Consumer" (sarva-hara) because He withdraws everything at the time of dissolution; I am He.
Furthermore, I am the "Source" (udbhava), which means excellence or spiritual elevation, as well as the cause for attaining that state.
Of whom? Of those who are destined for future welfare—meaning, those capable of attaining excellence.
Among women, fame, fortune, eloquence, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness—I am these supreme qualities.
By the mere connection with whose radiance even the world considers itself to have achieved its purpose.
Among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-Sāman; among meters, I am the Gāyatrī;
among months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and among seasons, I am the flower-bearing spring.
Likewise, among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-sāman, the foremost;
and among the meters (chandas), I am the Gāyatrī—the meaning is that among the Ṛks distinguished by meters such as the Gāyatrī and others, I am the Gāyatrī verse.
Among the months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa.
Among the seasons, I am spring, the source of flowers. Of those who deceive, I am gambling; of the radiant, I am splendor;
of victors, I am victory; of the resolute, I am resolve; and of the virtuous, I am goodness.
I am gambling, characterized by the casting of dice and so forth, among those who practice deception;
I am the splendor of the splendid;
I am victory among victors.
Among those who possess resolve, I am resolve;
among those endowed with goodness, I am the goodness of the virtuous.
Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, I am Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among poets I am Uśanas, the poet.
Among the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas, I am this very Vāsudeva, your friend;
among the Pāṇḍavas, you yourself are Dhanañjaya;
and even among the sages—those of contemplative nature who know all things—I am Vyāsa.
Among poets who perceive the truth, I am Uśanas, the sage.
Of those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; of those who seek victory, I am statesmanship.
Among secrets, I am silence; and among the wise, I am knowledge itself.
Of those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; I am the chastiser of the unsubdued. Of those desiring victory, I am policy;
and of secrets to be guarded, I am silence.
I am the knowledge of those who possess knowledge. And that which is the seed of all beings, O Arjuna, that too I am;
there is no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me.

And furthermore, O Arjuna, that which is the seed and the cause of growth for all beings— that, for the purpose of concluding the section, He states as a summary of His manifestations: "There is no being, whether moving or unmoving, that exists without Me."
That which would exist without me—that is, withdrawn by me or abandoned by me—would indeed be soulless and void. Therefore, the meaning is that everything has me as its essence. (BhG 10.39)
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
this detailed exposition of my glory has been declared by me only in brief.
There is no end to the extent of my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
for it is not possible for anyone to describe or even to know the limit of the divine manifestations of the Lord who is the Self of all.
This detailed account of my manifestation has been declared by me only in brief, as a single portion.
Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or power,
know that to be born from but a fragment of My splendor.

Whatever being in the world is possessed of power—whether it be a thing endowed with majesty, or glorious, or even exalted; whether it be accompanied by *śrī* (fortune), that is, by *lakṣmī*, or endowed with energy—all that you should understand, know, to be born from a portion of My, the Lord’s, splendor—that which has its origin in a single part of My splendor is "born from a portion of splendor" (*tejo’ṃśa-sambhavam*). Understand this.
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge to you, O Arjuna?
Sustaining this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world.
Or rather, what would be the use for you, O Arjuna, of knowing much more of this kind and so forth, since it would remain incomplete?

Listen, however, to the matter being stated in its entirety: having specially supported—that is, having made firm—this entire world with one part, that is, with one limb or one foot, which is the very nature of all beings.
And thus says the Vedic hymn: "A foot of Him are all beings" (Ṛgveda 8.4.17.3).
"I am established [in that foot]" (BhG 10.42).

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Eleven:
The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form.
(Commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda:
The manifestations of the Blessed One have been described.

In that context, having heard what was declared by the Blessed One—"By a single portion of myself, I stand supporting this entire world" (Gītā 10.42)—[Arjuna asks about] that which is the form of the world-soul.
Desiring to directly perceive that primordial, divine [form], Arjuna said:
"By those words which You have spoken for my benefit—supreme, secret, and known as the Adhyātma—this delusion of mine has vanished. (BhG 11.1)

For the sake of my grace—that is, for the purpose of favoring me—by that speech which You have uttered, which is supreme (paramam), unsurpassed (niratiśayam), secret (guhyam), to be guarded (gopyam), designated as "the inner self" (adhyātma-saṃjñitam), and concerning the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self (ātmānātma-viveka-viṣayam)—by that speech of Yours, this delusion (moha) of mine has departed; the meaning is that my non-discriminating intellect (aviveka-buddhi) has been removed. (BhG 11.1)
Moreover:
"The origin and dissolution of beings have indeed been heard by me in detail from you, O lotus-eyed one, as well as your imperishable majesty. (BhG 11.2)
"Becoming" is birth and "dissolution" is destruction; these two, becoming and dissolution, have indeed been heard by me in detail from you—
not in brief—
from your presence.

O lotus-petal-eyed one! "Lotus-petal" (kamala-patra) refers to the petal of a lotus; you are so called because your eyes are like that, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Furthermore, the state of being a great soul is "māhātmya," which is also imperishable and inexhaustible.
The word "heard" (śrutam) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].
"It is exactly as you have described yourself, O Supreme Lord.
I desire to see your divine form, O Supreme Person."
"It is exactly so, not otherwise, in whatever manner and by whatever means you describe yourself, O Supreme Lord.
Nevertheless, O Supreme Person, I desire to see Your divine Vaiṣṇava form, endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor.
"If You think it possible for me to see that, O Lord," BhG 11.3.2.
O Lord of Yoga, therefore show me Your imperishable Self.

O Lord, O Master, O Lord of Yoga— if you think, if you consider that it is possible for me, Arjuna, to see that [form], then [I shall show it to you]; "yogeśvara" means the Lord of Yogas, the master of those who possess yoga.
O Lord of Yoga!
Since I am exceedingly desirous to see [Thee], therefore, for my sake, show Thyself as the Imperishable Self.
Thus urged by Arjuna, the Blessed One said:
"Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands—
divine, of various kinds, and of many colors and shapes."
Behold my forms, O Pārtha, by the hundreds and by the thousands;
that is to say, in great numbers.

And those various forms are of many kinds, celestial, belonging to heaven, and non-material; they possess various colors and shapes—colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth, being of diverse types, and likewise shapes, which are specific arrangements of parts—and thus they are "of various colors and shapes. (BhG 11.5)
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the two Aśvins and the Maruts;
behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before.
Behold the twelve Ādityas,
the eight Vasus,
and the eleven Rudras.
The two Aśvins; the Maruts, who consist of seven groups of seven;
and likewise many others never before seen in the world of men by you, or by anyone other than you.
Behold these wonders and marvels, O Bhārata!
(BhG 11.6) It is not merely this much—
behold today, all here in one place, the entire universe with its moving and unmoving beings.
O Guḍākeśa, whatever else you wish to see within my body, [tell me that].
Behold here today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe— everything together with the moving and the unmoving— situated in one place, within my very body;
and whatever else you fear, such as victory and defeat.
As for what you said, "Whether we shall conquer them or they shall conquer us," if you wish to see that as well— [BhG 11.7]—
nevertheless:
But you are not able to see Me with these very eyes of yours;
I shall give you divine vision; behold My sovereign yoga.
But you are not able to see me, the bearer of the universal form, with this very same natural eye of yours;
however, that divine eye with which you may be able to see it, that divine eye I give to you.
"Therefore, behold my divine yoga"—the meaning is: behold my divine yoga, which is the supreme excellence of the power of yoga, belonging to me, the Lord.
Sanjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the Great Lord of Yoga, then—
He revealed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.

Having spoken thus in the manner described, immediately thereafter, O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great Lord of Yoga— the one who is both great and the Lord of Yoga, the Great Lord of Yoga, Hari Nārāyaṇa— revealed, he showed, to Pārtha, the son of Pṛthā, his supreme form, the universal form, the sovereign form.
With many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders,
adorned with many divine ornaments, and wielding many uplifted divine weapons.
"Having many mouths and eyes" means that form in which there are many mouths and many eyes; "having many wonderful sights" means that form in which there are many wonderful, astonishing appearances;
likewise, "having many divine ornaments" means that in which there are many divine ornaments.
Likewise, [He] showed [Himself] with many divine weapons raised; that is, [He] in whom many divine weapons such as swords and so forth were raised—that is "divyānekodyatāyudham.
This is to be connected with the preceding verb "darśayāmāsa" (He showed).
Furthermore—
The Lord who wears celestial garlands and garments, who is anointed with celestial perfumes,
who consists of all wonders, who is infinite, and whose faces are everywhere.

Wearing divine garlands and garments—that Lord by whom divine garlands (mālya), flowers, and garments (ambara) are worn; anointed with divine perfumes—that one whose divine perfumes and ointments (anulepana) are present; the God consisting of all wonders, abounding in every marvel; the Infinite—He who has no end (anta).
He showed him that which has faces everywhere—that is, faces on all sides—because He has become the self of all beings;
it is to be supplied that Arjuna saw Him. (BhG 11.11)
Furthermore, an analogy for that radiance of the Blessed One, who possesses all forms, is stated: "It would be like the simultaneous rising of a thousand suns in the sky."
If that light were similar to the light of that Great-Souled One, it would be so.

Or in the atmosphere, or in heaven, if there were a thousand suns— that is, a thousand suns— rising simultaneously, the radiance of those thousand suns rising together would be like the radiance of that Great-Souled One who possesses the Universal Form.
Or if it were not so, then the splendor of Viśvarūpa alone would be excessive; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore—
Then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld the entire universe, divided into many parts, situated within the body of the God of gods.

Then, in that single universal form, Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, beheld the entire world situated within it, existing as one yet divided manifoldly through the distinctions of gods, ancestors, humans, and so forth; he saw this in the body of Hari, the God of gods. (BhG 11.13)
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the Lord and spoke with palms joined in reverence: Bhagavad Gītā 11.14.

Then, having seen him, Dhanañjaya was overcome with wonder; his hair stood on end, and he became one whose body hairs were thrilled. Having bowed down—having performed a profound salutation—and being deeply humbled, he spoke with his head to the God who bears the universal form, with palms joined in reverence for the purpose of paying homage.
How so? Revealing his own experience by saying, "I see that universal form which was shown by you," Arjuna said:
"O God, I see the gods within your body."
All the hosts of various beings,
Brahmā the Lord seated upon the lotus-throne,
all the sages, and the divine serpents— [I see them all].

I see, O Lord, I perceive within your body all the gods, as well as the hosts of various classes of beings— the multitudes of distinct types of beings, both stationary and moving, possessing diverse forms and characteristics.
Furthermore: Brahmā, the four-faced Lord, the ruler of creatures, seated upon the lotus—meaning seated on the Meru-calyx in the midst of the earth-lotus;
and all the sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest;
and the divine serpents, Vāsuki and others, who dwell in heaven.
I see you on all sides with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms; I see neither your end, nor your middle, nor again your beginning.
I behold you, O Lord of the Universe, in your universal form.

I see You, who possess many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes—that is, You whose arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes are many—as having infinite forms, meaning You whose forms are endless; "endless" (*ananta*) refers to that which has no end, where "end" (*anta*) means a limit or conclusion. I see You everywhere, in all places.
Nor is there a middle;
for "middle" is the interval between two extremes.
Furthermore, I do not see your beginning—nor do I see the end of the God.
I do not see the middle,
nor again do I see the beginning, O Lord of All, O You of Universal Form! BhG 11.16.
Furthermore: [I see] him wearing a crown, holding a mace and a discus, a mass of splendor blazing on all sides.
I behold You, difficult to gaze upon, with the immeasurable splendor of blazing fire and the sun on all sides.

To Kirīṭin, who possesses a *kirīṭa*—a specific kind of head ornament—and thus is called Kirīṭin; likewise to Gadin, who possesses a mace (*gada*) and is thus called Gadin; and likewise to Cakrin, who possesses a discus (*cakra*) and is thus called Cakrin.

I see You as a mass of splendor, a heap of radiance, blazing on all sides; "blazing on all sides" (*sarvatodīptimān*) means that which possesses a blaze extending in every direction. I see You, who are difficult to behold from every side—that is, everywhere—possessing a luster like that of a blazing fire and the sun; "fire and sun" (*analārkau*), "blazing fire and sun" (*dīptānalārkau*), and the luster of those two blazing fire and sun.

You, whose splendor is light—that is, you who possess the brilliance of a blazing fire and the sun—are one of blazing fire and solar radiance; you are that immeasurable one, "immeasurable" meaning not subject to measurement and impossible to define.
From this very manifestation of your yogic power, I infer:
You are the supreme imperishable to be known;
you are the ultimate refuge of this universe;
you are the undecaying protector of the eternal dharma.
You are considered by me to be the eternal Puruṣa.
You are the Imperishable (akṣara), so called because you do not decay; you are the Supreme Brahman, to be known—that is, to be realized—by those seeking liberation.
You are the supreme, most excellent repository (nidhāna) of this entire universe; "repository" means that in which everything is deposited, meaning the ultimate support.
Furthermore, you are imperishable (*avyaya*); because no decay exists for you, you are "imperishable.

You are the protector of the eternal dharma (*śāśvata-dharma-goptā*); that which exists eternally is "eternal" (*śāśvata*), meaning constant; you are the protector of that dharma. You are considered by me to be the ancient, primeval Supreme Person (*sanātana-puruṣa-parama*). (BhG 11.18)
Furthermore:
[He is] without beginning, middle, or end; with infinite vigor and infinite arms; with the moon and sun as his eyes.
I see you with a mouth like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with your own splendor.
"Without beginning, middle, or end" means that for you there is no beginning, middle, or end; thus, you are "without beginning, middle, or end.
"Of infinite vigor" means that there is no end to your vigor; thus, you are "of infinite vigor."
To you, who possess infinite valor;
likewise, to you who have infinite arms— he whose arms are infinite is "ananta-bāhu," to you, that one with infinite arms.
I behold you, whose eyes are the moon and the sun— that is, you whose two eyes are the moon and the sun;
I behold you, whose mouth is blazing fire— that is, you whose mouth is both blazing and fire.
To you, whose mouth is a blazing fire,
who heats this entire universe with your own splendor—
[for this space between heaven and earth...]
All the directions are pervaded by you alone;
having seen this wondrous and fierce form of yours, O Great-Souled One, the three worlds are deeply distressed.

Indeed, this space between heaven and earth, the intermediate region, is pervaded by you alone who bear all forms; and all the directions are pervaded as well. Having seen—having perceived—this wondrous and astonishing form of yours, which is fierce and terrible, the three worlds, the triple universe, are deeply distressed, terrified, or shaken.
O Great-Souled One!
"Of noble nature.

Now, the Blessed One proceeds with the intent of demonstrating the absolute victory of the Pāṇḍavas in order to resolve that doubt which previously existed in Arjuna— namely, "whether we shall conquer, or whether they shall conquer us."
Beholding him, he said: "Moreover—these hosts of gods are indeed entering into you;
some, overcome with fear, offer praise with palms joined."
Saying "May it be well!", the hosts of great seers and perfected beings praise you with abundant hymns of praise.
For these warriors who are fighting— those hosts of gods such as Vasu and others who have descended here in human form to remove the burden of the earth— are seen entering you;
as they enter, some are seen praising and glorifying you with joined palms out of fear, while others are unable even to flee.

When battle is imminent, having observed omens such as portents, the hosts of great seers and perfected beings— those assemblies of maharṣis and siddhas— saying, "May there be well-being for the world," praise You with abundant and complete hymns of praise.
(BhG 11.21) Furthermore:
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas;
the Viśvedevas, Aśvins, Maruts, and Uṣmapās;
and the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas.
And they all gaze upon you, filled with wonder.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas; the hosts beginning with the Rudras; the Viśvedevas and the two Aśvin deities; the Maruts and the Pitṛs who drink the steam;

the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas—the Gandharvas such as Hāhā and Hūhū, the Yakṣas such as Kubera, the Asuras such as Virocana, and the Siddhas such as Kapila—all these, having become filled with wonder, gaze upon You. 11.22.
Because— O mighty-armed one, your form is vast, with many mouths and eyes, and many arms, thighs, and feet.
Seeing You with many bellies and formidable with many tusks, the worlds are terrified, as am I.
Your form is great and of immense proportions; it has many mouths and eyes—that form in which there are many faces and eyes is "many-mouthed-and-eyed. O mighty-armed one!
It has many arms, thighs, and feet—that form in which there are many arms, thighs, and feet is "many-armed-thighed-and-footed."
Furthermore, "bahūdaram" means that in which there are many bellies;
"bahu-daṃṣṭrā-karālam" means that which is formidable and distorted with many fangs. Having seen such a form, the worldly beings—ordinary living creatures—were terrified and shaken by fear.
So am I as well. //BhGS 11.23// ============================== The reason for this is as follows:
[I am] touching the sky, blazing, and multicolored.
O Viṣṇu, seeing You with Your mouth wide open and Your vast eyes blazing, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
"Touching the sky" means touching the heavens;
"blazing" means flaming up;
"of many colors" means you in whom there are many terrifying colors and various forms—such a You are "of many colors."
Having seen you with wide-open mouths— that is, you in whom the mouths (*ānana*) are wide open (*vyātta*)—

and with blazing, large eyes— that is, you in whom the eyes (*netra*) are blazing (*dīpta*), inflamed, and large (*viśāla*), my inner self is indeed deeply distressed; that is, it is greatly pained and terrified.

I, whose inner self (antarātmā) is the mind, being thus deeply distressed in my inner self, find no steadfastness (dhṛti)—that is, no fortitude—and I obtain no tranquility (śama), nor the peace of mental contentment. O Viṣṇu!
Why is this?
Having merely seen your mouths, terrifying with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction,
I no longer know the directions nor do I find any peace.
Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe!

Having seen— that is, having perceived— your mouths, which are formidable with tusks (*daṃṣṭrā-karālāni*), distorted by their tusks, and resembling the fire of time (*kālānala-saṃnibhāni*)— the fire of time being that which burns the worlds at the end of the cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*)— having seen your mouths resembling that fire of time.
I do not know the directions due to my inability to distinguish between east and west; I have become disoriented. Therefore, I find neither peace nor happiness.
For this reason, be gracious, O Lord of Gods, and be well-disposed toward me.
O Abode of the Universe!
//BhG 11.25// ============================== That fear of defeat which I once had regarding them has now vanished;
for—these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [are gazing at You].
All of them together with the hosts of kings—
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Kṛṣṇa),
along with our own foremost warriors as well.

And these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, are entering in haste—all together, united with the hosts of rulers of the earth (avanipālas)—those who protect the earth (avanīm) are called avanipālas; with their multitudes. This is the connection with the word "entering" which is placed further on.

Moreover, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the Sūta’s son Karṇa, and likewise those others, together with our own foremost warriors such as Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the rest— along with these leaders and preeminent among combatants—
enter your mouths, hastening toward them.
Terror-striking and formidable with their fangs,
some are seen caught between the teeth with their heads crushed to powder. (BhG 11.27)
Your mouths—your faces—enter [them] while being in a state of haste, possessed of speed. Of what kind are those mouths?
Terrifying, formidable, and fearsome, with fangs that are jagged and gaping.

Furthermore, some are seen and perceived among those who have entered the mouths, stuck between the teeth as if they were meat being eaten, with their heads—their upper parts—crushed and reduced to powder. How do they enter the mouths? To this he says:
Just as the many currents of water in rivers flow toward the ocean, so do these heroes of the world of men [flow] toward you.
They enter the blazing mouths.

Just as the many and numerous currents of water—the various velocities of the waters—of flowing rivers rush toward and enter the ocean headlong, even so do these heroes of the world of men, Bhīṣma and the others, who are valiant in the human world, enter Your blazing, radiant mouths.
To the question, "For what purpose do they enter, and how? He says:
Just as moths with full force enter a blazing fire for their own destruction,
even so do worldly beings enter it for their destruction.
Even your mouths [will be filled] by those of great speed.
Just as moths and winged insects, with full force— that is, those whose speed or motion has become fully developed and intense— enter a blazing, flaming fire for their destruction,
even so do living beings, with full force, enter your mouths for their destruction. Furthermore, you—
Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths,
you lick them while filling the entire universe with your splendors.
Your fierce rays blaze forth, O Viṣṇu.

You lick—that is, you taste—swallowing as you draw them inward from all sides; you fill and pervade the entire world together with its extremities, using your mouths—your faces—which are ablaze, being suffused with radiant splendors.
"The entire world" means everything together with its front, that is, the whole.
Furthermore, O Viṣṇu, whose nature is all-pervading, your fierce and cruel rays shine—that is, they exert their scorching heat.
Since you are thus of such a terrible nature, tell me: who are you in this fierce form?
Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious.
I desire to know you, the Primordial One, for I do not understand your manifestation.
Tell me, declare to me who you are, you of fierce form and cruel appearance.
Homage be to you, O best of gods, foremost among deities;
be gracious, show favor.
I desire to know you specifically— that is, I wish to know you as the primordial one, existing from the very beginning— for I do not understand your activity, that is, your course of action.
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown powerful and engaged here in withdrawing the worlds;
even without you, all shall cease to exist.
Those warriors who are stationed in the opposing armies.

I am Time, the destroyer of worlds; "the destroyer of worlds" means one who brings about the destruction of all beings. Having increased—that is, having reached full maturity—listen to the purpose for which I have increased: I have set out at this time to gather together, that is, to annihilate, the worlds. Even without you, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and all the others shall cease to exist.
"Those from whom you have apprehension,
those who are stationed in the opposing ranks— in each opposing rank, that is, in the enemy forces standing as adversaries— there are warriors, namely fighters.
(BhG 11.32) Since it is thus:
Therefore, arise and win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone.
Be merely a sign, O Savyasācin!
Therefore, arise! Attain the glory that Bhishma and the other great car-warriors—invincible even to the gods—were defeated by Arjuna;
for that is attained solely through merit.
Having conquered your enemies, Duryodhana and the others, enjoy the prosperous kingdom, free from rivals and thorns.
By me alone have these been slain; they were already deprived of life by me beforehand.
You are merely the instrument.
O Savyasācin!
Because he shoots arrows with both his right and his left hand, Arjuna is called Savyasācin.
[He who can slay] Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and likewise other heroic warriors—
Slay those already slain by me; do not be distressed.
Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.
And as for Droṇa, the Blessed One points out each and every warrior of whom Arjuna was apprehensive, saying, "He has been slain by me.
In this regard, the cause for apprehension concerning Droṇa and Bhīṣma is well known;
for Droṇa was a teacher of the science of archery, endowed with divine weapons.
Moreover, his own preceptor was especially venerable;
and Bhīṣma, who possessed the power to die at will and was endowed with divine weapons, engaged in a duel with Paraśurāma and was not defeated.
Likewise, Jayadratha [was born], whose father was performing ascetic penance with this resolve: "Whoever shall cause my son's head to fall upon the earth,
his head too shall fall."
Karna, the son of Surya, was also endowed with the unerring spear given by Vasava; since he was born of a maiden, he is designated by that very name.
"Slay those slain by me, acting as a mere instrument."
"Do not be distressed; do not fear them.
Fight, and you shall conquer your rivals—the enemies such as Duryodhana and others—in the battle.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava,
Kirīṭin, trembling and with palms joined in reverence,
bowed down again and spoke further to Kṛṣṇa.
Bowing down with great fear, he spoke with a faltering voice.

Having heard these words previously spoken by Keśava, Kirīṭin—with palms joined in reverence, trembling and shaking—having offered salutation, spoke again to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice. This faltering arises from being overcome by fear due to the impact of grief, and from the emergence of joy due to being overwhelmed by affection;
it occurs when the throat is constricted by phlegm upon the eyes being filled with tears.

And then, "with faltering voice" (*sa-gadgada*) means that which is accompanied by a lack of fluency in speech, a dullness of sound, and a stammer; this is an adverbial modifier for the act of speaking, meaning he spoke these words with such a voice. "Extremely terrified" (*bhīta-bhītaḥ*) means having a mind repeatedly overcome by fear; "having bowed down" (*praṇamya*) means having become prostrate. This connects with the word "spoke" (*āha*), which is separated [from its modifiers]. (BhG 11.35)
Arjuna said:
"It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that the world rejoices and is filled with devotion by the proclamation of your glory."
The *rakṣas* flee in all directions out of fear,
and all the hosts of *siddhas* pay homage.
It is fitting;
what is it? It is by hearing the proclamation of Your greatness—the chanting of Your majesty—O Hṛṣīkeśa!
The meaning is that it is "fitting" (sthāne), that is, appropriate, that the world rejoices and attains great joy. Alternatively, "fitting" (sthāne) is an adjective qualifying the object [of joy].
The Blessed One is the proper object of joy and other such emotions, because He is the Lord, the Self of all, and the friend of all beings;
thus one becomes attached to Him and attains devotion.
And that [fleeing] should be understood as occurring "in the domain" (viṣaye).
Furthermore, the *rakṣas*—terrified, meaning overcome with fear—flee, that is, they go toward the various directions; and that occurs "in the domain," meaning within their sphere of activity.

All the hosts of perfected beings—the assemblies of Siddhas such as Kapila and others—bow down and pay homage; and that is only fitting. [BhG 11.36] He shows the reason why the Blessed One is an object of joy and so forth:
And why should they not bow down to you, O Great-Souled One, who are greater even than Brahmā, the original creator—
O Infinite One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe?
You are the imperishable, that which is being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.

And for what reason, O Great-Souled One, should they not bow down—that is, offer salutation—to You? Because You are more venerable, that is, weightier, than even Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha; since You are the primal creator, the cause [of him], therefore [they should bow] to the Primal Creator.
How could they not pay homage?
Therefore, the meaning is that you are the worthy object—the proper locus—for joy and other such emotions, as well as for salutation.
O Infinite One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe, you are that supreme Imperishable.
That which is heard in the Vedāntas—what is it? "Being" (sat) and "non-being" (asat). "Being" means that which exists.
The unreal is that regarding which there is the cognition "it does not exist.
That syllable for which both the real and the unreal serve as its substratum— that is,
by means of which the designations "real" and "unreal" are metaphorically applied— is [the supreme reality].
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, that imperishable is beyond both being and non-being, which those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable (akṣara).
The intention is that you alone are that, and nothing else. (Gītā 11.37)
He praises him once more:
"You are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe."
You are the knower and the object of knowledge, and the supreme abode;
by You the entire universe is pervaded, O You of infinite forms.

You are the primordial god (*ādi-deva*) because you are the creator of the world; you are the Puruṣa because you dwell within the city [of the body]; and you alone are the ancient (*purāṇa*), eternal one, the supreme and most excellent repository (*nidhāna*) of this universe, in which the entire world is deposited at the beginning of the great dissolution (*mahā-pralaya*). Furthermore, you are the knower (*vettā*).
You are the knower of every class of object to be known;
and that which is to be known, which is worthy of being felt, You are that, the supreme abode, the highest station of Viṣṇu.
By You the entire universe is pervaded and encompassed.
O you of infinite forms!
No end to your forms is found.
Furthermore—
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, and the Great-Grandfather;
homage, homage be to you a thousand times over.
And yet again, once more, salutations, salutations unto you!
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the lord of waters, Śaśāṅka, Candramas, Prajāpati, Kaśyapa and the rest, and the Great-Grandfather—the Great-Grandfather being the father even of the Grandfather;
that is to say, the father even of Brahmā. Homage, homage be unto you a thousand times!
And again, "namo namaḥ" (homage, homage) to You;
this is said by performing the repetition and counting of the act of salutation many times.
The phrase "and again, yet once more" demonstrates one's own lack of satisfaction due to the intensity of faith and devotion. (BhG 11.39)
Likewise: Homage to you from the front, and from behind; let there be homage to you from every side, O All!
You possess infinite vigor and immeasurable prowess;
you pervade everything, and therefore you are all.
Homage to you from the front, in the eastern direction;
and homage to you from behind, even from your back— homage be to you from every side, to you who abide everywhere in all directions, O All!
"Ananta-vīryāmita-vikrama" means that his vigor (*vīrya*) is infinite and his prowess (*vikrama*) is immeasurable;
"vīrya" signifies capability (*sāmarthya*), while "vikrama" signifies valor (*parākrama*).
Even some who possess vigor do not exert themselves in matters such as the slaying of enemies,
or they are of feeble prowess;
you, however, possess infinite vigor and immeasurable valor, and thus you are "the one of infinite vigor and immeasurable valor."
Since you pervade the entire world completely with your single self, therefore you are "all.
The intended meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from you.
Since I have offended You due to my ignorance of Your majesty, therefore—thinking You were merely a friend—I spoke rashly, saying, "O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O friend!"
Not knowing this greatness of yours,
whether through negligence or even out of affection, [I have acted thus].

Thinking and perceiving [Him] as a friend of equal age, and having overcome Him by force through a perverted understanding—having spoken thus, "O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O Friend!"—what was said by the ignorant, the one lacking knowledge, the fool?
To the question "What did the ignorant say?", He replies: "Your majesty, Your greatness, this universal form of Yours as the Lord."
The connection is one of grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya), meaning "not knowing this greatness of yours.
If the reading is *tavemam* ("this of yours"), then it is indeed a case of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Whether through negligence, by way of a distracted mind,
or even out of affection—
affection being defined as confidence born of love.
For that reason also, I have said what I have said:
"And whenever you were treated with disrespect for the sake of mockery,
during recreation, sleep, sitting, or eating..."
Or even alone, O Acyuta, in Your presence, I seek forgiveness from You, the immeasurable one.
And as for the fact that you have been treated with disrespect or have been humiliated for the sake of mockery, for the purpose of derision—where? In matters of dwelling, bedding, seating, and food.
"Dwelling" (*vihāra*) refers to movement, specifically the exertion of the feet.
Lying down is reclining; sitting is remaining seated; eating is consuming food.
Thus, while you were alone and out of sight in these matters of lodging, bedding, seating, and food, you were treated with disrespect and held in contempt;
or else, O Acyuta!
"In Your presence"—the word "tat" (that) is used here as an adverbial modifier;
that is, "in Your direct presence. Whatever disrespect I have shown You, for all that multitude of offenses, I beg forgiveness from You, the immeasurable One who transcends all means of knowledge.
Since you are the father of this world of the moving and the unmoving,
you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher.
There is no one equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior, even in the three worlds, O You of incomparable power?
You are the father, the progenitor of the world—the multitude of living beings, both moving and unmoving, stationary and animate.
You are not only the father of this universe; you are also venerable, worthy of worship.
Since the Guru is weightier and more venerable, one asks: "Why are you so much more venerable? He replies: "There is no one equal to you, none who is your peer.
For two Lords cannot possibly exist.
Because it is impossible for there to be multiple supreme beings,
for no other being equal to you can possibly exist;
how much less could there be another superior to you, even throughout all the three worlds?
O You of incomparable power!
That by which something is measured is a *pratimā* (measure or likeness);
since there is no such measure for Your power, You are one whose power is incomparable (*apratima-prabhāva*). O incomparable one of power—this means that Your power is unsurpassed.
Since this is so—
therefore, having bowed down and prostrated my body,
I shall gladden you, the Lord worthy of praise.
O God, as a father bears with his son, a friend with a friend, and a lover with his beloved, so you ought to bear with me.
Therefore, having bowed down— that is,
having paid homage by holding the body low with great intensity—
I seek to propitiate you, the Lord, the Sovereign.
You are worthy of praise and hymn. Furthermore, you forgive the offense of a son just as a father forgives him,
and every offense of a friend just as a friend does.
Or, just as a lover forgives an offense committed by his beloved, so too, O Lord, you ought to forgive—
meaning to endure or to bear with it. (BhG 11.44)
I am thrilled to see what has never been seen before,
yet my mind is distressed with fear;
therefore, O Lord, show me that very same form.
Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe!
This universal form of yours has never been seen before by me, nor by anyone else;
having seen it, I am filled with joy,
yet my mind is deeply agitated by fear.
Therefore, O Lord, show me that very form which is my friend;
be gracious, O Lord of gods,
O Abode of the World, the dwelling place of the universe!
O Abode of the Universe!
// BhG 11.45 // I wish to see You likewise, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in Your hand.
O you of universal form, become thousand-armed with that very same four-armed form!
"I desire—that is, I pray—to see you as you were before: wearing a crown (*kirīṭin*), likewise bearing a mace (*gadin*), and with a discus in hand.
Since this is so, therefore, in that very form as the son of Vasudeva, with four arms."
O thousand-armed one!
By means of your present universal form,
become manifest, O you whose body is the universe!
"Having withdrawn the universal form,
become [endowed] with that very form"— this is the meaning. [The Lord],
perceiving that Arjuna was afraid...
Having withdrawn His universal form and consoling him with kind words, the Blessed Lord said:
"O Arjuna, this [has been shown] by Me, being pleased with you."
By my own power, I have shown you this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primordial— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.
By me being pleased—
pleasure meaning a disposition of favor toward you— by me who possess that [favor], toward you.

O Arjuna, this supreme form, the universal form, has been shown by means of my own yoga—that is, through the power of my own sovereignty. It consists of light, being primarily composed of splendor; it is the universe in its entirety, infinite and without end, existing from the very beginning, the primordial.
That form of mine which has never been seen before by anyone other than you—[He praises you, saying:
"By the sight of My own form, you have indeed become one who has accomplished his purpose; [for] it cannot be attained through Vedic knowledge, sacrifices, study, or gifts."
Nor can I be seen in such a form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus, through ritual acts or through fierce austerities. (BhG 11.48)
Nor by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices— that is, by the study of the four Vedas as they truly are,

and by the study of sacrifices (the separate mention of the "study of sacrifices" is for the purpose of indicating the knowledge of sacrifice, since the study of sacrifice is already accomplished by the study of the Vedas themselves)— nor by gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others.

Nor can I— who possess such a form as the universal form (viśva-rūpa) displayed here— be seen in the world of men (nṛ-loka), that is, in the human realm, by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus, even through ritual acts such as the Agnihotra prescribed in the Śrutis, nor through fierce austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, which are severe and formidable.
Let there be no distress in you, nor any state of bewilderment,
upon seeing this terrible form of mine; with your fear dispelled and your mind gladdened, look upon me once more.
Behold this very form of mine.
Let there be no distress for you, let there be no fear, and let there be no state of delusion or mental confusion,
having seen and perceived such a terrible form as this which has been shown by me.

Free from fear and with your anxiety gone, and being joyful in mind, behold once again that very four-armed form of yours, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace— this form which is dear to you. Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed him his own form once more and comforted him who was terrified.
Having again assumed his gentle form, the Great-Souled One.
Having spoken these words to Arjuna who was in such a state, Vāsudeva again showed his own form, born in the house of Vasudeva;
and he comforted him, having consoled this frightened one.
Having again assumed a gentle form, the Great-Souled One’s body became serene.
Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, [I am restored to my natural state].
Now I have become restored to my senses and have returned to my natural state.
O Janārdana, having seen this human form of yours, which is my friend, serene, and gentle,
I have now— this very moment— become restored.
What? With a conscious mind, with a serene heart, I have returned to my own nature, my true self.
The Blessed Lord said: You have seen this form of Mine which is very difficult to behold.
Even the gods always long for a vision of this form.
It is "sudurdarśa," meaning that its vision is very difficult to obtain.
You have seen this form of mine;
even the gods always and at all times long for a vision of this form of mine.
The intention is that even those desiring to see [Me] have not seen Me as You have, nor will they see Me.
Why is this? — [as follows: The intention is that even those desiring to see [Me] have not seen Me as You have, nor will they see Me.
Why is this? — [as follows:]
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity,
nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen Me.

Neither by the Vedas— the four Vedas of Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan— nor by fierce austerity such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, nor by giving gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, am I [to be known].
Neither by sacrifice, nor by ritual, nor by worship can such a one as I—of the manner shown here—be seen, as you have seen Me.
How, then, can I be seen? It is said:
"But by unswerving devotion, O Arjuna, I can be known in this way."
To know and to see it in its true essence, and to enter into it, O scorcher of foes.
He explains by what kind of devotion [this is attained]: "by undivided" (ananyayā), meaning not separate;
that devotion which never at any time exists apart from the Blessed One is "undivided" devotion.
That by which nothing other than Vāsudeva is perceived through any of the senses is [also] undivided.
Devotion is exclusive;
by that devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I— of such a nature as this universal form—
capable of being known through the scriptures.
O scorcher of foes, it is not merely for the sake of knowing through the scriptures, but also for seeing and realizing it in its true essence,
and for entering and attaining liberation.
Now, the essential meaning of the entire Gītā scripture, which has liberation as its goal, is stated in summary as that which is to be practiced:
"O Pāṇḍava, he who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme, who is my devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward all beings—he comes to me. (BhG 11.55)

"Mat-karma-kṛt" means one who performs my work; "mat-karma" is work for my sake, and he who does that is "mat-karma-kṛt. "Mat-paramaḥ" means one for whom I am the supreme goal—just as a servant performs the work of his master.
One does not, however, approach the Lord with the thought, "This is the supreme goal to be reached by me after death.
But one who thinks, "He performs actions for Me alone and reaches Me as his supreme goal," is *mat-paramaḥ*;
that is, he for whom I am the supreme—the highest goal—is *mat-paramaḥ*.
Likewise, my devotee worships Me alone in every way—with his whole being and with all his energy; thus he is "my devotee.
He is "free from attachment," meaning free from attachment—attachment being affection or fondness—to the circle of wealth, sons, friends, wife, and kinsmen.
He is "without enmity," meaning one whose enmity has departed, being devoid of the state of an enemy toward all beings, even toward those who are engaged in doing him extreme harm.
Such a devotee of mine comes to me;
I alone am his supreme goal, and there is no other goal whatsoever for him.
This instruction, which is pleasing to you, has been taught by me, O Pāṇḍava. Thus [ends the eleventh chapter].

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 12:
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Devotion" (with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda).

In the chapters beginning from the second up to the chapter on the Vibhūtis, the meditation upon the Supreme Self, Brahman, the Imperishable, who is divested of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), has been described.

Furthermore, the meditation upon the Lord (Īśvara), who possesses the attributes of all yogic sovereignty and the power of omniscience through the limiting adjunct of pure being (sattva), has been taught in various places therein.

However, in the chapter on the Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpa-adhyāya), Your own cosmic form—the primordial form of the Lord which is the self of the entire universe—was shown by You solely for the purpose of meditation.
Having shown that [vision], You said, "He who performs My work" (Gītā 11.55), and so forth.
Therefore, desiring to know which of these two positions is superior, Arjuna said:
"Those devotees who, being ever-steadfast, worship You in this manner..."
And those who [worship] the imperishable, the unmanifest—of these, which are the best knowers of yoga? BhG 12.1.
The word "thus" (evam) refers back to the meaning stated in the immediately preceding verse by the words "performing My work" (mat-karma-kṛt) and so forth.
The meaning is that they are "ever steadfast" (satata-yuktāḥ), being engaged in the aforementioned matters such as the Lord's work with uninterrupted concentration.
Those devotees who, possessing no other refuge, worship and meditate upon you as the Cosmic Form (viśva-rūpa) as it has been shown;

and others who have abandoned all desires and renounced all actions, who worship the Imperishable Brahman as it has been specifically described— that which is unmanifest because it is free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and beyond the reach of the senses—
for that which is within the range of the senses is called "manifest" (vyakta).
Because the verbal root *añj* has that as its object;
however, this syllable is the opposite of that,
being distinguished by the qualifiers stated by the learned.
Among those who also attend upon them, which of these two groups are the best knowers of Yoga? The meaning is: which are the most excellent practitioners of Yoga? // BhG 12.1 //
The Blessed Lord said: Let those who are worshippers of the Imperishable, who possess right vision, and whose desires have ceased, remain for now;
what is to be said regarding them, we shall explain later. But as for the others—
Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined.
Those devotees who, having fixed and concentrated their minds upon Me, the Supreme Lord of universal form, worship Me—

the omniscient Sovereign of all yogas and the best of boons, whose vision is freed from the darkness of afflictions such as attachment— and who are ever-steadfast, being constantly disciplined according to the principle of the meaning of the verse stated at the end of the immediately preceding chapter, endowed with supreme and most excellent faith; [they come to Me alone].
They are my opinion, my preference, because they are the most disciplined. For they pass their days and nights continuously with their minds fixed on Me;
therefore, it is appropriate to say that they are the most disciplined. (BhG 12.2)
Are the others not the most disciplined? No;
however, listen to what must be said regarding them:
"But those who worship the Indestructible, the indefinable, the unmanifest..."
All-pervading, inconceivable, immovable, unchanging, and eternal.
But as for that which is imperishable and indefinable—
because it is unmanifest, it lies beyond the range of words and thus cannot be defined; therefore, it is "indefinable."
The "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is so called because it is not manifested by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); they "worship" (*paryupāsate*) it, meaning they worship it on all sides.

What is called "worship" (*upāsana*) is this: having approached proximity by making the object of worship the focus of one's attention according to the scriptures, one remains for a long time in a continuous flow of identical cognitions, like a stream of oil; that is what they call "worship."
He states the qualification of the Imperishable: it is all-pervading, like space; and it is inconceivable because of its unmanifest nature.
For whatever falls within the range of the senses is conceivable even by the mind.

Because it is the opposite of that, the Imperishable (akṣara) is inconceivable. In common worldly usage, the word *kūṭa* is well known in such expressions as "a fixed object" (*kūṭastha*), "an object appearing with qualities but possessing internal defects," "a forged form" (*kūṭarūpa*), and "false testimony" (*kūṭasākṣya*). In these cases, *kūṭa* refers to something that is deceptive or counterfeit. Since this [Imperishable] is the opposite of such things, it is called *akūṭastha*. Furthermore, because it is eternal, it is not subject to change; thus, it is called *akūṭastha* in the sense of being unchanging. Alternatively, it is called *akūṭastha* because it is the opposite of that which is perishable (*kūṭastha*) due to its nature of constant transformation.
