And likewise, that which is well-known from such passages as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10) and "My Māyā is difficult to overcome" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.14)— being the seed of manifold saṃsāra beginning with ignorance (avidyā), possessing internal defects, and denoted by terms such as 'Māyā', 'Vyākṛta', and so forth— is the *kūṭa*.
It is "stationed on the peak" (kūṭastha) because it stands upon that peak by virtue of presiding over it;
or else, it is "stationed on the peak" because it stands like a heap, and for that very reason it is immovable.
Since it is immovable, [it is called kūṭastha].
Therefore, "firm" means eternal.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, those whose intellect is equal toward all things—
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, they attain Me alone.

Having fully restrained— that is, having properly controlled and withdrawn— the aggregate of the senses, those whose intellect is equal— meaning those whose intellect is the same and uniform in the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable at all times and in all circumstances—
they, being such as these and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain Me alone.
But it should not be said of them that "they reach Me," for it has been stated:
"The man of wisdom, however, is My very Self; this is My view.
Indeed, regarding those who exist as the very nature of the Blessed One, it is not appropriate to speak of them as being either the most disciplined or the least disciplined. (BhG 12.4)
But rather—greater is the suffering for those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest;
for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by those who possess bodies. (BhG 12.5)
Affliction is greater.
Although affliction is indeed great for those devoted to My rituals and so forth,
affliction is even greater for those who perceive the ultimate reality as the imperishable Self, arising from the cause of abandoning the conceit of the body.
"For those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest" means those whose minds are attached to that which is unmanifest; for them, "those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest.
Since the goal consisting of the Imperishable is indeed unmanifest, it is attained with difficulty by embodied beings who possess the conceit of a body.
Therefore, the affliction is greater.
The conduct of those who worship the Imperishable (Akṣara) we shall explain further below.
But as for those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are intent on Me—
Meditating on Me with undivided yoga, they worship Me.

But those who, having surrendered all actions unto Me, the Lord, being "intent on Me"—meaning those for whom I am the supreme goal—worship Me by means of yoga, that is, through meditative concentration (samādhi), with undivided devotion; "undivided" meaning that for which no other object of support exists, having set aside the Self who is the God of universal form. By what means? By yoga, that is, by contemplation, they meditate upon and worship Me.
What of them?— O Pārtha, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me, I become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence before long.

For them, who are solely intent upon my worship, I am the Lord and the deliverer. Why? He says: "From the ocean of the cycle of death"—the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) conjoined with death is "mṛtyu-saṃsāra," and that itself is like an ocean, hence "sāgara."
Because it is difficult to cross, I shall soon become their deliverer from that ocean of death and saṃsāra;
what then? Very quickly indeed, O Pārtha.
"For those whose minds are absorbed in Me"—those whose minds are absorbed in, that is, concentrated upon, Me in My universal form (viśvarūpa), they are "those whose minds are absorbed in Me.
Since this is so, therefore:
"Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me."
From this time forward, you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt.
Fix—place—the mind, which consists of volition and doubt, upon Me alone, the Lord who possesses the universal form;
fix—establish—the intellect, which performs determination, upon Me alone.
Then hear what will happen to you: you shall dwell—you will surely abide—with your self merged in Me, making your home in Me.
Thus, after the fall of the body;
there is no doubt—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (BhG 12.8)
But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me,
then seek to reach me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of constant practice.
Now, if you are unable to concentrate and stabilize the mind upon me in such a way as I have described— making it firm and unshakable— then afterwards, through the yoga of practice (*abhyāsa-yoga*),
you must repeatedly place the mind upon a single object after withdrawing it from all other directions; this is practice.

Yoga preceded by that [devotion], characterized by steady concentration—by means of that yoga of practice, O Dhanañjaya, desire Me, who am the Cosmic Form; pray for Me, seeking to attain Me. If you are unable even to practice, become one whose supreme goal is My work.
Even while performing actions for my sake, you shall attain perfection.

If you are unable even to practice—that is, if you are incapable—then become one for whom my work is supreme (*mat-karma-parama*). "My work" (*mat-karma*) means work performed for my sake; "one for whom that is supreme" (*tat-paramaḥ*) means one for whom my work is the highest priority;
the meaning is that you should make my work your primary concern.
Even if you perform actions solely for My sake without practice, you will attain perfection by way of the purification of the mind, yoga, and the acquisition of knowledge.
But if you are unable even to do this, then, taking refuge in My yoga,
renounce the fruits of all actions with a self-controlled mind.
Furthermore, if you are unable to perform even that which was mentioned— namely, being intent on my work—
then [perform] my yoga.
Having renounced actions performed with reliance upon Me—that is, their performance through that [reliance]—that is My yoga.

Relying upon that, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions—the abandonment of the results of all works—thereafter, being self-controlled, meaning with a restrained mind. This is the sense.
Now he praises the renunciation of the fruits of all actions:

"Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from such renunciation, peace follows immediately. (BhG 12.12)
For knowledge is indeed more excellent—that is, more praiseworthy—than the former.
Why? Because it arises from practice preceded by discrimination.
Even compared to that knowledge, meditation preceded by knowledge is superior.
It follows that for one who possesses knowledge, the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior even to meditation. Thus,
from the renunciation of the fruits of action by one endowed with the aforementioned qualifications, peace— that is, tranquility— of saṃsāra along with its causes would occur immediately thereafter,
and does not depend upon another time.

For one who is ignorant and engaged in action, when unable to practice the means previously taught, the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is taught as the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*),

but not from the very beginning. And therefore, by teaching the progressive superiority of each stage— beginning with "Knowledge is indeed better than practice"— the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is praised.
Because it is heard as something to be performed even when one is incapable of performing the complete means [of attainment].
By what similarity is there praise?
When [the text says], "When all are liberated," immortality is stated through the abandonment of all desires.
That is well known:

all desires are the fruits of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. And for the wise man established in meditation, peace follows immediately upon their renunciation. Thus, there is a commonality between the renunciation of all desires and the renunciation of the fruits of action by the ignorant; because of this commonality, there is praise for the renunciation of the fruits of all actions.
This is for the purpose of encouragement:
just as the ocean was drunk by the Brahmin Agastya, so too are present-day Brahmins praised because of their commonality with the state of being a Brahmin;
likewise, [one is praised] due to the renunciation of the fruits of action.
The superiority of Karma-yoga as a means to the highest good has been declared.

Herein, moreover, having relied upon the distinction between the Self and the Lord, Yoga— characterized by the concentration of the mind on the Lord in His universal form (viśva-rūpa)— has been described,
as well as the performance of action for the sake of the Lord and so forth.

Furthermore, by the statement "But if you are unable even for this" (Gītā 12.11), which indicates that ignorance is the cause [of action], he shows that the yoga of action is not appropriate for one who perceives non-difference and is a worshiper of the Imperishable;
likewise, he shows the impossibility of the worshiper of the Imperishable performing the yoga of action.
Having stated the independence of the worshipers of the Imperishable regarding the attainment of liberation in the words "They attain Me alone" (Gītā 12.4),...
He has shown that for others there is dependence on another, namely subordination to Īśvara, as in the statement: "I am their deliverer" (Gītā 12.7).

For if they were considered to have become the very self of Īśvara due to their vision of non-difference, then they would be of the very nature of the Immutable (akṣara), and in that case, the mention of the act of delivering them would be inappropriate.

Furthermore, because the Blessed Lord is exclusively intent on Arjuna’s welfare, He teaches him the yoga of action— which is devoid of right vision and characterized by the perception of duality— rather than teaching him to regard Himself as the Lord; for no one, having known the Self as the Lord through valid means of knowledge, would desire to become subordinate to anyone else, due to the contradiction involved.

Therefore, for the sake of those renunciants who worship the Imperishable, who are established in right vision, and who have abandoned all desires, I shall declare the collection of virtues beginning with "one who is not hateful toward any being," which is the direct cause of immortality; thus [the Lord] proceeds:
"One who is not hateful toward any being, friendly and compassionate..."
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, equal in pain and pleasure, and patient.
"One who is not hateful toward any beings" means one who does not hate;
he does not hate anything, even that which is a cause of suffering for himself,
for he perceives all beings as his own self.
*Maitra* means the state of being a friend; one who acts with friendliness is *maitra*. And likewise, *karuṇa*:
*karuṇā* is compassion, pity, or sympathy for those who suffer.
One who possesses that is compassionate,
a bestower of fearlessness to all beings;
this is the meaning of "renunciant" (saṃnyāsī).
"Free from possessiveness" means being devoid of the notion of "mine. "Free from egoism" means having departed from the notion of "I.
"Equal in suffering and happiness" means one for whom suffering and happiness are equal, such that neither aversion nor attachment arises toward them.
Forgiving and endowed with patience, he remains entirely unperturbed even when reviled or struck.
The yogi is always contented, self-controlled, and firm in his resolve.
He who has dedicated his mind and intellect to Me—that devotee of Mine is dear to Me.
He is always and constantly content whether he obtains or does not obtain the means for the maintenance of the body, having conceived the sense of sufficiency;
likewise, he is content whether he obtains things of great quality or the opposite.
Thus the yogi is always one whose mind is concentrated in meditative absorption.

"Self-controlled" means one whose nature is restrained. "Firmly resolved" means one whose resolve—his firm, steady determination—is fixed upon the reality of the Self; he is one who has firmly resolved. "With mind and intellect dedicated to Me": the mind consists of volition and conceptualization.
Intellect has the characteristic of determination;
that renunciant in whom both of these are offered—that is, established—unto Me alone is one whose mind and intellect are offered unto Me.
Such a devotee of Mine is dear to Me.
For it was indicated in the seventh chapter that "I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me";
that [point] is here elaborated upon.
Because the world is not agitated by him, and he is not agitated by the world;
He who is free from joy, impatience, fear, and agitation—he too is dear to Me.

Because the world is not agitated by him— that is, it does not experience anxiety, does not feel distress, and does not become disturbed— nor does he himself agitate the world; and he who is free from joy, resentment, fear, and agitation— that is, liberated from joy, resentment, fear, and agitation.
Joy (*harṣa*) is an exaltation of the internal organ upon obtaining what is dear, characterized by signs such as horripilation and the shedding of tears.
Resentment (*amarṣa*) is intolerance.
Fear (*bhaya*) is terror.
Agitation is a state of being disturbed;
he who is freed from these is dear to Me.
One who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, and free from distress—
He who has renounced all undertakings and is my devotee is dear to me.
He is independent and free from longing regarding objects of dependence such as the body, the senses, and their corresponding objects.
He is pure, being endowed with both external and internal purity.
He is skillful, capable of immediately and correctly responding to tasks as they arise.
One who is indifferent and does not take the side of anyone— such as a friend or an enemy— is an indifferent ascetic;
he is one whose distress has departed and whose fear has vanished.

"One who has abandoned all undertakings": here, "undertakings" (*ārambhāḥ*) refers to those actions motivated by desire for the sake of enjoying fruits in this world or the next; one whose nature it is to abandon them is "one who has abandoned all undertakings. My devotee who is such is dear to Me. (BhG 12.16)
Moreover:
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion—he is dear to Me. (BhG 12.17)
He who does not rejoice upon obtaining what is desired, does not feel aversion upon encountering what is undesired, and does not grieve at the loss of what is dear;
Nor does he long for what has not been attained;
he whose nature it is to renounce both auspicious and inauspicious actions is one who has renounced the auspicious and the inauspicious. He who possesses such devotion is dear to Me.
Likewise, he who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor...
He who is the same amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment; // BhG 12.18 //
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor, respect and contempt,
cold and heat, and pleasure and pain.
And he is free from attachment everywhere.
Furthermore:
equal toward blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, [he remains steadfast].
The man who is homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion is dear to Me.
"Equal in censure and praise":
"censure and praise" (*nindā-stutī*) refers to both censure and praise; he for whom these two are equal is "equal in censure and praise" (*tulya-nindā-stutiḥ*).
A silent one is one who possesses silence, with speech restrained; one who is content with whatever is necessary merely for the maintenance of the body. And so it has been said:
"Whosoever is clothed in whatever manner, fed by whatever means,
and sleeps wherever he may be— the gods know him as a *brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, one who is "homeless" (*aniketa*) is one for whom no fixed dwelling, shelter, or residence exists.
"Nor in a house," and so forth, according to another Smṛti text.
"Steadfast-minded" (sthira-matiḥ): he whose mind is steady—that is, whose intellect has the ultimate reality as its object—is steadfast-minded.
Such a man, full of devotion, is dear to Me. (BhG 12.19)

The collection of duties for those renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) who are devoted to the knowledge of the supreme reality— who have desisted from all seeking and are worshippers of the Imperishable, as described in the passage beginning with "one who is not hateful toward any being" (Gītā 12.13)— is now concluded:
"But those who fully attend to this nectar of dharma as it has been described..."
Those devotees who possess faith, who regard Me as the supreme goal, are exceedingly dear to Me.
But those renunciants [should hear] this "dharmyāmṛtam"— that which is not departed from dharma (dharmya) and is also immortal (amṛta),
because it is the cause of immortality—
as it has been described here.

With the words beginning "one who is not hateful toward any being," those who are faithful and regard Me as the Supreme— meaning those for whom I, the Imperishable Self as described, am the Supreme and unsurpassed Goal— practice and perform [these duties];
they are My devotees who have taken refuge in the highest devotion characterized by the knowledge of ultimate reality.
"They are exceedingly dear to Me.
Having explained what was indicated by the statement, "For the man of knowledge is exceedingly dear to Me" (Gītā 7.18), it is here concluded: "Those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me.
Because one who practices this nectar of dharma as described becomes exceedingly dear to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Controller.
Therefore, this nectar of dharma should be practiced with effort by one desiring liberation who wishes to go to the supreme abode dear to Viṣṇu; such is the meaning of the passage. (BhG 12.20)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).

The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall declare that knowledge, along with the object of knowledge, and the knower, having fully understood which, one attains the supreme goal. The field, knowledge, and the knower—these are what I shall briefly describe according to their nature. This body is called the *kṣetra* (the field). One who knows it is called the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) by those who perceive the truth. Know me, O descendant of Bharata, to be the *kṣetrajña* in all fields. The knowledge of the *kṣetra* and the *kṣetrajña* is what I consider to be true knowledge. What that field is, of what nature, and what its modifications are; from what cause it arises, and what that *puruṣa* is; And what powers belong to him, and with what qualities he is endowed—this will be stated in detail through Śruti and reasoning. That which is to be known is the beginningless Brahman, whose nature is neither being nor non-being. It is said to be neither existent nor non-existent. By means of the intellect, through the purification of the *guṇas*, one perceives the Supreme Self within the self by the self. When, through the eye of wisdom, one sees the same Lord dwelling equally in all beings, the source of the emanation of all, and the indestructible; Then, having become equal-minded toward all, one attains the supreme state of non-differentiation from Me, O Bharata. He who, by means of this knowledge and the object of knowledge, perceives Me as existing in all things—he, being established in Me, does not perish. [Verse 13.33 is missing in this edition. But those who, through the yoga of non-difference, perceive the same Lord dwelling equally in all beings, they too abide in Me, though they may think otherwise. Even if a person of evil conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he must be considered righteous, for he has rightly resolved. Swiftly he becomes virtuous and attains everlasting peace. Know for certain, O Kaunteya, that My devotee perishes never. For, O son of Kuntī, those who take refuge in Me are of various natures—women, vaiśyas, śūdras, and even those born of low origin. Having attained this transient and miserable world, even those of base birth, women, vaiśyas, and śūdras reach the supreme goal by My grace. How much more so the holy brahmins and the devoted royal sages! Having come to this impermanent and sorrowful world, worship Me with single-minded resolve. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow down to Me. Engaging yourself in yoga while making Me your supreme goal, you shall surely come to Me. Now begins the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field" (with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda).
In the seventh chapter, two natures (prakṛti) of the Lord were indicated: the lower one, consisting of the three guṇas and divided eightfold, which is the cause of transmigratory existence;
and another, higher one, which is the living being (jīva-bhūta), whose essence is the Lord characterized as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Through these two natures, the Lord attains the state of being the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

In this regard, the Chapter on the Field (Kṣetrādhyāya) is commenced by way of defining the two— the Field (kṣetra) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)— in order to determine the true nature of the Lord who possesses them. Furthermore, in the immediately preceding chapter, from the verse "One who is not hateful toward any beings" (Gītā 12.13) until the conclusion of that chapter, it was stated how those renunciants who possess knowledge of reality abide, according to their steadfastness.

Furthermore, by what knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) are they endowed such that, through the practice of the dharma as described, they become dear to the Blessed One? For this purpose, the present chapter is commenced.

Nature (prakṛti), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇātmikā), having transformed into the forms of all effects, instruments, and objects, combines with the Person (puruṣa) in the form of the body, senses, and so forth, for the sake of the Person's experience (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga).
This very aggregate is this body.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"O son of Kuntī, this body is called the field (kṣetra)."
Those who know that [reality] call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). // BhG 13.1 //
The word "body" (śarīram) qualifies that which was referred to by the pronoun "this" (idam).
O Kaunteya, it is called so because of its protection from injury (kṣata-trāṇāt), its decay (kṣayāt), and its perishability (kṣaraṇāt).
Because the fruit of karma is produced within this [body] as in a field, it is called a "field" (*kṣetra*).
The word *iti* has the sense of the word *evam* (thus).
It is designated and spoken of as "the field."
He who knows, that is, discerns this body as the field— making it an object of knowledge from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head,
making it an object of understanding either through innate or acquired wisdom part by part.
They call that experiencer the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*); the word *iti* here has the same meaning as the word *evam*, as before; they say, "He is the knower of the field."
Who are they? Those who know them—that is, those who know both the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*)—are "knowers of that" (*tad-vidaḥ*).
Thus, the field and the knower of the field have been described. Are they to be known by this much knowledge alone?
To this it is replied:
"And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata;
that which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field—that is considered by Me to be true knowledge. (BhG 13.2)

Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), possessing the characteristics already described, the Supreme Lord who is not subject to transmigratory existence. The intention is this: know that Knower of the Field—who, though divided by the various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of numerous fields from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is, when all distinctions of limiting adjuncts are cast off, beyond the reach of words and concepts such as "being" or "non-being."
O Bhārata,

since there remains nothing else within the scope of knowledge apart from the true nature of the field, the knower of the field, and the Lord, therefore, that knowledge which pertains to the field and the knower of the field— which are the objects of knowledge— is the knowledge by which the field and the knower of the field are made the objects [of cognition].
That knowledge is considered right knowledge; this is my intention, that of me, the Lord Viṣṇu.
Now, if it is argued that there is only one Lord in all fields and no other enjoyer exists apart from Him,
then it follows that the Lord himself is subject to transmigratory existence.
Alternatively, since there is no transmigrating being other than the Lord, it would follow that transmigration does not exist;
and both of these [consequences] are undesirable,
because it would entail the pointlessness of the scriptures concerning bondage, liberation, and their causes.
Furthermore, [this view] contradicts the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
First of all, by direct perception, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is apprehended as characterized by pleasure, pain, and their causes.
Moreover, because the diversity of the world is perceived, it is inferred that cyclic existence has merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as its cause.
All this is untenable if the self and the Lord were one;
it is not so, because knowledge and ignorance are established as being distinct.

"Far apart, opposite, and divergent are these two: ignorance and what is called knowledge" (KaṭhU 1.2.4). Likewise, a contradictory difference in the fruits of those two objects—knowledge and ignorance—is also specified: the higher good...

And [the text says]: "The higher and the lower" (KaṭhU 1.2.2). Here, the object of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the higher good (*śreya*), whereas the lower good (*preyas*) is the effect of ignorance (*avidyā*).
And likewise Vyāsa says: "Now, these two paths... (Mbh 12.241.6), and so forth, as well as "These indeed are the two paths," and so forth.
And here, two culminations have been stated.
It is understood from the Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning that ignorance, along with its effects, must be abandoned by means of knowledge.
As for the Śrutis, they state: "If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great ruin" (Kenopaniṣad 2.5).
"One who knows it thus becomes immortal here;
there is no other path for going" (ŚvetU 3.8). "The knower does not fear anything" (TaittU 2.9). But for the ignorant one: "Then fear comes to him" (TaittU 2.7).
"Existing in the midst of ignorance" (KaṭhU 1.2.5);
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (MuṇḍU 3.2.9);
"He who thinks 'He is one and I am another' does not know; he is like an animal to the gods" (BAU 1.4.10).

"He who knows the Self becomes all this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), "When [it becomes] like a hide" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20), and so forth—there are thousands [of such passages]. And the Smṛtis also: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded" (Bhagavad Gītā 5.15).
"Even here, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity" (Gītā 5.19),
"For seeing the same everywhere" (Gītā 13.29), and so forth;
and also from the standpoint of logic:
Knowing of snakes, the tips of kusha grass, and a well, people avoid them;
some fall into them through ignorance, while others do so when they possess knowledge.
"Behold the fruit, how distinguished it is! (Mbh 12.201.17).

And likewise: it is understood that the ignorant person, possessing the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth, impelled by passion, hatred, and the like, performs righteous and unrighteous deeds, and is thus born and dies.

However, for those who perceive the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, there is the cessation of engagement in righteous and unrighteous deeds due to the abandonment of passion, hatred, and the like; therefore, it cannot be denied by anyone on the basis of reason that such persons are liberated.
This being the case,

although the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is indeed the Lord himself, he appears as if subject to transmigratory existence due to the distinctions created by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) produced by ignorance (avidyā),
just as the Self appears to have the nature of the body and so forth.
For all living beings, the well-established and certain sense of selfhood regarding the body and other things that are not the self is produced by ignorance,
just as there is the certain perception of a person in a tree trunk.
Yet, by this much alone, the attributes of the person do not become properties of the tree trunk.
Or, as the property of a post belongs to a person,

so too it is not the case that consciousness is a property of the body, nor is corporeality a property of the conscious self; thus, attributes such as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion are not logically applicable to the self.
Because there is no difference in their being produced by ignorance, just like old age and death; [we reply:
no, because they are not comparable.
If this is argued—[we reply: the post and the person, being both objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), are superimposed upon one another by the knower through ignorance;
however, in the case of the body and the self, there is a mutual superimposition between two things that are respectively object and subject (*jñeya-jñātṛ*).
Thus, the illustration is not equivalent.
If it is argued that, for this reason, the attributes of the body—though they are objects of knowledge—belong to the knowing Self, we say no;
for it would entail the consequence of [the Self] being insentient and so forth.

For if the attributes of the knowable field, such as the body and the rest—namely pleasure, pain, delusion, desire, and so on—were to belong to the knower, [then the aforementioned faults would follow].
In that case,

a reason for the distinction must be stated as to why certain properties of the knowable field— such as those superimposed by ignorance— belong to the self, whereas others, such as old age, death, and so forth, do not.

There is an inference that they do not exist— namely, "because they are superimposed by ignorance, like old age, death, and so forth," as well as "because they are to be abandoned" and "because they are to be adopted," and so on.
This being so, transmigratory existence— characterized by agency and enjoyership— resides in the object of knowledge and is superimposed upon the knower through ignorance;
therefore, the knower is not affected by it in any way.
Just as space is [perceived] by the ignorant through superimpositions such as having a surface or being soiled,
so too, since this is the case,
not even a mere scent of transmigratory existence can be suspected in the Blessed One, who is present in all fields as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara).
For nowhere in the world is benefit or harm ever seen to be produced by a property superimposed through ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for what was said—that the illustrative example is not analogous—that is incorrect.
Why? Because the intended point of similarity between the example and the thing illustrated is simply the fact of being a superimposition through ignorance.
Therefore, it does not deviate [from its object].
As for your thought that it might deviate with respect to the knower,
its lack of necessity (anaikāntikatva) has also been demonstrated by means of old age and so forth.

If it is argued that the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is subject to transmigratory existence because he possesses ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for ignorance is of the nature of darkness (*tāmasa*).
Indeed, [ignorance] is a cognition characterized by darkness.
Because its nature is that of an obscuration, ignorance consists in grasping erroneously, or in giving rise to doubt, or in the nature of non-apprehension.

Because that [discernment] is absent when there is an absence of the light of discernment, and because the threefold ignorance consisting of non-apprehension and so forth is perceived when there is the defect of darkness and the like, which is of the nature of obscuration in the state of tamas.
Here it is said: "In that case, ignorance (avidyā) must be a property of the knower. No;
for defects such as cataracts and the like are observed in the eye, which is an instrument [of cognition].
As for what you think—that ignorance is a property of the knower—[that is not so].
And that very state of possessing the quality of ignorance is what constitutes the transmigratory nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Therefore, as for what was said—that the Lord alone is the Knower of the Field and not a transmigrator—that is incorrect; it is not so.

Just as, when the eye— the instrument— is seen to possess defects such as perceiving erroneously, neither the erroneous perception nor its cause, the defect of cataracts (*timira*) and so forth, belongs to the perceiver; for when the cataract is removed by the restoration of the eye, it is no longer observed in the perceiver, and thus it is not a property of the perceiver.
Likewise, in all cases, the cognitions of non-apprehension, error, and doubt, which have those [objects] as their causes, must belong to some instrument alone,
and not to the knower, the *kṣetrajña*. Furthermore,
because they are themselves objects of cognition, like the light of a lamp, they cannot be attributes of the knower.
Precisely because it is an object of cognition, its cognizability must be distinct from its own self;

furthermore, in the state of liberation (kaivalya), which is characterized by the disjunction of all instruments of perception, no proponent of any philosophical school accepts that the self possesses defects such as ignorance (avidyā).
If the self (*ātman*), as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), had its own inherent property (*svo dharma*) like heat in fire,
then there could never be a separation from it;
for since the self is immutable, all-pervading like space, and formless, conjunction with or separation from anything is logically impossible.
The eternality of the Knower of the Field’s lordship is established by such scriptural statements concerning the Lord as: "Because of being beginningless and devoid of qualities" (Gītā 13.32).

If it is argued that this being the case, there would be defects such as the futility of the scriptures due to the non-existence of saṃsāra and the transmigrating being, we say no; for [this objection] is accepted by all.
Indeed, a defect accepted by all proponents of the self (ātmavādin) is not to be avoided by one person alone.
How is this accepted?
For it is accepted by all proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) that for liberated souls there is an absence of the conventional designations "saṃsāra" and "one who transmigrates" (*saṃsārin*).
Nor is it accepted that they incur defects such as the uselessness of the scriptures.
Likewise, for us who maintain that the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) are one with the Lord,
let there be the purposelessness of scripture;
yet it possesses utility within the realm of ignorance— just as, for all dualists, scripture and the like possess utility only during the state of bondage.
It is not so in the state of liberation.
Surely, for all dualists, the states of bondage and liberation of the self are indeed real entities from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthatas*).
Therefore, since there exists that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be attained, along with the means for them, the scriptures and other authorities would possess purposeful meaning.
But for the non-dualists (*advaitin*), on the other hand—
If it is argued that because duality is not ultimately real,

and because the state of bondage is produced by ignorance, the Self's lack of ultimate reality would render the scriptures and other means of knowledge purposeless due to their having no object, we say: no.
Because it is impossible for there to be distinct states of the self.
If, first of all, the states of bondage and liberation were to belong to the self, they would have to occur either simultaneously or successively.
First of all, they cannot exist simultaneously due to contradiction, like staying and going in a single [entity]. And if they occur sequentially,
is it without a cause or with a cause?
If it were signless (*nirnimitta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation;

if it were with signs (*sanimitta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of its not being ultimately real because it lacks intrinsic existence (*svato 'bhāvāt*). Such being the case, your own tenet would be abandoned.
Furthermore, when determining the sequence between the states of bondage and liberation, the state of bondage must be conceived as preceding [liberation];
yet that state would be both beginningless and finite,
which is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, an infinite [self] possessing states such as liberation is accepted despite being contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is impossible to establish the permanence of that which possesses states while transitioning from one state to another.
Now, if, in order to avoid the fault of impermanence, the distinction between the states of bondage and liberation is not postulated; [then...]
Therefore, even for the proponents of duality, defects such as the futility of the scriptures are indeed unavoidable;
thus, since the situation is the same, this defect need not be avoided by the proponent of non-duality.
Nor is the scripture purposeless, because it concerns persons who are as they are known—namely, the ignorant.
For the ignorant perceive the fruit and the cause, which are not the Self, as the Self; this is not the case for the wise.
For when the wise perceive the Self as distinct from both the fruit and the cause, it is impossible for them to perceive those two as the "I," that is, as the Self;
for not even one who is utterly deluded or insane perceives identity between water and fire, or between shadow and light.
How much more so for one who possesses discernment?
Therefore, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions does not apply to one who perceives the Self as distinct from both the fruit and the cause. For it is not [addressed] to "Devadatta,"...
When one is appointed to a certain task with the words, "Do this," the person standing there understands the appointment even while hearing it, thinking, "I, Viṣṇumitra, have been appointed.
This understanding is possible because of the failure to grasp the distinction between the separation [of the self from the body] and the object [of the action].
The same applies to the fruit and the cause as well.

[Objection: Is it not indeed appropriate that, with respect to the natural relationship [between teacher and pupil], there should be an understanding of the subject matter of the scripture—namely, "I am impelled toward the cause of desired results and restrained from the cause of undesired results"—even while there exists the realization of the Self as distinct from those results and causes?

Just as, for example, fathers, sons, and others, despite perceiving their mutual difference as selves, still understand the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions directed toward one another. [Reply: No.
Because the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the fruit and the cause is already established even prior to the realization of the vision of a distinct Self;
for it is only after one has understood the injunction that one realizes the Self's difference from the fruit and the cause for the purpose of avoiding what is prohibited, not before.
Therefore, it is established that the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions has as its domain the ignorant person.

If it is argued that, because those who perceive the self as distinct from the body would not engage in such acts as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 10.2.1), and those who view only the body and so forth as the self would likewise not engage,
there is therefore an absence of an agent and the scriptures are rendered purposeless— this is not so.
Since engagement and withdrawal are established precisely through what is conventionally recognized:
first, the knower of Brahman who perceives the identity of the Lord and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) does not engage [in worldly activity];
likewise, the proponent of selflessness (nairātmyavādin) also does not engage [in such activity], thinking that there is no other world.

However, for those who— based on what is well-known— have inferred the existence of the self through the otherwise inexplicable hearing of the scriptures concerning injunctions and prohibitions, yet remain ignorant of the specific nature of the self and possess a thirst born of the fruits of action, proceed [in their practice] out of faith;
thus, [the self] is not perceptible to all.
Therefore, the treatise is not purposeless.
If it is argued that because those who possess discernment are seen to refrain from action, the scriptures would be useless since those who follow them would likewise refrain from action, we say no;
for discernment arises in some individuals alone.
Indeed, among many living beings, only a certain one might possess discernment.
Just as it is now:
fools do not follow the discerning person,
because their activity is dependent upon defects such as passion and the like.
Furthermore, because we observe engagement in rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*),
and because engagement occurs by its own nature—
it has been said: "But it is nature that acts" (Gītā 5.14).
Therefore, saṃsāra is merely ignorance, pertaining only to the object as it is perceived;
ignorance and its effects do not belong to the isolated *kṣetrajña*.
Furthermore, false knowledge is not capable of defiling an ultimate reality.
For the water of a mirage cannot turn a saline wasteland into mud by means of its moisture;
likewise, ignorance can do nothing at all to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Therefore, this has been said: "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field."
And: "Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance" (Gītā 5.15).

Now, why is it that even among the learned there is this sense of "I am this" and "this is mine," as if they were transmigrating beings? Listen: that which is called learning is merely the perception of the Self within the field alone.
If, however, they were to perceive the Knower of the Field as changeless, then they would not desire enjoyment or action, thinking, "May this be mine.
For enjoyment and action consist precisely in change.
This being so, [the objection remains].
The ignorant person engages in action because of a desire for results;

however, for the wise person—who perceives the Self as changeless—since there is an absence of desire for results, activity is untenable, and thus "cessation" is figuratively attributed to the stopping of the operations of the aggregate of the body and the senses.

Furthermore, let someone else possess this kind of cleverness: "The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is indeed the Lord (īśvara), and the Field (kṣetra) is something other than him, being the object of the Knower of the Field alone;
whereas I am a transmigrating being, experiencing pleasure and pain."

"And the cessation of saṃsāra must be accomplished by me through the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field, and by directly perceiving the Lord as the knower of the field through meditation and abiding in His true nature. He who understands thus—
And he who thinks that "he who awakens [to consciousness] is not the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) is one who uses the term "pandita" as a mere empty sound.

Thinking, "I shall establish the meaningfulness of both saṃsāra and liberation, as well as of the scripture," he is a destroyer of the self, being himself deluded and misleading others due to his lack of the traditional transmission of the meaning of the scriptures;
thus he effects the loss of what was heard and the fabrication of what was never heard.
Therefore, one who does not know the tradition should be disregarded like a fool, even if he is a knower of all the scriptures.

As for what was said— that if the Lord were identical with the individual knower (kṣetrajña), he would become subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva), and if the individual knowers were identical with the Lord, there would be no transmigrating beings, leading to the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of transmigratory existence—
these two objections have been answered by the acceptance of the distinction between knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā).
How so? Because an object that is ultimately real is not defiled by a defect imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, an illustration has been shown: a desert region is not turned into mud by the water of a mirage.

Furthermore, the objection that the non-existence of transmigrators would entail the non-existence of *saṃsāra* is answered by the logical proof that both *saṃsāra* and the transmigrator are imagined through ignorance.
If it is argued that the very possession of ignorance is the defect of transmigratoriness for the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
and that the resulting states of happiness, suffering, and so forth are perceived through direct experience, we say no;
for [ignorance] is a property of the field (kṣetra), which is the object of knowledge.
Because it is impossible for the Knower, the Kṣetrajña, to incur the defects produced by that [body];
for whatever collection of defects you ascribe to the Kṣetrajña while it does not actually exist,
since those are established as objects of knowledge, they possess the nature of the field (kṣetra) alone.
It does not constitute the nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
nor is the Knower of the Field defiled by it, because a connection between the knower and the object of knowledge is logically impossible.
For if there were indeed a conjunction [of the self with attributes], the very state of being an object of knowledge would not be possible.
If ignorance, suffering, and so forth were properties of the self, how, my friend, could they be perceived through direct perception?
Or how can there be the property of being the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña-dharma*)?

For when it is determined that everything knowable is the "Field" (*kṣetra*) and the Knower alone is the "Knower of the Field," then to assert that ignorance, suffering, and so forth are qualifiers of the Knower of the Field— that is, properties of the Knower of the Field— and yet maintain their perceptibility, is a contradiction spoken out of reliance on mere ignorance.
Only.
Here it is asked: "To whom does that ignorance belong? It belongs to him by whom it is perceived. To whom is it perceived? [This is the question.]
To this it is replied: The question "Whose ignorance is seen? is meaningless.
Why? If ignorance is seen, you must also see the one who possesses it.
Furthermore, when that which possesses [the property] is being perceived, the question "To whom does it belong? is not appropriate;
for when one possessing cows is being perceived, one does not ask, "Whose are the cows?"
Thus, the question becomes meaningful.
But is it not the case that the example is dissimilar?
Since both the cows and their possessor are perceptible, their relationship is also perceptible; therefore, the question would be purposeless.
Neither ignorance nor its possessor are perceptible,
such that the question would be rendered meaningless;
for it is only when the connection between ignorance and the ignorant one is known through something imperceptible [that the question arises].
What would happen to you?
Since ignorance is the cause of misfortune, it must be abandoned.
For whom there is ignorance...
He will avoid that [ignorance].
But is ignorance not yours alone? Then you must know both ignorance and the self that possesses it.
I know it, but not through direct perception.
If you know it through inference, how is the apprehension of the relationship [between the middle and the major terms] established?
For it is not possible to apprehend a connection at that time between you, the knower, and ignorance, which has become the object of knowledge,
because the knower is already occupied solely with ignorance as its object;
nor is there any apprehender of the connection between the knower and ignorance.
Furthermore, another cognition would have to exist to take that [first cognition] as its object,
because it would lead to an infinite regress.
If the connection between the knower and the knowable were itself known by yet another cognition, [the same problem would follow].
If one cognizer were to be postulated, another would have to be postulated for him,
and yet another for him; thus, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would be unavoidable.
Furthermore, if ignorance is an object of knowledge,
or if anything else is an object of knowledge, it is simply an object of knowledge;
likewise, the knower too is simply a knower.
It does not become an object of knowledge.
And when this is so,
nothing is impaired in the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the knower, by ignorance, suffering, and the like.
Is it not the case that this very same defect remains— namely, that the knower is a field characterized by defects?
No, for the designation "knower" is applied metaphorically to that which is of the nature of consciousness itself and is changeless.
Just as the metaphorical designation of "burning" is applied to fire by virtue of its mere heat, so it is here.

Just as the Blessed One has shown that the self is inherently devoid of the nature of action, agent, and fruit—such that action, agency, and so forth are merely metaphorically attributed to the self through the superimposition of ignorance—so too in various places [it is said]: "He who perceives him as the slayer... (Gītā 2.19).
This has been demonstrated in such passages as "All actions are performed in every way by the qualities of material nature" (Gītā 3.27) and "He does not take on the sin of anyone" (Gītā 5.15),
and it has been explained by us in exactly that manner.
And we shall demonstrate this in the subsequent sections.
Well then, since the nature of action, agent, and fruit does not exist in the Self by its own nature,
and is merely superimposed through ignorance,
ritual acts are indeed to be performed only by one who is ignorant.
It follows, then, that this does not apply to the wise.
True, this is indeed what follows; however, we shall demonstrate this very point under the verse beginning with "for it is not possible for one who bears a body."

And in the section summarizing the meaning of all the scriptures, we shall demonstrate this specifically under the verse, "O Kaunteya, that which is the supreme culmination of knowledge," by means of a brief summary alone.
Enough with this extensive elaboration;
thus, the chapter is concluded.

This summary verse—beginning with "That field" (*tat kṣetraṃ yac ca*) and so forth—is presented as a compendium of the subject matter of the Chapter on the Field (*kṣetrādhyāya*), which was taught in the verse beginning with "This body" (*idaṃ śarīram*).
For it is proper to present a summary of the meaning one intends to explain.
Thus: "That field, what it is, of what nature, what its modifications are, and from whence it arises..."
Hear from me briefly who he is and what his power is.

That which was indicated as "this body" is referred to by the word "that" (tat). And that which was indicated as "the field" (kṣetra), he describes as being of such and such a nature (yādṛk) with respect to its own inherent qualities (svakīyaiḥ dharmaiḥ).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya).
"Yad-vikāri" means that which undergoes modification; "yo vikāro yasya" means the modification belonging to which.
And "yataḥ" means from which; the ellipsis of the sentence is "from which a product (kārya) arises."

And as for that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) who has been pointed out—he is "of such power" (yat-prabhāva), meaning he possesses those powers which are capacities produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Listen from my words to the essential nature of both the Field and the Knower of the Field, exactly as it has been specified, in brief—that is, in summary.
The meaning is: having heard it, retain it firmly.
He praises that true nature of the field and the knower of the field—which He intends to explain—in order to stimulate the interest of the listeners:
"It has been sung in many ways by the seers, in various distinct Vedic hymns, and also in the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are reasoned and definitive. (BhG 13.4)

It has been sung—that is, narrated—in many ways and in various manners by the seers, such as Vasiṣṭha and others. It has been sung through various meters—that is, the *ṛc* and other meters—with diverse states and in manifold ways, each distinctively and separately. Furthermore, it has been expressed through the words of the *Brahma-sūtras*, which are sentences that indicate Brahman.

They are called "padas" because one goes to them and understands them; and by those very words, the true nature of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is sung—this is understood to follow [from the context].
The Self is known through such words of the Brahma-sūtras as "One should meditate upon [the Self] as the Self," and so forth.
The meaning is: [words] that possess reasons, are joined with logic, are well-determined, have the nature of being free from doubt, and produce a firm conviction.
To Arjuna, who had been made attentive by this praise, the Blessed One said:
"The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest itself;..."
The faculties are eleven, and the objects of the faculties are five.

The "great elements" (mahābhūtāni) are both great because they pervade all transformations and are elemental; however, the subtle ones will be designated by the term "objects of the senses," while the gross ones will be referred to by that same term. Ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra) is the cause of the great elements, characterized by the notion of "I."
The intellect (*buddhi*), characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*), is the cause of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
its cause, in turn, is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) itself, not the manifest.
It has been said: "The unmanifest is the undifferentiated power of the Lord; it is my *māyā*, difficult to overcome."
The word "eva" (only/just) has the sense of restricting the primordial nature (*prakṛti*); that is, the primordial nature is divided into eight parts only to this extent.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction of divisions.
The sense organs (*indriyāṇi*) are ten.
The five beginning with the ear are the sense organs (buddhīndriya) because they produce cognition;
the five beginning with speech and the hands are the action organs (karmendriya) because they accomplish action. These constitute ten.
And one more:
what is that? The mind, which is the eleventh and consists of volition and so forth;
and the five objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.
The Sāṃkhyas call these the twenty-four principles (tattvas);

now, as for those which the Vaiśeṣikas call the "qualities of the self" (ātma-guṇas), the Blessed One declares that they too are indeed attributes of the field (kṣetra-dharma) and not of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the physical aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—
this, in brief, is declared to be the field along with its modifications.
Desire is that by which, having previously perceived an object of a certain kind as a cause of happiness,

one, upon perceiving another object of that same kind, desires to acquire it because it is a cause of happiness. This desire, being a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is the "field" (kṣetra) because it is an object of knowledge.
Likewise is hatred: having experienced an object of a certain kind as a cause of suffering, upon perceiving another object of that same kind, one feels hatred toward it.
Thus, this hatred, because it is an object of knowledge, is indeed a field;
likewise, pleasure, which is favorable and consists of a serene mental state, because it is an object of knowledge, is indeed a field; and suffering, which is adverse by nature, is likewise a field.
Because it is an object of knowledge, that too is a field.
A "conglomeration" (saṃghāta) is the collection of the body and the senses;
within that, there is the manifestation of the activity of the internal organ.
Like fire in a heated iron ball,
consciousness is permeated by the essence of the reflection of the self's sentience;
and that [body] is the field (kṣetra), because it is an object of knowledge.
Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is that by which the body and the senses, having reached a state of exhaustion, are sustained;
and because it is an object of knowledge, it is the field (*kṣetra*).
The mention of desire (*icchā*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating all the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Since...
He concludes what has been said with the words "this" (etat).
This field, together with its modifications—that is, along with the transformations such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth—has been briefly described or stated.
[This refers to] that aggregate of various types of fields which was called "the body, the field" in Gītā 13.2.

That field has been explained as divided into the various categories beginning with the great elements and ending with fortitude. The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) will be described by specific qualifications—the Blessed Lord Himself will speak of Him along with His attributes in the passage beginning with, "I shall declare that which is to be known, by the thorough knowledge of which the Knower of the Field, who possesses power, attains immortality. That very object of knowledge, together with its qualifications, he himself will explain.
Now, however, [the Lord describes] that group of means for attaining that knowledge, characterized by humility and so forth,
in the presence of which one becomes fit and qualified for the thorough realization of that which is to be known—
that toward which the renunciant is devoted and is called "established in knowledge."
The Blessed One declares that this group of qualities, beginning with humility (*amānitva*), is denoted by the word "knowledge" because it is the means for attaining knowledge:
"Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint. (BhG 13.7)
Humility (*amānitva*) is the absence of the state of pride; pride is the praising of oneself, and its absence is humility.
Deceitfulness (*adambhitva*) is the absence of hypocrisy, which is the ostentatious display of one's own religious duty (*svadharma*).
The absence of that is non-hypocrisy. Non-violence is the non-injuring of living beings. Patience is the absence of agitation when encountering the offenses of others.
Straightforwardness is uprightness and the absence of crookedness.
Service to the teacher is the attendance upon the teacher—who instructs in the means for liberation—through acts such as obedience.
Purity is the cleansing of bodily impurities with earth and water.
Furthermore, purity (*śauca*) consists in the removal of the impurities of passion and so forth through the cultivation of their antidotes within the mind.
Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the state of being firm;
it is the state of having formed a firm resolve upon the path to liberation alone.

Self-restraint (ātma-vinigraha) is the restraint of that aggregate of causes and effects denoted by the word "self" which acts as one's own adversary; it is the curbing, by its very nature, of that which is active in every direction, within the path of virtue alone—this is self-restraint.
Furthermore—
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism, and the contemplation of the defects of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. (BhG 13.8)
Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the state of dispassion toward the objects of the senses—sound and so forth—whether perceived or unperceived, and toward enjoyments.

Non-egoism (*anahaṃkāra*) is simply the absence of the sense of "I. The contemplation of the defects in birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering means the contemplation of the defects in each of these, beginning with birth and ending with the sufferings of death, old age, diseases, and sorrows.
In birth, the defect is the emergence from the womb through the gateway of the birth canal; the contemplation of that is its thorough observation.
Likewise, there is the contemplation of defects in death.
Likewise, regarding old age, there is the observation of the defects consisting in the cessation of wisdom, power, and vitality, as well as being treated with contempt;
likewise, regarding diseases such as headaches and the like, there is the observation of their defects;
and likewise, regarding sufferings caused by internal, external, and celestial factors.

Alternatively, suffering itself is the defect; this is the "defect of suffering. The observation of this [defect] in birth and so forth is as previously described: birth is suffering, death is suffering.
Aging is suffering;
diseases are suffering,
because they are the causes of suffering.
Birth and the rest are suffering,
but they are not suffering by their very nature alone.
Thus, through the contemplation of the defects of suffering within birth and the rest, dispassion arises toward the body, the senses, and the enjoyment of sense objects.
Consequently, there arises an inclination of the senses toward the inner self for the purpose of perceiving the Self.
Thus, because it is a cause of knowledge, the perception of the defects of suffering inherent in birth and so forth is called "knowledge.
Furthermore—
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (BhG 13.9)
Non-attachment (*asakti*) is the absence of attachment; attachment is merely affection for objects that cause clinging, and its absence is non-attachment.
Non-possessiveness (*anabhiṣvaṅga*) is the absence of possessiveness.
What is called "intense attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is a specific form of clinging characterized by the cultivation of the thought that there is no self other than [the object], such as thinking,
when another is happy or suffering, "I alone am happy" or "I am suffering."
Whether he lives or dies, [the fool thinks], "I alone shall live, and I shall die.

Where? He says: "Among sons, wives, houses, and so forth"—that is, among sons, wives, houses, and by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," among others as well who are exceedingly dear, such as the class of servants and the like.
And both of these are called "knowledge" because they have knowledge as their purpose.
Furthermore, there is constant even-mindedness, which is the state of having an equal mind.

Toward what? Toward the occurrences of the desirable and the undesirable; that is, toward the attainments—the acquisitions—of both the desirable and the undesirable, there is always indeed an equal state of mind.
He does not rejoice in the occurrence of the desirable, nor does he become angry at the occurrence of the undesirable; and this constant state of equanimity of mind is knowledge. (BhG 13.9)
Moreover:
"Unswerving devotion to Me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
resorting to solitary places; and a distaste for the assembly of people. (BhG 13.10)

When, through *ananya-yoga*—that is, through non-dual meditative absorption (*apṛthak-samādhi*)—one possesses a firm and unerring conviction that "there is nothing other than the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva; therefore, He alone is our refuge," this is *ananya-yoga*.
Devotion (*bhakti*) is worship performed by means of that [yoga], and it is "unswerving" (*avyabhicāriṇī*), meaning it does not have the nature of wavering.
And that is knowledge:
the practice of frequenting secluded places.

A secluded place is one that is naturally or through human effort free from impurities and the like, as well as from snakes, tigers, and so forth; it is a place secluded by means of forests, riverbanks, temples, and the like.
One whose nature is to resort to that is a "resorter to secluded places" (*vivikta-deśa-sevī*);
the state of being such is "resorting to secluded places" (*vivikta-deśa-sevitvam*).
For it is because the mind becomes serene in secluded places that the cultivation of the self and so forth arises in a state of seclusion.

Therefore, dwelling in a secluded place is called knowledge. "Dislike and lack of delight in the assembly of people" refers to the assembly or gathering (*saṃsada*) of common folk— those who are devoid of refinement and lacking in discipline.

There is no association with those who possess worldly dispositions, even if they are disciplined, because that [association] is an aid to knowledge. Therefore, detachment from the assembly of ordinary people is knowledge, since its purpose is knowledge. (BhG 13.10)
Furthermore:
"Constancy in the knowledge of the Self and the perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is contrary to this is ignorance. (BhG 13.11)
"Constancy in the knowledge of the Self" (adhyātma-jñāna-nityatvam): knowledge concerning the Self and so forth is "knowledge of the Self" (adhyātma-jñāna);
constancy is the state of being constant in that [knowledge].
It is the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) which arises from the ripening of the cultivation of the means to knowledge, such as humility (amānitva) and the rest.
Its purpose is liberation, which is the cessation of saṃsāra.
The examination of that is the vision of the object of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
For when there is an examination of the fruit of the knowledge of reality, there will be engagement in the practice of its means.
This knowledge, beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the reality of the goal of knowledge, has been described as "knowledge" because its purpose is knowledge.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is that which is other than this aforementioned [knowledge], being its opposite:
pride (*mānitva*), hypocrisy (*dambhitva*), violence (*hiṃsā*), lack of forbearance (*akṣānti*), dishonesty (*anārjava*), and so forth; this ignorance should be understood for the sake of avoidance.
"Because it is the cause of the operation of saṃsāra. [BhG 13.11] In response to the inquiry, "What is to be known by means of the knowledge described above?", he says:
I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality:
the beginningless Supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being.
Now, it may be objected: the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), such as humility (amānitva) and the rest, do not cause the Knowable to be known;
for humility and so forth are never observed to be the determiners of any object whatsoever.
And in every case, it is observed that only that cognition which has a particular object as its domain is the determiner of that very object of knowledge;
for one thing is not perceived by a cognition whose object is something else, just as fire is not perceived by a cognition whose object is a jar.
This is not a fault;
for we have already stated that it is called "knowledge" because it is the cause of knowledge,
and also because it is a cooperative cause for knowledge.
That which is to be known—that which ought to be understood—I shall declare; I shall explain it thoroughly and correctly.
To what end?
In order to attract the listener by means of an incentive, he says: "Having known that which is to be known, one attains immortality—immortal state."
The meaning is that it does not die again. That which has a beginning is "beginning-possessing" (*ādimat*); that which does not have a beginning is "beginningless" (*anādimat*).
What is that? It is the supreme, unsurpassed Brahman, which is the subject under discussion as "that which is to be known.
In this regard, some divide the phrase *anādi mat-param* [into *anādi-mat* and *param*].
Since the meaning has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the addition of the possessive suffix *-matup* would be redundant and undesirable.
Furthermore, they demonstrate a specific meaning: "That of which I am the supreme power (*parā śakti*) called Vāsudeva—that is *mat-param*.
This is true; in this way, there would be no tautology.
If a purpose were possible;

however, no purpose is possible, because Brahman is intended to be made known precisely through the negation of all attributes, as expressed in the statement: "It is said to be neither being nor non-being."
To demonstrate the possession of a specific power and to deny that very specificity are contradictory.

Therefore, although the suffix *matup* has the same meaning as the *bahuvrīhi* compound, its use here is for the purpose of completing the verse. Having attracted the listener's attention with the inducement, "The object of knowledge, which has immortality as its fruit, will be spoken by me," he says: "That object of knowledge is said to be neither existent (*sat*), nor is it said to be non-existent (*asat*)."

Now, one might object: "Having made a great preparation and proclaimed with a loud voice that you would teach the Knowable, you have spoken something inconsistent when you say, 'It is neither existent nor non-existent.
No; what you have said is indeed consistent."

How so? For in all the Upaniṣads, Brahman, the object of knowledge, is indicated solely through the negation of specific attributes—such as "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) and "neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8)—because it is beyond the reach of speech, such that one cannot say, "This is it."
Is it not the case that there is no such thing which is not denoted by the word "exists"?
For if it were not denoted by the word "exists," [it would not exist].
There is no such object of knowledge; and it is contradictory to say that "it is an object of knowledge" while also saying "it is not expressed by the word 'exists'.
It is certainly not non-existent.
Because it is not an object of the cognition "it does not exist."
Is it not the case that all cognitions are indeed followed by the notions of "existence" or "non-existence"?

This being so, the object of knowledge (jñeya) must also either be the objective domain of a cognition followed by the notion of existence, or the objective domain of a cognition followed by the notion of non-existence.
No, because, being beyond the reach of the senses, it is not the object of a cognition that is followed by both [types of] cognitions;
for whatever object is accessible to the senses, such as a jar and so forth, it must be the object of a cognition followed by the cognition "it exists."
Alternatively, it might be an object of a cognition accompanied by the notion of non-existence.

However, this object of knowledge, because it is beyond the senses and is accessible through the single means of cognition that is verbal testimony, is not an object of a cognition accompanied by both [existence and non-existence] like a jar or similar things; therefore, the statement that "it is neither existent nor non-existent" is not contradictory.

"That which is to be known is said to be neither existent nor non-existent" is not contradictory, because of the Śruti: "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover above the unknown. (Kenopaniṣad 1.3)

If it is argued that even the Śruti contains contradictory meanings—just as, for instance, having begun the sacrificial hall for the sake of the sacrifice, one says, "Who indeed knows whether he exists in that world or not? (TaittS 6.1.1)—we say no. This is because the scripture’s teaching on being other than the known and the unknown is intent upon establishing an object that must necessarily be known; whereas the passage beginning with "whether in that world" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) supplementary to an injunction.
And because of logical possibility, Brahman is not denoted by words such as "existent" or "non-existent.

For every word, when employed to illuminate an object and heard by listeners, causes the object to be understood only by depending on the grasping of convention through the medium of genus, action, quality, or relation, and not otherwise, since it is never observed to function in any other way.
For example: as "cow" or "horse" by way of genus;
or "he cooks" or "he reads" by way of action;
or "white" or "black" by way of quality.
Or [the term "possessor"] may apply through a relationship, as in "wealthy" or "owner of cows";
however, Brahman does not possess a genus (jāti), and therefore it is not denotable by words such as "existent" (sat) and so forth.
Nor is it possessed of qualities, such that it could be designated by the word "quality," because it is devoid of qualities.
Nor is it denotable by words signifying action, because it is devoid of action, according to the Vedic scripture: "It is partless, actionless, and tranquil" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
Nor is it a possessor of relations, because it is one; and because it is non-dual, beyond the scope of objects, and the Self itself, it is not related to anything whatsoever.
It is logical that it is expressed by the word,
as also from such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).

Since there might be a suspicion of non-existence regarding the Knowable because it is not an object of the word or the concept "existent," [the Lord], demonstrating its existence through the medium of the adjuncts of the organs of all living beings, does so for the purpose of removing that suspicion.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands pervading everything. (BhG 13.13)
"Having hands and feet everywhere" means that it has hands and feet on all sides; that is the object of knowledge.

The existence of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is discerned through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the organs of all living beings. And the Knower of the Field is said to be [defined] by the limiting adjunct of the field (kṣetra).
The field (kṣetra) is divided in many ways by the hands, feet, and so forth;
the multitude of distinctions produced by these various adjuncts of the field belong only to the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) in a false sense.
Thus, by the removal of those [adjuncts], its state of being "knowable" is stated, and it is said that "it is neither existent nor non-existent."

Although the false form produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) does not truly exist, it is spoken of as if it were a knowable property (*jñeya-dharma*) for the sake of attaining an understanding of existence; thus, it is said, "hands and feet everywhere," and so forth.
For there is this statement of those who know the tradition: "The non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*) is conceptualized through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*).

Hands, feet, and the rest, which are perceived everywhere as parts of all bodies, are the effects of their own causes—the presence of the power of the knowable (*jñeya-śakti*). Thus, they serve as signs (*liṅga*) of the existence of the knowable, being so designated through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
It is said:
"In that same way, the rest should be explained.
"That has hands and feet on all sides."
It is to be known as having eyes, heads, and faces on every side—that which has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides is "sarvato'kṣi-śiro-mukham. It is possessed of ears on every side;
"śruti" refers to the sense organ of hearing.
That which possesses that [Self] is "possessed of hearing" (śrutimat).
In the world—that is, among the multitude of living beings—it stands pervading and encompassing everything, attaining its stability. (BhG 13.13)

The purpose of beginning this verse is to prevent the suspicion that the object of knowledge possesses those [limbs] due to the superimposition of the sense organs, such as hands and feet, which serve as its limiting adjuncts (upādhi):
"Appearing through the functions of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses;
unattached, yet the sustainer of all; free from qualities, yet the experiencer of qualities. (BhG 13.14)
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses— all those senses known as the organs of perception (buddhīndriya) and the organs of action (karmendriya), such as the ear and so forth—
as well as the internal organs, namely the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas), because they are equal in their nature as limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for the object of knowledge.
They are grasped by the term "all the senses.

Furthermore, since even the ear and other [external senses] possess their status as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) only by way of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it shines forth through the qualities of all the senses—which serve as the limiting adjuncts of both the internal and external organs—such as determination, volition, hearing, and speaking; thus, it is said to be "reflected in the qualities of all the senses" (*sarvendriyaguṇābhāsam*).
The meaning is that this Knowable appears as if engaged in the operations of all the senses;
for the Śruti says, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (BAU 4.3.7).
But for what reason is it not actually perceived as being engaged? To this he says: "devoid of all senses."
The meaning is that it is devoid of all instruments of action;
therefore, that object of knowledge is not engaged by the operations of the senses.
As for this mantra: "He who has neither hands nor feet, yet is swift and a grasper; who sees without eyes and hears without ears" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19), and so forth.
This is intended to demonstrate that the Knowable possesses the power to assume qualities in accordance with the adjuncts of all the sense organs;
it is not, however, intended to demonstrate that it directly possesses activities such as moving swiftly.
The meaning of this mantra is like the meaning of the mantra beginning with "The blind man found the jewel" (TaittĀ 1.11).
Since that which is to be known is devoid of all instruments [of cognition],
it is therefore unattached, being free from all connection.
Even though this is so,
Nevertheless, it is indeed the sustainer of all,
for everything has a real locus because the cognition of existence follows everywhere;
even mirages and the like do not exist without a locus.
Therefore, it is the sustainer of all because it sustains everything.
