Furthermore, there is this other gateway for attaining the reality of the knowable:
that knowable is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), meaning it is free from those qualities known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Nevertheless, that which is the enjoyer of the qualities (guṇas)—that is, the experiencer and perceiver of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas when they have transformed into the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion by means of sound and the other sense objects—that is the Knowable; this is the meaning.
Furthermore:
it is both outside and inside of beings, and it is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
With reference to the body—which is imagined as the self through ignorance and extends outward to the skin—that very [skin] is made the limit and is called "outside.
Likewise, with reference to the inner self (pratyag-ātman), the body itself is made the limit and is called "inside.
When both "outside" and "inside" are mentioned, it might follow that there is an absence in the middle.
This is said: that which is both the immobile and the mobile, and even that which appears as the body— the moving and the non-moving— is to be known as that very [reality],
just like the appearance of a snake in a rope.
If that which is non-moving were indeed moving, then all objects of worldly transaction would be knowable; why, then, is this not understood by everyone as "this"?
To this it is said: True, it appears as everything.
Nevertheless, it is subtle like space.
Therefore, because of its subtlety, although it is knowable in its own form, it is unknowable to the ignorant.

But for the wise, it is eternally known through such authoritative means as, "All this is indeed the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.7) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
It is far away because it is unknown, since it cannot be attained by the ignorant even in ten million billion years;
yet it is near, because it is the very Self for those who know. (BhG 13.15)
Moreover:
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among beings;
it is to be known as the sustainer of beings, as well as their devourer and their progenitor. (BhG 13.16)
And it is undivided, yet like space it is one;

though it exists as if divided among all beings, that is to say, among all living creatures, because it is perceived only within bodies. Furthermore, it is the sustainer of beings (*bhūtabhartṛ*); it sustains all beings during the time of their maintenance, and thus it is to be known as the sustainer of beings.
At the time of dissolution, it is *grasiṣṇu*, having the nature of devouring;
and at the time of origination, it is *prabhaviṣṇu*, having the nature of bringing forth—just as a rope or similar object [is the substrate] for a snake or other such things falsely imagined upon it.
(BhG 13.16) Furthermore, if it were not perceived even while existing everywhere, [it would not be the Self].
Is darkness, then, the object of knowledge? No. What then?
"That is said to be the light even of lights, beyond darkness."
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge—this dwells within the heart of every being.
That which is to be known is the light even of the luminaries such as the sun;
for the luminaries such as the sun shine only when kindled by the light of the consciousness of the Self, as it is said:
"By that splendor kindled, the sun shines" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "By its light all this shines" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14),
and from the Smṛti as well, beginning with, "The splendor that resides in the sun" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.12).
It is said to be beyond darkness— that is, untouched by ignorance (ajñāna).
For the sake of encouraging one who has become despondent through the thought that knowledge and so forth are difficult to attain, he says: "Knowledge consists of humility and the like.

That which was described in the passage beginning with, "I shall declare that which is to be known" (Gītā 13.12), is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). When that very object of knowledge is known, it becomes the fruit of knowledge; therefore, it is called "attainable through knowledge" (*jñāna-gamya*).
That which is being known is the object of knowledge.
These three are established—meaning they abide specifically—in the heart, that is, in the intellect (buddhi) of every living being;
for it is precisely therein that the triad is perceived.
This verse is begun for the purpose of summarizing the meaning as it has been stated:
"Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
My devotee, having understood this, attains to my own state of being. (BhG 13.18)

Thus, the field (*kṣetra*)—beginning with the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and ending with fortitude (*dhṛti*); likewise, knowledge (*jñāna*)—beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the purpose of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*);

and the knowable (*jñeya*)—beginning with "that which is to be known" (*jñeyaṃ yattat*) and ending with "it is said to be beyond darkness" (*tamasaḥ param ucyate*)—has been stated in brief, that is, in summary.
Indeed, this entire meaning of the Vedas and the meaning of the Gītā has been stated in summary.
To the question, "Who is qualified for this right vision?
it is said: one who is my devotee—that is, one who has surrendered their entire being to me, the Lord, the omniscient, the supreme teacher, Vāsudeva.

He whose intellect is possessed by such a conviction—that whatever he sees, hears, or touches is indeed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—that devotee of Mine, having understood this aforementioned right vision (*samyag-darśana*), attains *mad-bhāva*;
*mad-bhāva* means "My state of being," which is the state of being the Supreme Self (*paramātma-bhāva*). To that state of My being, he attains.
...one goes to liberation.

// BhGS 13.18 // ============================== In that seventh chapter, two natures of the Lord were introduced—the higher and the lower, characterized as the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
And it was stated: "All beings have this as their source" [Gītā 7.7].
The following point is now stated: how it is that the field and the knower of the field constitute the two sources of the origin of beings—"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the modifications and the qualities are born from Prakṛti. (BhG 13.19)
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are the two natures of the Lord;
know that both those two, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, are beginningless— that is, they are "anādī," meaning those for whom no beginning exists.
Since God is eternal, it is logical that His two primal natures (*prakṛti*) must also be eternal;
for God’s very nature as Lord consists precisely in possessing these two natures.
Those two natures, by which God is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, are beginningless, real, and the cause of *saṃsāra*.
Some explain *nādī* as *anādī* using a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
by this, it is said that the causality of Īśvara is established.
If, however, only *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* were eternal, then the world would be produced solely by them.
That the Lord is the creator of the world is not tenable;

for prior to the origination of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa), there would be no object over which to exercise lordship, resulting in the absurd consequence that the Lord is not actually a lord.

If saṃsāra were without a cause, there would follow the consequence of no liberation, the consequence of the futility of the scriptures, and the consequence of the non-existence of bondage and liberation.
However, if God and the two primal natures (*prakṛti*) are eternal, all of this becomes logically consistent.
How so? "And the modifications, and the qualities (*guṇa*s) indeed."

Know—that is, understand—that the modifications to be described hereafter, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the body and the senses, as well as the qualities (*guṇas*) transformed into the forms of the notions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are born from *prakṛti*.

*Prakṛti* is the Lord’s power that causes modification, consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is *māyā*. Those modifications and qualities whose origin is that [power] are "born from *prakṛti*"; know those modifications.
And know that the qualities (guṇas) arise from Nature (prakṛti); they are transformations of Nature.
What, then, are those modifications and qualities arising from Nature? To this he says:
"Nature is said to be the cause in the agency of the body and the senses."
The Puruṣa is said to be the cause for the experiencing of pleasures and pains.
Regarding "the state of being the agent of the effect and the instruments": the "effect" (kārya) is the body; the "instruments" (karaṇa) are the thirteen located therein.
The five elements that originate the body and the objects of the senses—which are modifications arising from *prakṛti*—are included here under the term "effect," as they were previously mentioned.
Furthermore, the qualities (*guṇa*) arising from *prakṛti*, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are included under the term "instruments" because they reside within the instruments.

The agency—that is, the state of being a producer—belonging to those effects and instruments is called "agency of effects and instruments. In that agency of effects and instruments, *prakṛti* is said to be the cause or the agent by virtue of its initiating activity.
Thus, through this agency of effects and instruments, *prakṛti* is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
Even in this reading, "kārya-kāraṇa-kartṛtve," it means:

that which is the transformation of something is its effect (kārya), while the transformer is the cause (kāraṇa); [the text refers to] the agency (kartṛtva) with respect to those two, the effect and the cause, namely the transformed and the transformer.

Alternatively, the sixteen transformations are the effect (kārya), and the seven primary causes and their modifications are the cause (kāraṇa); these very things are called "effect and cause" (kārya-kāraṇa), and Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause of their agency.
It is precisely by virtue of being the initiator [of action].
And as to how the person (*puruṣa*) may be the cause of *saṃsāra*, that is stated: "Person," "living being" (*jīva*), "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), and "experiencer" (*bhoktṛ*) are synonyms;
he is called the cause for the state of being an experiencer—that is, an apprehender—of pleasures and pains which are objects of experience.

But how is it stated that *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* together constitute the cause of *saṃsāra* by means of this agency of the effect and the instrument, and the state of being the experiencer of pleasure and pain?

To this it is replied: [it is so] because, in the absence of the transformation of *prakṛti* into the form of effects, instruments, pleasure, and pain—which consist of cause and fruit—and in the absence of the conscious *puruṣa* being their perceiver, [neither could exist].

From what would there be saṃsāra? When, moreover, there occurs a conjunction in the form of ignorance between Prakṛti— which has transformed into the nature of effects and instruments, pleasure and pain, and consists of cause and effect, and is thus the object of experience— and the Puruṣa, who is its opposite and is the experiencer.
"In that case, there would be transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).

Therefore, it is logical that what was stated—that the cause of transmigratory existence consists in the nature of Prakṛti and Puruṣa acting as the instrument and the agent, and as the experiencer of pleasure and pain—is correct. But what indeed is this so-called transmigratory existence?
The experience of pleasure and pain is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
And for the *puruṣa*, the state of being an experiencer of pleasures and pains constitutes its transmigratory condition.
Regarding that which was stated—that the *puruṣa*’s state of being an experiencer of pleasures and pains constitutes its transmigratory condition—it is now explained what the cause of that is:
For the person, abiding in material nature, experiences the qualities born of nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs.
The person is the enjoyer situated in nature (*prakṛti-stha*).
"Situated in nature" means abiding within *prakṛti*, which is characterized by ignorance and has transformed into the form of the body and the senses;
that is to say, he has come to regard *prakṛti* as the self.
For because of this, he "enjoys," which means he perceives;
he experiences the qualities born of nature— that is, produced from nature— which are manifested in the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and thus [he is called] "happy."
"I am suffering," "I am deluded," or "I am wise"— thus [one conceives].

Even though ignorance persists, when the qualities of pleasure, pain, and delusion are being experienced, that attachment which constitutes the sense of "I" (ātma-bhāva) is the primary cause of worldly existence (saṃsāra) for a person's birth;
as stated in such scriptural passages as, "As is one's desire, so is one's resolve" (BAU 4.4.5).
This very point he expresses: "The cause, the reason, is attachment to the qualities (guṇa-saṅga)—that is, the attachment of this experiencer (bhoktṛ), the person, to births in good and evil wombs."
The wombs are both true and untrue; these are the "true-and-untrue wombs. Births within those true-and-untrue wombs are "births in true-and-untrue wombs.
With respect to those births in true-and-untrue wombs, which serve as the objects [of experience], the cause is attachment to the *guṇas*.

Alternatively, the phrase "attachment to the qualities" (*guṇa-saṅga*) is the cause of this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—which consists of births in good and evil wombs—and the term "cycle of existence" (*saṃsāra*) is to be supplied from within the middle of the verse.
"Good wombs" (*sad-yoni*) refers to the wombs of gods and so forth;
"evil wombs" (*asad-yoni*) refers to the wombs of animals and so forth.
By implication, it should be understood that human births, as well as births in the realms of the existent and non-existent, are not contradictory.

This is what is meant: ignorance known as abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti), along with attachment to the qualities (guṇas) which is desire, is the cause of saṃsāra; and this is stated for the purpose of its complete abandonment. Furthermore, the cause for its cessation—namely knowledge, dispassion, and renunciation—is well-known in the Gītā scripture.

And that knowledge concerning the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), by knowing which one attains immortality, was introduced previously [in Gītā 13.12]: "Having known it, one attains immortality. It has also been described through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and by the superimposition of what is not its nature (*atad-dharmādhyāropa*). Now, a direct definition of that very same [knowledge] is being provided: [The Blessed Lord said: "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and also the end of beings. (Gītā 10.20) This is the direct instruction regarding that very [Self]. The meaning is as follows: I, the Supreme Lord, am the Self—meaning the inner controller (*antaryāmin*)—residing in the hearts of all beings. And how? As the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings. That is to say, I am the cause of their origin, their subsistence, and their dissolution. Or, alternatively, I am the Self residing in the hearts of all beings, and I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of those very beings. Just as the clay is the beginning, middle, and end of jars and other earthen objects, so too am I the Self of all beings. Therefore, there is nothing else apart from Me. Since I am thus the Self of all, there is no distinction whatsoever between Me and them. Consequently, the entire universe is non-different from Me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because I am the Self of all, I am the inner witness (*sākṣin*) of everything, free from the qualities of the material nature (*guṇa*), and devoid of all particularity (*viśeṣa*). Thus, the meaning is that I am the supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality. By this, the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established. This is the intention. Alternatively, the word *ātman* may be interpreted as "nature" (*svabhāva*). In that case, the meaning is: I am the nature of all beings, existing as their beginning, middle, and end. That is to say, I am the constituent essence (*prakṛti*) of all beings. Just as gold is the nature of bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments, so too am I the nature of all beings. Therefore, since I am the nature of all, there is no difference between them and Me. Hence, the entire universe is non-different from Me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because I am the nature of all, I am the inner witness of everything, free from the qualities of the material nature, and devoid of all particularity. Thus, the meaning is that I am the supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. Or again, the word *ātman* may be taken in the sense of "abode" (*adhikaraṇa*). In that case, the meaning is: I am the abode of all beings, existing as their beginning, middle, and end. That is to say, I am the support (*ādhāra*) of all beings. Just as space (*ākāśa*) is the support of jars and other objects, so too am I the support of all beings. Therefore, since I am the support of all, there is no difference between them and Me. Consequently, the entire universe is non-different from Me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because I am the support of all, I am the inner witness of everything, free from the qualities of the material nature, and devoid of all particularity. Thus, the meaning is that I am the supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. Or yet again, the word *ātman* may be understood in the sense of "measure" (*mātra*). In that case, the meaning is: I am the measure of all beings, existing as their beginning, middle, and end. That is to say, I am the limit (*maryādā*) of all beings. Just as the fathom (*vyāma*) is the measure for measuring cloth and other things, so too am I the measure of all beings. Therefore, since I am the measure of all, there is no difference between them and Me. Consequently, the entire universe is non-different from Me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because I am the measure of all, I am the inner witness of everything, free from the qualities of the material nature, and devoid of all particularity. Thus, the meaning is that I am the supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. Or finally, the word *ātman* may be taken in the sense of "essence" (*svarūpa*). In that case, the meaning is: I am the essence of all beings, existing as their beginning, middle, and end. That is to say, I am the true nature (*tattva*) of all beings. Just as fire is the essence of heated iron, so too am I the essence of all beings. Therefore, since I am the essence of all, there is no difference between them and Me. Consequently, the entire universe is non-different from Me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because I am the essence of all, I am the inner witness of everything, free from the qualities of the material nature, and devoid of all particularity. Thus, the meaning is that I am the supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. In this way, the Blessed Lord has taught the oneness of the individual soul and the Supreme Self through various methods. However, some people, due to their dull intellect, do not understand this oneness even when it is taught in such ways. For them, the Blessed Lord spoke another verse to establish that very oneness: "I am the taste in water, O son of Kuntī, and the radiance in the moon and the sun; I am the sacred syllable *oṃ* in all the Vedas, and the sound in space, and the manliness in men. (Gītā 7.8) The meaning is as follows: I am the essential nature of the taste in water. Just as sweetness is the inherent nature of sugar-cane juice, so too am I the inherent nature of the taste in water. Similarly, I am the radiance in the moon and the sun. Just as light is the inherent nature of the moon and the sun, so too am I the inherent nature of the radiance in the moon and the sun. Likewise, I am the sacred syllable *oṃ*, which is the source of all the Vedas, in all the Vedas. Just as the *oṃkāra* is the inherent nature of the Vedas, so too am I the inherent nature of the sacred syllable *oṃ*. Similarly, I am the sound in space. Just as sound is the inherent nature of space, so too am I the inherent nature of the sound in space. Likewise, I am the manliness in men. Just as vigor is the inherent nature of men, so too am I the inherent nature of the manliness in men. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. Furthermore, the Blessed Lord spoke another verse to establish that very oneness: "And I am the pure fragrance in the earth, and the brilliance in the fire; I am the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics. (Gītā 7.9) The meaning is as follows: I am the pure fragrance in the earth. Just as the sweet scent is the inherent nature of sandalwood and other fragrant substances, so too am I the inherent nature of the pure fragrance in the earth. Similarly, I am the brilliance in the fire. Just as heat is the inherent nature of fire, so too am I the inherent nature of the brilliance in the fire. Likewise, I am the life in all beings. Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the inherent nature of all beings, so too am I the inherent nature of the life in all beings. Similarly, I am the austerity in ascetics. Just as self-restraint is the inherent nature of ascetics, so too am I the inherent nature of the austerity in ascetics. By this, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established. This is the intention. Furthermore, the Blessed Lord spoke another verse to establish that very oneness: "And I am the consciousness in all beings, and the power of resolution in the senses; and I alone am the object of knowledge to be known, and I am the state of liberation among states. (Gītā 7.10) The meaning is as follows: I am the consciousness in all beings. Just as awareness is the inherent nature of all beings, so too am I the inherent nature of the consciousness in all beings. Similarly, I am the power of resolution in the senses. Just as the capacity for determination is the inherent nature
The supreme Person within this body is called the witness, the permitter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also the Supreme Self.
The *upadraṣṭṛ* is a witness who, while remaining proximate, is himself uninvolved;

just as when the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) are occupied with the sacrificial rites, another person standing aside, unoccupied and skilled in the science of sacrifice, observes the merits and defects of the activities of those priests and the sacrificer—
so too, the *upadraṣṭṛ* is a witness who, by virtue of proximity, observes the operations of the body and the senses while they are engaged in their respective functions.
Alternatively, the body, the eye, the mind, the intellect, and the self are the seers.
Among these, the body is the external seer;
starting from that, the innermost one—the self—is the seer, being most proximate and inward-facing.
Since there is no other seer more internal than he,
he may be called the "witness" (upadraṣṭṛ) because of his supreme proximity to the act of seeing;
or, like a witness to a sacrifice, he is the witness because he takes everything as his object.
And the "consenter" (anumantā):
consent is the act of approving; he is the consenter who rejoices in those performing actions.
Alternatively, the consenter is one who, though not himself engaged in the activities of performing an action, is nevertheless engaged [in it].

Because he appears as if favorable toward that [action], he is the "consenter" (anumantṛ). Alternatively, being a witness to their activities as they proceed in their own functions, he never restrains them; thus, he is the "consenter."

The Supporter (*bhartṛ*). What is called "supporting" (*bharaṇa*) is the maintenance of the nature of the body, senses, mind, and intellect—which are composite and possess the appearance of consciousness—by means of the Self as the conscious principle acting as their instrumental cause; since this is performed by the conscious Self alone, the Self is called the "Supporter.
The Experiencer (*bhoktṛ*).

Just as heat is inseparable from fire, the cognitions of the intellect—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and having all objects as their domain—arise as if swallowed by the conscious self; yet, though appearing distinct, they are perceived [as such]. Thus, the Self is called the "experiencer" (bhoktā) and the "Great Lord" (maheśvara).
He is Maheśvara because he is the Great Lord, being both the self of all and independent.
He is the Supreme Self (Paramātman).

Since he is the supreme Self characterized by being the witness and so forth, with respect to the body and everything else up to the intellect—which are falsely imagined as the inner self through ignorance—he is called the Supreme Self.
He is also spoken of and declared by the word "the inner Supreme Self" (antaḥ-paramātmā) in the Śruti. Where is He? In this body, He is the Person beyond the unmanifest;
for "the Supreme Person is indeed another, called the Supreme Self."
[Thus, that which was introduced in Gītā 13.2, "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field," and which will be explained in Gītā 13.3,
has been concluded. He who thus knows this Self, characterized as described above— the Person together with Nature and its qualities— [attains liberation].
Even though acting in every way, he is not born again.

He who knows the Puruṣa directly as his own self in the manner described— "I am this"— and who knows Prakṛti, characterized by ignorance, along with its modifications, to have been brought to non-existence and withdrawn by means of knowledge;
such a person, even though existing in every way and in all circumstances, is not born again— that is, he does not arise for another body— once this body of the wise man has fallen away.
The meaning is that he does not take up another body.
By the word "api" (even), what more need be said?
The intention is that one who remains established in his own duty is not born again.

Now, although it has been stated that there is no further birth after the arising of knowledge, nevertheless, it might be argued that the destruction— without yielding their fruit— of those actions performed prior to the arising of knowledge, as well as those occurring in subsequent times, and those performed over many past births, is not logical; thus, there would be three types of births, for the perishing of what has been done is indeed not tenable.
Just as there is no distinction perceived among actions that have begun to take effect in their results and have already initiated their birth,
so too all three types of karma would initiate three births.
Or else, all [atoms] combined together might initiate a single birth [of an effect];
otherwise, if what has been produced were to perish [immediately], there would follow the consequence of a lack of confidence in everything, and the treatises (śāstra) would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, this statement—that "he is not born again"—is incorrect. No; for it is said:
"his karmas are exhausted" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8), and "he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).

The burning away of all karma for the knower is declared by hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "For him, that long a time only," and "All his actions are consumed like the pith of a reed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).
And here too, the burning away of all karma has been stated by the verse beginning with "Just as firewood... (Gītā 4.37), and he will state it further on the grounds of logical reasoning:
for karmas, which have ignorance, desire, and the afflictions as their seeds and causes, initiate the sprout of future births.

Moreover, in this regard also, the Blessed One has stated in various places that actions accompanied by the underlying intention of egoism (*sāhaṃkāra-abhisaṃdhi*) initiate results, whereas others do not;
"Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again."
And it is said: "Likewise, the self is not joined again with afflictions that have been burnt by knowledge" (Mbh 3.200.10).
Let it be granted, for now, that there is a burning of those karmas performed after the arising of knowledge, because they coexist with knowledge.
But it is not tenable that there is a burning away of the karmas performed in this very life prior to the arising of knowledge, nor of those performed in past lives. No;
for there is the qualification "all karmas.
If it is argued that this refers only to all karmas occurring after the time of knowledge, we say no.
Because there is no logical ground for contraction [of the soul].
As for what was said— that just as the karmas that initiated the present birth do not perish even when knowledge has arisen because they have already begun to yield their fruit,
so too it is not reasonable for karmas whose fruits have not yet begun to perish— that is incorrect.
How so? Because their fruit has already begun to operate, like an arrow that has been released.

Just as an arrow previously released from a bow for the purpose of piercing a target continues its motion even after the target has been pierced, until it finally ceases only through the exhaustion of the momentum already initiated by falling to the ground;
in the same way, the karma that initiated the body continues even when the purpose of maintaining the body has ceased.

It continues to function just as before until the momentum of its formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is exhausted. Just as that very arrow, even when released from the bow, is brought to a halt if it has not yet initiated the momentum for its flight,
so too are those karmas whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest rendered seedless by knowledge while they still abide in their own substratum.
It is established that it was rightly said: "When this body of the wise man has fallen, he is not born again.
In this regard, these various means for the realization of the Self—meditation and so forth—are now described:
"Some perceive the Self within the Self by means of meditation. (BhG 13.24)
Others by means of the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.

By means of meditation (*dhyāna*). Meditation is defined as follows: having withdrawn the sense organs, such as the ear and others, from their objects such as sound and so forth, and having drawn the mind into the inner conscious Self (*cetayitṛ*), that which is contemplation with one-pointedness is meditation.
Likewise, because of the employment of similes in the passage: "The crane meditates as it were, the earth meditates as it were, the mountains meditate as it were" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1).
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is a continuous, uninterrupted cognition, like a stream of oil. By means of that meditation,

some yogins perceive the Self within their own intellect (*buddhi*), seeing the Self as immediate consciousness through their own immediate consciousness— the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) refined by meditation— while others do so through the yoga of Sāṃkhya.

That which is called Sāṃkhya is the contemplation that "these qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are the objects of perception for me; I am other than them, the eternal witness of their activity, the Self distinct from the qualities. This is the Yoga of Sāṃkhya.
By means of this, they perceive the Self through the self; thus it continues.
By *karma-yoga*:
action itself is the *yoga*;
it is of the nature of a disciplined application (*ghaṭana*) performed with the intention of dedicating it to the Lord.
It is called "yoga" figuratively because it is the object of yoga;
by means of that [yoga], through the purification of the mind and the arising of knowledge, others [attain liberation].
Others, however, not knowing thus, worship having heard from others.
And they too, being devoted to the sacred scriptures, certainly transcend death.

But others, among these various options, not knowing the Self in the manner described even through any one of them, hear from other teachers who say, "Meditate upon this very thing," and being faithful, they worship; being thus faithful, they meditate.
They too certainly cross over, they indeed transcend death—that is to say, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) joined with death.
"Devoted to the Śruti": for those whose supreme resort (*param ayana*) is the Śruti—that is, hearing (*śravaṇa*)—which is the highest means (*sādhana*) for setting out upon the path to liberation;
the meaning is that they rely solely on the instruction of others as their authority and are themselves devoid of discrimination (*viveka*).
What need is there to say that those who are independent regarding the means of knowledge and possess discrimination transcend death? This is the intended meaning. (BhG 13.25)

The knowledge concerning the identity of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord, expressed in the passage "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (Gītā 13.3), is the means to liberation, as it was stated:
"Having known which, one attains immortality" (Gītā 13.13).
For what reason is that so?
Thus, to demonstrate the cause of that, the following verse is commenced:
"Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the Knower of the field. (BhG 13.26)

Whatever being or object whatsoever is born or produced—without exception? No; he says: "Know, O bull of the Bharatas, that the stationary and the moving—that which is immobile and that which is mobile—is born from the union of the field and the knower of the field. Thus you should understand and know.
What, then, is this "conjunction" (saṃyoga) between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) that is intended?
It cannot be a specific kind of relation consisting of the joining of parts, like that of a jar to a rope, because the knower of the field lacks parts, being partless like space.

Nor is their connection characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), as in the case of threads and cloth, because it is not admitted that there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

Thus it is said: the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the field and the knower of the field—which are object and subject and possess distinct natures—is characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of each other's attributes; this is based on the absence of discrimination regarding the true nature of the field and the knower of the field, just like the superimposed conjunction of a snake or silver upon a rope or mother-of-pearl due to the absence of knowledge that discriminates them.

This very conjunction of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whose nature is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and which is characterized by false knowledge, is to be understood as the knowable in its true nature as Brahman— devoid of all specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)— by means of the verse, "That which is neither existent nor non-existent" (Gītā 13.13), after first attaining a thorough knowledge of the distinction between the characteristics of the field and the knower of the field according to the scriptures, and having separated the knower of the field, defined as previously described, from the field just as one extracts a blade of grass (*iṣīkā*) from the *muñja* reed.
And the field, like an illusory elephant, a dream-object, or a city of Gandharvas, appears as if real though it is entirely unreal;
for one whose consciousness has reached such certainty,
false knowledge departs due to its opposition to the aforementioned right vision.

Because the cause of his birth has been removed, what was stated— that "the wise man who thus knows the Puruṣa and Prakṛti along with the Guṇas is not born again" (Gītā 13.25)— is logically established.

By the statement "he is not born again" (Gītā 13.24), the fruit of perfect realization (samyag-darśana) was described as the absence of birth through the cessation of the seeds of transmigratory existence, such as ignorance (avidyā).
The cause of birth has been stated to be the conjunction of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), which is conditioned by ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, although the right vision (samyag-darśana) that removes that ignorance has already been mentioned, it is stated once more in different words:
"The Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings..."
He who sees the Imperishable within the perishing—he truly sees.
"Equally," meaning without distinction, "abiding," meaning remaining present;
where? "In all," that is, in every single being, from Brahmā down to the immovable plants, among all living creatures.
Whom? The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara)—who is called the Supreme Lord in relation to the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the unmanifest self.
Him who abides equally in all beings—
distinguishing them by saying "while they perish"—
and that Supreme Lord as "the imperishable."
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the absolute difference between living beings and the Supreme Lord.
How so? For among all the modifications of existence (*bhāva-vikāra*), the modification characterized by birth is the root.
All other modifications of existence that occur subsequent to birth end in destruction.
There is no modification of an entity beyond destruction, because [destruction] is the non-existence of the entity;
for attributes exist only when there is a substratum.
Therefore, by restating the absence of the final modification of existence, all prior modifications of existence are negated along with their effects.
Consequently, the absolute distinction of the Supreme Lord from all elemental beings is established.
It is the state of being without distinction and the state of oneness.
He alone who perceives the Supreme Lord in the manner thus described truly sees;
for does not the entire world also see?
"What is the use of the qualification?
[The answer is: "He sees the truth, but he sees it erroneously."
Therefore, he specifies: "only that [person] sees.
Just as one who perceives a single moon is distinguished in relation to one with cataracts who sees many moons—by saying "only that person sees"—so too is this specified.
In the same way here also, he who perceives the one undivided Self as described is distinguished from those who perceive it as divided— that is, contrary to its true nature as the one Self;
he alone truly sees, while the others, though seeing, do not see.
The meaning is: because of seeing things erroneously, like one who sees many moons.
Now, a verse is begun in order to offer praise for the aforementioned right vision by stating its fruit:
"For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere," etc.
He does not destroy himself by himself; therefore, he goes to the supreme goal.

For, seeing and perceiving equally—that is, seeing with equanimity—the Lord, whose characteristics were described in the immediately preceding verse, as abiding everywhere and established identically among all beings; what does he do by seeing thus? He does not harm, that is, he does not commit violence against himself by means of his very own self.
By refraining from each of those forms of injury, one attains the supreme, most excellent state known as liberation.
But surely no living being whatsoever destroys its own self;
how then can it be said that "one does not destroy what has not been reached"?
It is just as in the passage: "Fire is not to be piled up on earth, nor in the atmosphere, nor in heaven," and so forth.
This is not a fault, because it is possible for the ignorant to disregard the Self.
For every ignorant person, having disregarded the Self— which is extremely well-known, immediate, and directly perceived— mistakes the non-Self for the Self.
Having performed merit and demerit, one destroys the self already acquired and acquires another new self;
having destroyed that as well, one acquires yet another.
Thus, by destroying each successively acquired self, every ignorant person is a "slayer of the self" (ātmahā).
But as for that which is the supreme Self, even that is, as it were, slain by ignorance at all times because its fruit is not realized; thus, all the ignorant are indeed "slayers of the Self.
However, the other who perceives the Self as described does not, in either way, harm or slay the Self by means of the self.
Then he goes to the supreme goal; the meaning is that the aforementioned fruit accrues to him.
(BhG 13.28) It was stated: "Seeing the Lord dwelling equally in all beings, one does not destroy the self by means of the self" (Gītā 13.28).
That [statement] appears untenable, given that the selves are divided by differences arising from the distinctness of their own qualities and actions.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise sees the Self as the non-agent—he truly sees. (BhG 13.29)
By nature, the *prakṛti* of the Blessed One is *māyā*, consisting of the three *guṇas*, according to the wording of the mantra: "One should know *māyā* to be *prakṛti*" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10].

And by that very *prakṛti*—and not by anything else—transformed into the form of effects and causes such as the *mahat* and so forth, actions initiated through speech, mind, and body are performed and brought to completion in every way and in all their various modes.

He who sees and perceives the Self as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), devoid of agency and free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—he truly sees; such is the intended meaning: he is the seer of ultimate reality (paramārtha).

The meaning is that, for that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), non-agent (*akartṛ*), and without distinction (*nirviśeṣa*), like space (*ākāśa*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can establish its division.
Furthermore, he elaborates upon that same right vision (*samyagdarśana*) by means of another expression:
"When one perceives the distinct existence of beings as situated in the One..."
And from that very [state], Brahman then attains expansion.

When, at whatever time, one perceives the separate existence of the elements— the distinctness of the elements— residing as a single unity within the one Self, following the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and perceives the Self through direct experience according to the teaching "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);

And from that very source—from that very Self—he perceives the expansion, the origin, and the manifestation: "From the Self comes breath; from the Self comes hope; from the Self comes memory; from the Self comes space; from the Self comes fire; from the Self comes water; from the Self come appearance and disappearance; from the Self comes food"—when he perceives the expansion in such ways as these, he attains Brahman; he becomes it.
"At that time" means at that moment.
When the Self, being one, is the Self of all bodies, the connection with those defects [of the bodies] would follow; therefore, this is said:
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this immutable Supreme Self,
O son of Kuntī, does nothing and is not tainted, even though it dwells within the body.
Because it is beginningless. "Beginninglessness" (*anāditva*) means the state of being without a beginning;
a "beginning" (*ādi*) is a cause.
That which does not have such a [cause] is beginningless.
For whatever has a beginning perishes by its own nature;
this [Self], however, does not perish because it is without beginning and partless,
and likewise because it is devoid of qualities.
For that which possesses qualities departs through the departure of its qualities;
but this one, because it is devoid of qualities, does not depart.
Thus, this Supreme Self is immutable.
Because no expenditure of this is found, it is "indestructible" (avyaya).
Since this is so, although it is said to be "dwelling in the body"— meaning that the Self is perceived within bodies— it is called "dwelling in the body."
Nevertheless, he does not act;
precisely because of that non-action, he is not stained by its fruit. For it is the agent who is stained by the fruit of action.
But this [Self] is a non-doer; therefore, the meaning is that it is not tainted by the fruit [of action].
Who, then, among the bodies is the doer and is tainted?

If, first of all, the embodied soul (*dehī*) were other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and were both the agent and the one who is tainted, then this which has been stated— the identity of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) in such passages as "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (Gītā 13.2)— would be untenable. Alternatively, if there is no embodied soul other than the Lord...
"Who acts and who is tainted?"—this must be explained.

Or else, [if one holds that] "there is no other," then it is entirely difficult to understand and difficult to express; thus the Vaiśeṣikas, Sāṃkhyas, Ārhatas, and Buddhists have rejected the Upaniṣadic vision proclaimed by the Blessed One.
To this, the Blessed One himself has stated the following resolution: "But it is nature (svabhāva) that acts" (Gītā 5.14).
For it is only through the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) that the conventional expressions "one acts" and "one is stained" occur;
in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), however, these do not exist within the one Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Therefore, for those wandering mendicants (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas*) who are established in this ultimate Sāṃkhya philosophy and are steadfast in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭha*):

The Blessed One has shown in various places that those for whom the functioning of ignorance has been discarded have no eligibility for action. Regarding the question of what it is that one does not do and is not tainted by, he provides an illustration:
"Just as space, though all-pervading, is not tainted because of its subtlety."
Likewise, the Self, though situated everywhere within the body, is not tainted.

Just as space, though all-pervading and omnipresent, is not tainted nor bound due to its subtlety— that is, its subtle nature— so too the Self, though situated everywhere within the body, is not tainted. Furthermore—
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field.

Just as the one Sun, the illuminator, the Aditya, reveals and illumines this entire world, so too, being one, does He reveal the field (kṣetra), beginning with the great elements and ending with the sustaining faculty (dhṛti). Who is He? The meaning is: the Knower of the Field (kṣetrī), the Supreme Self.
In this context, the illustration of the sun serves a dual purpose regarding the Self:
like the sun, the Self is one and the same in all fields, and it is untainted. (BhG 13.34)

This verse is intended as a summary of the meaning of the entire chapter: "Those who thus know the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and the liberation from the material nature of the elements, they go to the Supreme. (BhG 13.35)

Of the field and the knower of the field, as they have been explained, there is thus— in the manner demonstrated— an interval, a specific mutual distinction; by the eye of knowledge— that is, by the eye which is knowledge born from the grace and instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and which is self-convincing— by that eye of knowledge.

And those who know—that is, who understand—the liberation of the elements from their primordial nature; for the "primordial nature of the elements" is that which is called the Unmanifest (avyakta) and is characterized by ignorance (avidyā); [they know] the liberation from that primordial nature of the elements, which is the attainment of its cessation.
"They go" means they proceed to the Supreme, the reality of the Supreme Self, Brahman;
the sense is that they do not take up a body again.
Thus [ends the commentary] of the venerable wandering ascetic teacher, the worshipful feet of the blessed Lord Govinda.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field," in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.
Bhagavad Gītā 14:
Now begins the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Classification of the Three Guṇas."

(Śrīmad-Śaṅkara-Bhagavat-pāda-viracitaṃ Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣyam) It has been stated that everything which arises arises from the conjunction of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). How is that so?
To demonstrate this, the subsequent chapter beginning with "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ) is commenced.

Alternatively, it is for the purpose of showing that the field and the knower of the field, being dependent on the Lord, are the cause of the world, and not as independent entities as the Sāṃkhyas maintain.
It has been stated that abiding in material nature (prakṛti) and attachment to the qualities (guṇas) are the causes of transmigratory existence.
In what quality is there attachment, and how?
What are the qualities, and how do they bind?
And how can there be liberation from the qualities?
Furthermore, the characteristic of one who is liberated must be stated; for this purpose, the Blessed One said:
Furthermore, I shall again declare the supreme knowledge among all forms of knowledge,
knowing which all the sages have attained the highest perfection beyond this world.

The phrase "supreme knowledge" (paraṃ jñānam) is to be connected with the distant word [pravakṣyāmi]. Furthermore, although it has been stated repeatedly in all the preceding chapters, I shall declare it again;
and that is "supreme" because its object is the supreme reality.
What is that? It is knowledge, the highest of all forms of knowledge, because it possesses the highest fruit.
By "of all forms of knowledge," he means of those beginning with humility (amānitva).
What then? [It refers to] those [knowledges] whose objects are things to be known, such as sacrifice and so forth.

He praises this [knowledge] with the words "those" and "the supreme among all," meaning that while those do not lead to liberation, this one does, in order to generate interest and conviction in the minds of the listeners.

Having known that knowledge—having known and attained which all sages, characterized by reflection and having renounced the world, have gone from here, from this bondage of the body, to the supreme perfection called liberation; and to show the exclusivity of this perfection, He says: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained My own nature."
Even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer.

Having relied upon this aforementioned knowledge— that is, having performed the practice that is the means to knowledge— they have attained my state of similarity, meaning they have reached the very nature of me, the Supreme Lord.

But similarity is not the state of having common properties (*sādharmya*), because in the *Gītā-śāstra* no difference between the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is admitted;
furthermore, this discourse on the fruit is spoken for the purpose of praise.
Even at the time of creation (*sarga*), they are not born;
they do not arise.
And even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), when even Brahman perishes, they do not suffer; they do not undergo affliction.
The meaning is that they do not fall away.
[14.2] He states that such a conjunction of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is the cause of all beings:
"My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed."
From that, O Bhārata, the origin of all beings occurs.

My own being—my *māyā*, consisting of the three *guṇas*, *prakṛti*—is the womb (*yoni*), the cause of all beings. Because it is greater than all effects, because it is the cause, and because it nourishes (*bṛṃhaṇāt*) its own transformations, it is called "the Great Brahman" (*mahad brahma*); thus the womb itself is specified. Into that great Brahman, the womb, I place—that is, I deposit—the embryo, the seed of the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the seed which is the cause of the birth of all beings; for I am the possessor of the two powers of the *prakṛtis* of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
The meaning is: "I am the Lord; I join the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who conforms to the nature of its limiting adjuncts consisting of ignorance, desire, and action, with the field.
"Origination" (saṃbhava) means birth; it occurs for all beings through the gateway of the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, and from that, namely, from the act of conception (garbhādhāna).
O Bhārata!
//BhGS_14.3// O son of Kuntī, whatever forms arise from all wombs, of those the Great Brahman is the womb, and I am the father who provides the seed. //BhG_14.4//

O son of Kuntī, among all wombs— whether those of gods, ancestors, humans, cattle, wild animals, and so forth— those forms which arise, characterized by the configuration of the body and consisting of congealed limbs and parts,
of those forms the Great Brahman in its entirety is the womb, the cause; I, the Lord, am the provider of the seed, the father who performs the act of impregnation.
What are the qualities? How do they bind? It is said:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of Prakṛti bind the imperishable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one. (BhG 14.5)
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas" are technical terms for the *guṇas*. These *guṇas* are not qualities dependent upon a substance, as are color and other such properties.
Furthermore, it is not intended here that there is any difference between the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*).

Therefore, like the *guṇas*, being eternally dependent on another and consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) with respect to the *kṣetrajña*, they bind the *kṣetrajña* as it were; for, taking the *kṣetrajña* as their locus, they obtain their own existence, and thus they are said to "bind.
And these, arising from *prakṛti*—that is, arising from the *māyā* of the Blessed One—bind him as it were.
O Mahābāho!
He whose two arms are great, powerful, and extend down to his knees is Mahābāhu; O Mahābāho!
[I see] the imperishable embodied one within the body, the physical frame.

And its immutability has been stated in the verse beginning with "Because it is beginningless" (Gītā 13.32). Now, it was previously said that "the embodied one is not tainted" (Gītā 13.32); how then is it stated here otherwise, that "they bind"?
We have already indicated this by using the word "as it were" (*iva*) in the phrase "as if they were binding.
Now, among the qualities beginning with *sattva*, the characteristic of *sattva* itself is stated:
"Therein, *sattva* is illuminating and healthy because of its stainlessness."
O sinless one, it binds by attachment to pleasure and by attachment to knowledge.
Because of its purity, like a crystal gem, it binds that sattva which is luminous, healthy, and free from affliction.

How? Through attachment to pleasure—by falsely effecting a union of the self, which is the subject, with pleasure, which has become an object, thinking "I am happy"—this is what is meant by being attached to pleasure.
This very thing is ignorance (avidyā).
For the attribute of the object does not belong to the subject.
And it has been stated by the Blessed One that everything from desire up to fortitude is indeed an attribute of the field, which is the object.

Therefore, by ignorance alone—which is its own attribute and characterized by the non-discrimination between object and subject—one becomes, as it were, attached to pleasure that is not one's true self.
It makes the attached appear unattached, the unattached appear attached, and the unhappy appear happy.
Likewise, there is attachment to knowledge; and since "knowledge" is associated with pleasure, it is an attribute of the field alone—namely, of the object and the internal organ—and not of the Self.
For if it were an attribute of the Self, attachment would be impossible.
And because bondage is impossible [in their case],
attachment to knowledge and the like should be understood as being like [attachment to] pleasure— O sinless one, O you who are free from addiction. (BhG 14.6)
Know that *rajas* is of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action. (BhG 14.7)

Know that *rajas* consists of passion (*rāga*); because it causes coloring, it is called passion, just as red ochre (*gairika*) colors. Know it to be of an impetuous nature. It arises from thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) and attachment (*āsaṅga*). Thirst is the longing for what has not yet been obtained.
Attachment is the clinging of the mind, characterized by delight, toward an object already obtained.

That passion (rajas), O son of Kuntī, binds the embodied being through attachment to action—attachment to actions performed for the sake of visible and invisible results, that is, devotion to them; it binds by arising from thirst and attachment (tṛṣṇāsaṅga). It is "arising from thirst and attachment" (tṛṣṇāsaṅgasamudbhavam). It binds by means of that attachment to action. Thus, rajas binds the embodied soul.
But know that *tamas* is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, indolence, and sleep.

Know that *tamas* is the third quality, born of ignorance—that is, produced from ignorance. It causes delusion, creating a lack of discrimination for all embodied beings. O Bhārata, it binds one through negligence, laziness, and sleep—namely, by means of negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*ālasya*), and sleep (*nidrā*).
Furthermore, the function of the qualities is stated briefly:
"O Bhārata, sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action;
but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence. (BhG 14.9)
Sattva attaches and binds one to happiness;
rajas, O Bhārata, attaches one to action—the word "binds" carries over from the previous verse.
Furthermore, tamas, by its nature as a veil, obscures and covers the knowledge produced by sattva—that is, discrimination—and binds one to negligence.
Heedlessness (pramāda) is the non-performance of what has been undertaken to be done.
[BhG 14.9] It has been stated: "When do the qualities (guṇas) perform their functions? To this it is replied: O Bhārata, when sattva prevails by overcoming rajas and tamas.
Rajas, sattva, and tamas; likewise, tamas, sattva, and rajas.
When sattva overcomes both rajas and tamas, it becomes manifest, arises, and increases; then,
having attained its own nature, sattva begins its own effects, such as knowledge and happiness, O Bhārata.
Likewise, when the quality of rajas overcomes both sattva and tamas and increases,
it then initiates its own effects, such as action and craving. Similarly, when the quality known as tamas overcomes both sattva and rajas and increases, [it likewise initiates its own effects].
Then [the intellect] begins its own effects, such as the obscuration of knowledge (jñānāvaraṇa) and so forth.
When a particular quality (guṇa) becomes manifest, what is its characteristic mark? This is explained:
When light arises through all the gates of this body, and knowledge [dawns], then one should know that sattva has increased. (BhG 14.11)
In all the gates— that is,
in all the instruments such as the ears and so forth, which are the gateways for the self’s perception—
in all those gates, the activity of the internal organ, the intellect (buddhi), arises as a manifestation within this body.
That itself is knowledge.

When such a light called knowledge arises, then one should know by the sign of the light of knowledge that *sattva* has increased—that is, it has become manifest—or else [one should know this]. (BhG 14.11)
This is the mark of rajas when it has arisen: greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing;
these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas.
Greed (lobha) is the desire to take another's property. Activity (pravṛtti) is the act of engaging in action. Undertaking (ārambha) is general exertion.
Of what? Of actions (*karman*).
Lack of tranquility (*aśama*) is the absence of calm, the engagement in joy, passion, and so forth.
Longing (*spṛhā*) is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) directed toward objects that are common to all.
When the quality of passion (rajas) is predominant, these signs arise, O bull of the Bharatas.
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion— these are the marks of passion.
These are born when darkness has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
Non-illumination is non-discrimination (*aviveka*).
Furthermore, absolute non-engagement—that is, the absence of activity—is its effect, namely negligence (*pramāda*) and delusion (*moha*) itself.
The meaning is that non-discrimination is a state of bewilderment (*mūḍhatā*).
When the quality of *tamas* has increased, these signs arise, O descendant of Kuru.
Showing that even the fruit obtained through the door of death is entirely secondary (*gauṇa*), being caused by attachment and passion, He says:
But when the embodied soul meets its end while goodness (sattva) is predominant, then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest.

When the *sattva* quality has increased and become predominant, and the embodied self undergoes dissolution—that is, death—then he attains, that is, reaches, the stainless worlds, which are free from impurity; this refers to those who know the highest, namely those who know the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Great One (*mahat*). (BhG 14.14)
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
When the quality of *rajas* has increased, having undergone dissolution—that is, death—one is born among those human beings who are attached to action, those possessed of attachment to karma.
Likewise, in exactly the same way, one who has dissolved—meaning one who is dead—is born among the wombs of the deluded, such as the wombs of animals and so forth, when *tamas* has increased.
A summary of the meaning of the preceding verse is now stated:
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by goodness (sattva);
the fruit of passion (rajas) is suffering, and the fruit of darkness (tamas) is ignorance.
The meaning is that for well-performed action characterized by *sattva*,
the learned declare the fruit to be exclusively pure and of the nature of *sattva*;
however, the fruit of passion (*rajas*)— that is, of action characterized by *rajas*— is suffering.
Because it falls under the domain of karma, its fruit is also nothing but suffering;
since it conforms to its cause, it is purely of the nature of passion (rājasa).
Likewise, ignorance is the result of *tamas*, of tamasic action, and of unrighteousness (*adharma*), as previously described.
Furthermore, that which arises from the *guṇas* is as follows:
from *sattva* knowledge is born, and from *rajas* greed alone.
From tamas arise negligence, delusion, and ignorance as well.
From *sattva*, which has attained its own nature, knowledge arises and is produced;
from *rajas* comes greed alone;
and both negligence and delusion arise from *tamas*.
And ignorance itself arises.
Furthermore:
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle.
Those established in the conduct of the lowest quality, being characterized by darkness (tamas), go downwards.
Those established in *sattva*—meaning those who abide in the conduct characterized by the quality of *sattva*—go upward and are born in the worlds of the gods and other such realms.

Those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle and are born among human beings. Those established in the lowest quality and conduct—the "lowest quality" (*jaghanya-guṇa*) being that which is both low and a quality, namely *tamas*—[are born in the lower realms].

Their conduct consists of sleep, laziness, and so forth; those situated in that, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality—the deluded ones who are characterized by darkness (tāmasa)—go downwards and are born among animals and other such beings.

For a person joined with false knowledge in the form of being established in material nature (prakṛti), there is attachment to the qualities that serve as objects of experience, which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

That attachment consisting of the notions "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded"— which is the cause for a person’s worldly existence (saṃsāra) characterized by birth in good or evil wombs— was briefly described in the previous chapter. Here, beginning with the words "The qualities (guṇas), sattva, rajas, and tamas, arise from Prakṛti," the true nature of these qualities is explained.
The functioning of the guṇas,
the binding nature of the guṇas through their own functioning, and the destiny of the puruṣa bound by the functioning of the guṇas.

Having thus explained in detail that all this—rooted in false knowledge—is the cause of bondage, [the Lord now says] that liberation must be declared as resulting from right vision; therefore, the Blessed One says:
"When the seer perceives no agent other than the gunas..."
And he who knows that which is beyond the qualities attains My state of being.
When the wise seer, being enlightened, perceives no agent other than the *guṇas*— which have transformed into the forms of effects, instruments, and objects—
and sees that the *guṇas* alone in all their states are the agents of all actions, and knows that which is beyond the *guṇas*, being the witness to the activity of the *guṇas*; [he does not grieve].
He shall attain my state—my very being.
How does he attain it? It is said:
"Having transcended these three qualities that arise from the body, the embodied soul..."
Freed from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, he attains the immortal.

Having transcended these aforementioned qualities—having passed beyond even while living those three which constitute the limiting adjunct of Māyā and are the seeds for the arising of the body—the embodied soul, being liberated even while alive, the wise one attains immortality, free from birth, death, old age, and suffering. (Birth, death, old age, and sufferings are collectively termed *janma-mṛtyu-jarā-duḥkhāni*. By means of these, being liberated even while living, the wise one attains the immortal state.
The meaning is that he thus attains my own state.

Having received the seed of the question—"While still living, having transcended the qualities, one partakes of the immortal"—Arjuna said: "By what marks, O Lord, does one become a transcender of these three qualities?"
What is his conduct, and how does he transcend these three qualities?
By what marks and signs, O Lord, does one become transcendent—having passed beyond these three qualities thus explained?
What is his conduct? That is to say, "what is his behavior" (kim-ācāraḥ)?
And in what manner, by what means, does he transcend—passing beyond—these three qualities? ||| BhG 14.21 ||| ==============================

Having been questioned by Arjuna regarding the characteristics of one who has transcended the *guṇas* and the means for transcending the *guṇas*, the Blessed One spoke this verse as a response to both questions.
Listen first to that which concerns the marks endowed with which one becomes transcendent of the *guṇas*:
"O Pāṇḍava, [freedom from] illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and even delusion (*moha*)..."
He does not hate what has arisen, nor does he long for what has ceased.

He does not hate illumination, which is the effect of *sattva*; activity, which is the effect of *rajas*; or even delusion, which is the effect of *tamas*, when these have fully arisen—that is, when they have properly manifested as objects of experience—thinking, "A tamasic cognition has arisen in me;
therefore I am deluded."
Likewise, a rajasic activity of a painful nature has arisen within me; therefore, impelled by that rajas, I have been set in motion and displaced from my true nature.
Alas, my condition is wretched, for this is a fall from the state of abiding in my own essential nature.

Likewise, the *sāttvika* quality, being luminous in nature, binds by bringing about discrimination toward Me and attaching one to pleasure; thus, due to imperfect vision, one hates those [qualities]. Therefore, one who has transcended the qualities does not hate them when they are active.

And just as a person characterized by *sattva* and so forth desires the effects of *sattva* and the other qualities to cease after they have manifested themselves to him, [so too does the transcender of qualities].
The meaning is that one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*) does not desire [the cessation of suffering] in such a manner.
This is not a mark (*liṅga*) perceptible to others;
rather, because it is perceptible to one's own self, it is for the sake of the self.
This indeed is its characteristic:
for another does not perceive hatred or desire directed toward one's own self.
Now, what is the conduct of one who has transcended the qualities?
Thus he gives the answer to this question: "He who sits like one indifferent, who is not shaken by the qualities;
who remains established in the thought that it is only the qualities that are acting, and does not waver. (BhG 14.23)

"Just like one who is indifferent"—just as an indifferent person does not take the side of anyone, so too this knower of the Self (*ātmavit*), established on the path of the means for transcending the qualities (*guṇātītatva*), remains seated; he is the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) who is not shaken from the state of discriminative vision by the qualities.
He clarifies this: "He who remains [steadfast], [observing] that the qualities—transformed into the forms of the body, the senses, and their objects—exist within one another."
The use of the *parasmaipada* ending is due to the fear of violating the meter;
alternatively, there is another reading, "yo 'nutiṣṭhati" (he who practices).
It does not stir, it does not move.
The meaning is that he remains established in his own true nature (svarūpa).
Furthermore:
equanimous in pain and pleasure, self-abiding, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
The steadfast one is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and equal toward blame and self-praise.

One who has equal suffering and happiness is "sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ. One who is established in oneself, abiding in one's own self, is "svasthaḥ" and serene. One for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal is "samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ. One for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant are equal—that is, the pleasant and the unpleasant are the same—is "tulyapriyāpriyaḥ."
Steadfast and wise, regarding censure and self-praise as equal: "censure" (nindā) and "self-praise" (ātma-saṃstuti) constitute the compound *nindātmasaṃstutī*;
that ascetic for whom censure and self-praise are equal is one who regards censure and self-praise as equal.
Furthermore:
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe,
and who has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
He is equal toward honor and dishonor, remaining the same and unchanging;
he is the same toward the factions of friends and enemies,
even if some remain indifferent according to their own inclinations.
Nevertheless, since they arise according to the perspective of others—just as [one might speak of] the factions of friend and enemy—it is said that "the factions of friend and enemy are equal.
One who has abandoned all undertakings (*sarvārambha-parityāgī*):
actions are undertaken for the sake of seen or unseen ends; thus, they are called "undertakings" (*ārambhāḥ*).
One whose nature is to renounce all undertakings is a "renouncer of all undertakings" (sarvārambha-parityāgī).
The meaning is that he is one who has abandoned all action except for that which is necessary merely for the maintenance of the body.
Such a person is said to have transcended the qualities (guṇātītaḥ).

From the words "as one who is indifferent" up to "he is said to have transcended the qualities," that which was taught is the means for attaining the state beyond the qualities (*guṇātītatva*), which must be practiced by a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) as long as it requires effort. Once this has become firmly established and self-evident, it becomes the characteristic of the ascetic who has transcended the qualities. Now, however, how does one transcend the three qualities?
He provides the answer to this question:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman. (BhG 14.26)
And that ascetic or worker who, with unswerving devotion— devotion being worship (bhajana) itself as a yoga— serves Me, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the hearts of all beings; he,
having transcended these aforementioned qualities.
"For becoming Brahman" (*brahma-bhūyāya*):
"becoming" (*bhūya*) means the state of being; the meaning is that it conduces to, or becomes capable of, the state of becoming Brahman—that is, liberation (*mokṣa*). (BhG 14.26)
Why is this so? It is said:
"For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss" (BhG 14.27).
For I am the support (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Brahman, the Supreme Self; "support" means that in me the [Self] is established (*pratitiṣṭhati*), thus I am the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*).
Of what kind of Brahman?
Of the immortal, the imperishable.
Of the immutable and changeless;

of the eternal and constant Dharma—that is, the knowledge of Dharma which is attainable through the yoga of knowledge; of bliss, which is of the nature of joy, absolute, unerring, characterized by immortality and so forth, and consisting of supreme bliss.
The inner self (pratyag-ātman) is the foundation of the supreme self (paramātman);
through right knowledge, it is determined to be identical with the supreme self.
Thus it has been said: "This leads to becoming Brahman."
And that power of the Lord by which Brahman is established— that is, proceeds— for the purpose of bestowing grace upon devotees and so forth,
that power is none other than I, who am Brahman;
the intention is that there is no difference between power and the possessor of power.
Alternatively, because it is denoted by the word "Brahman," Brahman is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Of that Brahman, I alone—and no other—am the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) foundation and support.
Of what kind [of Brahman]?
I am the foundation of the immortal—that which possesses the nature of non-death—and of the imperishable, which is devoid of decay;

furthermore, I am the foundation of the eternal and constant Dharma characterized by the culmination of knowledge, and of the bliss produced thereby, which is absolute and invariably certain. Thus it continues. (BhG 14.27)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjya-pāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka).
Bhagavad Gītā 15:
Now begins the fifteenth chapter, named "The Yoga of the Supreme Person."

(Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Bhāṣya composed by Śrīmac-Chaṅkara-Bhagavatpāda): Since the fruit of action for those who perform rites, as well as the fruit of knowledge for those who possess it, are dependent upon Me,
therefore those who serve Me through the yoga of devotion attain liberation after transcending the qualities (guṇas) by means of attaining knowledge through My grace.

What need is there to say that those who correctly understand the very nature of the Self [possess such knowledge]? Therefore, the Blessed One, desiring to explain the nature of the Self even without being asked by Arjuna, spoke beginning with the words "Rooted above," and so forth.

Therein, first of all, for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*), He describes the true nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) through the metaphor of a tree; for only one who is dispassionate toward *saṃsāra* has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the knowledge of the reality of the Blessed One, and no other.
The Blessed Lord said: They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below.
The Vedic hymns are its leaves; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.
"Rooted above" means that it is "above" because of its subtlety, its causality, its eternity, and its greatness;
it is called the unmanifest Brahman, which possesses the power of Māyā.
Since that [unmanifest] is its root, this tree of worldly existence is said to be "rooted above."
And from the Śruti: "This eternal Aśvattha tree has its roots above and its branches below" (KaṭhU 2.3.1). And in the Purāṇa:
"Its origin is rooted in the Unmanifest; it arises from His very grace;
it consists of the trunk of the intellect, and the cavities within it are the sense organs."
The great elements are its branches, and it possesses leaves in the form of sense objects;
it has the flowers of merit and demerit, and the arising of pleasure and pain as its fruit.
This eternal Brahma-tree is the means of subsistence for all beings;
this is his Brahma-forest, and Brahma moves within it like a witness.
"Having cut this and having shattered it with the supreme sword of knowledge, and then having attained the state of the Self, one does not return from there again. Thus it begins.
They call that tree of saṃsāra, which consists of illusion (māyā), one whose roots are above.

It has branches below; since the great *ahaṃkāra*, the *tanmātras*, and so forth are like its branches extending downwards, it is "one whose branches are below" (*adhaḥ-śākha*). They call this *aśvattha*—which does not stand even for tomorrow (*na śvo 'pi sthātā*)—the *aśvattha*, meaning that which perishes in an instant. Yet they call it "imperishable" (*avyaya*) because the illusion of *saṃsāra* has been proceeding from beginningless time. This is that tree of *saṃsāra*.
For that which is well-known as the substratum for the beginningless and endless continuum of the body and so forth is indeed imperishable;
