this is another qualification of that very tree of worldly existence: "the Vedas are its leaves."
The Vedas— characterized as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*— are the "leaves" of this tree of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-vṛkṣa*) because they conceal [it]. Just as leaves serve to protect a tree,
so too do the Vedas serve to protect the tree of worldly existence, because they reveal dharma and adharma, along with their causes and effects.
He who knows that tree of worldly existence (saṃsāra-vṛkṣa), together with its root, exactly as it has been described— he is a knower of the Veda;
the meaning is that he is a knower of the purpose of the Veda.

Indeed, there is not even an atom's worth of anything remaining to be known other than this tree of transmigratory existence along with its root; therefore, [the Lord], being all-knowing and the knower of the meaning of all the Vedas, praises the knowledge of the tree of transmigratory existence together with its root. Now, the conceptualization of the further parts of this very tree of transmigratory existence is stated:
Its branches extend downward and upward,
nourished by the *guṇas* with sense-objects as their sprouts;
and its roots, likewise, stretch downward in continuous succession.
In the world of men, they are bound by their karma.

From below, starting from humans and so forth down to the stationary objects, and from above, up to the abode of Brahmā the creator of the universe— up to this limit, the fruits of knowledge and action have spread forth and extended like the branches of that tree, according to one's karma and according to what has been heard.
"Increased by the qualities" means increased, that is, made gross, by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which serve as their material cause (*upādāna*).
"Sprouts of objects" means that objects such as sound and so forth are like sprouts; they emerge like buds from the branches, which are the fruits of actions belonging to the body and so forth.
Therefore, the branches have the objects as their sprouts.

The primary root of the tree of saṃsāra, namely *upādāna* (clinging), was explained previously. Now, however, those latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth, produced by the fruits of karma— which act as intermediate causes for the engagement in *dharma* and *adharma* like secondary roots— are continuous and have entered below, relative to the gods and other realms.
"Following after karma" means that karma— characterized by merit and demerit—
is the "following," which occurs subsequently;
those [results] arise following the arising of that [karma].
Those actions follow one specifically in the world of men;
for it is here that the authority over action is well known to belong to human beings.
(BhG 15.2) As for this tree of transmigratory existence that has been described—
Its form is not perceived here in that way;
it has neither end nor beginning, nor any fixed foundation.
This is the *aśvattha* tree with its deeply rooted roots.
Having cut [it] with the firm weapon of non-attachment.
Its form is not perceived here in the manner described,
because it is equal to a dream, a mirage, water in a mirage, an illusion, and a city of the Gandharvas;
for its very nature is seen and then lost, and therefore it has no end, no limit, no finality, and no completion.
Likewise, there is no beginning;
no one perceives that "this has proceeded starting from this point.
Nor is its middle—its established duration—perceived by anyone.
This *aśvattha* tree— described as having well-developed roots, meaning that its roots have grown well, sprouted, and become very firm—

one should cut down with the sword of non-attachment; that is, by means of the weapon of detachment consisting of rising above the desires for sons, wealth, and worlds, which has been made firm by the resolve directed toward the Supreme Self, and sharpened on the whetstone of repeated practice of discrimination.
Having uprooted the tree of saṃsāra along with its seed,
one should thereafter seek that state,
having reached which they do not return again.
I take refuge in that very same Primal Person,
from whom this ancient course of worldly activity has issued forth.
Thereafter, that Vaiṣṇava state must be sought; "seeking" means searching for or knowing.
That state into which they have gone and entered from which they do not return—that is, they do not turn back again to worldly existence—is the goal.

As for how it is to be sought, he says: one should seek that very person who was designated by the word "pada" as the "first"—meaning existing at the beginning—as the "first person," by taking refuge in him;
this is the meaning.
Who is that person?
Thus it is said: from which Person (puruṣa) the activity of the illusory tree of saṃsāra has issued forth and emerged, like an illusion from a magician;
it is ancient (purāṇī), being of long standing. It is now stated in what manner they go to that state:
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the inner self, with desires turned away,
they are liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain.
Those who are undeluded go to that imperishable state.

"Nirmāna-mohāḥ" means those from whom pride and delusion have departed; "māna-mohau" refers to pride and delusion, and those from whom these two are gone are "nirmāna-mohāḥ," meaning they are free from pride and delusion. "Jita-saṅga-doṣāḥ": attachment itself is the fault, thus it is "saṅga-doṣaḥ"; those by whom this fault of attachment has been conquered are "jita-saṅga-doṣāḥ."

Those by whom the fault of attachment has been conquered are "those who have conquered the fault of attachment. Those who are "constantly devoted to the inner self" are those constantly intent on contemplating the nature of the Supreme Self; they are "devoted to that. Those whose desires have "turned away" are those from whom desires have specifically ceased through being untainted; they are "those whose desires have turned away."

The ascetics who have renounced the world, being liberated from the dualities such as the pleasant and the unpleasant, and having cast off the notions of pleasure and pain, go—being undeluded and free from delusion—to that imperishable state which has been described.
That very state is further specified:
"Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines it."
That supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return.
The word "dhāma" is connected with the distant word "dhāmnā.
That *dhāma*—that state which is of the nature of splendor—the sun, Āditya, does not illuminate, even though he possesses the power to illuminate everything.
Likewise, neither does the moon, Śaśāṅka.
Neither by fire nor even by Agni;
having gone to and attained that Vaiṣṇava abode, they do not return,
and which the sun and other luminaries do not illumine.
That is the abode, the supreme state of Viṣṇu, my own station.
[Objection: But surely every destination ends in return; it is well known that "all unions end in separation" (Mbh 11.2.3).
How is it said that for those who have gone to that abode there is no return?
Listen to the reason for this:
"In the world of living beings, an eternal portion of My very self becomes the individual soul."
It draws in the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their own nature.

Of Me alone—of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self—the *aṃśa* (portion), *bhāga* (part), *avayava* (limb), or *ekadeśa* (one part) are synonymous terms. In the world of living beings (*jīva-loka*), that is, in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), he is known as the "living being" (*jīva-bhūta*), celebrated as the agent and the enjoyer; he is eternal (*sanātana*), meaning ancient.

Just as the reflection of the sun in water is a portion of the sun and, upon the removal of the water, returns to the sun itself and does not return [to the water], but goes away by that very same self, even so is this case.

Just as the space within a jar or similar limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), being a portion of space, does not return once it has reached [the universal] space upon the removal of the cause—the jar or the like—therefore it is rightly said that "having gone there, they do not return.
But one might object: how can the partless Supreme Self have a part, a portion, or a limb?
And if it were to possess parts, there would be the consequence of its destruction due to the separation of those parts.
This is not a fault,
because a single location, delimited by an adjunct (upādhi) created by ignorance, is conceptualized as if it were a part.
And this matter has been shown in detail in the Chapter on the Field (Kṣetrādhyāya).

As for how that living being (jīva), conceived as a portion of Me, transmigrates and departs, it is said: He draws—meaning he attracts—the senses, beginning with the ear, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their own places, remaining in their material nature within the ear-cavities and so forth. (BhG 15.7)
At what time?—
When the Lord acquires a body and when He departs from it,
He goes forth taking these [senses] with Him, as the wind carries fragrances from their source. (BhG 15.8)

And as for the second quarter of the verse, "and when the Lord— the living soul (jīva), the master of the aggregate consisting of the body and so forth— departs," it is connected first by the force of the meaning:
"when he obtains another body from the previous one, then, having taken these senses with the mind as the sixth, he goes forth— he goes completely, he departs."
What is it like? He says: like the wind, the purifier, [carrying] fragrances from their source, such as flowers.
What, then, are those [senses]?—the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose.
Having presided over the mind, this [Self] experiences the objects of the senses.

The ear, the eye, the sense of touch (the skin), the tongue, the nose, and the mind as the sixth— presiding over each of these senses while stationed in the body, it experiences objects such as sound and the rest.
Thus, having transcended the body, [it perceives] that which resides in the body.
Whether it is departing, or remaining, or even enjoying experiences endowed with the qualities, the deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it.
Whether departing— leaving behind the body previously acquired— or staying in the body, or experiencing—
perceiving sounds and other objects— the Self is "endowed with qualities," meaning accompanied by, followed by, or joined with the qualities such as pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Even though He is thus situated and has come within the range of their vision, the deluded—whose minds are dragged away by the force of enjoyment of objects seen and unseen, and who are thus bewildered in many ways—do not perceive Him.
"Alas, what a tragedy! the Blessed One laments.
But those whose eyes are the knowledge born of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) do indeed see Him; that is to say, those with the eye of knowledge possess discerning vision. (BhG 15.10)
Striving yogis behold Him established within themselves;
yet even those who strive, if they are of unrefined soul and lacking discernment, do not behold Him.

Exerting effort, practicing yoga, and possessing concentrated minds, yogis behold this aforementioned Self, perceiving it as "This am I," established within their own intellect; yet even those who exert themselves by means of the scriptures and other valid authorities fail to perceive it if they are unrefined in soul— meaning their selves are not purified through austerity and mastery of the senses— and have not desisted from evil conduct.
Those who are undisciplined and arrogant, lacking consciousness and discrimination, do not perceive this even though they exert effort.
That state which, although it illuminates everything, is not illuminated by lights such as fire or the sun;
and having attained which, those seeking liberation do not return again toward the cycle of worldly existence.

And with four verses, the Blessed One, desiring to express the state of being the Self of all and the status of being the locus of all worldly transactions for that Reality— of which the individual souls are parts (just as the spaces within jars are parts of the one universal space) by conforming to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi)— speaks of the summary of His manifestations:
"That splendor residing in the sun which illumines the entire world..."
Know that splendor which is in the moon and that which is in the fire to be mine.
That which resides in the sun, having the sun as its support—what is that? It is the splendor, the radiance, the light which illumines, that is, makes manifest the entire, whole world;
and that splendor which exists as the illuminator in the moon, the bearer of the hare-mark.
And that light which is in the fire, know— that is, understand— it to be mine, belonging to me, Viṣṇu; or else,
that light consisting of consciousness which is in the sun, and that which is in the moon.
And know that light which exists in fire to be mine—belonging to me, Viṣṇu;
for indeed, that light consisting of consciousness is the same in both stationary and moving beings.
In that case, how is this qualification—"that which is in the sun," and so forth—appropriate?
This is not a fault, because its extensiveness is established by the predominance of *sattva*. For in the sun and other such luminaries, *sattva* is exceedingly luminous and exceedingly radiant.
Therefore, it is specified as "light" (*jyotis*) precisely because it is not manifest there, and not because it is superior there.
For just as in the world, even though the shape of the face is the same, the face does not appear in wood or a wall; [so too here].
But it manifests in a mirror and other such objects according to their degree of clarity and greater clarity; it is just like that.
Furthermore:
"And entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital power."
And having become the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all herbs.
Having entered—that is, having pervaded—the earth (*gāṃ*), I sustain all beings and the world by my *ojas*, that is, by my power.

That power, which is free from desire and passion, is my sovereign form that has entered the earth for the sake of supporting the world; by it, the earth, though heavy, does not fall downward nor does it split apart.
And thus says the Vedic mantra: "By whom the formidable sky and the earth were made firm" (TaittS 4.1.8).
And there is the verse beginning with "He has supported the earth" (Ṛgveda 8.7.3.1).

Therefore, it is rightly said: "Entering the earth, I support all beings, both moving and unmoving. Furthermore, having become Soma—the essence of sap—I nourish all the herbs born upon the earth, such as rice and barley, making them full of growth and full of delicious flavor, being Soma, whose nature is sap.
The nature of taste:
Soma is the source of all tastes, for he, consisting of the essence of all tastes, nourishes all plants by infusing them with his own essential juices. (BhG 15.13)
Moreover:
"Having become the Vaiśvānara fire and entered the bodies of living beings, joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the fourfold food. (BhG 15.14)

"I myself indeed, having become Vaiśvānara fire, abide within the stomach"—as stated in such scriptural passages as: "This is the Vaiśvānara fire which is within the person, by which this food is digested, that which is eaten" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9.1). Being Vaiśvānara, I have entered and taken refuge in the bodies of living beings—those possessed of vital breaths—united with the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

Joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I cook—that is, I prepare—the food; I make it into a fivefold offering, consisting of four kinds of eatables: that which is chewed, that which is eaten, that which is sucked, and that which is licked.
Indeed, the consumer is the monkey-fire (Vānara-agni).
Soma is the food to be consumed by Agni.
For one who perceives that both of these together constitute Agni-Soma and are everything, there is no taint from the defects of food.
Furthermore—
And I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known.
I alone am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
And being the Self of the entire multitude of living beings, I am seated within the heart—that is, in the intellect.
Therefore, from Me, who am the Self, come the memory and knowledge of all living beings, as well as their loss, which is their disappearance.
For those of meritorious deeds, memory and knowledge arise in accordance with their meritorious actions.
Likewise, for those of evil deeds, there is the removal—meaning the taking away and the disappearance—of memory and knowledge in accordance with their evil deeds.
Furthermore, by all the Vedas, I alone, as the Supreme Self, am to be known;
that is to say, I am the author of the Vedānta and the author of the tradition of the meaning of the Vedānta.
"I am indeed the knower of the Vedas and the knower of the meaning of the Vedas.

(BhG 15.15) The brief summary of the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign named Nārāyaṇa, conditioned by specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), has been stated in the passage beginning with "That splendor which resides in the sun" (Gītā 15.12).

Now, the subsequent verses are commenced with the desire to determine the true nature (*tattva-svarūpa*) of that very same Lord—He who is free from adjuncts and absolute—by way of distinguishing Him from the conditioned states of the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*).
In that regard, having grouped together all the subject matter of the intermediate chapters concerning the past and the future, He says:
"Two persons are there in this world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the unchanging is called the imperishable. (BhG 15.16)
In this world of *saṃsāra*, these two persons are said to be distinguished as two separate groups: one group is the perishable (*kṣara*), which decays and is subject to destruction;
the other person is the imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the opposite of that, being the Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).

The imperishable (akṣara) person is said to be the seed of origin for the perishable (kṣara) person, serving as the substratum for the impressions (saṃskāra) of desire, action, and so forth, belonging to the many transmigrating beings.
Who are those two persons?
The Blessed One himself says: "The perishable is all beings."
The meaning is "the entire collection of modifications.
*Kūṭāstha* means standing like a heap (*kūṭa*); that is, situated like a mass (*rāśi*). Alternatively, *kūṭa*, *māyā*, *vacanā*, *jihmatā*, and *kuṭilatā* are synonyms.
Established through various modes such as manifold illusory speech and the like, it is immutably fixed (*kūṭastha*).
Because the seeds of *saṃsāra* are infinite, it does not perish; thus it is called the Imperishable (*akṣara*). (BhG 15.16)

Distinct from these two—the perishable and the imperishable—and characterized by a nature different from them, untouched by the defects of the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the perishable and the imperishable, eternally pure, awakened, and free by nature—this is the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self (Paramātman):
"But the Supreme Person is another, called the Supreme Self;
the immutable Lord who, entering the three worlds, sustains them. (BhG 15.17)

But the Supreme Person is another, entirely distinct from these two, being the most excellent and supreme; He is called the "Supreme Self" (paramātman) in the Vedāntas because He is supreme (para) in relation to those selves conditioned by ignorance such as the body, and because He is the Self (ātman) of all beings, the inward-consciousness. Thus He is declared and spoken of as the Supreme Self.

He alone is distinguished who, having entered and pervaded the three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ by means of His own power of consciousness and strength, sustains them— sustaining them by the mere existence of His own essential nature.
He is "undecaying" (avyaya), meaning that no decay exists for Him.
Who? The Lord, the omniscient one named Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is that of ruling.
The name "Puruṣottama" (the Supreme Person) is well-known as the designation for the Lord as explained above.
By demonstrating the meaningfulness of this name through its established etymology, the Blessed One reveals himself as the unsurpassed Lord, saying: "I am the Supreme."
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

Since I have transcended the perishable— that is, I have gone beyond the tree of worldly illusion known as the *aśvattha*— and since I am even higher than the imperishable, which is the seed of the tree of worldly illusion, I am therefore the most excellent (*uttama*), the most sublime (*utkṛṣṭatama*), or the highest (*ūrdhvatama*).
Because of this superiority over both the perishable and the imperishable, I am celebrated and renowned in the world and in the Veda.
Devotees know me as "Puruṣottama" (the Supreme Person); poets also employ this name in their poems and other works, and they praise me by using this designation, "Puruṣottama. (BhG 15.18)
Now, the fruit of him who knows the Self as it has been described is stated:
"He who, being undeluded, thus knows Me as the Supreme Person,"
He, the all-knowing one, worships me with his whole being, O Bhārata.

He who, being undeluded—free from delusion—knows Me, the Lord, endowed with the aforementioned attributes, in the manner described, [realizing] "I am this Puruṣottama," he, knowing all by means of his entire self, is omniscient; he worships Me, who dwells in all beings, with his whole being, as the Self of all, O Bhārata.
In this chapter, having stated that the knowledge of the reality of the Blessed One results in the fruit of liberation, [the Lord now speaks:]
Now, he praises that [teaching]:
"Thus, O sinless one, this most secret instruction has been declared by me; having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that was to be done. (BhG 15.20)
Thus, this is the most secret, the most to be guarded, the ultimate mystery;
what is that? It is the scripture (śāstra).
Although the entire scripture known as the Gītā is spoken of [as "the scripture"],
nevertheless, this very chapter alone is here called "the scripture" for the sake of praise, because of the context;
for the entire meaning of the Gītā scripture has been stated in summary form in this chapter.
Not only is the meaning of the Gītā scripture complete here, but the entire meaning of the Vedas is also fully contained herein;
for it has been stated: "He who knows that, he is a knower of the Vedas" (Gītā 15.1), and "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known" (Gītā 15.15).
This has been spoken and declared by me, O sinless one;
having understood this scripture according to the meaning as it has been shown, one becomes wise, and not otherwise.
And one becomes one who has accomplished his duty, O Bhārata—that is, one by whom that which was to be done has been performed.
The meaning is that when the reality of the Blessed One is known, everything that ought to be performed by a Brahmin born of a distinguished lineage becomes accomplished;
the intention is that otherwise, nothing whatsoever can be brought to completion.
All action in its entirety—
And it has been said: "O Pārtha, one attains perfection in knowledge" (Gītā 4.33).
For this indeed is the totality of the birth of a Brāhmaṇa, especially so;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has fulfilled his duty, and not otherwise (Manu 12.93).
And such is the word of Manu.
Since you have heard this supreme truth from me,
therefore, O Bhārata, you have achieved your purpose.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 16:
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Distinction between the Divine and Demoniacal Natures."
(The commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda:
The divine, the demoniacal, and the rakshasa natures of living beings were indicated in the ninth chapter.
To demonstrate these in detail, the present chapter begins with the verse: "Fearlessness, purity of heart," and so forth.

In this regard, the divine nature leads to liberation from saṃsāra, while the demoniacal and rakshasa natures lead to bondage; therefore, the Blessed Lord spoke in order to demonstrate how to adopt the divine nature and how to avoid the other two:
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; BhG 16.1.
Fearlessness is the absence of timidity.

Purity of being (*sattva-saṃśuddhi*) is the complete purification of the inner organ (*sattva*); the meaning is that it is conduct characterized by a state of pure being, consisting in the total avoidance of deceiving others, guile, falsehood, and so forth, in all worldly dealings.

The "establishment in the yoga of knowledge" (*jñāna-yoga-vyavasthiti*) consists of knowledge and yoga. Knowledge is the comprehension of categories such as the Self through scripture and the teacher.
Yoga is the attainment of the state of being directly experienced by one's own self through one-pointedness and the withdrawal of the senses regarding those categories already understood.
The "establishment" (*vyavasthiti*) in these two—knowledge and yoga—is their firm foundation and steadfast devotion to them.
This is said to be the primary divine [gift], characterized by sattva.
Giving is the distribution of food and other things according to one's capacity;
and self-restraint is the pacification of the external organs.
He will describe the tranquility and peace of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Sacrifice (*yajña*) includes both the *śrauta* rites such as the *agnihotra*,
and the *smārta* rites such as the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the bodily and other forms that will be described later.
Rectitude (*ārjava*) is straightforwardness at all times. (BhG 16.1)
Furthermore:
non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice, compassion for all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness; BhG 16.2.

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the non-injury of living beings, the avoidance of causing them pain. Truthfulness (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to reality as it is, avoiding both what is unpleasant and what is false. Absence of anger (*akrodha*) is the pacification of anger when one is reviled or struck by others.
Renunciation (tyāga) is abandonment (saṃnyāsa),
since giving has already been mentioned previously;
tranquility (śānti) is the subsiding of the internal organ.
Absence of backbiting (*apaiśuna*) is the state of not being a backbiter.
Backbiting (*paiśuna*) is the exposing of another's faults;
the absence of that is *apaiśuna*.
Compassion is pity for living beings who are suffering;
lack of greed is the absence of agitation when the sense organs are in proximity to their objects;
gentleness is softness and the absence of cruelty.
Modesty (*hrī*) is shame.
Lack of fickleness (*acāpala*) is the state of not engaging the speech, hands, feet, and so forth when there is no purpose for doing so.
(BhG 16.2) Furthermore—
Energy, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with a divine nature.
*Tejas* is self-confidence, not merely a glow on the skin;
*kṣamā* is the non-arising of internal agitation when one is reviled or struck; we have already stated that *akrodha* (non-anger) is the pacification of such agitation once it has arisen.

Such is the distinction between forbearance (*kṣamā*) and the absence of anger (*akrodha*). Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa-vṛtti-viśeṣa*) that prevents despondency when the body and the senses have fallen into a state of exhaustion; by means of it, the faculties and the body do not succumb to dejection.

Purity is twofold: external, consisting of cleansing with earth and water, and internal, which is the clarity of the mind and intellect through the absence of the turbidity of illusion, passion, and so forth.
Thus, purity is of two kinds.
Non-malice is the absence of the desire to harm others; it is non-violence.
Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is pride that is beyond measure; one who possesses it is "excessively proud" (*atimānī*).
The state of being such is "excessive pride-ness" (*atimānitā*).
The absence of that is "lack of excessive pride," meaning the absence of the conception of one's own excellence as being worthy of supreme honor.
These qualities, beginning with fearlessness and ending with this, belong to one who is born into prosperity.
Of what kind of prosperity?

"Daivīm" means directed toward that which is the excellence (*saṃpat*) of the gods; it refers to one who has been born as one worthy of divine glory and destined for future welfare—this is the meaning.
O Bhārata!
Now, the demonic nature (*āsurī saṃpat*) is described:
Deceit, arrogance, and excessive pride, as well as anger, harshness, and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born for the demonic nature.
Deceit (*dambha*) is the state of bearing the banner of righteousness (*dharma-dhvajitva*). Arrogance (*darpa*) is the inflation [of the mind] caused by learning, wealth, kinsmen, and so forth.
Excessive pride (*atimāna*) has been explained previously.
And anger;
and harshness itself is harsh speech, such as [saying] to one with eyes, "You are one-eyed."
The ugly as beautiful, one of low birth as one of noble birth, and so forth;
and ignorance is non-discriminative knowledge, a false cognition regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, and other such objects.

"Of one who is born," O Pārtha. "Born into what? He says: "The demonic prosperity"—the prosperity of the Asuras is 'demonic' (āsurī); the meaning is "of one born into that. Now, the function of these two prosperities is stated: The meaning is "of one born into that.
Now, the function of these two prosperies is stated:
The divine nature is deemed to lead to liberation, while the demonic leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born with a divine nature.
The divine nature is that which leads to liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra;
the demonic nature is considered and intended as the fixed bond for the sake of bondage,
and the same applies to the Rākṣasa nature.

When this had been said, the Blessed One, perceiving the internal state of Arjuna—which consisted of the reflection, "Am I endowed with the demonic nature, or am I endowed with the divine nature?"—said: "Do not grieve; do not give way to sorrow."
"You have now been born with divine nature; you are born having aimed for excellence—the meaning is that you are destined for future prosperity, O Pāṇḍava. (BhG 16.5)
There are two types of created beings in this world: the divine and the demoniac.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demoniac.

The two classes of beings (*bhūta-sarga*) refer to the two types of creation (*sarga*) of living beings (*bhūta*), namely humans; "creation" (*sarga*) is so called because they are created (*sṛjyeta*). These two classes of beings are said to be "endowed with the twofold nature of the divine and the demonic," as stated in the Śruti: "There were indeed two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring: the gods and the asuras" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1).
"In this world"— that is, in saṃsāra—
because a twofold nature is established for all beings. What are those two types of created beings?

Thus it is said: "In the very nature (prakṛti) [of the two], the divine and the demoniac. He states the purpose for repeating what has already been mentioned: "The divine creation of beings (bhūta-sarga) has been declared in detail—that is, explained at length—by means of various detailed modes, beginning with 'Fearlessness, purity of being' (sattva-saṃśuddhi), and so forth;
however, the demoniac has not been declared in detail."

Therefore, for the purpose of avoiding that, O Pārtha, listen in detail and grasp what is being said by Me concerning the demonic nature. (BhG 16.6) From this point until the conclusion of the chapter, the demonic disposition is presented as a characteristic of certain types of beings;
and by making it directly perceptible, its avoidance can be accomplished.
Asuras do not understand what is to be engaged in and what is to be desisted from;
neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth is found in them.

And as for engagement— that activity directed toward that which must be done to accomplish the goals of human life— and cessation— which is the opposite of that, namely, turning away from that which causes harm—
Asura-like people do not know these, they do not understand them.
Not only do they not know engagement and withdrawal, but neither purity nor right conduct nor truth exists among them;
for these Asuras are indeed impure, ill-behaved, deceitful, and speakers of untruth.
Moreover:
"They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
born of mutual union, what else is it but caused by lust? (BhG 16.8)
"Just as we are mostly false, so too this entire world is unreal;
and it is without foundation, for its foundation is neither merit nor demerit, thus it is called 'without foundation'.
Those Asura people say that the world is "without a Lord" (anīśvara), meaning that there exists no ruling Lord who takes account of merit and demerit; therefore, they say the world is without a Lord.
Furthermore, the entire world has arisen from the mutual union of men and women engaged in desire, produced through their reciprocal interaction. What else could be the cause?
It is caused solely by desire; thus, it is "desire-caused" (*kāma-haituka*).
What else could be the cause of the world?
There exists no other unseen cause, such as merit (dharma) or demerit (adharma).
"Desire alone is the cause of living beings in the world"—this is the Lokāyatika view. (BhG 16.8)
Holding fast to this view, those ruined souls of small intellect,
performers of cruel deeds and enemies of the world, arise for its destruction.
Holding fast to this view, relying upon it, those of ruined souls— whose very nature is destroyed and whose means for attaining the next world have failed—

possessing little intelligence, that is, those whose intellect is limited to the objects of the senses; such people of small understanding arise, manifesting themselves as performers of fierce deeds, cruel in their actions, and violent by nature.
The connection is that they prevail for the destruction of the world.
The meaning is that they are enemies who bring harm to the world.
And they—
having resorted to desire, which is difficult to satisfy, and being possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance—
Having grasped false notions out of delusion, they engage in impure vows.

Relying upon and clinging to specific desires— which are difficult to satisfy and impossible to fulfill— those possessed of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance (dambha, māna, and mada), having grasped and adopted false notions and inauspicious certainties out of delusion and lack of discrimination, proceed in this world with impure vows.
Those whose vows are impure are called "impure-vowed.
Furthermore:
they have resorted to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death.
They are devoted solely to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, convinced that this is all there is.
And an immeasurable thought; that thought whose extent cannot be measured is "immeasurable," and [he considers] that immeasurable one.
"Having resorted to that which ends in dissolution and ends in death" means they are constantly intent on anxiety;
"having sensual enjoyment as their supreme goal."

They are called *kāmas* because they are desired; these are the sense objects, such as sound and the rest. Their supreme goal is the enjoyment of those objects. They are those whose minds are resolved that this alone is the highest aim of human life (*puruṣārtha*), namely the enjoyment of desires, and who are certain that "this much is all.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, they are wholly devoted to desire and anger.
They strive for the accumulation of wealth by unjust means for the sake of sensual enjoyment.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope— where hope itself is the snare— and being thus restrained and dragged from all sides,
those who are devoted to desire and anger— meaning those for whom desire and anger are their primary resort or support—
strive and exert themselves for the sake of enjoying desires, with the enjoyment of desires as their purpose, and not for the sake of dharma.
The meaning is: by unjust means, such as the seizing of another's property and so forth.
What? Accumulations of wealth—that is, heaps of riches. And their intention is as follows:
"This has been gained by me today; this desire I shall attain;
this is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again. (BhG 16.13)
"This wealth has been obtained by me today;
this other thing, which fulfills my heart's desire and brings satisfaction to the mind, I shall obtain.
This I have, and this too will be mine in the coming year—again, wealth; by means of that, I shall become famous as a wealthy man. (BhG 16.13)
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well;
I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (BhG 16.14)
"This invincible enemy named Devadatta has been slain by me;
I shall also slay others, even those who are wretched.
What can these poor things do?"
In every respect, there is no one equal to me.
How so? I am the lord; I am the enjoyer;
and in every way I am successful and endowed with sons and grandsons.
I alone am not merely human; I am powerful and happy,
whereas others have been cast down as a burden upon the earth.
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, and I shall rejoice"—thus they are deluded by ignorance. (BhG 16.15)
"I am possessed of wealth; I am of noble lineage, perfected in the learning of the Vedas for seven generations—even by that, there is no one who is my equal.
Who else is there who is similar or equal to me?"
Furthermore: "I shall sacrifice; by means of this sacrifice I shall also surpass others; I shall give gifts to actors and the like; and I shall rejoice, that is, I shall attain an excess of joy."
Thus, deluded by ignorance— meaning bewildered by lack of knowledge and having fallen into various states of non-discrimination—
[they fall]. Confused by many thoughts, enveloped in the snare of delusion,
and attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into impure hell.
"Perplexed by many thoughts" means they are variously bewildered by the many types of thoughts previously described;
"enveloped in the net of delusion" means that delusion (*moha*)— which is non-discrimination or ignorance— is like a net because it functions as an obscuration, and they are completely covered by it.
Addicted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and remaining fixed therein, they accumulate sin by that means and fall into impure hells such as Vaitaraṇī and others.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride,
they perform sacrifices merely in name, out of hypocrisy and contrary to the prescribed rules.
"Self-conceited" means those who have been honored by themselves alone on account of their own superiority in all virtues, rather than being honored by the virtuous;
"arrogant" means those whose minds are not humble.

Possessed of wealth, pride, and arrogance—pride and arrogance caused by wealth—they perform sacrifices merely in name; that is, they perform sacrifices by means of mere names out of hypocrisy and the desire for the banner of righteousness (*dharmadhvajitā*), without following the prescribed rules and devoid of the constituent parts and procedures ordained by the injunctions. (BhG 16.17)
Resorting to egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and wrath,
these envious ones hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others.

Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the act of identifying with the "I" (*ahaṃkaraṇa*). It is that by which one conceives of the self as qualified by qualities—both real and unreal—that have been superimposed upon it, thinking "I am.
This egoism, known as ignorance (*avidyā*), is most painful; it is the root of all defects and the source of all unwholesome activities. [The word *tam* refers to this.]

Likewise, *bala* (strength) is that which is characterized by the intent to overcome others and is accompanied by sensual passion (*kāmarāga*). *Darpa* (arrogance) is a specific defect residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the arising of which causes one to transgress the Dharma. *Kāma* refers to objects such as women and the like.
Anger toward undesirable objects—
these and other great defects they have resorted to;
moreover, hating Me, the Lord, who am the witness of the intellect and actions in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, they hate Me.
Transgression against My instruction is malice; those who act thus are envious, being unable to tolerate the virtues of those established on the true path.
To those hateful and cruel ones—the lowest of men—I consign them to the cycles of worldly existence.
I incessantly cast the impure into only demonic wombs.

I cast those who are hostile to me—those cruel haters of the virtuous who have become opponents of the true path, those lowest of men who, due to their possession of the fault of unrighteousness, perform impure deeds—into the very courses of many hells within the cycles of worldly existence; I cast these impure ones perpetually and continuously into the wombs of tigers, lions, and other such [beasts] belonging to the Asuras, which are characterized by cruel actions. This is the connection [of the verse].
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they fail to reach Me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state.

Having entered— that is, having attained— the womb of the asuras, these deluded ones, lacking discrimination, are born life after life in wombs abounding in darkness; thus descending, these fools, O Kaunteya, failing to reach— that is, failing to attain— Me, the Lord,
go from that state even further down to the lowest, most degraded, condition.
"Without even reaching Me"—this means that there is no possibility whatsoever of attaining Me;
therefore, the meaning is "without reaching the path of the virtuous who are My disciples.
This is stated as a summary of the entire demonic nature.
In this threefold [classification], all the infinite varieties of demonic endowment (āsurī-sampad) are included;
by avoiding it, they are avoided,
for it is the root of every misfortune.
This is what is said:
"These three are the gates to hell, the destroyers of the self:
lust, anger, and greed; therefore, one should renounce these three. (BhG 16.21)
This threefold, three-pronged gateway to the attainment of hell is the destroyer of the self;
for as soon as one enters this gateway, the self perishes,
such that it becomes unfit for any human goal (puruṣārtha).
Therefore it is said: "The door that leads to the destruction of the self—what is that? It is desire, anger, and likewise greed;
therefore, one should abandon these three."
Since this door is the destruction of the self, one should therefore abandon these three, beginning with desire.
This is a praise of renunciation:
"O son of Kuntī, a man who is liberated from these three doors to darkness..."
He practices what is for his own welfare, and thereby he goes to the supreme goal.
O son of Kuntī, one who is liberated from these gates of darkness— namely, from these three, beginning with desire, which are the doors of the hell of darkness consisting of suffering and delusion—
that person practices and pursues what is for his own highest good.
That which was previously not practiced because it was bound by something else, he now practices due to the removal of that obstacle;
then, by practicing that, he attains the supreme goal, even liberation. // BhG 16.22 //
The scripture is the cause for both this avoidance of the demonic nature and the practice of what is beneficial;
by means of the authority of the scripture, both can be accomplished, and not otherwise. Therefore—
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.

He who, having cast aside the injunctions of the scripture— the Veda being the scripture whose injunctions are the cause for knowing what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, specifically those called prescriptions and prohibitions— acts according to his own whims, impelled by desire, does not attain perfection, which is fitness for the goals of human life; nor does he find happiness in this world, nor the supreme goal, whether it be heaven or liberation.
Therefore, the scripture is your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having understood what is prescribed by the rules of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.

Therefore, the scripture (*śāstra*) is the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) for you to determine what ought and ought not to be done— that is, the determination of duty and non-duty. Hence, having known and understood what is declared by the scriptural injunction— where "injunction" (*vidhi*) means "prescription" (*vidhāna*), and thus "scriptural prescription" refers to that which is characterized as "one should do" or "one should not do"—
you ought to perform here that which is your own duty as stated therein.
The word "here" (iha) is for the purpose of indicating the stage of the sphere of action. // BhGS 16.24 //

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 17:
Now begins the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Threefold Division of Faith."
Having thus received the seed of his question from the Lord’s statement, "Therefore, the scripture is the authority" (Gītā 16.24), Arjuna said:

"Those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scripture, yet sacrifice endowed with faith—what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it goodness (sattva), or passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)? (BhG 17.1)

Whosoever, without distinction, having cast aside and abandoned the scriptural injunction— the scriptural ordinance, the mandate of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the scriptures— worship, that is, honor the gods and others, being endowed with faith, meaning possessed of a conviction rooted in belief; those who, not seeing any scriptural injunction characterized by Śruti or Smṛti, worship the gods and others solely out of faith based on observing the conduct of the elders.

Those who, having abandoned the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifice here while endowed with faith, are understood by the phrase "those who, having abandoned the scriptural injunctions, sacrifice. However, those who, despite perceiving some scriptural injunction, abandon it and worship the gods and others contrary to the rules, are not included here by the phrase "those who, having abandoned the scriptural injunctions, sacrifice."
Why? Because of the qualifying attribute "endowed with faith.

It is impossible to imagine that someone, while seeing a certain scripture dedicated to the ritual procedures for the worship of gods and so forth, would nevertheless reject it out of lack of faith and yet proceed with faith toward the worship of gods and so forth prescribed therein.
Therefore, those who were previously mentioned in the verse, "Those who, discarding the scriptural injunctions, sacrifice endowed with faith," are here intended.
For such persons as these, O Kṛṣṇa, what is their final state—is it *sattva*, or *rajas*, or *tamas*?
Does their state of final abiding consist in *sattva*?
Or is it *rajas*, or else *tamas*?
This is what is meant: their worship directed toward objects such as the gods, etc., [is characterized by these qualities].
Is it of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī), or rather of passion (rājasī), or else of darkness (tāmasī)? // BhG 17.1 //
"The Blessed Lord said: This question concerns a general subject and does not deserve an answer without further analysis.
Faith is of three kinds among embodied beings; it arises from their own nature.
It is of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī), passion (rājasī), and darkness (tāmasī). Listen to that. (BhG 17.2)
Faith is threefold and of three kinds—
that regarding which you ask concerning embodied beings; it is born of their very nature.
The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of dharma and so forth produced in a previous birth, which becomes manifest at the time of death, is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*);
that which arises from this is "born of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-jā*).
That which is characterized by *sattva* is "of the nature of *sattva*" (*sāttvikī*), being produced from *sattva*, and having as its object the worship of deities and the like.

That which arises from *rajas* is *rājasa*, having as its object the worship of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the like; that which arises from *tamas* is *tāmasa*, having as its object the worship of Pretas, Piśācas, and the like.
Listen and attend to this threefold faith as it is being described. (BhG 17.2)
This faith is of three kinds; O Bhārata, the faith of every being conforms to their own nature.
This person consists of faith; whatever one's faith is, that indeed one is.
O Bhārata, the faith of every class of living beings conforms to their own nature and corresponds to their internal organ, which is endowed with specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
If this is so, what follows from it?
It is said: this transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) consists of faith; he is composed primarily of faith.
How so? Whatever one has faith in—that is, whatever faith a particular living being possesses—that very living being is of that same nature, conforming precisely to that faith.

Consequently, since the steadfastness in *sattva* and the other qualities can be inferred from their effects, such as the worship of gods and others, he says: "Those characterized by *sattva* worship the gods; those characterized by *rajas*, the yakṣas and rākṣasas."
Others, who are people of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), worship the spirits of the departed (pretas) and the hosts of elemental beings (bhūtagaṇas).
Those of a sattvic nature, established in purity, worship the gods;
those of a rajasic nature worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas;
and others, who are tamasic people, worship the spirits of the dead, hosts of elemental beings, the Seven Mothers, and so forth.
Thus, by their effects, beings have been determined as being grounded in *sattva* and so forth regarding the performance or abandonment of scriptural injunctions.

Among them, only some in a thousand are devoted to the worship of the gods and the like, being grounded in *sattva*; however, for the most part, living beings are grounded in *rajas* and *tamas*. How so?—
Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures, being possessed of hypocrisy and egoism, and impelled by the force of desire and passion; BhG 17.5.

Those people who perform and carry out austerities that are not ordained by the scriptures— neither prescribed by the scriptures nor even terrible, causing pain to living beings and to themselves— are joined with hypocrisy and egoism;
"hypocrisy and egoism" (dambhāhaṃkārau) refers to those two,
and they are joined with them, thus being "joined with hypocrisy and egoism."

"Possessed by the power of desire and attachment": *kāma* is desire and *rāga* is attachment; the power produced by these two is the "power of desire and attachment" (*kāma-rāga-bala*). Those who are endowed with that are "possessed by the power of desire and attachment.
"Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements residing in the body, and likewise Me who am situated within the body—know them to be of demonic resolve. (BhG 17.6)

Emaciating—that is, making lean—the aggregate of elements (bhūta-grāma), which is the collection of instruments (karaṇa-samudāya) residing within the body; being devoid of discrimination (acetasaḥ), they likewise emaciate Me, Nārāyaṇa, who am situated within the body as the witness of the intellect and its activities.
Indeed, the failure to carry out My instruction is itself the emaciation of Me.
Know them to be of demonic resolve; those whose resolve is demonic are "of demonic resolve"—know them as such for the purpose of avoiding them. This is the instruction.

(BhG 17.6) Furthermore, here the preference of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* persons for food is shown according to its division into three groups—namely, those characterized by being savory, oily, and so forth.
Among these specific types of food, such as the savory and the oily, one's *sāttvika* nature is to be inferred from the mark of excessive personal pleasure.

Having understood the nature of *rājasika* and *tāmasika* states, this is for the purpose of avoiding foods characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, and for the purpose of adopting those characterized by *sattva*.

Likewise, the threefold classification of sacrifices and other acts according to the distinctions of the qualities such as *sattva* is taught here so that, having understood the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types, one might indeed abandon them and practice only the *sāttvika* ones; with this intent, he says:
Moreover, food is dear to everyone and is of three kinds;
likewise for sacrifice, austerity, and charity—listen now to this distinction between them.
Furthermore, for every living being who eats, food is dear and desired in three ways;
likewise are sacrifice, austerity, and charity. Listen to this distinction of those—food and the rest—which is about to be described. (BhG 17.7)

Foods that increase life-span, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and satisfaction—those which are savory, succulent, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—are dear to those of sattvic nature. (BhG 17.8)

Longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy—these are longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy; they increase these [qualities], thus they are "increasers of longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy. Furthermore, they are savory, endowed with flavor, smooth, and oily.

Firm foods are those that remain for a long time in the body; pleasant foods are those dear to the heart; these are the foods beloved by the *sāttvika*, desired by one of a *sāttvika* nature. (BhG 17.8)
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to those of the passionate nature (rājasa); they bestow suffering, grief, and disease. (BhG 17.9)

Regarding the phrase "bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning," the word *ati* ("excessively") is to be applied to each of the qualities beginning with bitter. Thus, it means "extremely bitter" (*atikaṭu*), "extremely pungent" (*atitīkṣṇa*), and so forth.
Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning—these are the foods desired by those of a rajasic nature.
They bestow suffering, grief, and disease; that is, they provide suffering, sorrow, and illness—thus they are called "bestowers of suffering, grief, and disease.
Food that has lost its savor, whose essence is gone, which is putrid and stale, as well as that which is leavings and impure—such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature.
"Yāta-yāma" means slightly overcooked,
since the term "gata-rasa" (devoid of essence) is used to denote that which has lost its potency;
"gata-rasa" means separated from its essence.
Foul and putrid, stale and cooked [the previous day] and kept overnight,
as well as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa), meaning that which remains after one has eaten; these are [impure].
Such food, consisting of impure things unfit for sacrifice, is dear to those characterized by tamas.
Now, sacrifice is described as being of three kinds:
that sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits; [is declared to be sāttvika].
He who resolves his mind that "one must certainly sacrifice" is one characterized by goodness (sāttvika).

By those who do not desire fruits—that is, by those who do not seek rewards—the sacrifice prescribed by rule is performed; that is, the sacrifice ordained by the injunctions of the scriptures is offered, having fixed the mind on the mere accomplishment of the essential form of the sacrifice itself, with the resolve: "The sacrifice must simply be performed," and having determined: "I have no personal goal to be achieved through this."
That sacrifice is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
But that which is performed after aiming for a fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
But that sacrifice which is performed with a specific intention, aiming for a fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be rajasic.
A sacrifice devoid of scriptural injunctions, where no food is distributed, lacking mantras and priestly fees, and bereft of faith— they declare such a sacrifice to be tamasic.

"Deficient in ritual" means contrary to what has been prescribed; "where food is not offered" means that food has not been prepared or given to the Brahmins— that sacrifice in which such food is absent is called "one where food is not offered."
A sacrifice devoid of mantras—meaning deficient in its mantras, whether by accent or by syllable;
lacking in sacrificial fees—meaning bereft of the prescribed dakṣiṇā; and devoid of faith—they declare such a sacrifice to be tāmasa, saying it is produced from darkness. (BhG 17.13)

Now, austerity is said to be of three kinds: worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity. (BhG 17.14)
Gods, twice-born ones, teachers, and the wise—these are "gods, twice-born ones, teachers, and the wise"; their worship is "the worship of gods, twice-born ones, teachers, and the wise.
Purity;
straightforwardness is uprightness.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) constitute bodily austerity (*śārīra-tapa*). That which is accomplished by means of all the instruments of action—the body being primary—such as the agent and so forth, is called bodily austerity.
For it will be stated later: "These five are its causes" (Gītā 18.15).
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial;
And the practice of reciting sacred texts is said to be austerity consisting of speech.

Speech that causes no agitation to living beings, that causes no suffering, and which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial—that is, pleasant and beneficial in terms of both seen and unseen purposes—is what is meant.
The speech is qualified by these attributes such as "causing no agitation" and so forth;
and the word "ca" (and) serves to indicate the conjunction of these qualifying attributes.
If a sentence uttered for the sake of another should lack even one, two, or three of the qualities of being true, pleasant, beneficial, and non-distressing,

it is not the austerity consisting of speech (*vāṅ-maya-tapas*). Likewise, if a truthful statement lacks even one, two, or three of the other [qualities], it does not possess the nature of the austerity consisting of speech.
Likewise, pleasant speech that is deficient in any one of the other [qualities], or in two, or in three, does not constitute austerity consisting of speech.
Similarly, beneficial speech that is deficient in any one of the other [qualities], or in two, or in three, does not constitute austerity consisting of speech.
What, then, is that austerity?
That speech which is truthful, non-provocative, pleasant, and beneficial—that is austerity consisting of speech;
for example: "Be at peace, my child."
Devote yourself to sacred study and yoga;
in this way, it will lead to your welfare.
The practice of private recitation according to the rules is called austerity of speech.
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint,
and purity of being— this is called austerity of the mind.
Tranquility of mind (*manaḥ-prasāda*) is the serenity of the mind; it is *prasāda*, which is the attainment of clarity. It is gentleness, what they call mental well-being (*saumanasya*).
This is a state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is to be inferred from its effects, such as the clarity of the face and so forth.
Since silence (*mauna*)—which is the restraint of speech—is also preceded by the restraint of the mind, the cause is expressed through its effect: "silence is the restraint of the mind.
Self-restraint (*ātma-vinigraha*) is the cessation of the mind; self-restraint is a general form applicable to all [objects].
The distinction is that silence is the restraint of the mind specifically with respect to the object of speech.

Purity of disposition (*bhāva-saṃśuddhi*) means being free from deceit (*amāyāvitva*) when dealing with others; this is called mental austerity (*mānasa-tapas*). Now, it is explained how the aforementioned austerity—whether physical, verbal, or mental—becomes threefold according to the distinction between the qualities of *sattva* and the others when practiced by men. *Bhagavad Gītā* 17.16: "Purity of disposition (*bhāva-saṃśuddhi*) means being free from deceit (*amāyāvitva*) when dealing with others; this is called mental austerity (*mānasa-tapas*). ============================== [The following explains: How does the austerity (tapas) performed by men—whether physical, vocal, or mental—become threefold according to the distinction between the qualities of *sattva* and the others? It is said:
That threefold austerity which is performed by men with supreme faith,
by those disciplined and free from desire for fruits, is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

That austerity which is performed— meaning practiced— with faith, that is, with a supreme and excellent conviction in the afterlife, and which is threefold, of three kinds, and has three bases, when it is performed by men who are practitioners free from desire for fruit, devoid of longing for results, and disciplined with concentrated minds— such is the austerity.
The learned declare that to be *sāttvika*, produced from *sattva*.
That austerity which is performed for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, and with hypocrisy, is declared here to be *rājasa*; it is unsteady and impermanent.
"Honor" (satkāra) refers to the act of praising, such as saying, "This ascetic brahmin is excellent"; "respect" (māna) refers to the act of honoring, such as rising from one's seat and saluting;

and "worship" (pūjā) refers to washing the feet, offering worship, providing a bed, and so forth—it is for these purposes that austerity is practiced. Thus, austerity is for the sake of honor, respect, and worship.
And that austerity which is performed with hypocrisy is declared here, O King, to be rajasic; it is unstable because its fruit is merely occasional, and thus it is impermanent.
That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself or for the sake of destroying another, is said to be tamasic.

That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp—that is, with a conviction based on a lack of discrimination—and which causes pain to oneself for the sake of destroying or ruining another, is declared to be *tāmasa* austerity.
Now, the threefold nature of giving is described: The threefold nature of giving is described now:
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who cannot return the favor,
at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient— that gift is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
Having formed the thought, "It must be given," whatever gift is bestowed upon one who does not return favor and is incapable of doing so,
or even upon one who is capable but to whom one gives without expectation;
and [given] in a meritorious place such as Kurukṣetra and the like.
At the proper time, such as during a solar transit (saṃkrānti) and so forth;
and to a worthy recipient, such as one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍ-aṅga-vid) and has mastered the Vedas— such a gift is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with a view toward a fruit, or again,
which is given with a sense of distress— that gift is declared to be rajasic.

But that gift which is given for the sake of a reciprocal favor— thinking, "This person will reciprocate with me at some time"— or for the sake of its fruit, thinking, "There will be an unseen result from this gift for me," and which is given with a specific aim, being afflicted and joined with weariness; [that is not a pure gift].
That gift is declared to be rajasic.
The gift that is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,
without respect and with contempt— that is described as tamasic.
Giving at an improper place and time means giving in an improper place—one crowded with barbarians, impure persons, and the like—or in an impious place;
at an improper time—one not renowned as a cause of merit, such as being devoid of specific occasions like the *saṃkrānti*; and giving to unworthy recipients—such as fools, thieves, and so forth.

Alternatively, even when there is excellence of place and other factors, it refers to that gift which is unaccompanied by respect—lacking kind words, washing of the feet, worship, and the like—and which is treated with contempt, involving an insult to the recipient.
That is declared to be tāmasa.
This instruction is now stated for the purpose of ensuring the excellence of sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth:
"Oṃ tat sat"—this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman.
By him, in ancient times, the Brahmins, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were established.

"Oṃ Tat Sat"—this is the designation (*nirdeśa*). It is called a "designation" because by means of it something is designated. This threefold designation of Brahman is recorded and contemplated in the Vedāntas by those who know Brahman.

By that threefold instruction, the Vedas and sacrifices were ordained and fashioned in the past; this is stated for the purpose of praising that instruction. (BhG 17.23) Therefore, having uttered "Om," the rites of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity, as prescribed by the rules, proceed constantly among those who discourse on Brahman. (BhG 17.24)

Therefore, having uttered— that is, pronounced— "Om," the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity— acts whose nature consists of sacrifice and the like, performed according to scriptural injunctions and impelled by the scriptures, proceed constantly and at all times for those who speak of Brahman, who have the habit of discoursing upon Brahman.
With "Tat," [one performs] acts of sacrifice and austerity without aiming for a fruit.
And various acts of giving are performed by those who long for liberation.

"Without aiming for that"— that is, having uttered the designation "That" (tad), which refers to Brahman, and without aiming for the fruit of sacrificial and other rites; [this includes] the performance of sacrifice and austerity (*yajña-tapaḥ-kriyā*), meaning both sacrificial acts and ascetic acts, as well as various acts of giving (*dāna-kriyā*) characterized by the bestowing of land, gold, and so forth.
They are performed—that is, they are brought to completion—by those desiring liberation, those seeking liberation, those who yearn for release.
The application of the two words *om* and *tat* has been explained. Now, the application of the word *sat* is being stated:
The word "sat" is used in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness;
likewise, O Pārtha, the word "sat" is applied to a praiseworthy action.

In the case of the existence of the existent, as when a son who was previously non-existent is born; likewise, in the case of the state of goodness—that is, the state of being good (*sādhu-bhāva*)—which occurs when one of bad conduct becomes possessed of good conduct, in that state of goodness, this designation "existent" (*sat*) is applied to Brahman; that is, it is expressed.
And likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is applied—that is, it is used—in reference to a praiseworthy action such as marriage and the like.
(17.26) Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is also called *sat*; and action performed for that purpose is likewise designated as *sat*. (17.27)
That state which exists in sacrifice, in the performance of sacrificial rites, in austerity, and in charity;
That is called "Being" (Sat) by the wise;
and action for its sake is that which has sacrifice, charity, and austerity as its purpose.
Alternatively, it is that which has as its purpose the three aforementioned designations—that is, having sacrifice, charity, and austerity as its purpose, or having the Lord as its purpose.
It is indeed designated as "Sat.

Thus, even those actions such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity that are of a non-sattvic nature and deficient in quality, become endowed with quality and sattvic when preceded by faith through the employment of the three designations of Brahman.
And because everything is accomplished therein by making faith the primary factor, therefore—
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit either after death or in this world.
An oblation offered without faith;
a gift given to Brahmins without faith;
austerity practiced without faith.
Likewise, O Pārtha, whatever praise, salutation, and so forth are performed solely out of lack of faith is said to be worthless, because it lies outside the path that is the means for attaining Me.
And even though it involves great effort, it yields no fruit either after death or in this world.
"Because it is censured by the virtuous. (BhG 17.28)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjya-pāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
